Issue #1973: feat(review): scope the RDD kill switch per worktree and announce its blast radius

## Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand that PRs will be rejected if the linked issue does not have `status:approved`

## 🔍 Affected Area

CLI (commands, flags)

## 💡 Problem Statement

The RDD kill switch has exactly two scopes, `global` and `clone`. There is no worktree scope, and **linked worktrees silently share the clone-local override** because it is stored under the Git common directory, which every linked worktree shares.

This makes the switch unusable for the multi-agent workflow the product otherwise encourages: several agents working in parallel, one worktree each, off a single clone. Turning reviews off for one of them turns them off for all of them, and nothing says so.

### Reproduction (verified on `main` @ `f25647d4`)

```bash
git init clone-a && cd clone-a
git commit --allow-empty -m init
git worktree add ../wt-b -b featb

# Disable in clone-a ONLY, using the narrowest scope available
gentle-ai review mode disable --scope=clone --cwd clone-a --json
#   "clone_local": "off"
#   "effective":   "off"
#   "source":      "clone_local"
#   "revision":    "sha256:abadcd392ac5189b49c99bdc9963b314d8d8099de11bc569fbd6ed5d07119ef1"

# Now read the sibling worktree, which was never touched
gentle-ai review mode status --cwd ../wt-b --json
#   "clone_local": "off"
#   "effective":   "off"
#   "source":      "clone_local"
#   "revision":    "sha256:abadcd392ac5189b49c99bdc9963b314d8d8099de11bc569fbd6ed5d07119ef1"   ← identical
```

A separate `git clone` is correctly unaffected (`effective: on`, `source: default`). The blast radius is precisely "one clone, all of its worktrees".

### Why it happens

`cloneLocalRDDModeRoot` derives the override directory from `identity.GitCommonDir`:

- `internal/reviewtransaction/rdd_mode.go:528` — `base := filepath.Join(identity.GitCommonDir, ...)`
- Stored at `<git-common-dir>/gentle-ai/review-transactions/rar-authority/v1/rdd-mode/gen-NNNNNNNNNN.json`

Linked worktrees resolve to the same `--git-common-dir`, so they read the same record. This is correct and deliberate for the *authority* store; it is the *policy* switch inheriting that placement that produces the surprise.

### Two aggravating factors

**1. `--scope` defaults to `global`.** `internal/cli/review_mode.go:57` — `flags.String("scope", reviewModeScopeGlobal, ...)`. A plain `gentle-ai review mode disable` writes to `os.UserHomeDir()` and disables RDD for **every repository, clone and worktree of that user**. The narrowest thing a hurried operator can type is also the widest thing the product can do.

**2. The reach is never announced.** `review mode status` reports `source` faithfully, but only if you go and read it *from the other worktree*. Neither `disable` nor `enable` says how far the write it just performed actually reaches.

Precedence (`ResolveRDDMode`, `internal/reviewtransaction/rdd_mode.go:215-231`) is `any off wins, a repository can never force on`. The clone-local override is off-only, so a worktree that needs RDD **cannot opt back in** while its sibling holds the switch off.

### Not in scope for this issue

The consent decline path is correct and should not change. `internal/cli/review_mode.go:619-628`: answering "not now" writes nothing, does not latch, and does not touch the mode — the next candidate is asked again. Only acceptance latches. That asymmetry is deliberate and documented, and it is working.

## 📦 Proposed Solution

Something along these lines, in rough priority order:

**1. Announce the blast radius on write.** Every `enable`/`disable` should state what it just reached — at minimum whether the clone has linked worktrees, and how many. Cheapest fix, closes the silent-surprise hole on its own.

```
Disabled review-driven development for clone /path/to/clone-a.
This reaches all 4 linked worktrees of this clone (wt-b, wt-c, wt-d).
```

**2. Add a `worktree` scope.** Stored per-worktree rather than under the common dir — `git rev-parse --git-dir` resolves to the per-worktree directory (`.git/worktrees/<name>`), which is the natural home. Precedence would extend to `worktree > clone > global`, keeping the off-only rule at every level so no scope can force RDD *on*.

**3. Reconsider the `--scope` default.** Either require `--scope` explicitly for the mutating operations, or default to the narrowest scope rather than the widest. Defaulting a policy write to "everything this user owns" is a sharp edge.

Whichever combination lands, `review mode status` should keep reporting the deciding source, extended to name the deciding *scope* when a worktree-level record exists.

## 🔄 Alternatives Considered

**Document the behavior and stop there.** Cheap, and item 1 above is most of the value. But it leaves the parallel-agent workflow with no way to isolate a single agent, which is the actual user need behind this report.

**Tell users to use separate clones instead of worktrees.** This works today and is the only current answer. It costs a full checkout per agent and gives up the shared object store, which is most of why worktrees are used for this in the first place.

**Make the clone-local override support an allow-list of worktrees.** More flexible than a worktree scope, considerably more state to reconcile, and it puts policy for worktree B inside a record that worktree B does not own. A per-worktree record is simpler to reason about.

Issue #2713: T-SQL: a bracketed FOREIGN KEY can drop the child table entirely and emit a self-referencing edge tagged EXTRACTED

## Summary

For some bracket-quoted T-SQL, a `FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES` clause causes the **child table to be
dropped from the graph entirely** and produces a **self-referencing edge on the parent, tagged
`EXTRACTED`**.

`EXTRACTED` means "explicit in the source". There is no `Customer → Customer` reference anywhere in
the input. So this is not a missing edge — it is a **fabricated edge carrying the highest confidence
grade**, which is worse, because the grade is what a reader uses to decide whether to trust it
without checking.

The identical input with brackets removed is extracted correctly.

## Repro

`s.sql`, alone in a directory:

```sql
CREATE TABLE [dbo].[Customer] (
    [CustomerId] INT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    [Name]       NVARCHAR(100) NULL
);
GO

CREATE TABLE [dbo].[Invoice] (
    [InvoiceId]  INT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    [CustomerId] INT NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT [FK_Invoice_Customer] FOREIGN KEY ([CustomerId])
        REFERENCES [dbo].[Customer] ([CustomerId])
);
GO
```

```
graphify . --code-only --force
```

## Actual

```
labels: ['s.sql', 'dbo].[Customer']
edges : [('s', 'contains',   's_dbo_customer', 'EXTRACTED'),
         ('s_dbo_customer', 'references', 's_dbo_customer', 'EXTRACTED')]
```

`[dbo].[Invoice]` is **absent from the graph**. The FK it declares appears as `Customer → Customer`.

## Expected

The same file with brackets removed gives the right answer, so this is the behaviour to match:

```
labels: ['s.sql', 'dbo.Customer', 'dbo.Invoice', ...]
edges : [..., ('s_dbo_invoice', 'references', 's_dbo_customer', 'EXTRACTED')]
```

## What I could and could not isolate

Reproduces deterministically, including with `--force` in a fresh directory, so it is not an
incremental-cache artefact.

I could **not** isolate the trigger. Four plausible causes were each tested and **refuted** — nearby
variants all extract correctly:

| Hypothesis | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Objects after the first are dropped | three bracketed `CREATE TABLE`, no FK | **all three extracted** — refuted |
| A bracketed FK breaks extraction generally | `[dbo].[Beta]` FK → `[dbo].[Alpha]` | **correct edge** — refuted |
| FK column name matching the referenced column name | `AlphaId` → `AlphaId` vs `AlphaId` → `Id` | **both correct** — refuted |
| A parameterised column type (`NVARCHAR(100)`) breaks statement boundaries | with and without | **both correct** — refuted |

So the minimal failing case above is the smallest input I have that fails, and structurally similar
inputs succeed. I did not want to guess further at a mechanism in someone else's parser — the repro
is deterministic, so hopefully it is quicker to bisect from inside.

## Why this matters for schema corpora

The stated value of the SQL path is that **declared foreign keys become high-confidence edges**, and
that is exactly the case failing here. A schema with many FKs is the corpus where the tool should be
strongest; instead some tables vanish silently and some relationships are replaced by self-loops
that look authoritative. Both failures are invisible in the build log — the run exits 0 and reports
a node and edge count that looks reasonable.

For scale, the schema we are indexing declares ~1,365 foreign keys.

## Environment

- graphify **0.9.39**, `tree_sitter_sql` present (confirmed importable)
- Python 3.14.2, Windows 11
- `--code-only`, so this is the local AST path with no LLM involved

## Related

The bracket-quoted identifier label mangling (`dbo].[Customer`) is filed separately. It is visible
in the output above but does not appear to share a trigger with this — every bracketed case mangles
labels, only some drop nodes.

|---|---|

| Re-checks `ADMINISTRATOR` | `device` (line 13), `sensor-configuration`, `guideline` (line 38) |

`device/delete.js` shows the intended shape: Moderator to soft-delete, Administrator required to escalate to permanent.

Consequence: a Moderator can irreversibly destroy caves, entrances and documents. `PERMISSION_SYSTEM.md` claimed permanent deletion was Administrator-only until this audit; the doc has been corrected to match the code, but the code is likely what's wrong.

### 2. Restore is Moderator-only for every entity except guidelines

12 of 13 restore controllers check `MODERATOR` alone. `guideline/restore.js` (lines 10-14) accepts Moderator **or** Administrator.

So guideline is the outlier here — either it should drop to `MODERATOR` only, or the other 12 should accept both.

A narrower instance of #2 between entities modelled almost identically: `device/restore.js` (line 9) and `sensor-configuration/restore.js` check `MODERATOR` only, while `guideline/restore.js` accepts either role. - **Permanent deletion** → require `ADMINISTRATOR` in all 10 core-content controllers, matching `device`/`sensor-configuration`/`guideline`.
- **Restore** → settle on one rule and apply it to all 13.

Issue #14: Add cycle and retry-bound rules

## Context

Cycles in an agent workflow are where "it retried forever and burned the budget"
lives. ZeroClaw has no structured loop construct, so a cycle in pure control edges
is a modeling error; a cycle through failure (`goto`) edges is a recovery loop
that the runtime bounds by other means.

That distinction drives the severities here, and the assumption behind the softer
one has to be recorded in the finding rather than left implicit — this is exactly
the kind of thing that makes a warning trustworthy or noise.

## Task

Implement `crates/egeria-analysis/src/rules/cycles.rs`:

- **`EGR-STRUCT-003`**: strongly connected components in the executable graph.
  A cycle using only failure edges is a **warning**, and the finding records in
  `model.scope` the assumption it rests on — that the runtime bounds revisits
  (`max_step_visits`). A cycle in pure control edges is an **error**: ZeroClaw has
  no loop construct, and structured loops are deferred (ADR-0009).
- **`EGR-RETRY-001`** (error): a retry policy with a missing, zero or absurd bound
  on directly-authored IR; and a failure-edge SCC with no exit path to the end
  node, which is structurally nonterminating regardless of retry bounds.

Witnesses carry the full cycle: nodes and edges, in order.

Issue #12: [I] Candidate pair generation and clustering (optional)

**What**

Build the candidate set from the union of: bare cross-reference pairs, same-milestone pairs (capped 40 per milestone), same `area:*` label pairs (capped 40), top-6 embedding neighbours per issue, path/symbol overlap pairs above 0.25, and all pairs inside a sub-issue tree. Dedupe, cap at 6n.

Then build the undirected candidate graph weighted by how many signals fired, partition it with greedy modularity or connected components, and split any component larger than 14 issues.

Two refinements that matter: each issue joins its **top 2** clusters, so cluster boundaries get double coverage; and a final **representatives cluster** takes the 2 highest-degree issues from each cluster (capped at 14) to catch genuine cross-cluster edges.

> **Optional — stretch work.** Off by default; only build this if the single-call path measurably underperforms on the gold set.

**⚠️ Scope change since this was written:** we now use `stealth/ox-alpha` with a **1M-token context**, so clustering is no longer needed for *capacity* at our scale — 45 issues is roughly 30k tokens. It is still needed for *precision*, because a model asked about 45 issues at once attends worse than one asked about 12.

So: make cluster size configurable via `LATTICE_CLUSTER_SIZE`, where `0` means one call for the whole backlog, and **default to a single call for n ≤ 40**. Then measure both paths against the gold set in #42 and report which wins. That comparison costs one extra run and is a genuinely interesting result.

**Why it matters**

This is the answer to the O(n²) problem for large backlogs, and the reason the project scales past a toy. Never ask the model about all pairs; never ask about a single pair either, since N² calls is the same problem wearing a hat. Ask about clusters.

Target: n=30 → ~5 requests. n=200 → ~32 requests at concurrency 5, roughly 50 seconds. Put these measured numbers in the README — scale claims backed by numbers are rare in hackathon submissions.

Note that **requests, not dollars, are the scarce resource**: the model is free, but OpenRouter's free tier allows 20/min and 50/day (1000/day with $10 of credits).

**Scope**

- `src/lib/infer/candidates.ts`

**Done when**

- [ ] Candidate count stays at or below 6n
- [ ] No cluster exceeds 14 issues
- [ ] Every issue appears in at least one cluster
- [ ] The representatives cluster exists and is capped
- [ ] Call count is reported

# Integrate PrefixSharing to verl: Generalizing PrefixGrouper for Arbitrary-Prefix Reuse in Agentic RL Training

## 1. Summary

GRPO, step-wise RL, and tree-structured agent training often place trajectories with identical token prefixes in the same batch. Standard actor and reference-policy training recomputes those prefixes for every trajectory.

We propose extending verl's existing PrefixGrouper feature from prompt-only sharing to **arbitrary-prefix sharing within a micro-batch**. The current PrefixSharing prototype uses differentiable KV injection, supports FSDP/Transformers and Megatron, and is designed to preserve baseline logits, log-probabilities, loss, and gradients.

Prototype: https://github.com/Jackie2049/PrefixSharing/tree/open-source

## 2. Motivation

Shared-prefix redundancy appears in several RL trajectory structures, with different requirements on the sharing algorithm.

### 2.1 GRPO-style trajectories

```text
trajectory 0: [prompt P][response A]
trajectory 1: [prompt P][response B]
trajectory 2: [prompt P][response C]
```

All trajectories share one prompt and diverge once. This is the workload that PrefixGrouper already handles well: one explicit prompt group is transformed into one prefix plus multiple suffixes. PrefixSharing supports this case, but does not aim to replace PrefixGrouper's simpler and more efficient prompt-only path.

### 2.2 StepRL-style trajectories

Step-wise RL can sample or optimize continuations from intermediate reasoning steps:

```text
trajectory 0: [prompt P][step 1][step 2A]
trajectory 1: [prompt P][step 1][step 2B]
trajectory 2: [prompt P][step 1][step 2A][step 3A]
trajectory 3: [prompt P][step 1][step 2A][step 3B]
```

There are multiple reusable prefixes: `[P]`, `[P, step 1]`, and `[P, step 1, step 2A]`. Their lengths differ, and a trajectory that reuses one prefix can become the provider of a longer prefix. A single `one prompt + many responses` group cannot express all these chained relationships at once. PrefixSharing detects provider/reuser relationships at arbitrary token boundaries and reuses each available prefix within the same forward.

### 2.3 TreeRL-style trajectories

Tree-search and multi-turn agent RL naturally produce nested branches:

```text
                         /-- [turn 2A] -- [leaf A]
[root][turn 1 shared] --+
                         \-- [turn 2B] -- [leaf B]
                                           \-- [turn 3B] -- [leaf C]
```

Different subsets of leaves share different ancestors. Flattening the leaves into independent sequences repeatedly computes the root and every internal branch. PrefixSharing represents these nested relationships as a provider/reuser plan, allowing internal tree nodes to be reused without requiring the workload to collapse into one prompt group.

Inference prefix caches do not solve this training-side problem. Actor updates and reference log-probability computation require differentiable execution, correct token-level outputs, and gradients through the shared prefix computation.

## 3. Design

### 3.1 Goals

- Reuse arbitrary shared prefixes within one micro-batch. The logical plan and activation-store abstraction are designed so that sharing can later be extended across micro-batches, but cross-micro-batch lifetime and scheduling are outside the first upstream scope.
- Preserve baseline forward and backward semantics. The optimized computation is mathematically equivalent to independent full-sequence forwards, and tests verify attention outputs, logits, log-probabilities, loss, and gradients against the baseline within dtype-appropriate numerical tolerance.
- Extend the existing PrefixGrouper user-facing feature in verl 0.8.0 instead of adding a competing top-level switch. Users can select the existing prompt-only PrefixGrouper algorithm or the arbitrary-prefix PrefixSharing algorithm according to their trajectory structure.
- Keep logical prefix relationships independent from the physical attention implementation.
- Upstream the FSDP/Transformers path first and retain Megatron as another backend.

### 3.2 Non-goals for the first upstream contribution

- Cross-micro-batch activation sharing.
- Context parallelism and every fused attention kernel.
- DeltaNet or other recurrent-state reuse.
- Upstreaming FSDP, Megatron, MindSpeed, and NPU support at the same time.
- Guaranteeing speedup for every batch composition or prefix ratio.

### 3.3 Overview

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["verl actor/ref micro-batch"] --> B["Shared-prefix mode dispatch"]
    B -->|"prompt_only"| C["PrefixGrouper"]
    B -->|"arbitrary_prefix"| D["PrefixSharing planner"]
    D --> E["Trim reuser inputs and create runtime context"]
    E --> F{"Training backend"}
    F --> G["FSDP / Transformers attention"]
    F --> H["Megatron attention"]
    G --> I["KV injection and attention"]
    H --> I
    I --> J["Restore token layout and prefix-last outputs"]
    C --> K["Standard verl training outputs"]
    J --> K
    K --> L["verl log-probability, loss, and backward"]

    classDef verl fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb,color:#111827,stroke-width:2px
    classDef prefixSharing fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,color:#111827,stroke-width:2px
    classDef existing fill:#f3f4f6,stroke:#6b7280,color:#111827,stroke-width:1px
    class A,B,K,L verl
    class D,E,F,I,J prefixSharing
    class C,G,H existing
```

Node colors indicate code ownership: blue marks verl integration touchpoints, green marks the self-contained PrefixSharing module, and gray marks existing components reused by the integration.

The proposed verl integration follows five steps:

1. **Prepare the verl micro-batch.** The actor or reference-policy path provides token sequences and masks using the normal verl batch contract.
2. **Select the sharing algorithm.** `prompt_only` keeps the existing PrefixGrouper path; `arbitrary_prefix` invokes PrefixSharing. The feature remains opt-in and the baseline path is unchanged when disabled.
3. **Build the logical plan.** PrefixS

Issue #148: `--deps` / `--importers` / `blast-radius` report `coverage: complete` on languages with no file-level imports


**Version:** 4.4.2 (Homebrew) · macOS · `ast-grep` installed

## Summary

In languages where files inside a module do not import each other by path — Swift is the clearest case, but the same applies to C#, Java within a package, and Kotlin — the dependency graph comes back essentially empty, yet the JSON still declares the analysis authoritative and complete.

## Repro

Any single-module Swift app (~290 source files in my test):

```
codemap --deps --json .
```

## Actual

```json
"coverage": {"status": "complete", "sources": [{"name": "ast-grep", "status": "authoritative"}], "issues": []}
```

Two edges found across the whole project. `blast-radius` on a 50-file change in the same project reports:

```
files_with_dependents=0
impacted_outside_diff=0/0
dependency_context_outside_diff=0/0
```

## Expected

Either real edges, or an honest `degraded` status.

## Why this is the worst of the bugs

Parsing is fine — 1068 functions were extracted correctly. The *edge model* is what doesn't apply: every import in that project resolves to a framework (`SwiftUI`, `Foundation`, …), never to another file in the project. So the graph is structurally empty, not wrong-by-accident.

The damage comes from pairing that with `status: complete`. A consumer — especially an automated one feeding an LLM — reads "complete" plus "0 dependents" and concludes the change is isolated. In my test the changed set included a type with **40** referencing files and another with **33**. Reported impact: zero, with full confidence.

A tool that says "I found nothing" is useful. A tool that says "I checked everything and there is nothing" when it cannot check is worse than not running.

## Suggested fix

1. When a language's import graph yields ~0 internal edges across a large file count, set `coverage.status = "degraded"` with an issue explaining that the language needs symbol-reference resolution rather than import resolution.
2. Longer term, resolve edges for these languages by **type name → declaring file**. `ast-grep` already extracts the declarations; the missing step is matching references to them. A plain ranking of `type name → count of other files referencing it` took 1.8s on the same repo and produced exactly the signal `blast-radius` reported as zero.

## Related false positives

The two edges it does find look like filename-against-directory-name matches:

```
VendorSDK  ───▶ src/Integrations/VendorSDK
OtherSDK   ───▶ src/Integrations/OtherSDK
```

Issue #18: Toposort cycle semantics mismatch

## Description:
`topologicalSort()` treats symmetric edges as non-dependencies (doesn’t count them in in-degree), but it still calls `hasCycle()` which can return true due to cycles formed by symmetric edges, causing `topologicalSort()` to throw even when the directed dependency subgraph is acyclic.

##  Code:
src/memory_graph/utils/traversal.cpp[R272-276]

```
std::vector<std::string> topologicalSort(const MemoryGraph &graph) {
  if (hasCycle(graph)) {
    throw std::runtime_error(
        "[utils:traversal] Graph has a cycle - topological sort impossible");
  }
```
## Relevance:
⭐⭐ Medium

## Evidence:
`topologicalSort()` explicitly ignores symmetric edges when computing in-degrees, but it still rejects graphs if `hasCycle()` detects any cycle via the full adjacency list, which includes symmetric edges. This is an internal semantic contradiction that can cause false 'cycle' failures relative to the dependency graph that topologicalSort actually processes.

## Agent Prompt:
The issue below was found during a code review. Follow the provided context and guidance below and implement a solution

### Issue description
`topologicalSort()` ignores symmetric edges for dependency/in-degree, but it gates execution on `hasCycle(graph)`, which detects cycles through symmetric adjacency too. This inconsistency can reject mixed graphs where only the symmetric relationships create cycles.

### Issue Context
A concrete example: symmetric triangle A-B, B-C, C-A plus a directed DAG elsewhere should still be sortable if symmetric edges are intended to be ignored for dependency ordering.

### Fix Focus Areas
- src/memory_graph/utils/traversal.cpp[225-276]
- src/memory_graph/utils/traversal.cpp[289-297]

### Suggested fix
Either:
1) Add a directed-cycle checker used by `topologicalSort()` that ignores symmetric edges entirely, or
2) Add a parameter to `hasCycle()` to optionally ignore symmetric edges, and call it in `topologicalSort()` with that mode enabled.

Factions are flat. A cell of a larger order, a merchant house inside a guild, a splinter that broke away — all render as peers.

## Schema

```sql
alter table public.factions
  add column if not exists parent_id text references public.factions(id) on delete set null;
```

`on delete set null` promotes orphans to top level rather than cascading a whole branch into oblivion — deleting a parent faction must never silently delete its children.

## Cycle guard — the thing that will bite

Nothing stops A → B → A, and a cycle hangs any recursive render. Guard in both places:

- **Client** — exclude the faction itself and its descendants from the parent picker.
- **DB** — a trigger, or accept the risk knowingly. The data is DM-authored, so a client-only guard is defensible for v1; the point is to decide it explicitly rather than by omission.

Issue #4: Add 0/1 Knapsack module (Dynamic Programming pattern gap)

## Problem

The repo currently implements three distinct algorithmic patterns — graph shortest-path (`dijkstra-shortest-path`), flood-fill/connected-components (`number-of-islands`), and constrained sliding-window optimization (`max-score-window`) — plus a geometry/coordinate problem (`queens-attack`). None of the four modules touch **dynamic programming**, which is one of the most heavily represented pattern families in any serious DSA/interview-prep collection (LeetCode's DP tag alone covers hundreds of problems; "Grokking the Coding Interview"-style pattern groupings treat it as a top-level category). For a repo whose own README states it's "a growing collection of classic algorithms and DSA challenges," DP is a conspicuous, specific gap rather than a vague "add more algorithms" ask.

## Proposed solution

Add a new standalone module, `knapsack`, implementing 0/1 Knapsack — the canonical entry point into DP (optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems, the two properties every other DP problem builds on).

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] New module following the existing structure (own `pom.xml`, `src/main/java`, `src/test/java`, module `README.md` with a complexity section and a Mermaid flowchart, matching the style of the other four modules).
- [ ] Package `ar.edu.utn.frc.tup.algorithms.knapsack` (matching the non-`queens-attack` naming convention — see the separate stale-metadata issue for why `piii` should not be reused).
- [ ] Solves 0/1 Knapsack: given item weights, values, and a capacity, return the maximum achievable value without exceeding capacity, each item usable at most once.
- [ ] Tests cover, at minimum: zero capacity, empty item list, a single item that alone exceeds capacity, an item exactly filling remaining capacity, and a case where excluding a higher-value-but-heavier item beats including it.
- [ ] **100% line and branch coverage**, enforced the same way as the other three modules (JaCoCo `check` bound to `verify`, `LINE`/`BRANCH` `COVEREDRATIO` minimum 1.00 at `BUNDLE` level) — the branch where an item is excluded because including it doesn't improve the subproblem result must be explicitly exercised by a test, not just the inclusion branches.
- [ ] `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s module matrix and `.github/workflows/codeql.yml`'s module list both updated to include the new module (both currently hardcode the 4-module list and will silently skip a 5th module if it's forgotten).
- [ ] Root `README.md` modules table updated with the new entry.

## Suggested approach

Standard bottom-up (tabulation) DP over a `[items][capacity]` table is the simplest to reach 100% branch coverage with deterministic tests; a memoized recursive version is also reasonable if it's what best demonstrates the recursion-based framing.

Issue #5: Add Kruskal's MST module (Union-Find pattern gap)

## Problem

`dijkstra-shortest-path` already establishes a weighted-graph domain (`Graph`, `Graph.Edge` in `dijkstra-shortest-path/src/main/java/ar/edu/utn/frc/tup/algorithms/dijkstra/Graph.java`) and a priority-queue-based algorithm on top of it. What's missing is the **Union-Find / Disjoint-Set** pattern — a distinct and heavily interview-tested technique (cycle detection, Kruskal's MST, dynamic connectivity) that nothing in the current four modules demonstrates, even though the graph building blocks to support it already exist in spirit.

## Proposed solution

Add a new module, `kruskal-mst`, implementing Kruskal's Minimum Spanning Tree algorithm backed by a Disjoint-Set (Union-Find) structure with path compression and union by rank/size.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] New module with its own `pom.xml`, `src/main/java`, `src/test/java`, and `README.md` (complexity section + Mermaid flowchart), matching the existing module structure.
- [ ] Package `ar.edu.utn.frc.tup.algorithms.kruskal`.
- [ ] Disjoint-Set implementation with path compression on `find` and union by rank (or size); Kruskal's algorithm sorts edges by weight and unions components while skipping edges that would form a cycle.
- [ ] Tests cover: a fully connected graph, a disconnected graph (assert the algorithm reports the result as a forest / signals no single spanning tree exists, rather than silently returning a partial tree), a graph with duplicate/parallel edges of different weights, and a single-node graph.
- [ ] **100% line and branch coverage** via the same JaCoCo `check` gate pattern as the other modules — specifically, both the "union succeeds" and "union skipped, edge would create a cycle" branches must be hit by tests, plus the path-compression branch in `find`.
- [ ] `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and `.github/workflows/codeql.yml` module lists updated to include the new module.
- [ ] Root `README.md` modules table updated.

## Suggested approach

Keep the Disjoint-Set as its own small class (`DisjointSet` or `UnionFind`) separate from the `Kruskal` driver class, so each has a focused, easily-100%-covered responsibility — mirrors how `dijkstra-shortest-path` already separates `Graph` from `Dijkstra`.

Issue #288: ops: isolate structured agent workloads from Viewer web server resources

## Problem

Structured Codex and Claude agents are launched through the production Viewer container wrapper. The wrapper uses nsenter into the host mount and PID namespaces, while the child keeps the Viewer container cgroup membership. Agent app servers and every descendant build or test process therefore compete directly with the production Next/Bun web server.

## Live evidence

Observed on 2026-07-15 at deployed revision 34bfd52:

- Docker process tree shows the Viewer Next/Bun process as the ancestor of nsenter, Codex app-server, and agent bun test processes.
- During two active verification suites:
  - Viewer Next/Bun used 87.8 percent CPU and entered D state.
  - One full bun test used 75.6 percent CPU.
  - One focused bun test used 8.4 percent CPU.
  - Root request latency grew from about 0.40 seconds to 2.53 seconds.
- Earlier contention samples reached 447 percent container CPU, 619 PIDs or threads, and 10-13 second root, files, board, accounts, and runtime snapshot latency.
- A reviewer spawn failed before binding with runtime host unavailable while the runtime host Unix socket itself returned a 488,926-byte snapshot in 38-39 ms.
- Once the test workload drained, runtime snapshot recovered to 0.283 seconds and the retry spawn succeeded.
- Dockerfile line 84 launches host-path commands through nsenter without CPU, IO, memory, or PID isolation.

## Scope

Separate interactive agent workloads from the Viewer web-serving resource budget for both Codex and Claude structured hosts. Preserve subscription authentication, transcript paths, host filesystem access, signal handling, delivery receipts, and attachability.

A staged approach may use low CPU and IO priority as an immediate guard, followed by a dedicated worker cgroup or host-side supervisor for durable isolation.

- Codex and Claude app servers, code-mode hosts, shell tools, and all descendants inherit the worker resource policy.
- Worker overload yields an explicit queued, throttled, or resource-limited receipt instead of a false runtime-host-unavailable classification.
- Runtime-host socket calls and Viewer API calls remain observable as separate latency metrics.
- Agent completion, interrupt, kill, resume, signal forwarding, cleanup, and no-orphan invariants remain covered.
- Worker process exits release every cgroup or supervisor record.
- Managed account homes, auth mounts, cwd access, Docker or tmux wrappers, and transcript durability keep current behavior.
- Deployment includes a production load gate with two Viewer-managed builders running full suites while a clean Ctrl+Shift+R trace is recorded.

Issue #145: Drift guard cannot detect code on main that depends on an uncommitted migration

`scripts/check-migration-drift.mjs` compares **committed** migration files against the
`supabase_migrations.schema_migrations` ledger. Both directions are covered:

- committed but not applied -> `LOCAL_NOT_APPLIED`
- applied but not committed -> undocumented drift

code *was*. That is how the stock work reached production with the old `deduct_recipe_stock`
still in place while production reported a clean 121/121.

## Proposed checks, cheapest first

1. **Referenced-object check (highest value).** Grep `main` for `.rpc("<name>")` calls and
   assert every name is created by some committed migration or appears in
   `supabase/schema.sql`. Would have caught `check_stock_sufficiency` immediately -- the RPC
   name exists in code on a branch while no committed migration creates it.

2. **Live object check.** For each `.rpc()` name found in `app/` and `lib/`, query the target
   DB for a matching `pg_proc` entry before allowing a deploy. Catches drift the repo alone
   cannot see, and is what would have flagged production directly.

3. **Test-gate parity.** Run the same Build Verification on production deploys as on staging
   (#141). `recipe-deduction.test.ts` fails without its migration, so a test gate on main
   would have surfaced this on the first production deploy after the stock work landed.

   today found unmerged migrations on `cloudflare-staging`, `feat/whatsapp-ingress-foundation`

Issue #171: [Epic] Free Molecular Flow Aerodynamic Drag with STL Panel Model

## Overview

Replace the simple ballistic-coefficient drag model (`Cd * A` cannonball/flat-plate) with a panel-level **Sentman free molecular flow** model that operates on arbitrary STL mesh geometry. This bridges the existing Phase 1 atmospheric drag foundation (`aero/atmospheric_drag.rs`, `DragSurfaces` component) with the Phase 4 aerodynamic database vision (issue #131, task 4.2).

## Motivation

The current drag model (`components/drag_surfaces.rs`) uses a simple coefficient drag model: each surface contributes `F = 0.5 * rho * v^2 * Cd * A * proj_factor`. This is adequate for cannonball ISS propagation but cannot model:

- Arbitrary vehicle geometry from CAD/STL exports
- Per-panel incidence-angle-dependent pressure and shear under free molecular flow
- Multi-body spacecraft (bus + articulated solar panels) with independent winding correction
- Attitude-dependent drag moments for 6DOF torque computation

## Scope (8 Tasks)

| Task | Title | Dependencies |
|------|-------|-------------|
| 1 | STL Mesh Parsing & Geometry Primitives | — |
| 2 | IShape Trait Abstraction | — |
| 3 | Connected Components Detection (Multi-Body Decomposition) | 1 |
| 4 | Per-Component Centroid & Winding Correction | 3 |
| 5 | Sentman Free Molecular Flow Panel Model | 1, 2 |
| 6 | Frame Transformation Pipeline | 1, 2 |
| 7 | AerodynamicDragEffector | 1–6 |
| 8 | Integration Tests | 7 |

Tasks 1–2 can start in parallel. Task 3 depends on 1. Task 4 depends on 3. Tasks 5–6 depend on 1+2. Task 7 depends on everything. Task 8 depends on 7.

## Architecture

### Integration with existing code

- **Units**: All physical quantities use `apogee_common::units` types (`Area<f64>`, `Density<f64>`, `Kilograms<f64>`, `AccelerationVector`, `ForceVector`, `TorqueVector`, `Meters<f64>`, `Dimensionless<f64>`). No raw `f64` in public APIs.
- **ForceModel trait**: The new `AerodynamicDragEffector` implements `crate::systems::force_model::ForceModel` (same as `DragSurfaces` and `SrpSurfaces`), plugging into the existing `ForceContext` / `aggregate_forces` pipeline.
- **ECS**: The effector is an ECS component, consistent with `DragSurfaces` / `SrpSurfaces` pattern. Entities without it are skipped.
- **Module location**: New code goes in `crates/apogee-core/src/aero/` (existing aero module). New submodules: `stl.rs`, `geometry.rs`, `sentman.rs`, `winding.rs`, `effector.rs`.
- **nalgebra**: All vector/matrix math uses `nalgebra::Vector3<f64>`, `nalgebra::UnitQuaternion<f64>`, `nalgebra::Isometry3<f64>`.
- **TDD**: All tasks follow RED-GREEN-REFACTOR. Failing test first, minimal implementation, then refactor.

### Key design decisions

1. **IShape trait**: Unified interface so both STL meshes and primitive shapes (Box, Sphere, Cylinder) plug into the drag effector. STL-based shapes use the Sentman panel model; primitives fall back to the simple coefficient drag model.
2. **Per-component winding correction**: Each connected component in a multi-body STL gets its own area-weighted centroid. A global centroid would place it between bodies, causing incorrect winding flips on panels.
3. **Sentman closed-form equations**: Per-panel pressure coefficient `Cp` and shear coefficient `C_tau` under free molecular flow, using `libm::erf` or Abramowitz & Stegun 7.1.26 rational approximation (~1e-7 accuracy).
4. **Frame chain**: inertial → vehicle body → component-local → STL coordinate system, stored as `Isometry3<f64>` for composability. Supports articulated panels that update per-timestep.

### Visibility determination

A triangle panel is visible (illuminated by flow) if `normal . (-flow_direction) > 0`. Back-face culling skips shadowed panels.

## Exit Criteria

- [ ] STL parser handles both binary and ASCII formats with recomputed normals
- [ ] Connected components detection correctly identifies discrete bodies in multi-body meshes
- [ ] Winding correction produces consistent outward normals per component
- [ ] Sentman panel model computes `Cp` and `C_tau` validated against analytical solutions
- [ ] Frame transformation pipeline transforms freestream through full frame chain
- [ ] `AerodynamicDragEffector` implements `ForceModel` and integrates with `aggregate_forces`
- [ ] STL sphere `Cd ≈ 2.0` in hypersonic limit (S → infinity, fully diffuse)
- [ ] CSA symmetry: `CSA(+X) == CSA(-X)` for all axes after winding correction
- [ ] Multi-body satellite + solar panels: exactly 3 connected components detected
- [ ] Enable/disable per-component functionality works
- [ ] All tests pass with `cargo test --workspace`, zero clippy warnings

## Dependencies

- Phase 1 atmospheric models (NRLMSISE-00 — exists, validated)
- Phase 1 force aggregator and `ForceModel` trait (exists)
- Phase 1 units library (exists, `Quantity<T,U>` / `VectorQuantity<T,N,U>`)
- Phase 1 ECS architecture (exists, `World` / `Arena<SpacecraftBundle>`)

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

In the database tree, project folders have activation checkboxes. However, activating a parent project folder does not activate the projects contained in its subfolders. Users must open the complete folder tree and activate every nested project separately.

### Describe the solution you'd like

When the activation checkbox of a project folder is checked, all project folders contained below it should also be activated and loaded into the workspace. Unchecking the parent folder should likewise deactivate all nested projects.

The existing checkbox should be used. No additional context-menu commands or buttons are required.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

An alternative would be separate commands such as “Load all projects in this folder branch into the workspace” and “Remove all projects in this folder branch from the workspace”. This would duplicate the purpose of the existing checkbox and make the interface more complicated.

Using groups as additional containers would not solve the problem because the existing project-folder hierarchy already expresses the required structure.

### Give a reason why someone else should spend time on that request

The existing checkbox visually suggests that it controls the selected folder and its contents. Recursive activation would make the database tree behave consistently with this expectation and would save repeated manual activation for every user who organizes projects in nested folders.

# EPIC-02 — Cognitive Gateway v0.2

## Adaptive Knowledge, Retrieval & Memory Plane

## Vision

Cognitive Gateway v0.1 establishes the **deterministic control plane**: explicit intent and situation, declarative planning, capability resolution, process authority, policy checks, context compilation and explainable execution boundaries.

EPIC-02 adds the next layer:

> **Cognitive Gateway shall not only control what may happen; it shall be able to acquire, relate, evaluate, refresh and reuse the knowledge required to make each controlled execution step better.**

The goal is **not** to bolt a vector database onto the gateway and call it RAG. The goal is to build a model-independent **Knowledge, Retrieval & Memory Plane** with typed contracts, bounded retrieval loops, provenance, trust, freshness, evidence sufficiency, graph relationships and governed memory.

This EPIC turns Cognitive Gateway from a deterministic one-pass control plane into a **controlled adaptive knowledge system** while preserving the architectural rule that probabilistic retrieval and model output can provide information, but can never grant authority.

---

```text
EPIC-01 / v0.1
CONTROL

Intent
  ↓
Situation
  ↓
Delta / Plan
  ↓
Resolver
  ↓
Process

EPIC-02 / v0.2

Observe

Plan Retrieval

Retrieve from multiple sources

Relate / Merge / Rerank

Evaluate trust, freshness and sufficiency
  ↓
Compile minimal context

Execute

  ↓
Reassess

Bounded replan
  ↓
Remember what remains useful
```

EPIC-02 is therefore the bridge between a controlled execution platform and a later learning cognitive runtime.

---

# Core Architectural Principle

The central separation remains non-negotiable:

```text
Retrieval answers:
  What relevant information can be found?

Situation / Planner answers:
  What appears to be needed?

Resolver answers:
  Which registered capabilities can satisfy it?

Process Engine answers:
  What lifecycle transition/activity is legal now?

Policy answers:
  What is allowed now?

Runtime answers:
  How is the authorized activity executed?
```

Or, compactly:

> **Retrieval supplies information. Evidence supports claims. Memory preserves validated experience. None of them grants permission, capability or process authority.**

---

# Why a Dedicated EPIC

The first Cognitive Gateway EPIC intentionally keeps full RAG, vector databases and graph databases out of the v0.1 delivery path so the deterministic product core can become usable first.

That boundary must remain intact.

EPIC-02 therefore owns the **advanced knowledge plane** without delaying completion of the v0.1 product slice.

The v0.1 contracts must only provide clean extension points such as:

```text

RetrievalResult
Evidence

Freshness
ContextFragment
```

Concrete advanced retrieval behavior belongs here.

# Retrieval is a Plan, Not an Unbounded Agent Loop

A central new concept is a typed, inspectable and bounded `RetrievalPlan`.

Conceptually:

```text
RetrievalPlan
├── purpose
├── queries[]
├── required_information[]
├── sources[]
├── strategies[]
├── trust_requirement
├── freshness_requirement
├── max_results
├── max_rounds
├── cost / latency budget
├── evidence_requirement
└── stop_condition
```

Example:

```yaml
purpose: determine_worker_failure

queries:
  - docker worker readiness failure
  - overlay network failure
  - matching historical incidents

sources:
  - repository
  - runtime
  - documentation
  - incident-memory

strategies:
  - lexical
  - semantic

freshness:
  runtime: current
  documentation: latest-valid

max_results: 30
max_rounds: 3

stop_condition:
  evidence_sufficient
```

An SLM/LLM may later **suggest** or refine a RetrievalPlan, but the plan must be normalized and constrained before execution.

Unbounded behavior such as:

```text
while not sure:
    search somewhere
```

is prohibited.

Issue #89: canPerformAction() fails open on an unregistered permission id — team member role changes and removals are effectively unguarded

### Summary

Two independent defects compound into a privilege escalation that any
authenticated team member can trigger against any other member below them in
the role hierarchy: they can change that member's role to **any non-owner
role, including `admin`**, and they can remove them from the team outright.

Both defects are in the framework, not in application code. Any consumer that
uses the generated team-member routes inherits them.

### Defect 1 — the permission check is skipped, and skipping means "allowed"

The generated member routes ask for permission using a two-segment id:

```js
// app/api/v1/teams/[teamId]/members/[memberId]/route.ts
membership.canPerformAction('members.update_role')   // PATCH
membership.canPerformAction('members.remove')        // DELETE
membership.canPerformAction('members.invite')        // POST (sibling route)
```

The ids actually registered in the permissions registry are three-segment:
`team.members.update_role`, `team.members.remove`, `team.members.invite`,
`team.members.view`.

`canPerformAction()` then does this:

```js
const [entity, actionType] = action.split(".");   // 'members.update_role' -> ['members','update_role']
const permission = `${entity}.${actionType}`;      // rebuilds 'members.update_role' — the 'team.' prefix is gone
if (PermissionService.isValid(permission)) {       // false: not in ALL_PERMISSIONS_SET
  if (!this.hasPermission(permission)) {
    return { allowed: false, /* ... */ }
  }
}
// no other branch denies — control falls through to:
return { allowed: true }
```

Because `'members.update_role'` is not a registered id, `isValid()` returns
`false`, the entire permission block is skipped, and the function returns
`allowed: true`. The role check does not merely fail to match — it never runs.

The naming mismatch is the trigger, but the deeper problem is the **fail-open
default**: an unrecognized permission id should deny, and ideally be loud about
it. As written, any typo or refactor that changes a permission id silently
disables the check it was supposed to perform, with no error and no log.

### Defect 2 — hierarchy is compared against the old role, never the new one

With the permission check inert, the only remaining guard is
`validateRoleTransition`, which calls:

```js
canManageRole(actorRole, fromRole)   // fromRole = the target's CURRENT role
```

and

```js
function canManageRole(actorRole, targetRole) {
  const hierarchy = getHierarchyFromRegistry();
  return (hierarchy[actorRole] ?? 0) > (hierarchy[targetRole] ?? 0);
}
```

Nothing ever compares the actor's hierarchy against `toRole` — the role being
assigned. So an actor only needs to outrank the target's *current* role, and
may then promote that target to any level, including one far above the actor's
own.

This is a defect on its own: even with Defect 1 fixed, an actor who legitimately
holds `members.update_role` could still promote someone above their own level.

### Reproduction

Roles and hierarchies as registered by default (`owner=100, admin=50,
professional=20, receptionist=15, member=10, viewer=1`); any two roles where
the actor outranks the target reproduce it.

1. Create a team with an owner, plus two members: one at hierarchy 20 (the
   actor) and one at hierarchy 15 (the target).
2. Authenticate as the hierarchy-20 member. That role does **not** hold
   `team.members.update_role` or `team.members.remove` in the registry — both
   are restricted to owner/admin (and remove to owner only).
3. `PATCH /api/v1/teams/{teamId}/members/{targetMemberId}` with
   `{"role":"admin"}`.
   **Actual:** `200`, and the target's row is updated to `admin` (hierarchy 50)
   in the database.
   **Expected:** `403` — the actor holds neither the permission nor a hierarchy
   above `admin`.
4. `DELETE /api/v1/teams/{teamId}/members/{targetMemberId}`.
   **Actual:** `200`, and the membership row is deleted.
   **Expected:** `403`.

Confirmed end to end against a running instance with real sessions, verifying
the database after each call — not by reading code alone.

### Impact

Any team member can remove any lower-ranked member, and can promote one to
`admin`. Two low-privileged members can therefore bootstrap each other:
A promotes B to `admin`, and B — now `admin` — promotes A. Neither needed any
member-management permission to begin with.

`POST .../members` (invite) shares Defect 1 but is currently shielded **by
accident**: that route performs its own additional `canInviteToRole()` check
which does compare against the destination role. The `PATCH` and `DELETE`
routes have no such backstop, which is why they are fully exposed. That
accidental coverage is worth noting precisely because it should not be relied
on — it means the invite path is one refactor away from the same exposure.

### Suggested fix

1. **Make `canPerformAction()` fail closed.** An unregistered permission id
   should return `allowed: false` (and warn), never fall through to allowed.
   This alone converts the whole class from "silently unguarded" to "visibly
   broken", which is the safer failure mode.
2. **Fix the ids at the call sites** to the registered three-segment form, or
   make the lookup prefix-aware — but do this *in addition to* (1), not instead
   of it, since (1) is what prevents the next occurrence.
3. **Validate the destination role**: `validateRoleTransition` should reject
   when the actor's hierarchy is not strictly greater than the hierarchy of
   `toRole`, in addition to the existing check against `fromRole`.

Item 1 is the one that closes the class; items 2 and 3 close the two live
instances.

The worker token cannot push `.github/workflows/**` in `Nishfleet/fleet-ops`. This issue tracks the workflow change needed to close fleet-ops#92.

That does not update the dedicated `systemd-analyze` job. README still claims that job verifies every `systemd/*` file. It does not.

Apply this patch to `Nishfleet/fleet-ops .github/workflows/ci.yml` on a branch from `origin/main`:

```diff
diff --git a/.github/workflows/ci.yml b/.github/workflows/ci.yml
--- a/.github/workflows/ci.yml
+++ b/.github/workflows/ci.yml
@@ -128,9 +128,9 @@ jobs:
           # Do NOT use set -e: we want to collect all failures, then exit.
           shopt -s nullglob
           rc=0
-          for f in systemd/*.service systemd/*.timer; do
-            if ! systemd-analyze verify --man=no "$f"; then
+          for f in systemd/*.service systemd/*.timer systemd/*.slice; do
+            if ! systemd-analyze verify --man=no --recursive-errors=no "$f"; then
               rc=1
             fi
           done
```

Why `--recursive-errors=no` is in this patch:

Default `systemd-analyze verify` (no flag) exits 0 even when the unit has an unknown key or a missing section. It prints `Unknown key name … ignoring.` and returns success. Adding `systemd/*.slice` to the loop without this flag would not make a bad key fail the job.

`--recursive-errors=no` fails on warnings in the specified unit only. It does not fail on unrelated host units. On this VPS, every current `systemd/*.service`, `*.timer`, and `*.slice` already passes with that flag.

Once the glob lands, close Nishfleet/fleet-ops#92.

## Change

Task assignment becomes a **typed relationship to a person node**, replacing the free-text `assignee` field.

Today `assignee` is a `text` field on task (`packages/core/src/models/core_schemas.rs`), and its own description says what it is:

> *"Person responsible for the task, as a free-text name or identifier — **not a relationship to a person node**. Absent means unassigned."*

That was always a placeholder. Two more signals confirm it:
- `TaskNode::assignee_id()` / `set_assignee_id()` (`packages/core/src/models/task_node.rs:580-586`) exist but merely alias the free-text `assignee: Option<String>` field
- The module doc example (`task_node.rs:28`) advertises `"assigneeId": null` — a field the struct does not actually have

With person gaining a task relationship (#2111), keeping the string field too would let a task be assigned to the *string* `"Michael"` while simultaneously edged to a *different* person node, with nothing reconciling them and every query forced to check both. The edge supersedes the field.

Pre-release: no migration, no compat shim — reset the database.

**Remove** the `assignee` field from task's schema; assignment is expressed solely as the person↔task edge declared from person's side (see #2111). ### Goal

Make parent tombstone cascades scale with the number of affected children, rather than with every historical child row owned by the user. *Depends on #161*

### Tasks

- Extend the RemelonDB Drizzle-store transaction API with a typed, transaction-bound lookup for live child IDs by a declared indexed relation. Do not couple `sync-validation.ts` directly to a PostgreSQL/Drizzle transaction or bypass the store's per-scope push lock.
- Represent the cascade relations centrally: deck -> `user_note_decks` by `deck_id`; note -> `user_cards` and `user_note_decks` by `note_id`; card -> `review_events` by `user_card_id`.
- Batch every requested parent ID for an edge in one scoped lookup, filtering `user_id = scope`, `deleted_at is null`, and `foreign_key in (...)`; return only child IDs. Preserve the existing deepest-child-first tombstone order.
- Add PostgreSQL partial composite indexes for those lookups: `(user_id, deck_id) where deleted_at is null`, `(user_id, note_id) where deleted_at is null` on both cards and memberships, and `(user_id, user_card_id) where deleted_at is null` on review events. - Deleting a deck, note, or card never loads all of that user's memberships, cards, or review events into application memory.
- Every cascade lookup is scoped, live-row-only, batched, and performed inside the same push transaction as its tombstones.
- Parent deletion continues to tombstone all and only its live descendants, including reviews before their cards.

Issue #77349: [Feature Request]: Multi-Agent Visual Workflow Orchestration — Complement to cron/blueprint system

## Summary

Hermes already has a powerful cron/blueprint system that manages individual scheduled tasks. But real-world automation is often not a single task — it is a directed graph of tasks with dependencies, branches, parallel paths, and human-in-the-loop review points.

Currently the only way to describe such a workflow is through free-text prompts, which is unreliable for complex scenarios (5+ nodes, 3+ branches, human review gates).

This feature adds a **visual workflow builder** in the Dashboard that renders as a node-graph, with an underlying YAML/JSON serialization that reuses the existing cron job engine — no second scheduling system.

## Use Case

Real-world examples:

- Task A (agent: fetch GitHub PRs) completes → conditional branch: if PRs > 5, route to "urgent review" path; else "weekly digest" path
- Two parallel tracks (security audit + performance analysis) run concurrently → join node waits for both → results delivered together to Telegram
- A critical decision requires human approval before proceeding to the next step
- Task B completes → notifies Task A that its input is ready, so Task A can resume

In company terms: each node is a "role" on a workflow. When one role finishes its job, the next role is notified. This is fundamental for multi-agent collaboration at scale.

## Proposed Architecture

### Workflow = Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)

- **Nodes** = tasks (reusing cron.jobs.create_job as the atomic unit)
- **Edges** = dependency relationships (sequential, parallel, conditional, join)
- **Serialization** = YAML/JSON files stored in ~/.hermes/workflows/
- **Scheduler** = resolves DAG topology, dispatches each node via the existing cron engine

### Node Types

| Type | Description | Example |
|------|-------------|---------|
| trigger | Event trigger: cron schedule / webhook / API | Every Monday 09:00 starts the flow |
| agent | An agent executes a task (prompt / skill / tool chain) | Fetch GitHub PRs and summarize |
| branch | Conditional branch — output determines the path | If new PRs > 5 → path A, else path B |
| human | Human review gate — blocks until user approves | Key decisions need human sign-off |
| parallel | Parallel fan-out — multiple downstream nodes start at once | Security audit + performance analysis in parallel |
| join | Convergence — waits for all upstream paths to finish | Continue only when both parallel tasks complete |
| output | Deliver results to Telegram / Discord / Obsidian / file | |

### Integration with Existing Systems

1. Workflow files live in ~/.hermes/workflows/ (YAML/JSON, versioned with git)
2. Node definitions reuse blueprint_catalog.py slot schema — same source of truth for Dashboard form / CLI slash command / agent prompt
3. Existing cron jobs are completely unaffected; workflow is a new entry point, not a replacement
4. Blueprint templates can render directly as "preset workflows" in the visual canvas
5. Agent can read/write workflow files, understand the topology, and explain the flow

## Why This Complements GASP, Not Competes

The GASP loop (issue #18092) solves "how a single agent improves itself over time" — discover problems, fix prompts, improve execution quality.

A visual workflow builder solves "how multiple agents / multiple tasks collaborate" — inter-task dependencies, conditional routing, human intervention, parallel acceleration.

The two layers are orthogonal and together form a complete automation capability:
- **GASP** makes each node get better over time
- **Visual workflow** makes nodes form reliable collaborative chains

## Design Principles

- **No second job engine.** Workflow execution dispatches into existing cron.jobs.create_job — we are orchestrating, not replacing.
- **Progressive disclosure.** Dashboard users get the visual canvas. CLI/TUI users keep their existing text-driven path; no forced migration.
- **Convention over configuration.** Default templates for common patterns (sequential pipeline, parallel review, human-in-the-loop). Users customize, not build from scratch.
- **Profile-safe.** Workflow files anchored on get_hermes_home() so each profile has its own isolated workflows.

## Not in Scope

- Not a replacement for cron/blueprint text creation
- Not a new job engine
- No impact on CLI/TUI surfaces
- No multi-agent message passing — Hermes Gateway already handles that

## Implementation Suggestion

1. Define Workflow DSL: a YAML schema for node/edge/condition definitions
2. Add workflow.py in the cron/ package: DAG resolution, topology sorting, conditional evaluation
3. Add a React node-graph component in web/src/pages/ (using react-flow or similar)
4. Wire up workflow serialization to ~/.hermes/workflows/ with atomic writes
5. Add a /workflow slash command for CLI/TUI users
6. Expose workflow topology to the agent (so agent can read, explain, and propose modifications)

Issue #87690: No CLI path to append to a list config field (hooks), while write_file/patch refuse config.yaml

## Problem

There is no supported way to **append** an element to a list-typed config field from the CLI. `_set_nested` deliberately does not grow lists ("the referenced index must already exist"), so:

```bash
# hooks.pre_llm_call currently has exactly 1 entry
hermes config set hooks.pre_llm_call.1.command "/path/new.py"
# IndexError: list index out of range
```

Editing an existing element works fine (`hooks.pre_llm_call.0.timeout 9`). Only appending is impossible.

## Why it matters

Registering a new shell hook is the common case, and `hooks:` is exactly the surface where hand-editing is discouraged: `write_file`/`patch` refuse `~/.hermes/config.yaml` outright with *"Agent cannot modify security-sensitive configuration. Edit ~/.hermes/config.yaml directly or use 'hermes config' instead."*

So an agent (or a scripted install) that wants to add a hook is left with:

1. `hermes config set` — cannot append
2. `write_file` / `patch` — refused by the security guard
3. hand-editing YAML through a shell one-liner — **works, and bypasses the guard entirely**

Option 3 is the only thing that functions, which means the guard is currently training people to route around it. On a multi-session box that is actively dangerous: a naive `yaml.safe_load` → mutate → `yaml.safe_dump` rewrite drops comments/formatting and will silently clobber a concurrent writer's change, since it rewrites the whole file with no compare-and-swap.

## Requested

Any one of these closes the hole:

- **Append syntax**, e.g. `hermes config set hooks.pre_llm_call.+.command "/path/x.py"` or an explicit `hermes config append <dotted.list.path> <json>`
- **A dedicated `hermes hooks add <event> <command> [--timeout N] [--matcher RE] [--fail-closed]`** — preferable for the hook case, since it can also handle the allowlist entry in the same step (today a hook must additionally be approved in `~/.hermes/shell-hooks-allowlist.json`, and there is no `hermes hooks approve`; `hooks list`/`test`/`revoke`/`doctor` exist, but the only way to approve non-interactively is to write that JSON by hand)
- At minimum, make the `IndexError` a friendly error that names the supported alternative

## Related

- #17876 added dot-index list navigation (edit-in-place); this is the missing append half.
- Filed alongside a separate bug where `name[N]` bracket syntax silently creates a literal junk key instead of erroring.

## Environment

Hermes on macOS 26.x, `_config_version: 37`, `hermes_cli/config.py::_set_nested`.

Issue #24: Decompose the elastic stiffness into its own material so the graph can order (and recompute) it

## Summary

`linear_elasticity` owns its tangent and builds it once in the constructor. That is
optimal while `K` and `G` are fixed, but it leaves no way to recompute it — and,
more awkwardly, no way to recompute it **correctly** even if one were added.

## The ordering problem

A material reading its own property creates no edge in the property graph. The
engine builds edges from `input_dependencies` and from material-level input wiring,
so `elastic::stress` and `elastic::tangent` both hang off the same single edge from
the strain source, and their relative order falls out of constructor registration
order. Measured:

```
=== Property execution order ===
  strain_in::strain
  elastic::stress          <- reads m_C
  elastic::tangent         <- writes m_C, too late
```

Attaching an update callback to `tangent` — the obvious, idiomatic fix — therefore
produces a stress lagging the constants by one call, **silently**. Verified: the
order is unchanged with the callback attached.

This is a latent trap beyond this material. Anyone who binds a callback to a
material's second output that its first output reads gets the same staleness, with
no diagnostic.

## Proposal

Split the stiffness into its own material. Consuming *another* material's property
creates a real Global edge, which the topological sort honours:

```
  stiffness::tangent       <- produced first
  elastic::stress
```

Same physics, different graph shape, ordering guaranteed by construction rather than
by registration order.

* `isotropic_tangent` — params `K`, `G`, `recompute`; output `tangent`
* `linear_stress` — inputs `tangent` + `strain`; output `stress`

### `recompute`

The update callback is bound **only** when `recompute` is true. `add_output` ignores
a null callback, so with `recompute=false` the property carries no callback at all
and the engine skips it outright — per-call cost is zero, not merely small, matching
`linear_elasticity`. The tangent is built once in the constructor either way, so it
is valid before the first `update()` regardless.

| | |
|---|---|
| `recompute = false` | constants fixed (Abaqus: `PROPS` cannot vary per name) |
| `recompute = true` | constants vary per call (CalculiX temperature interpolation) |

Defaults to `false`, matching `linear_elasticity`. The failure mode of the wrong
setting is worth naming: `recompute=false` while the constants move leaves a stale
tangent with the **stress still correct**, so it costs convergence rate rather than
accuracy and produces no diagnostic. A debug assertion catches it, and
`RecomputeFalseIgnoresALaterParameterWrite` pins the behaviour so it is recorded
rather than discovered.

## Why this is additive

Nothing existing changes. `linear_elasticity` is untouched and remains the better
choice whenever the moduli are fixed — one fewer material in the graph, tangent
computed once. `j2_plasticity` needs no change either: its `elastic_source` only
requires *some* material producing `tangent`.

Beyond the immediate problem, the generators become interchangeable — anisotropic,
temperature-dependent, damage-degraded stiffness all producing the same property,
with consumers indifferent to which. This is the decomposition `isotropic_damage`
already uses (state function + yield + damage law + assembler).

## Open question

Whether `recompute` should default to `false` (matches `linear_elasticity`; a
CalculiX user who forgets gets a stale tangent) or `true` (safe by default; everyone
else pays a rank-4 rebuild per integration point until they opt out).

## Branch

`feature/tangent-generator` (89b640b), stacked on `feature/material-set-parameter`
(#23) — the write-and-retrigger test needs `set_parameter`, and `recompute=true` has
no purpose without it. 191/191 tests pass.

Issue #1: Adopt R-universe as the publishing framework for the OSP R packages

## Proposal: adopt R-universe as the publishing framework for the OSP R packages

This repository is a newly created [R-universe](https://r-universe.dev) registry for the Open Systems Pharmacology R packages. It is already wired up and building at:

**https://open-systems-pharmacology.r-universe.dev**

This issue explains what it is, why it is worth adopting, and the one thing that currently blocks the builds from going fully green. I would like to propose R-universe as the standard way we distribute the OSP R packages, and get a maintainer decision on making it official.

### The problem it solves

The OSP R packages (`rSharp`, `ospsuite`, and the packages built on top of them) embed pre-compiled binaries in `inst/lib`: the .NET assemblies and the computational core. CRAN forbids binary executables in source packages, so these packages cannot be submitted to CRAN as they are. Today users install them with `remotes::install_github(...)` or by downloading pre-built archives from the GitHub releases and installing them in the correct order by hand.

R-universe removes that friction. It builds each package from source on Windows, macOS, and Linux, serves the resulting binaries from a CRAN-like repository, and imposes none of CRAN's no-binary or package-size rules. The committed `inst/lib` payloads are fine as they are.

### What users get

A plain `install.packages()` that resolves the whole dependency chain automatically:

```r
install.packages(
  "ospsuite",
  repos = c(
    OSP = "https://open-systems-pharmacology.r-universe.dev",
    CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"
  )
)
```

R-universe resolves the internal chain (`rSharp` -> `ospsuite.utils` -> `tlf` -> `ospsuite`) across the universe and pulls everything else from CRAN. No manual ordering, no `Remotes:` handling, no archive downloads. `pak` works the same way once the repository is added.

### How it works and its current state

The registry is a single `packages.json` in this repository listing the package repositories to build. The R-universe GitHub App is installed on the organization and watches these repositories; each new release is picked up and rebuilt automatically. The registry currently tracks the nine OSP R packages that publish GitHub releases:

`rSharp`, `ospsuite.utils`, `tlf`, `ospsuite`, `ospsuite.plots`, `ospsuite.reportingengine`, `ospsuite.parameteridentification`, `ospsuite.globalsensitivity`, `ospsuite.reportingframework`.

Three packages are left out for now because they do not cut GitHub releases (`ospsuite.addins`, `ospsuite.qualificationplaneditor`, `ospsuite.VBEToolbox`); they can be added as soon as they have a release.

The dashboard is live and builds are running now.

### The one thing that currently blocks green builds

`rSharp` needs a .NET runtime to load, and its `.onLoad()` currently calls `stop()` when a suitable runtime is not present. Because installing a package test-loads it, `rSharp` (and therefore everything that imports it) fails to install in any environment without the runtime, including the R-universe build machines. This is a property of the package and the build environment, not of the registry.

There is a version-specific reason this bites right now. The current `rSharp` release targets .NET 8 and declares `SystemRequirements: dotnet8`. The R-universe build machines run Ubuntu 26.04, and Ubuntu 26.04 does not distribute a `dotnet-runtime-8.0` package; it ships the .NET 10 line instead. So even though R-universe installs declared system requirements automatically, `dotnet8` cannot be satisfied on that distribution, and the runtime is simply not there for `rSharp` to load against.

This resolves itself with the rSharp V13 work. Once V13 lands on `main` (and a release is cut), `rSharp` targets .NET 10 and declares `dotnet10`, which the R-universe machines can install from the Ubuntu 26.04 archive. At that point the build environment has all the required system dependencies, and the Linux builds here should go green, with the packages that depend on `rSharp` following.

A complementary change makes `rSharp` install and load gracefully when a runtime is absent (deferring the hard error to the first actual call into .NET), proposed in Open-Systems-Pharmacology/rSharp#224.

### What I am asking for

1. A decision on adopting R-universe as one of the "official" publishing channel for the OSP R packages, alongside or ahead of the current GitHub-release install path.
2. Landing the rSharp V13 work (move to .NET 10), which is the primary unblock for the builds here, and reviewing the complementary Open-Systems-Pharmacology/rSharp#224.

Happy to walk through any of this or adjust the approach.

Issue #78: [P1][Phase 5] Enforce complete performance budgets and privacy-safe Core Web Vitals monitoring

## Outcome

Replace incomplete historical bundle checks with a measurable performance contract covering the actual shipped dependency graph, lab diagnostics, field Core Web Vitals, long tasks, enhancement tiers, and production regressions.

## Hard targets

Measure mobile and desktop separately.

### Core Web Vitals at p75

- LCP ≤ 2.5 s
- INP ≤ 200 ms
- CLS ≤ 0.1

### Delivery/runtime budgets

- Initial JavaScript ≤ 75 KB gzip, excluding a clearly opt-in/lazy full demo.
- Initial CSS ≤ 35 KB gzip.
- No render-critical remote JavaScript.
- No hero dependency larger than its static poster before interaction.
- No layout shift from fonts, proof data, demo, product cards, or release metadata.
- No initial-interaction long task above 200 ms on the selected representative mid-tier mobile profile.
- No WebGL initialization before primary content/controls are interactive.
- No continuous work while an enhancement is offscreen or the document is hidden.
- No installer buffering in page memory.
- No horizontal overflow at 320 px.

## Scope

### Correct dependency accounting

- Traverse every initial local module, including URLs with query strings.
- Include dynamic imports that execute before user intent/idle gates.
- Include import-map/CDN dependencies or ban render-critical remote dependencies.
- Report raw, transferred, parsed, and gzip/brotli sizes where useful.
- Separate static tier, lightweight enhancement, WebGL enhancement, and optional full demo.
- Account for inline scripts and inlined CSS accurately.
- Emit a human-readable and machine-readable budget report in CI.

### Lab performance

Run repeatable Lighthouse/WebPageTest-equivalent profiles for:

- homepage static tier;
- homepage enhanced tier;
- key secondary route;
- 4× CPU slowdown / mobile network profile;
- warm and cold caches where meaningful;
- light/dark and reduced-motion states;
- WebGL unavailable;
- stats API unavailable.

Capture:

- milestones and Core Web Vitals;
- request waterfall;
- code coverage;
- long tasks/main-thread work;
- memory trend;
- layout shifts and source attribution;
- animation/background work;
- image/font behavior.

### Privacy-safe RUM

Using the approved mode from #69:

- collect only Core Web Vitals and bounded technical context needed to diagnose regressions;
- avoid full URLs/query strings, repository names, user-entered text, commands, filenames, or raw error contents;
- document sampling, retention, region, and provider;
- distinguish static/enhanced hero tier without fingerprinting the user;
- publish a dashboard or repeatable report for p75 mobile/desktop;
- allow complete disablement.

### Regression policy

- Define hard-fail budgets versus warning trends.
- Require explicit reviewed budget changes with before/after evidence.
- Store preview performance artifacts per PR.
- Compare against the canonical #67 baseline and prior main.
- Add scheduled production checks without making CI depend on unstable third-party uptime.

## Non-goals

- Optimizing solely for one Lighthouse score while degrading comprehension or accessibility.
- Collecting invasive telemetry to debug a marketing page.
- Hiding optional WebGL cost in a separate unreported graph.

Issue #790: release.mjs leaves published shrinkwrap metadata on the previous version

## Summary

`scripts/release.mjs` updates the root `package.json` version but leaves both version fields in `package-lock.json` unchanged. If `--publish-npm` is used, the package prepack hook copies that unchanged lock verbatim to `npm-shrinkwrap.json`. The resulting npm tarball declares the new release version in `package.json` and the previous release version in its shrinkwrap metadata.

## Environment

- `upstream/dev`: `2aef244301f5d181624662fdad53e18e83e80bd9`
- Node.js: `24.15.0`
- Clean disposable Docker development worker
- Synthetic build and VSIX fixture; no package was published and no GitHub release was created

## Reproduction

In a disposable copy of the repository, I ran the exact release script with a synthetic `npm` fixture that only acknowledged the build command and materialized the expected VSIX path:

```bash
PATH="$PWD/fake-bin:$PATH" node scripts/release.mjs \
  --version 9.9.9 --no-publish --no-release
node scripts/package-shrinkwrap.mjs prepare
```

The release command completed successfully and left this metadata:

```json
{
  "package": "9.9.9",
  "packageLock": "1.7.2",
  "packageLockRoot": "1.7.2",
  "shrinkwrap": "1.7.2",
  "shrinkwrapRoot": "1.7.2"
}
```

Packing that disposable tree without lifecycle scripts preserves the mismatch in the release artifact:

```bash
npm pack --ignore-scripts --workspaces=false --json
tar -xOf pasko70-pibo-9.9.9.tgz package/package.json
tar -xOf pasko70-pibo-9.9.9.tgz package/npm-shrinkwrap.json
```

Observed:

```json
{
  "archive": "pasko70-pibo-9.9.9.tgz",
  "package": "9.9.9",
  "shrinkwrap": "1.7.2",
  "shrinkwrapRoot": "1.7.2"
}
```

I repeated the equivalent minimal synthetic package reproduction twice; both runs packed `package.json=2.0.0` with `npm-shrinkwrap.json=1.0.0`. As a control, running `npm install --package-lock-only` in the unpacked artifact rewrote both shrinkwrap version fields to `2.0.0`, confirming that npm regards the generated metadata as stale.

## Expected behavior

The release process should keep the root package manifest, lockfile root metadata, and published shrinkwrap root metadata on the same release version. Alternatively, prepack should reject a version mismatch before publication.

## Actual behavior

The release process can complete its build and package stages with the root manifest on the new version while the lockfile remains on the previous version. The publish lifecycle then packages that stale lock unchanged as `npm-shrinkwrap.json`.

## Cause and impact

`scripts/release.mjs:107-111` updates only the root and VS Code extension manifests. `scripts/package-shrinkwrap.mjs:14-18` validates package names but not versions, then copies `package-lock.json` verbatim. The existing shrinkwrap test exercises only matching manifest and lock versions.

Consequently, `--publish-npm` can emit a self-inconsistent package artifact. Fresh package tooling sees the shrinkwrap as needing a metadata rewrite even though it came directly from the release process, defeating the intended reproducible-package metadata lifecycle.

## Duplicate check

Searched all open and closed issues and pull requests for `release.mjs`, `npm-shrinkwrap.json`, shrinkwrap, package-lock version mismatches, stale lock metadata, npm packing, and published package metadata. No matching defect was found. #530 introduced the generated shrinkwrap and validates a matching-version tarball; #782 concerns malformed SemVer validation; #776 and #740 concern GitHub release assets. None covers stale npm package version metadata.

When the SCCM module is executed with the following option:
`-o REC_RESOLVE=TRUE`
the module crashes during recursive object resolution.

### Root Cause
The resolve_recursive() method builds an LDAP filter using a Distinguished Name (DN) without escaping LDAP special characters. If the DN contains characters that require escaping, the resulting LDAP filter is malformed, causing the LDAP query to fail and the module to terminate unexpectedly.

`o REC_RESOLVE=TRUE`

### Expected Behavior
The DN should be properly escaped before being incorporated into the LDAP filter, allowing recursive resolution to complete successfully without errors.

### Actual Behavior
The module constructs an invalid LDAP filter, causing the LDAP query to fail and the SCCM module to crash.

### Proposed Fix
Escape the Distinguished Name before it is inserted into the LDAP filter within the resolve_recursive() method. This ensures that LDAP filters remain valid regardless of the DN contents and prevents crashes when recursive resolution is enabled.
