Issue #4339: Add declarative PR dependency and rollout gates

## Problem

Agents frequently produce independently reviewable stacked or follow-up PRs, but the dependency between them is currently informal. A later PR can be merge-ready according to GitHub even when:

- another PR has not merged yet; or
- an unrelated commit/image has not reached production through Flux yet.

This comes up often enough that the dependency should be machine-readable and enforced rather than left in prose.

Examples:

- PR 1234 must wait for PR 1233 to merge.
- PR 1234 must wait until commit `abcdef123`, which is not necessarily part of PR 1234, has reached production.

## Goal

Add a general, repo-owned, open-source dependency gate that continuously publishes merge eligibility for the waiting PR's current head SHA.

Do not depend on a paid merge-management service.

A possible PR-body interface:

```text
Depends-On: #1233
Wait-For-Prod: abcdef123
```

The exact syntax is part of the design. Prefer something simple for agents to emit and humans to review.

## Required behavior

- A PR with no declared dependencies passes the gate immediately.
- A PR dependency remains pending until the referenced PR is merged.
- A production dependency remains pending until the exact commit/image is proven to have reached the named environment.
- The gate is recreated or reevaluated for every new PR head SHA.
- State is reconciled when PR descriptions or dependency states change.
- Flux/deployment events should trigger prompt reevaluation; periodic reconciliation should repair missed events.
- The UI explains every unresolved or invalid dependency.
- Invalid syntax, unknown dependency types, inaccessible references, and ambiguous image/tag matches fail closed.
- Use immutable commit SHAs or image digests for rollout predicates.
- Avoid circular dependency deadlocks and report detected cycles clearly.
- Work with GitHub branch protection/rulesets so the gate actually prevents merging.
- Continue to work with independently reviewable PRs; do not require stacked branches or serialize PR creation.

## Production evidence

Define what “reached production” means for each supported target. It should prove the relevant live path, not merely that an image exists or that ImagePolicy selected it. Likely evidence includes the applicable Flux reconciliation plus the deployed workload's exact image digest and readiness.

Keep the evaluator extensible so later predicates can cover migrations, releases, or other declarative prerequisites without turning the PR body into executable code.

## Evaluate Prow/Tide as a general coordination plane

Treat Prow/Tide as a serious candidate, not merely heavyweight prior art. Its reconciled merge pools, required and forbidden labels, required or conditional status contexts, presubmit handling, dashboards, commands, and external-plugin interface could support broader agent-authored PR coordination beyond this first dependency gate.

Evaluate at least:

- Whether Tide can manage merge eligibility while retaining the existing GitHub Actions → BuildBuddy CI architecture and consuming its status contexts.
- How PR dependencies and Flux rollout predicates would be represented: labels, status contexts, a Prow external plugin, or a small upstreamable Prow extension.
- Whether Prow's other general capabilities would replace enough bespoke GitHub automation to justify operating it.
- GitHub App permissions, branch-protection ownership, failure modes, reconciliation behavior, upgrades, and operational cost.
- How agents discover and emit the supported dependency declarations.
- A narrow repo-owned Action/controller as the comparison baseline.

Avoid adopting all of Prow by inertia, but also avoid building a one-off gate before checking whether Prow provides the right durable control plane.

Other small prior art worth inspecting:

- `gregsdennis/dependencies-action`: MIT Action enforcing PR/issue dependencies.
- `Levi-Lesches/blocking-issues`: event-driven dependency updates.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A short design comparison recommends Prow/Tide, a narrow local controller, or another open-source design with concrete operational reasoning.
- [ ] A documented PR-body declaration can reference another Ducktape PR.
- [ ] A documented declaration can reference an unrelated commit/image rollout to production.
- [ ] An enforced GitHub gate transitions automatically as dependencies change.
- [ ] The implementation has tests for satisfied, pending, invalid, inaccessible, cyclic, and changed-head cases.
- [ ] The rollout predicate is demonstrated against the actual Flux-to-workload path.
- [ ] Credentials and any cluster-side observer are declaratively managed through the existing GitOps ownership paths.

Issue #1245: bug: tool engine silently converts unknown node types to no-op FnNode when rebuilding workflow cache

## Current Behavior

The tool engine (`factory workflow tool *`) runs each command in a fresh process, so it serializes the workflow graph to `.factory/tool_session/workflow_cache.json` in `tool_init()` and rebuilds it from JSON on every subsequent `tool next` / `tool submit` / `tool status` call. `_rebuild_workflow()` only reconstructs `AgentNode`, `GateNode`, `Study`, `FnNode`, `ForkNode`, and `JoinNode`. Any other node type falls into a generic `else` branch that silently constructs an empty `FnNode(command="", notes="")` — losing all node-specific fields with no error and no validation failure.

Affected node types that exist in the codebase and are used by a registered built-in workflow (`parallel-improve`):
- `SubgraphForkNode` — loses `subgraph_entry`, `subgraph_exit`, `parallelism`, `worktree_isolated` (primitives.py:181-193)
- `SelectionNode` — loses `strategy` (primitives.py:196-201)
- `LLMNode` — loses `system_prompt`, `instance_prompt`, `model`, `provider`, `tools`, etc. (primitives.py:223-242)

The damage happens in two places, both silent:
1. **Serialization** (`tool_init`) only writes type-specific fields for `AgentNode`/`GateNode`/`Study`/`FnNode`/`ForkNode` — the other node types are stored with only common fields, so their semantics are already gone in the JSON.

```python
    while queue:
        nid = queue.pop(0)
        if nid in visited:
            continue
        visited.add(nid)
        if nid == exit_node:
            continue
        for target in edges_by_source.get(nid, []):
            if target not in visited:
                queue.append(target)

    return visited
```

## Problem

No data catalog exists. As of today:
- No one can answer "what tables exist in ClickHouse and what do they mean?"
- No lineage: "this `fact_claims_monthly` table — where did it come from? what processes produced it?"
- No data ownership: who is accountable if `dim_employee` has wrong department codes?

- ISO 27001 A.8.1 (asset inventory) is partially unmet for data assets

## Solution: OpenMetadata

OpenMetadata is the open-source unified metadata platform. It provides:
- Automated metadata ingestion from ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Airflow, dbt
- End-to-end data lineage (source DB → Debezium CDC → NATS → ClickHouse raw → dbt → mart → Grafana)

Issue #818: Idea: expose transitive Python dependencies through ansible-builder introspect

## Summary

Would the project be open to extending `ansible-builder introspect` with opt-in Python dependency resolution?

I have implemented an initial proof of concept in my fork:

> [!NOTE]
> Assisted by GPT 5.6 Sol.

[PoC feature branch](https://github.com/dbrennand/ansible-builder/tree/codex/introspect-transitive-python-deps)

The PoC adds:

```
ansible-builder introspect \
  --write-python-dependency-report=python-dependencies.json \
  --write-transitive-python=transitive-requirements.txt \
  /path/to/collections
```

The first option preserves pip’s installation report. The second produces a sorted, unpinned list containing only transitive package names. When both are requested, pip resolves the requirements once.

I'd like to open this idea for discussion.

## Motivation

`ansible-builder introspect` currently identifies Python requirements declared directly by collections and users, but it does not expose the dependencies introduced by those packages.

Transitive discovery could help collection maintainers and execution environment authors:

- Identify the complete resolved Python package set.
- Find vulnerable transitive packages that are not declared directly.
- Detect unexpected changes in upstream dependency graphs.
- Understand which versions and artifacts pip selected.
- Provide structured dependency data to CI and security tooling.

Existing YAML output, `--write-pip`, and `--write-bindep` behavior would remain unchanged.

## Potential SBOM and CRA value

This idea would not generate an SBOM or claim regulatory compliance. However, pip’s report contains useful inputs for future [SPDX](https://spdx.dev/) or [CycloneDX](https://cyclonedx.org/) generation, including package names, versions, artifact locations, hashes, and metadata.

This may also be relevant to both roles recognized by the [EU Cyber Resilience Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2847/oj/eng):

- Manufacturers of products with digital elements must meet vulnerability handling requirements. Annex I includes identifying and documenting components and producing a machine readable SBOM covering at least top level dependencies.
- Qualifying open-source software stewards have a tailored regime requiring a documented cybersecurity policy that promotes secure development, effective vulnerability handling, and the sharing of information about discovered vulnerabilities.

Better visibility into the dependency chain could greatly improve supply chain security and help manufacturers understand the Ansible content incorporated into their products. It could also provide useful information to open-source stewards supporting collections or related ecosystem tooling, particularly for vulnerability identification and remediation.

## Feedback requested

I would particularly appreciate feedback on:

- Whether dependency resolution belongs in `ansible-builder introspect`.
- Whether the raw pip report and transitive dependency name list are useful outputs.

the filesystem refuses.

capability, and degrade to the previous backend rather than failing the worker. A worker

## Environment

- Claude Code CLI 2.1.201

- Repo: a Next.js/TypeScript monorepo using git worktrees as the standard per-lane isolation mechanism, with a repo-local `PreToolUse` hook that gates mutating Bash/Edit/Write calls on repo custody state (not itself the bug, but it's how several bleeds were first detected — a command reporting the wrong branch)

## Summary

`EnterWorktree(path: …)` is documented (and reasonably assumed) to rebind only the calling agent's own working-directory context. In practice, under concurrency, it behaves like a **single mutable slot shared by the whole session tree**: when *any* agent — a subagent, or even a subagent several dispatch-levels deep — calls `EnterWorktree(path:)`, it silently repoints the cwd seen by **every other live shell in that session**, including the orchestrator's own persistent shell and sibling subagents' shells. The tool's contract implies isolation; the observed behavior is global, last-writer-wins mutation.

This has been reproduced repeatedly (~43 logged incidents across many sessions over roughly a week of heavy worktree-based fleet usage) and is the single highest-frequency, highest-severity harness friction item we've logged for this workflow.

## Expected behavior

Each agent (orchestrator and every subagent) that calls `EnterWorktree(path:)` should get its **own** cwd binding, independent of what any other concurrently running agent in the same session does. A parent session's shell should never be silently relocated by a child subagent's worktree operations, and two sibling subagents should never observe each other's cwd.

## Actual behavior

- Any `EnterWorktree(path:)` call, by any agent, clobbers one session-wide cwd slot.
- Every shell in the session tree — including the orchestrator's — re-reads that slot on its next Bash call, surfacing as an unprompted "Shell cwd was reset to `<newest lane's worktree>`" notice.
- A bare `cd` back to the intended directory does not stick once the slot has been externally pinned by another agent's `EnterWorktree` call — the next tool call snaps back to whichever worktree was most recently entered by anyone.
- This is bidirectional and not limited to parent→child: sibling subagent A can end up executing inside sibling subagent B's worktree, and vice versa, when both bootstrap around the same time.
- **The bleed does not require any `EnterWorktree` call at all**: in a 2026-07-09 session with three concurrent `Agent`-tool lanes and zero `EnterWorktree` invocations that turn, the orchestrator's shell was still repeatedly reset into a lane's worktree between tool calls. - The failure is invisible until something downstream contradicts expectation — a `git status`/`git branch --show-current` showing the wrong branch, a custody/intake tool reporting a foreign lane's state, a `git add <path>` failing on an unexpected pathspec, or file content not matching what was just written.

Issue #80800: Windows: superseded PowerShell recursive searches keep consuming CPU

## Summary

On Windows, Claude Code left two CPU-active `pwsh.exe` tool children running after it had already moved on to newer work. They were not OS zombies: both were still recursively scanning the workspace and consuming CPU, but their original tool calls no longer appeared relevant to the active Claude workflow.

## Environment

- Windows 11
- Claude Code launched as `claude.exe`
- Large local workspace with `.claude/worktrees` (35 worktrees; 29 contained `node_modules`)

## What happened

Two direct `pwsh.exe` children of one active `claude.exe` parent were still running:

```powershell
Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File -Path scripts,.claude -Include *.mjs,*.js |
  Select-String ...
```

and a similar `.claude,scripts` recursive search.

Both searches traversed `.claude/worktrees`, including many `node_modules` directories. The Claude parent later spawned a newer child for unrelated work, but the old PowerShell children kept running. The expected completion/handoff output for the old calls was absent.

During a 10-second sample, the two old children consumed approximately 5.72 CPU seconds and 1.66 CPU seconds respectively. This caused visible desktop slowdown; Defender and DWM load increased secondarily.

## Expected behavior

When a tool invocation becomes superseded, cancelled, or no longer awaited, Claude Code should terminate or reap its still-running child-process tree. For recursive file searches, it should also avoid unbounded PowerShell `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` through `.claude/worktrees` / `node_modules` (for example, prefer a bounded ignore-aware search).

## Workaround

I manually terminated only the two stale `pwsh.exe` child trees. They were read-only searches, and the newer Claude work continued.

Could the tool-process lifecycle be checked for cases where Claude advances to a new action while the prior PowerShell child remains CPU-active?

Issue #17206: Scan planning fails permanently with "Can't index multiple DVs" when a snapshot has duplicate deletion vectors for one data file (read-side recovery)

### Apache Iceberg version

main (development)

### Query engine

Spark

### Please describe the bug 🐞

**Summary:** Once a table ends up with more than one deletion vector (DV) referencing the same data file in a snapshot, **every scan of that table fails during planning** with:

```
Can't index multiple DVs for <data-file>: <dv1> and <dv2>
```

thrown from `DeleteFileIndex.Builder.add(Map<String, DeleteFile> dvByPath, DeleteFile dv)` (`core/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/DeleteFileIndex.java`, ~L529-533). The table becomes effectively unreadable and there is no built-in way to recover it. This is core scan-planning code, so it affects every query engine, not just Spark.

**Why it throws:** The DV index is built by iterating all live delete-manifest entries in the snapshot (`DeleteFileIndex.Builder.build()` -> `loadDeleteFiles()` -> the loop at ~L501). For each DV, `add(...)` does `dvByPath.putIfAbsent(dv.referencedDataFile(), dv)` and throws a `ValidationException` if an entry already exists for that path. There is no deduplication or merge.

**Spec context:** The spec forbids more than one DV per data file per snapshot ("there can be at most one deletion vector for a given data file in a snapshot"; "Writers must ensure that there is at most one deletion vector per data file and must merge new deletes with existing vectors or position delete files"). So two DVs for one data file is always metadata corruption, and the `ValidationException` is a *correct* detection of an invalid state - but it leaves the table permanently unreadable.

**How a table reaches this state:** This is the read-side manifestation of a write-side conflict-detection gap (see #15966). When two concurrent row-level writers use a `conflictDetectionFilter` that is narrower than the set of data files they actually touch, `validateAddedDVs` can miss the conflict and allow two DVs for the same data file to be committed. #15966 fixes the *write* side and prevents future corruption, but it cannot heal tables that are **already** corrupted - those remain bricked.

**Steps to reproduce:** Produce a snapshot containing two live DV entries that reference the same data file (for example via the concurrent narrow-`conflictDetectionFilter` path described in #15966, or by crafting two delete manifests that each contain a DV for the same data file), then run any scan. Planning fails with `Can't index multiple DVs`.

**Expected behavior:** A reader should be able to recover from an already-corrupted table without data loss. Rather than throwing (and leaving the table unreadable), `DeleteFileIndex` should:

1. **Byte-identical duplicates** (same `location()`, `contentOffset()`, `contentSizeInBytes()`) - the same DV referenced from two manifest entries (e.g. a manifest-rewrite race): deduplicate silently, logging at DEBUG.
2. **Genuinely different DVs for the same data file**: **merge (union) their position bitmaps** by reading both Puffin blobs and combining them, analogous to the merge already performed on the write path, and log a WARNING about the spec violation. This preserves **all** deletes.
3. **Never silently pick one DV**, which would drop the other's deletes and resurrect deleted rows - a correctness violation worse than a scan failure.

**Proposed fix (I can contribute):** In `DeleteFileIndex.Builder.build()`, collect DVs per referenced data file, and in a post-pass deduplicate byte-identical DVs and union the position bitmaps of any genuinely different DVs (reusing the existing DV merge utility), logging a WARNING; index only the resulting merged DV. `FileIO` is available on the Builder. This is a read-side recovery/self-heal that complements the write-side fix in #15966. I would include a reproducer test.

- [ ] I would be willing to contribute a fix for this bug with guidance from the Iceberg community

Issue #1063: build: ship the release binary with frame pointers (-C force-frame-pointers=yes)

Extends the #847 profiling contract: the shipped binary keeps its symbol table
so function-level flame graphs work in the field. This asks for one more
property with the same rationale: build the release binary with
`-C force-frame-pointers=yes`, so the frame-pointer half of the profiling
ecosystem works on the shipped image too.

## What we measured against the shipped binary

While validating an external CPU profiler against the release image (as
shipped, no rebuild), we needed an independent reference for the call chains.
Both of `perf`'s modes failed on the shipped binary:

- **`perf record --call-graph fp`**: unusable — the release profile does not
  emit frame pointers, so the kernel's rbp walk has nothing to follow.
- **`perf record --call-graph dwarf`**: libdw fails to evaluate this binary's
  call-frame information. Measured on a 6.18 KVM guest under a
  `bench/pgo-training` load: only **22 of 618** sampled chains ever crossed
  the libc-to-aisix boundary; everything else stopped there. The CFI data
  itself is fine — `readelf --debug-dump=frames-interp` parses all **36,928
  FDEs** cleanly — it is elfutils' evaluator that gives up on the fat-LTO
  output. Upstream's bug, but it ships in every distro's `perf`.

So today, no stock profiling tool can walk the shipped binary's stacks. To get
a working reference at all we had to rebuild the pinned release commit with
`RUSTFLAGS="-C force-frame-pointers=yes"`. On that build, `perf --call-graph
fp` walked **99.9%** of samples to the thread entry with user-chain depth p90
of 44 — essentially perfect. One flag is the difference between "no external
tool works" and "everything fp-based works".

## Cost

- Industry measurements put `force-frame-pointers` at **under 1%** on x86-64
  (16 GPRs; losing `rbp` as a scratch register stopped mattering a decade
  ago). Fedora 38+, Ubuntu 24.04+ and Arch now build their entire
  distributions with frame pointers on this reasoning.
- +8 bytes of stack per frame; binary-size delta is noise next to the
  symbol table #847 already ships (~10 MiB).
- Fat LTO, `codegen-units = 1`, and PGO are unaffected — frame pointers are a
  per-function prologue property, orthogonal to inlining and layout.

## What it buys

- `perf record -g` (fp is its default), bcc/bpftrace stack helpers, and every
  other rbp-walking tool work on the release image **as shipped** — support
  and customers can profile without a rebuild.
- Profiling validation stops rebuilding the world: the flag makes the shipped
  artifact its own reference target.

## Honest limits

- It does not fix libdw's fat-LTO problem; `--call-graph dwarf` stays broken
  until elfutils does.
- rbp walkers still lose the frames below any call into a library built
  without frame pointers (today: glibc in the base image). That blind spot
  belongs to the base image's libc, not to this flag; it shrinks as distros
  ship fp-built libc.

## Implementation sketch

The release binary's `RUSTFLAGS` are set in the Dockerfile's PGO phases
(`-Cprofile-generate=...` and `-Cprofile-use=...`) and unset in the
`PGO=off` branch. Append `-C force-frame-pointers=yes` to all three — keeping
both PGO phases' flags identical so the trained layout matches the shipped
shape — or hoist it into one `ARG`/`ENV` so it cannot drift between branches.

The #847 CI check already pins the symbol table because "a future strip step,
RUSTFLAGS change, or base-image swap would break flame graphs silently".
Frame pointers deserve the same pin once added: assert a sampled function
prologue starts with `push %rbp; mov %rsp,%rbp` (e.g. `objdump -d` on `main`)
in the same job, so the property cannot regress silently either.

## Verification

```sh
objdump -d --no-show-raw-insn /usr/local/bin/aisix | grep -A2 '<main>:' | head -3
# expect: push %rbp / mov %rsp,%rbp
```

A maintainer on the project arnaud18o5/sysml-ai-copilot (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #59: import_stmt is modeled as a regular :Element, polluting vector search results

`_walk_node`'s `import_stmt` case in `sysml_copilot/parser.py` records each import as a full-blown model element, same as a `PartUsage` or `RequirementDefinition`:

```python
elif node.data == "import_stmt":
    path = _import_path_str(node.children[0])
    elem = model.add_element("Import", path, scope_path)
    if container_id:
        model.add_relation(container_id, elem.id, "CONTAINS")
```

Repro:

```python
from sysml_copilot.parser import parse_sysml
text = '''
package Demo {
    import Utilities::Common;
    part def Widget;
}
'''
elements, _ = parse_sysml(text)
```
```json
[
  {"id": "Demo", "kind": "Package", "name": "Demo", "qualified_name": "Demo", "doc": null},
  {"id": "Demo.Utilities::Common", "kind": "Import", "name": "Utilities::Common", "qualified_name": "Demo.Utilities::Common", "doc": null},
  {"id": "Demo.Widget", "kind": "PartDefinition", "name": "Widget", "qualified_name": "Demo.Widget", "doc": null}
]
```

Two knock-on problems once this reaches `ingest.py`/`query.py`:

- `ingest.py` embeds every element via `element_text()` (`embeddings.py`), so this pseudo-element gets an embedding too — `"Import - Utilities::Common"`. It's then a real candidate in `resolve_element`'s vector search: an NL query that happens to mention a name matching the imported path segment (e.g. "Common") can resolve to the `Import` pseudo-element instead of an actual part/port/requirement, which is a confusing and wrong answer for a tool whose whole job is resolving "what is the user talking about."
- `qualified_name` mixes the `.`-scope separator with the import path's own `::` separator (`Demo.Utilities::Common`), which doesn't match the qualified-name convention every other element kind follows (dot path from the package root, per CLAUDE.md's architecture invariant) — a wildcard import (`import Utilities::*;`, once #57 lands) would produce an even stranger id/name like `Demo.Utilities::*`.

CONTAINS is excluded from impact-analysis traversal (`IMPACT_RELATIONSHIP_TYPES` in `query.py`), so this doesn't currently pollute impact-analysis *results* for other elements — the concrete, reachable bug is `resolve_element` surfacing an `Import` node as the top NL-query match.

Suggested fix: don't create an `:Element`/embedding for imports at all — either drop the `model.add_element(...)` call and just keep a note of unresolved import paths on the `_Model` (matching the "unresolved, just recorded" framing already used for imports in CLAUDE.md/README), or if a graph representation is wanted, give imports their own non-`Element`-labeled node (or a property on the package) so they're excluded from `embed_texts`/the vector index by construction rather than by accident.

Noticed while implementing #45 and scanning `parser.py`/`ingest.py` for other gaps not yet covered by an existing issue.

refusals, and its own reason to exist:

1. a claim stays adjacent when a stage arrives;
2. relabelling a step keeps the flow connected;
3. a step is inserted between two steps;
4. an unused, non-canonical stage is removed;

five can merge upward**: each is a different act, on a different write, with a different refusal, and
three of them amend different normative sentences. On the rubric alone this would be five issues.

**The owner was shown that analysis and chose one issue.** It is recorded here so a reviewer meets
the decision at the top of the body rather than discovering it at spec review.

touch the same surface — automation configuration and the board that arranges it — so as five issues

A project has a canonical workflow it cannot lose. The loop this product runs on — **grill →
propose → implement → sync** — exists from the project's first minute, and an Admin can relabel it,

Issue #175: Perf: reduce remaining cache.db connection churn after one-time schema verification

## Problem

`session_summarizer._connect()` opens a **fresh** `sqlite3.Connection` to `~/.ccstory/cache.db`, runs `PRAGMA schema_version`, and executes `_run_migrations()` (with `PRAGMA user_version` check) **every single time** it is called. In one typical `ccstory week` run, `_connect()` is invoked **20+ times** across:

- `upsert()` — once per session being summarized
- `get_many()` — bulk fetch summaries
- `_classify_cache_get_many()` — bulk fetch cached classifications
- `synthesize_overall_for_period()` / `synthesize_category_for_period()` — narrative cache
- `invalidate_*()` — cache invalidation
- `import_from_claude_recap()` — one-time migration

Each call pays:
1. File open overhead
2. `PRAGMA schema_version` (forces SQLite header parse)
3. `_run_migrations()` (checks `PRAGMA user_version`, compares against `CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION`)

### Why it matters

For the critical path of the first-run experience, this compounds with the double-scan issue (#174). The user sees the "Generating fallback narratives" progress bar, during which `upsert()` is called once per session, each opening and closing the DB.

### Proposal

Use a process-lifetime singleton connection with a `_migrated` flag:

```python
_singleton_conn: sqlite3.Connection | None = None
_migrated: bool = False

def _connect() -> sqlite3.Connection:
    global _singleton_conn, _migrated
    if _singleton_conn is not None:
        return _singleton_conn
    DB_PATH.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    conn = sqlite3.connect(str(DB_PATH))
    conn.execute("PRAGMA schema_version").fetchone()
    if not _migrated:
        _run_migrations(conn)
        _migrated = True
    _singleton_conn = conn
    return conn
```

Callers that currently call `conn.close()` in `finally` blocks would need updating to not close the singleton. Add an explicit `close_cache()` for process shutdown if needed.

### Affected files

- `ccstory/session_summarizer.py` — 20 call sites

Issue #3213: Add configurable gRPC message size limits for server

  ## Problem

  When using `LookupSubjects` with complex permission schemas involving recursive
  relations (e.g., `group#downwards_member`) and set operations, requests fail with:

  rpc error: code = ResourceExhausted desc = grpc: received message after decompression larger than max 4194304

  ### Why client-side options don't help

  - Client-side `grpc.MaxCallRecvMsgSize()` only affects the client connection
  - The limit is hit on **internal dispatch calls** where `CollectingDispatchStream`
    buffers results during Union/Intersection/Exclusion operations
  - The server uses gRPC's default 4 MiB limit with no way to configure it

  ### Use case

  - Org with ~100k users
  - Complex permission schema with recursive group membership (`group#downwards_member`)
  - `LookupSubjects` to find all users with a permission on a resource

  ## Proposed Solution

  Add configurable gRPC message size limits to `GRPCServerConfig`:

  - `--grpc-max-recv-msg-size` (default: 4194304)
  - `--grpc-max-send-msg-size` (default: 4194304)

  Since `GRPCServerConfig` is shared, this also enables:
  - `--dispatch-cluster-max-recv-msg-size`
  - `--dispatch-cluster-max-send-msg-size`

  ## Implementation

  I have a working implementation ready to submit as a PR if this approach is acceptable.

  Changes:
  - Add `MaxRecvMsgSize` and `MaxSendMsgSize` fields to `GRPCServerConfig` struct

Issue #2275: `#[commentable]` hard delete: the FK cascade crosses record scope, under-reporting and corrupting another record's counter

Follow-up from #2261 (`#[commentable]`, closes #1367). Raised by Codex review; filed per the review budget on that PR.

## The problem

With `#[commentable(..., soft_delete = false)]`, `delete_subtree` removes the subtree with a real `DELETE`, and the `comments` table's `parent_id` carries `REFERENCES comments(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`. The recursive query that collects the subtree is correctly scoped to one record — it only follows children sharing the root's `(commentable_type, commentable_id)`.

The database cascade is not so scoped.

An imported or hand-written row can name a comment in this subtree as its `parent_id` while carrying a *different* `(commentable_type, commentable_id)`. The recursive query rightly excludes it, so it is absent from `ids`. But when the `DELETE` lands, the FK cascade removes it anyway, along with its descendants. So:

- those rows are gone without ever appearing in `ids.len()`, and
- the **other** record's `comment_count` is never decremented, leaving that counter permanently overstated.

The delete reports a smaller number than it removed, and it silently corrupts a counter belonging to a record the caller never named.

## Scope

Hard-delete only (`soft_delete = false`). The default soft-delete path marks `deleted_at` rather than deleting rows, so no cascade fires.

Reachable only with cross-record `parent_id` edges, which the framework's own write path cannot create — `add_comment` rejects a `reply_to` naming a comment on a different record (that check is tested). So this needs imported data, a migration, or hand-written SQL. That makes it unlikely but not unreachable, and the failure is silent.

## Options

1. **Account for the cascade** — before deleting, collect every descendant by `parent_id` *without* the record-scope filter, then decrement each affected parent's counter by its own share. Correct, and makes `delete_comment`'s return value honest, but turns a single-record operation into a multi-record one.
2. **Reject cross-record edges** — detect them in the subtree walk and fail the delete with a directed error, so the corrupt data is surfaced rather than silently propagated. Cheapest, and arguably right: a cross-record edge is already a violated invariant.
3. **Drop the FK cascade** and delete the subtree explicitly by id. Removes the database's ability to reach outside the scoped set at all, at the cost of the cascade's safety net for the soft-delete path.

(2) is probably the right default — the framework refuses to create these edges, so encountering one means something else is wrong and quietly widening a delete is the least helpful response.

## Reproduce

A `#[commentable(soft_delete = false)]` model; a comment tree on record A; then `UPDATE comments SET parent_id = <a comment in A's tree> WHERE id = <a comment on record B>`. Delete A's root: B's comment vanishes, `delete_comment` under-reports, and B's `comment_count` still counts it.

Issue #1644: [W6 blocker] Route Show Runtime repair through one verified owner

## Problem

The Settings Dependencies action calls `_prepare_show_runtime_job()`, which calls `prepare(force=True)` without first proving that the installed Show Runtime cannot start. A healthy runtime can therefore be replaced merely because the user pressed Install/Repair.

That is unsafe before W6 because same-identity forced replacement mutates or deletes the path a live runtime may still reference. The exposure is documented by [PR #1634 thread 14](https://github.com/avibe-bot/avibe/pull/1634#discussion_r3834840296) and owned by [the authoritative availability plan's W6 section](https://github.com/avibe-bot/avibe/blob/master/docs/plans/show-runtime-availability.md#w6--make-the-switch-atomic-repo-avibe).

## W6 blocker contract

- One manager-owned verified-repair path serves both Doctor and Settings; callers cannot invoke an ungated forced replacement directly.
- The path proves startability first. A healthy runtime is reported healthy and is not replaced; only an observed start failure authorizes repair.
- Replacement creates a new immutable install path and never overwrites bytes reachable through a command already handed to a caller or running process.
- Pruning retains installs by live/cached reference, not only by a fixed `keep_previous` count. Distinct identities are not safe when cleanup can still delete a referenced older directory.
- Install-versus-install keeps the existing thread and cross-process serialization; no lock is stretched across the runtime lifecycle.

## Acceptance

- Pressing Settings Repair on a healthy runtime performs no replacement.
- Doctor and Settings use the same startability evidence and report the same three outcomes: healthy, observed start failure repaired, or verification undetermined/failed without destructive action.
- A forced repair cannot invalidate a cached command or a running runtime, including through cleanup of an older distinct identity.
- Hermetic concurrency and retention tests cover cached command reuse, a running runtime that lazily loads files after startup, same-identity replacement, distinct-identity pruning, and both UI/CLI repair callers.

This issue blocks W6. It does not block PR #1634: the destructive repair path already exists on `master`, and #1634 reduces its trigger by reporting the installed version truthfully.

Issue #347: Harden setNested in fix-i18n.mjs so prototype protection is structural, not a denylist

## Summary

`setNested` in `voc-datalake/frontend/scripts/fix-i18n.mjs` already guards against prototype pollution, but it does so in a shape CodeQL does not recognise as a sanitizer, so `js/prototype-pollution-utility` (medium, alert 6, first raised 2026-03-25) keeps firing on it. The guard should be restated so the protection is structural rather than a denylist the scanner has to infer.

## Current state

```js
const UNSAFE_KEYS = new Set(['__proto__', 'constructor', 'prototype'])

function setNested(obj, key, val) {
  const parts = key.split('.')
  if (parts.some(p => UNSAFE_KEYS.has(p))) return
  let cur = obj
  for (let i = 0; i < parts.length - 1; i++) {
    if (!cur[parts[i]] || typeof cur[parts[i]] !== 'object') cur[parts[i]] = {}
    cur = cur[parts[i]]
  }
  cur[parts[parts.length - 1]] = val
}
```

The early return covers every path segment, terminal and intermediate, against the three dangerous keys, so **this is not currently exploitable**. Two reasons the risk is low regardless:

- It is a local build script. It never ships to a browser, and it processes locale JSON that is already committed to this repository, so reaching it requires a malicious key in a tracked file.
- The denylist covers the keys that actually matter for pollution.

## Why change it anyway

A denylist is a maintenance liability: it is correct only as long as the list is complete, and nothing enforces that. Making the containers non-prototypal removes the class of bug instead of enumerating it, and has the side benefit of satisfying the scanner so the alert stops needing manual triage on every PR that carries this file.

Suggested direction:

- Create intermediate objects with `Object.create(null)` so there is no prototype to pollute.
- Keep the existing `UNSAFE_KEYS` early return as belt and braces rather than replacing it.
- If the parsed locale objects need to stay plain (for `JSON.stringify` round-tripping and deep-equality assertions), verify that with the existing i18n gates before switching — the scripts and their tests are sensitive to object shape.

## Acceptance criteria

- Writing a key containing `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype`, at any position in the path, cannot modify `Object.prototype`, and there is a check that fails if that protection is removed.
- The i18n scripts and their existing gates still pass, and generated locale files are byte-identical to before the change.
- CodeQL no longer reports `js/prototype-pollution-utility` for this file, or the remaining report is dismissed with reasoning recorded on the alert.

## Context

Surfaced while reviewing #346 (merging `development` into `main`). The alert is **not** a regression from that PR: the file is byte-identical to `development` and does not exist on `main` at all, so it arrives with that merge and CodeQL reports it against main's baseline for the first time. Alert 6 is being dismissed on #346 as a false positive with that reasoning recorded, and this issue tracks the hardening separately so the merge stays scoped to dependency resolution.

Issue #1165: [lambda_http] Fallible response body panics during buffered conversion instead of propagating the body error

## Description

`lambda_http` accepts response body types whose `HttpBody::Error` is fallible, but the buffered response conversion calls `expect()` when collecting the body.

If the body returns an error—for example, when a proxied HTTP/1.1 chunked response is truncated—`IntoResponse::into_response()` panics instead of propagating the body error. This affects both the text and binary conversion paths.

When the handler runs under `lambda_http::run`, the panic may be caught by `lambda_runtime`'s `CatchPanicService` and reported as an invocation error, so the process can survive when built with the default `panic = "unwind"` strategy.

However, this relies on `catch_unwind` as the error channel instead of propagating the body error:

- With `panic = "abort"`, which may be used for size-optimized Lambda builds, the process terminates.
- The diagnostic says that the user handler panicked even though the panic originates inside `lambda_http`.
- The structured body error is flattened into a panic message.
- Outside `lambda_http::run`, such as in custom runtimes, tests, or other adapters, calling `IntoResponse::into_response()` directly panics the process, as demonstrated below.

## Versions

- `lambda_http`: 1.3.0
- No modifications to `lambda_http`
- The same behavior is present in earlier releases
- `rustc`: 1.88.0 (6b00bc388 2025-06-23)
- `cargo`: 1.88.0 (873a06493 2025-05-10)
- OS: Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm)
- Architecture: aarch64
- Reproduction environment: official `rust:1.88-bookworm` Docker image

## Minimal reproduction

`Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[package]
name = "lambda-http-body-error-repro"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
lambda_http = "=1.3.0"
bytes = "1"
futures-util = "0.3"
http-body = "1"
http-body-util = "0.1"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt"] }
```

`src/main.rs`:

```rust
use bytes::Bytes;
use futures_util::stream;
use http_body::Frame;
use http_body_util::StreamBody;
use lambda_http::{IntoResponse, Response};
use std::io::{self, ErrorKind};

#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]
async fn main() {
    let frames = vec![
        Ok(Frame::data(Bytes::from_static(b"partial response"))),
        Err(io::Error::new(
            ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof,
            "simulated truncated response body",
        )),
    ];
    let body = StreamBody::new(stream::iter(frames));

    let response = Response::builder()
        .header("content-type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")
        .body(body)
        .unwrap();

    // Panics in lambda_http::response::convert_to_text().
    let _ = response.into_response().await;
}
```

Run:

```bash
cargo run
```

## Actual behavior

The process exits with status 101 and produces the following panic:

```text
thread 'main' panicked at /usr/local/cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/lambda_http-1.3.0/src/response.rs:412:42:
unable to read bytes from body: Custom { kind: UnexpectedEof, error: "simulated truncated response body" }
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
```

A real transport-level example is an HTTP proxy returning a `Response<hyper::body::Incoming>` where the upstream server closes an HTTP/1.1 chunked response before completing the current chunk.

Hyper exposes the premature closure as a body error. That error reaches the same `expect()` call in the buffered response conversion and is converted into a panic.

## Expected behavior

A response body error should be propagated as an error rather than surfaced through `panic!` and `catch_unwind`, so that:

- the failure is reported as an invocation error regardless of the configured panic strategy;
- the original body error is preserved in the diagnostic instead of being flattened into a panic message attributed to the user handler;
- callers of `IntoResponse` outside `lambda_http::run` are not taken down by a request-level I/O failure.

If the existing `IntoResponse` API cannot propagate the error without an API change, returning a deterministic error response from the conversion would still be preferable to panicking.

## Affected code

`ConvertBody` explicitly accepts fallible body types, with bounds including:

```rust
B: HttpBody + Unpin + Send + 'static,
B::Data: Send,
B::Error: fmt::Debug,
```

However, both buffered conversion paths use `expect()`:

```rust
body.collect()
    .await
    .expect("unable to read bytes from body")
```

Source at the `lambda_http-v1.3.0` tag:

- [`convert_to_binary` and `convert_to_text`](https://github.com/aws/aws-lambda-rust-runtime/blob/lambda_http-v1.3.0/lambda-http/src/response.rs#L377-L420)
- [`expect()` in `convert_to_binary`](https://github.com/aws/aws-lambda-rust-runtime/blob/lambda_http-v1.3.0/lambda-http/src/response.rs#L387)
- [`expect()` in `convert_to_text`](https://github.com/aws/aws-lambda-rust-runtime/blob/lambda_http-v1.3.0/lambda-http/src/response.rs#L412)

## Impact

A single malformed or prematurely closed upstream response turns a request-level I/O failure into a panic inside the runtime's response conversion path.

This is especially relevant for HTTP adapters and reverse proxies that return a live, fallible `HttpBody`, because transport-level failures are expected to be represented and handled as normal body errors.

In environments using `panic = "abort"`, this can also terminate the runtime process instead of failing only the affected invocation.

This appears to be different from #1051.

That issue concerns an early client closure in the streaming runtime path involving `lambda_runtime` and `send_data().unwrap()` under local Lambda emulation.

This report concerns `lambda_http::IntoResponse` collecting a fallible application response body in the buffered conversion path.

- Lambda response streaming;

- a Lambda emulator;
- an actual HTTP server.

  ```python
      Item(name="Bar", amount=3.0),
      Item(name="Baz", amount=4.0),

                      include_confusion_matrix=True,
                      document_non_matches=True,
  ```

Issue #222: luna: what still depends on it, and what a disconnect is actually worth

> **2026-08-07 — references corrected.** Three rows and two problems have moved. `luna.gateware.interface.jtag` is down from 18 to **one** import — the deliberate negative control in `scripts/soc_jtag_registers_sim.py` — because `gateware/probes/jtag_registers.py` replaced it (#204). Problems 2 and 4 are **done** (#221, #215). Files mentioning each module today, over `gateware/ scripts/ firmware/ tests/`: `architecture.car` 18, `interface.psram` 10, `luna_soc…spiflash` 4, `interface.i2c` 4, `debug.ila` 1. The remaining substance is problem 1 (the fork pin, #194) and problem 3 (spiflash).

Parking a full inventory so the disconnect is one decision rather than a rediscovery each time it comes up.

## Why now

Retiring `hello_soc.py` and `cpu_area.py` (`fb6f330`) removed the last importers of `luna_soc.gateware.cpu.VexRiscv` and of `LunaECP5DomainGenerator` from anything the SoC builds. What is left is smaller and can be characterised exactly.

## What still depends on luna, by module

| upstream module | imports | where |
|---|---|---|
| `luna.gateware.interface.jtag` | 18 | probes, `bist.py` — `JTAGRegisterInterface` |
| `luna.gateware.architecture.car` | 18 | probes — `LunaECP5DomainGenerator` |
| `luna.gateware.interface.psram` | 9 | probes + the SoC — `HyperRAMPHY`, `HyperRAMInterface` |
| `luna_soc.gateware.core.spiflash.*` | 8 | the SoC — `peripherals/flash.py`, `flash_cdc.py` |
| `luna.gateware.interface.i2c` | 5 | probes |
| `luna.gateware.usb.*`, `luna.usb2` | ~20 | probes, LED demos, the SoC's USB console |
| `luna.gateware.debug.ila` | 1 | the SoC |

**The SoC itself** (`gateware/soc/`) imports luna in 8 places and luna_soc in 8. Everything else is probes and demos, which are cheaper to convert or retire.

## The four distinct problems

1. **The `awto-luna-soc` fork pin buys nothing** — it is zero commits behind upstream (#194).
2. **`board/` inherits `LUNAApolloPlatform` → `LUNAPlatform`**, which is what actually pins the fork, not any code we call (#221). The pin map itself is already vendored.
3. **`luna_soc.gateware.core.spiflash.*` is live and load-bearing** — the SPI flash controller, PHY, mmap and port. This is the one that needs real work: 8 imports across `peripherals/flash.py` and `flash_cdc.py`, and three of our own peripherals exist precisely because upstream's had defects (a hold expressed as a ready).
4. **`HyperRAMPHY` / `HyperRAMInterface`** — the DQS controller is already vendored (`peripherals/hyperram_dqs_controller.py`) so tCSHI and the latency branch could be fixed. The **non-DQS** path still uses upstream's and carries both defects (#215).

## What a disconnect is worth

Not independence for its own sake. Concretely: it removes the fork pin, it lets the three defect-driven replacements stop being described as divergence, and it makes `upstream-boundary.md` a shorter document. Against that, `luna.gateware.usb.*` is a large, working USB stack that we have no reason to reimplement — a full disconnect is probably not the goal, and the useful target is narrower.

**Suggested order, cheapest first:** (2) unhook the platform base classes, (1) drop the fork pin, (4) vendor the non-DQS controller alongside the DQS one, (3) decide whether the spiflash core is worth vendoring or whether the defects are worth upstreaming instead.

Related: #194, #215, #221, and `docs/upstream-boundary.md` for the policy on what we reserve.

# Spec 1000: AST-aware recursive chunking with relationship metadata

**Status:** draft stub.
**Origin:** Graph-substrate research ingest (docs/notes/2026-06-08-graph-substrate-research.md, candidate C7, axis GraphRAG & graph-as-retrieval).

## Context

`TokenChunker::chunk_source_with_symbols` in `crates/banso-context/src/chunking.rs` uses an all-or-nothing symbol-span strategy: each valid `SymbolSpan` is emitted as exactly one intact `SourceChunk` "even when the symbol body is larger than `target`" (line 150-151), and adjacent small symbols are never merged — the loop just walks spans and fills non-symbol gaps with the legacy token chunker. The resulting `SourceChunk` tracks only `content`, `start_line`, `end_line`, and `symbol_name: Option<String>`, so there is no scope hierarchy, imports, or signature attached even though `crates/banso-graph/src/builder/source_parser.rs` already computes `SourceSymbol.signature: Option<String>` and `line_end` via `detect_end_line`. This yields oversized chunks for large functions and semantically thin chunks for tiny siblings, degrading the embeddings being wired up in spec 988's retrieval path. The fix is size-aware recursive split-and-merge over AST nodes (cAST) plus enriching `SourceChunk` with scope/imports/signature metadata sourced from the existing `SourceSymbol` records (code-chunk, AstraAI); the AST-derived-KG work validates symbol-boundary chunking as the prerequisite quality step before real embeddings land.

Source techniques: cAST: Structure-Aware Code Chunking via Abstract Syntax Trees — https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15655 ; code-chunk: AST-Aware Chunking with Contextualized Text — https://github.com/supermemoryai/code-chunk ; AST-Derived Knowledge Graphs for Code RAG — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.08773 ; AstraAI: AST-Guided Retrieval for HPC Codebases — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.27423
Research: docs/notes/2026-06-08-graph-substrate-research.md

## Scope

- Add size-aware recursive split of oversized symbol spans in `TokenChunker::chunk_source_with_symbols` so a span exceeding `target` is subdivided rather than emitted whole.
- Add merge of contiguous small sibling spans up to `target` so tiny adjacent symbols are not emitted as semantically thin chunks.
- Extend `SourceChunk` in `crates/banso-context/src/chunking.rs` with scope-hierarchy, imports, and signature metadata fields.
- Propagate the `signature` (and end-line) already produced by `SourceSymbol` in `crates/banso-graph/src/builder/source_parser.rs` into the enriched `SourceChunk` rather than recomputing it.

## Non-Goals

- Choosing the concrete recursive split/merge algorithm parameters or token-budget tuning (plan phase).
- Replacing the regex-based `parse_source_symbols` in `crates/banso-graph/src/builder/source_parser.rs` with a full tree-sitter AST walk.
- Wiring embeddings or retrieval ranking (owned by spec 988).

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC-1** — A symbol span whose body exceeds `TokenChunker.target` is emitted as more than one `SourceChunk`, each within the target budget, instead of a single oversized chunk.
- [ ] **AC-2** — Contiguous symbol spans each well under `target` are merged into a combined `SourceChunk` up to the target budget, reducing chunk count versus per-symbol emission.
- [ ] **AC-3** — `SourceChunk` exposes scope-hierarchy, imports, and signature metadata, and a chunk derived from a symbol with a known `signature` carries that signature populated from `SourceSymbol`.
- [ ] **AC-4** — Files with no symbol spans retain the existing legacy token-chunking fallback (no regression in `chunk_source_with_symbols` output for unsupported inputs).

## Dependencies

- **Blocks:** none yet
- **Blocked by:** none yet (extends 988)

## References

- crates/banso-context/src/chunking.rs (TokenChunker.chunk_source_with_symbols, SourceChunk, SymbolSpan)
- crates/banso-graph/src/builder/source_parser.rs (parse_source_symbols, SourceSymbol)

- https://github.com/supermemoryai/code-chunk
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.08773
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.27423

# Move a table to another database within the same workspace

## Summary

Allow a user to move an existing table from one database (application) to another
database **in the same workspace**, without duplicating it. Today a table's parent
database is fixed at creation; the only workarounds are duplicate-then-delete or a
full CSV/export round-trip, both of which mint new ids and break every reference
into the table.

Scope is deliberately narrow: **same workspace only.** Cross-workspace moves are
explicitly out of scope (see "Non-goals") because they invalidate a much larger set
of workspace-scoped invariants.

## Motivation

Users reorganise their data over time — a table created in the wrong database, or a
database that has grown and should be split. There is currently no first-class way
to relocate a table while preserving its id, its rows, its views, and the references
other objects (builder data sources, automations, dashboards, API tokens) already
hold against its table id.

## The good news: it's a metadata reparent, not a data migration

The heavy lifting people assume this needs (copy rows, rename tables, rebuild
indexes) is **not** required for a same-workspace move:

- The physical Postgres table is named `database_table_<table_id>`
  (`table/models.py:937`, prefix in `table/constants.py:2`) — it encodes the **table
  id only**, never the database id. No `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME`, no data copy.
- Link-row junction tables are named `database_relation_<link_row_relation_id>`
  (`fields/models.py:532`) from a **global** sequence
  (`database_linkrowfield_link_row_relation_id_seq`, `fields/fields.py:266`) with
  `db_constraint=False` (`fields/field_types.py:3108`) — globally unique, not scoped
  to any database, and resilient to the row tables being reparented.
- `table.database.workspace` is unchanged, so user files, `TokenPermission`s scoped
  to the *table*, table-scoped RBAC assignments, and every table/field-id reference
  travel with the table untouched.

The precedent to mirror is **`FieldHandler.move_field_between_tables`**
(`fields/handler.py:1384-1411`) — the existing "an object literally jumps parents"
primitive: reassign the FK, `save()`, invalidate the source & destination model
caches, fix ordering, fire signals. Its docstring already warns that "field
instances can literally jump tables, and any other systems working with fields need
to handle this fact" — the same warning applies here, one level up.

The core operation is roughly:

```python
old_database_id = table.database_id
table.database = destination_database
table.order = Table.get_last_order(destination_database)
table.save()
invalidate_table_in_model_cache(table.id)  # both DB contexts
# re-evaluate cross-database references, fire signals for BOTH databases
```

Everything below is about the "re-evaluate cross-database references" step, which is
where the real work is.

---

  (`table/models.py:929`), `get_database_table_name` (`:937`).
- **Ordering** is per-database (`Table.get_last_order` filters by database). Append to
  the destination's end (like `create_table`/`duplicate_table` do); the vacated slot
  in the source just leaves a harmless gap. Optionally accept a target position.
- **Model cache** must be invalidated for the source (so it stops listing the table)
  and the destination — reuse `invalidate_table_in_model_cache`.
- **Undoable action** `MoveTableActionType` in `table/actions.py`. Subtlety: a move
  spans **two** databases, so the action scope must cover both source and destination
  (or be workspace-scoped) for undo/redo to surface in both sidebars. Existing table
  actions scope on a single `ApplicationActionScopeType.value(database_id)`
  (`table/actions.py`), which is insufficient here. Undo must restore both the
  original `database_id` and `order`.
- **Permissions on both sides.** Require the actor to hold update/delete on the source
  table **and** create/update on the destination database — mirror how
  create/duplicate-table is checked. Add a `MoveTableToDatabaseOperationType` in
  `table/operations.py` and register it in the permission managers. Do **not** rely on
  source-side permission alone.
- **API**: new endpoint (e.g. `POST /database/tables/<table_id>/move/` taking
  `new_database_id` + optional position) rather than overloading
  `TableUpdateSerializer`, which currently only accepts `name`
  (`api/tables/views.py`, `serializers.py`, `urls.py`). Consider making it async

- Every **future edit** of either side now raises `LinkRowTableNotInSameDatabase`.

Issue #47: Add a path mode to syn links

## What's wrong
`syn links` answers one question: what surrounds this memory. `graph_subgraph` walks BFS from a single id, bounded by `MAX_GRAPH_DEPTH` and the node/edge budgets. There is no way to ask how one memory reaches another, so a chain of supersessions or a contradiction two hops away is only findable by walking the neighbourhood by hand and joining the hops yourself.

## Why it's wrong
The relations synapse models are the ones where the path is the answer. `supersession` is transitive and already has `superseders_of` and `effective_pinned` reading it as a chain; a `contradiction` reached through a superseder tells the reader that the memory in front of them inherits a dispute. BFS from one endpoint shows neither, because it reports a neighbourhood rather than a route.

## How to fix it

After the edge count leaves single figures. A shortest path over a sparse graph mostly reports that no path exists, so this waits on the same signal as the graph recall leg — and is worth less than that leg, so it should not go first.

Graphify (Graphify-Labs/graphify) pairs a BFS query mode with `path A B` and a per-answer token budget, for the same reason: the neighbourhood question and the route question need different walks.

Issue #381: Any belt cycle anywhere zeroes ALL sink deliveries, even for disjoint working arms

## Symptom

`calc_throughput` returns zero deliveries for the **entire world** when any belt cycle exists anywhere on the grid — including cycles completely disjoint from every source→sink path. Found while diffing checkpoint rollouts (the owner spotted two SPLITTER_MERGE_SIDELOADED scores that looked wrong).

## Minimal repro

7×7 world: `source →(E) 3 belts → sink` on row 0, plus a disjoint 2×2 belt loop at (1,3)-(2,4):

```
S> b> b> b> K> .. ..
.. .. .. .. .. .. ..
.. .. .. .. .. .. ..
.. b> bv .. .. .. ..
.. b^ b< .. .. .. ..
.. .. .. .. .. .. ..
.. .. .. .. .. .. ..
```

`py_sink_deliveries`: **with loop `[]`; without loop `[(4, 0, 'iron_plate', 15.0)]`.**

Real-world instances (deterministic): greedy rollouts of the SFT base `h76h80yb` on `SPLITTER_MERGE_SIDELOADED` size 11, seeds **9009** and **9011** — both contain an accidental belt loop plus a disjoint working source→splitter→sink arm; both score 0.00. Deleting the loop tiles yields 7.5 items/s on the untouched arm.

## Cause

`throughput.rs:70-81`: step 1 of the flow computation is "Detect cycles → return no deliveries if any exist" — a global bail-out before Kahn's algorithm runs.

## Why it matters for training

- The terminal reward is throughput-based. Any episode where the policy incidentally places a loop among its junk gets reward 0 **regardless of a working factory elsewhere**. Trial episodes place 40–60 junk entities; incidental loops are plausible at a meaningful rate, silently zeroing exactly the episodes that matter most (partial successes).
- Same discontinuity hits greedy eval: 2 of 12 sampled SPLITTER_MERGE_SIDELOADED seeds of the SFT base score 0.00 for this reason at size 11.
- It also makes the reward landscape locally deceptive: adding one belt that closes a loop drops reward from positive to 0.

## Proposed fix

Remove the global bail. Kahn's algorithm already handles cycles gracefully: nodes on a cycle (and nodes only reachable through one) never reach in-degree 0, are never processed, and contribute zero flow — while the rest of the graph computes normally. Cycle nodes should count toward `unreachable` (orphans) rather than poisoning the world. The existing `has_cycle` DFS can stay for tests, or be dropped.

Small diff in `factorion_rs/src/throughput.rs` + a regression test mirroring the repro above. Not started — awaiting go-ahead (experiment hold is in effect).

Found via `scratchpad/diff_checkpoints.py` (checkpoint-diff tool, see #371).

Issue #264: Soak policy semantics: recompute-always, policy-at-decision-time, 1d emergency floor

Design decisions for how soak interacts with time, policy change, and emergencies (maintainer-driven, 2026-08-23). Nomenclature context: candidate selection is *backtracking version resolution* (pip's term; PubGrub is the CDCL-strengthened form) under *lexicographic optimization criteria* (CUDF/opam `-removed,-changed,-notuptodate`; the Mancoosi competition's "paranoid" vs "trendy" tracks are precisely our minimal-sufficient vs maximally-recent policies). Hard constraints: `in-patched-range ∧ reachable ∧ non-yanked ∧ soaked`; policy is only the tiebreak among survivors (#255 item 1 implements the constraint checks).

## 1. Soak-held findings are recomputed, never filed as dates
Soak status is a pure function of `(publish_date, current_policy, today)` — no stored verdicts, no dated TODOs to rot. The weekly explore run recomputes every candidate and prints held fixes as "fix exists, soaks in Nd (actionable ~DATE under current policy)" — informational, fresh each run. **Stateless newly-soaked flag**: `age ∈ [soak, soak + cadence)` marks candidates that crossed the threshold since the previous run, with zero stored state. Max notice latency = one cadence (weekly), or dispatch manually.

## 2. Policy change: current-policy-always
Because nothing stores soak verdicts, a threshold change automatically re-evaluates everything next run. Tightening (7→14) applies immediately to all candidates — the `max(old,new)` instinct satisfied for free. Loosening (7→3) also applies — deliberately: pinning `max()` forever would make policy irreversible. The safety property lives in **soak policy changes only by reviewed PR** (the policy value is code), not in remembering superseded values.

## 3. Emergency waiver — narrow, recorded, floored
Only for a fix to a **reachable AND actively-exploited HIGH/CRIT** on a current pin:
- **`MIN_SOAK = 1 day`, never waivable** — the floor IS the fresh-malicious-release defense; no emergency justifies ingesting a version published hours ago.
- Explicit freeze flag naming the advisory + required justification (exploitation evidence, reachability); recorded in the freeze report and the resulting ack. Per-instance, never a default, never reusable — same shape as `--allow-added-advisories`: using the escape hatch IS the record.
- Everything else about the pipeline still applies: patched-range, non-yanked, 3-axis evaluation, human sign-off.

Issue #22: RFC: cache invalidation contract for compiler-emitted artifacts

## Problem

`xark build` emits `circuit.json`, `r1cs.json`, and optionally `profile.json` as rustc side effects. Cargo fingerprints the Rust build, not the extraction inputs, so it can cache-hit when:

- the installed xark compiler changed;
- `--field`, profile mode, or the output directory changed;
- a required side-effect artifact was deleted.

There are also two independent correctness bugs in the current success path:

1. a failed Cargo invocation can be reported as success when an old `circuit.json` remains;
2. `r1cs.json` is not required, while an intentionally absent large-circuit `graph.dot` can trigger pointless rebuilds.

PR #12 proves these failures and replaces source-mtime mutation with an exact extraction stamp plus package-scoped `cargo clean -p`.

## What is already decided

These changes do not need an architecture decision and should be safe to land separately:

- check `cargo_status.success()` before accepting any existing artifact;
- require `circuit.json` and `r1cs.json` (plus `profile.json` in profile mode);
- treat `graph.dot` as optional;
- never touch user source mtimes;
- cover failed compilation and missing-artifact regeneration with a real nested-Cargo test.

## Decision required

How should Xark make extraction inputs participate in Cargo invalidation?

### A. Package-scoped clean, as in #12

Hash the compiler binary plus field/profile/output/schema into a stamp. On mismatch or a missing required artifact, run `cargo clean --package <circuit-package>` in Xark's isolated target and rebuild.

Advantages: simple, tested, does not invalidate dependencies, and works with the current `RUSTC=xark cargo build` flow.

Costs: deleting the primary package's cached outputs is an external cache policy; alternating output directories or modes causes repeated package rebuilds, and workspace/multi-target behavior becomes part of Xark's contract.

### B. Put the extraction key in the final crate's Cargo fingerprint

Use a final-package-only compiler input, for example through a carefully selected `cargo rustc` invocation, so Cargo rebuilds the circuit crate when the extraction key changes without an explicit clean.

Advantages: invalidation is expressed as a build input rather than deletion.

Costs: `cargo rustc` forwards arguments only to the selected final target and requires target disambiguation when a package has multiple targets. Xark would need a precise package/target selection contract and evidence that dependencies remain cached.

Cargo reference: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-rustc.html

### C. Decouple extraction from Cargo compilation

Compile normally, then run extraction as a separate explicitly keyed phase over an artifact Cargo already produced.

Advantages: clean ownership of side effects and cache keys.

Costs: this is a larger compiler-driver change and may not be justified for the current toolchain.

## Proposed sequencing

1. Split or narrow #12 so the Cargo-status and artifact-completeness correctness fixes can land without waiting.
2. Choose A, B, or C here.
3. Add the extraction stamp/invalidation mechanism with tests for compiler change, field/profile/output change, deleted `r1cs.json`, unchanged cache hits, workspace packages, and packages with multiple targets.

## Acceptance gates

Whichever mechanism is chosen must satisfy:

1. Broken Rust always exits non-zero even if old artifacts exist.
2. A missing required artifact is regenerated without mutating source files.
3. Changing the xark executable, field, profile mode, or output directory regenerates artifacts.
4. An identical build remains a Cargo cache hit.
5. Dependency crates are not rebuilt solely because extraction inputs changed.
6. Large circuits without `graph.dot` do not rebuild forever.
7. Workspace/package/target selection behavior is explicit and tested.
8. Stamp publication happens only after a successful build with a complete artifact set.

This RFC is only about the invalidation mechanism. It does not question the underlying stale-artifact bug.

Issue #18: Dedupe dependency fetches and edges: shared imports are read once per importer, and repeated imports produce parallel edges

Two related deduplication gaps in the crawl logic in `src/Main.elm`:

## Shared dependencies are fetched once per importer

When two crawled modules both import a not-yet-crawled module (without `--include-external`), `filesToFetch` is only filtered against the graph — not against `pending` — so the file is added to `pending` and read once per importer.

Correctness currently survives this, but only by accident of two behaviors:

- `List.filter ((/=) file.name) pending` removes *all* copies when the first response arrives, and
- the late duplicate response is dropped because the `Ready` state subscribes to `Sub.none`.

So completion detection works, but it's fragile and does wasted I/O. Filtering `filesToFetch` against `pending` (or tracking a visited set) would make it principled:

```elm
|> List.filter (\f -> not (List.member f state.pending))
```

## Repeated imports produce parallel edges

`dependencies` from `parseModules` isn't deduplicated, so a file importing the same module twice yields duplicate entries, which render as parallel edges in the DOT output (and trigger a redundant fetch). Deduplicating the list in `parseModules` fixes both.

Issue #132: Android: sync-adapter deletes/updates (#59) never propagate to the server — Google resurrects "deleted" events, one duplicate per cycle

## Summary

`device_calendar_plus_android` 0.7.1 performs `deleteEvent`, `deleteRecurring`, and the recurring-update paths with `CALLER_IS_SYNCADAPTER=true` plus the calendar's **real** Google account (introduced in #59, android 0.4.0). On a Google-synced calendar this makes the plugin impersonate Google's own sync adapter. `CalendarProvider2.deleteEventInternal` then takes the sync-adapter branch: it hard-deletes the local row with no `DELETED`/`DIRTY` marker and notifies with `syncToNetwork=false`. The server is never told, so:

- The next account sync re-downloads the "deleted" event under a fresh local id.
- Because creates are plain inserts (which *do* upload), every delete → recreate → sync cycle nets **one extra copy** of the event, including for brand-new events created after the "fix" in #59.
- On a real device this makes any bulk "delete and re-mirror" flow effectively un-clearable: every deletion appears to succeed locally, then the copy comes back, and the following sync adds another.

Verified against AOSP `CalendarProvider2.deleteEventInternal` and the [Calendar Provider sync adapter guide](https://developer.android.com/guide/topics/providers/calendar-provider#sync-adapter) — the non-sync-adapter branch is documented as the one that sets `DELETED=1, DIRTY=1` specifically "so that the sync adapter has a chance to tell the server about the deletion."

## Why #59 was the wrong fix for a real symptom

#59's stated motivation was correct as an observation, wrong as a diagnosis: after an app-level delete, the `DELETED=1` tombstone still showed up in `EventsService`'s own reads, because neither `getEvent` (non-recurring path) nor `readEventRow` filters `AND DELETED = 0`. That's a missing reader-side filter, not a provider bug — the docs put that burden on the reader. The `Instances` reads used by `listEvents` were already correct (the provider removes instances at soft-delete time), so the symptom was scoped to those two direct `Events` table reads.

Using `CALLER_IS_SYNCADAPTER` for the *update* paths (`updateEventAsSyncAdapter`) doesn't have even that motivation — the comment there claims `CalendarProvider2` "silently strips protected columns like RRULE from non-sync-adapter updates." That's not correct: `scrubEventData` runs only for sync-adapter callers and never touches `RRULE`; restricted columns (`verifyNoSyncColumns`) throw rather than get stripped, and `RRULE` isn't in that restricted set. The plain update path is the one that sets `DIRTY=1` + `MUTATORS`, requests an upload sync, and recomputes the `Instances` expansion — so the sync-adapter updates have the same non-propagation defect as the deletes, applied to recurring-series edits.

## Repro

1. Create an event on a calendar backed by a real Google account (not a local-only calendar).
2. `deleteEvent`/`deleteRecurring` it.
3. Trigger (or wait for) an account sync.
4. The event reappears under a new event id. Re-deleting and re-syncing adds a second copy, and so on — the duplication is cumulative, not a one-time glitch.

This reproduced on a real device (not the emulator) across multiple sync cycles, both for legacy events created before the app-side workaround and for **new events created and deleted after** the workaround — confirming the defect is in this plugin layer, not in the caller's engine logic.

## Suggested fix

Revert #59: use plain (non-sync-adapter) `Events.CONTENT_URI` operations for `deleteEventMaster`/`deleteEventInstance`/the update paths, and instead fix the actual symptom #59 was chasing by adding `AND DELETED = 0` to the two direct `Events`-table reads in `getEvent` and `readEventRow`. That combination:

- Lets deletes and RRULE-updates propagate to the server normally (no resurrection, no duplication).
- Still keeps soft-deleted rows out of `EventsService`'s own reads, which was the original bug #59 was fixing.

The one legitimate use of `CALLER_IS_SYNCADAPTER` we found is `CalendarService`'s use of it to create `ACCOUNT_TYPE_LOCAL` calendars — that's unaffected by this change.

We've patched exactly this in a local fork (plain delete/insert/update operations + the `DELETED = 0` filter on those two reads) and verified deletes now reach the server and stop resurrecting on a real device. Happy to share the diff or open a PR if that's useful, given this repo's contribution process.

## Environment

- `device_calendar_plus_android` 0.7.1
- Android API 24+ (target/compile 35)
- Google-synced calendar account (not `ACCOUNT_TYPE_LOCAL`)

Issue #2232: getComputedStyle infinite-loops on cyclic custom property (var()) references

Note: I used Claude to help file this issue, but I've reviewed and agree with the findings.

**Describe the bug**

When two custom properties reference each other (`--a: var(--b)` / `--b: var(--a)`), calling `window.getComputedStyle(element)` — or reading any property value off the returned declaration — hangs forever. In a real browser, cyclic `var()` references resolve to the property's "guaranteed-invalid value" (effectively falling back to initial/inherited value) rather than looping infinitely.

This was found while migrating a test suite from jsdom to happy-dom: a test asserting graceful handling of cyclic `var()` references (which passed under jsdom, since jsdom returns the raw stored value without attempting resolution) hung indefinitely under happy-dom.

**To Reproduce**

```js
import { Window } from "happy-dom"

const window = new Window()
const { document } = window
document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--a", "var(--b)")
document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--b", "var(--a)")

// hangs forever
const styles = window.getComputedStyle(document.documentElement)
console.log(styles.getPropertyValue("--a"))
```

Root cause looks to be in `CSSStyleDeclarationComputedStyle.parseCSSVariablesInValue`:

```js
parseCSSVariablesInValue(value, cssVariables) {
    let newValue = value;
    let match;
    while ((match = newValue.match(SINGLE_CSS_VARIABLE_REGEXP)) != null) {
        newValue = newValue.replace(match[0], cssVariables[match[1]] || '');
    }
    ...
}
```

When `cssVariables["--a"]` is `"var(--b)"` and `cssVariables["--b"]` is `"var(--a)"`, the `while` loop alternates between `"var(--a)"` and `"var(--b)"` forever — there's no cycle/visited-set guard or iteration cap.

**Expected behavior**

`getComputedStyle` should not hang. Ideally it would detect the cycle and treat the value as invalid (per spec), but at minimum it should cap substitution iterations so a cyclic reference fails fast instead of hanging the process.

**Environment**

Issue #54: Scheduled dependency upgrades never update transitive dependencies

The generated `upgrade` task runs `pnpm update` against an **explicit list of direct dependencies**:

```
pnpm update @action-validator/cli @action-validator/core ... typescript --config.minimum-release-age=5760
```

Named-package `pnpm update` only re-resolves the packages you name. A transitive-only package therefore stays pinned in `pnpm-lock.yaml` indefinitely, even when a newer version satisfies its parent's range — it moves only when some direct parent's own range changes.

## Evidence

Reproduced against this repo at `b1e98a1` (immediately before #48), where the lockfile carried `js-yaml@3.15.0` and `js-yaml@4.3.0`, both flagged high by [GHSA-5p4m-2wfm-xmqj](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5p4m-2wfm-xmqj).

| run | js-yaml after | `pnpm audit --audit-level high` |
|---|---|---|
| the upgrade task's exact command (named direct deps) | `3.15.0`, `4.3.0` — unchanged | 2 high |
| bare `pnpm update --config.minimum-release-age=5760` | `3.15.1`, `4.3.1` | **No known vulnerabilities found** |

The patched versions had been published 2026-07-31, 18 days old and well clear of the 4-day cooldown, and both satisfied their parents' existing ranges (`@istanbuljs/load-nyc-config` needs `js-yaml ^3.13.1`; `@eslint/eslintrc` needs `^4.1.0`). Three consecutive weekly upgrade runs (8/3, 8/10, 8/17) succeeded without moving them. It took the hand-written #48 to fix.

## Why it matters

`auditDeps` runs `pnpm audit --audit-level high` on every build. When a transitive advisory lands, the audit gate turns builds red — blocking provider-version PRs from auto-merging and blocking releases — for something the upgrade workflow structurally cannot fix. Every occurrence needs a manual PR, per repo, across the fleet.

Dependabot is only a partial net here. `.github/dependabot.yml` is deliberately `versioning-strategy: lockfile-only` with `open-pull-requests-limit: 0`, so it covers **security** updates only, not ordinary transitive drift. In the js-yaml case it never raised an alert — though the vulnerable versions were only on `main` for ~13 hours after the advisory published (2026-08-06 20:27Z → #48 merged 2026-08-07 09:27Z), so that is plausibly just timing rather than a broken integration. `dependabot_security_updates` is enabled and the dependency graph does see all 703 packages including transitive ones.

## Possible direction (not yet validated)

Adding a bare `pnpm update` fixes the resolution, but it also rewrites direct-dependency ranges in `package.json` — `^22` becomes `^22.20.1`, `^29` becomes `^29.5.14`. The task's trailing `pnpm exec projen` reverts most of that (15 changed lines down to 5), but not all: `@types/jest` and `jest` stayed narrowed in my test. So this needs more thought than dropping the flag in.

Other angles worth weighing: `pnpm audit --fix` (writes `pnpm.overrides` entries), or `pnpm dedupe`. Whatever is chosen has to keep honouring `--config.minimum-release-age`, and must not fight projen's own `package.json` regeneration.
