Issue #330: JS/TS: top-level bootstrap code (IIFE, callbacks, bare calls, initialisers) loses its call-graph edges in any multi-unit file

## Summary

In a JS/TS file that contains at least one real function or class, code at **module top level** —
IIFEs, callbacks passed to top-level calls, bare driver calls, and initialiser calls — belongs to no
extracted unit. The call graph only scans emitted units' code, so calls made by that code, including
calls to sinks, do not become edges — as the executed run below shows.

A sink reachable through top-level bootstrap code alone therefore gets no incoming edge from it, as
the `x.js` run below shows. This is the false-negative direction.

## Reproduced at `b501962`, with a control

`x.js` — the sink is a defined function so edges to it are recordable, and the file has real functions
so the empty-file fallback (below) is suppressed:

```javascript
function sink() { return 1; }
function realFn() { sink(); }              // CONTROL
(function boot() { sink(); })();           // IIFE
[1].forEach(function () { sink(); });      // callback
main();                                    // bare driver call
function main() { return 2; }
const initv = sink();                      // initialiser
```

Run through the real `TypeScriptAnalyzer` + `DependencyResolver`:

```
UNITS: ['x.js:sink', 'x.js:realFn', 'x.js:main']
CALL GRAPH:
    x.js:realFn -> ["x.js:sink"]
edges to sink: [["x.js:realFn",["x.js:sink"]]]
```

The control edge `realFn -> sink` is present, so edges to defined sinks are recordable and a null
result is not a broken harness. The IIFE, the callback, the bare `main()` and the initialiser contribute
nothing to the graph above — the only edge printed is the control's — and `boot` is absent from the
UNITS list.

## Root cause — three parts

**1. Only named module-level `FunctionDeclaration`s become units.**
`libs/openant-core/parsers/javascript/typescript_analyzer.js:285-303`:

```
285|    const STOP = new Set([
286|      ts.SyntaxKind.FunctionDeclaration,
287|      ts.SyntaxKind.FunctionExpression,
...
301|    return sourceFile
302|      .getDescendantsOfKind(ts.SyntaxKind.FunctionDeclaration)
303|      .filter((fn) => fn.getName() && isModuleLevel(fn));
```

Function *expressions* at statement level — which is what an IIFE and a callback are — are excluded
by this filter, which collects `FunctionDeclaration` kinds only. That is reasonable for naming; the consequence below is the problem.

**2. The only capture for unattributed top-level code is a fallback that fires on empty files.**
`libs/openant-core/parsers/javascript/typescript_analyzer.js:1041`:

```
1041|  _extractTopLevelSideEffects(sourceFile, relativePath) {
1042|    // Only synthesise when the regular extractors produced nothing for this
1043|    // file — otherwise we'd duplicate real functions/methods.
1044|    const filePrefix = `${relativePath}:`;
1045|    const hasAny = Object.keys(this.functions).some((id) =>
1046|      id.startsWith(filePrefix),
1047|    );
1048|    if (hasAny) return;
```

In any file with at least one unit, `hasAny` is true and the function returns immediately.

**3. The call graph scans only emitted units' code.**
`libs/openant-core/parsers/javascript/dependency_resolver.js:69-71`:

```
69|  buildCallGraph() {
70|    for (const [funcId, funcData] of Object.entries(this.functions)) {
71|      const calls = this._extractCalls(funcData.code, funcId);
```

A top-level statement belonging to no unit is not reached by this loop, so it is not passed to
`_extractCalls`.

Net: there is no general module-scope unit, so top-level outgoing edges are lost whenever the file has
at least one real unit.

## The fix must exclude by line range, not by statement containment

This is the part worth specifying carefully, because the obvious formulation fabricates edges.

A general module-scope unit has to exclude text already covered by emitted units. If exclusion is done
by *whole-statement containment* — drop any top-level statement that contains an emitted unit — then
class members and object-literal methods leak in, because those units live **inside** a top-level
statement (a class declaration, a `const` object literal). Their bodies then land in the synthetic
module unit and their calls are attributed to module load, which is not when they run.

Measured on `b.js`:

```javascript
class K {
  constructor() { this.v = 1; }
  method() { classOnlyHelper(); }
}
const handlers = {
  handle() { objLitHelper(); }
};
function classOnlyHelper() { return 1; }
function objLitHelper() { return 2; }
bootstrapCall();
function bootstrapCall() { return 3; }
```

`bootstrapCall()` is the only call that actually runs at module load. A containment-based exclusion
yields `b.js:module -> [classOnlyHelper, handlers.handle, objLitHelper]` — three calls that never run
at module load, and it drops the one that does.

**The repository already solved this, and wrote down why.**

# 2525minishop Growth & Cashflow Improvement Program

## Context from the business chat

2525minishop operates in Asahi, Chiba. Recent sales have fallen; the discussion raised a hypothesis that changes in the environment for Thai, Vietnamese and Chinese residents in Japan may have reduced demand, but this must be tested against seasonality, assortment, price, stock availability, competition and store traffic before treating it as a cause.

Current operating facts to carry into the work:
- Loyverse POS is the current sales system; a daily report and an off-platform backup are desired.
- The store has around 28 categories and closes around 20:00, sometimes earlier.
- The current tax setup has 8% consumption tax included, with at least one non-tax item.
- Consignment goods can inflate reported revenue; consignment sales, cash received, owned margin and tax treatment must be separated.
- The goal is not only more revenue: it is more owned gross margin, faster cash conversion, lower dead stock and more repeat customers.
- This repository is the Tanjai POS/ERP platform and can become the implementation surface for the operating and digital-channel work.

## Program objectives

1. Establish a trusted baseline for sales, margin, inventory, consignment and cash.
2. Find the highest-probability causes of the decline and test them cheaply.
3. Add sales channels that serve local Japanese customers, existing Thai/Vietnamese/Chinese communities and suitable Thailand-facing pre-order demand.
4. Improve cash conversion without discounting below a verified contribution margin.
5. Turn successful experiments into reliable POS/ERP workflows and recurring reporting.

## Phase roadmap

- **P0 — Diagnose and control (7–14 days):** data baseline, KPI definitions, customer/demand diagnosis, inventory/consignment/cash controls and multi-agent operating rules.
- **P1 — Quick wins and pilot channels (0–30 days):** assortment and promotion tests, multilingual/local acquisition, low-risk order capture and repeat-purchase actions.
- **P2 — Build the operating system (1–3 months):** POS/ERP data integration, CRM/loyalty with consent, B2B/community sales and fulfillment economics.
- **P3 — Scale what works (3–12 months):** forecasting, replenishment, marketplace/subscription decisions and continuous growth governance.

## Multi-agent delivery contract

Every agent must:
- Read this Epic and its assigned child Issue before acting.
- Work only inside the child Issue scope and name any out-of-scope discovery.
- Distinguish measured facts, assumptions and hypotheses; cite the source or export used.
- Keep consignment revenue/margin separate from owned goods.
- Avoid collecting unnecessary personal data and never commit secrets, passwords or payment credentials.
- Never enable live payment, external messaging or production writes without an explicit owner-approved gate.
- Return a concise handoff: files/PRs, evidence, tests or calculations, unresolved gaps, and the next dependency.
- Comment status as `ready`, `blocked` or `done`; link follow-up Issues instead of silently expanding scope.

## Program Definition of Done

- Baseline and KPI dictionary are reproducible.
- At least two revenue experiments have measured results and unit economics.
- At least one new channel reaches a controlled pilot with attribution.
- Inventory and consignment reporting no longer confuses gross sales with owned profit.
- POS/ERP changes pass tests, preserve auditability and have a rollback path.
- A weekly review can answer: what sold, what earned margin, what converted to cash, what is stuck, and which experiment should continue.

Issue #46: Proposal: reusable declarative skill groups


## Problem

Skiletto can install several skills from one source with `--all` or repeated `--skill`, and its manifest and lockfile reproduce the resulting environment. It cannot currently give a reusable name to a set of skills drawn from multiple sources and apply that set to a project or machine scope.

This would support configurations such as:

- `baseline`: general skills used everywhere
- `code-quality`: includes `baseline` plus review and testing skills
- `frontend`: includes `code-quality` plus framework-specific skills

A user could then apply `frontend` to a repository or install it globally in one operation.

## Proposed capability

Add declarative, named skill groups with these properties:

- A group can contain skills from multiple repositories.
- A group can include other groups.
- The same group can be applied at project or machine scope.
- Recursive inclusion detects cycles.
- Duplicate members are deduplicated deterministically.
- Conflicting definitions fail with an actionable error rather than silently choosing one.
- Every resolved member continues through Skiletto’s existing manifest, lockfile, content-hash, drift, hook, and harness behavior.
- Group definitions contain data only. They cannot introduce executable hooks.
- Ideally, the selected group remains part of the scope’s desired state so that a later `sync` can reconcile membership changes. A one-time expansion could be a smaller initial version if preferred.

The exact file format and CLI spelling are open for discussion. Possible commands might look like:

```console
skiletto group add code-quality
skiletto group add --global code-quality
skiletto group list
```

A first version could load groups only from local project or machine configuration. Remote catalog discovery and distribution could remain separate.

## Example use case

```toml
# Illustrative only, not a proposed final schema.

[groups.baseline]
skills = ["documentation", "testing"]

[groups.code-quality]
include = ["baseline"]
skills = ["security-review", "code-review"]
```

Each referenced skill would still have an explicit source, path, and optional ref somewhere in the declarative configuration. Applying `code-quality` would resolve all four skills and pin them through the normal lockfile flow.

## Existing functionality checked

I searched the open and closed issues and pull requests for groups, bundles, collections, profiles, packs, and manifests. The existing multi-skill selection work handles several skills within one source, but I did not find a proposal for reusable, composable groups spanning sources and scopes.

## Contribution question

Would this feature fit Skiletto’s direction, and would you be open to reviewing pull requests that add it?

If so, I would be happy to split the work into small reviewable changes, starting with an agreed behavioral contract and schema tests, followed by group expansion, CLI integration, lockfile behavior, and documentation.

A maintainer on the project kunchenguid/firstmate (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #2787: Lock acquisition recurses through .steal suffixes when initial lock creation fails

## Summary

When the lock parent exists but is not writable, `fm_lock_try_acquire` recursively appends `.steal` after the initial lock creation fails. The recursion continues until paths reach `ENAMETOOLONG` and produces a very large stderr stream.

## Reproduction

1. Use the canonical process-event claim root from an execution context that can read it but cannot create the requested lock directory.
2. Run `bin/fm-procevent.sh reconcile`.
3. Observe repeated paths ending in `.lock.steal.steal` and eventually `File name too long`.

In the observed run, stderr exceeded 1 MB. The calculated `.steal` paths were not created on disk. The claim root remained 4 KiB with one valid active claim.

## Cause

`fm_procevent_source_lock_acquire` delegates to `fm_lock_acquire_wait`. After `fm_lock_try_create` fails, the requested lock is still absent. `fm_lock_try_acquire` then treats the absent path as stale and recursively tries a sibling whose name adds `.steal`. Each creation fails for the same reason, so recursion is bounded only by the filesystem path limit.

Unix ownership and modes were valid. The triggering condition was an execution boundary that denied writes to the canonical claim root.

## Expected behavior

Lock acquisition should fail once with a bounded diagnostic when lock creation fails and the lock path is still absent. It must not enter stale-lock recovery because there is no stale lock to recover.

## Suggested fix

Immediately after `fm_lock_try_create` fails, return failure when the lock path is still absent and is not a symlink. Preserve the existing stale-lock recovery only when an actual path exists.

## Regression test

Use an existing non-writable lock parent and assert:

- acquisition fails within a bounded time
- stderr remains bounded
- no `.steal` path is created
- no recursive retry occurs

Issue #8: RFC: Decision authority, mission modes, evidence maturity, and stagnation escalation

## Summary

Explore a protocol-level extension for four orthogonal semantics that are currently implicit in Agent Relay:

1. **decision authority** — who is allowed to decide *what*;
2. **mission mode** — what kind of work a pass is actually performing;
3. **claim/evidence maturity** — how strongly a relied-upon claim is established;
4. **stagnation escalation** — when repeated failure should trigger a role/lens change instead of another same-role retry.

A fifth concept, **planning-context completeness**, is included as an exploratory/non-normative mechanism for deciding how much execution autonomy is safe without rating or profiling the human user.

This RFC is informed by Anthropic's June 16, 2026 research report, ["Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise"](https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-code-expertise), based on a privacy-preserving analysis of ~400,000 Claude Code sessions between October 2025 and April 2026.

The useful lesson is not that Agent Relay should score user expertise or optimize for longer autonomous action chains. The useful lesson is that effective agentic work separates **planning authority**, **execution autonomy**, and **verifiable success**.

Agent Relay already has the primitives needed to make those distinctions explicit: five stable roles, Reviewer lenses, mutation boundaries, immutable snapshots, evidence hierarchy, Verifier checkpoints, finding lifecycle, and Integrator readiness authority.

## Relationship to RFC #6

This RFC is deliberately separate from #6, **Runtime adapters and bounded iterative review loops**.

The intended boundary is:

> **RFC #6 governs control flow. This RFC governs decision semantics.**

RFC #6 asks:

- how repeated passes execute;
- how review cycles are bounded;
- how runtime state, cancellation, budgets, and termination work;
- how external runtimes/adapters may execute Agent Relay passes.

This RFC asks:

- who owns mission, architecture, implementation, verification interpretation, and readiness decisions;
- what category of work is occurring;
- how strong the evidence for a claim actually is;
- when repeated failure requires escalation or replanning.

A runtime or bounded review cycle defined by #6 MAY consume these semantics, but should not define them.

## Prior art / research signal

Anthropic's report describes several observations that map cleanly onto Agent Relay protocol concerns:

### Planning versus execution decisions

The report separates meaningful session decisions into:

- **planning** — what to do, which approach to take, what counts as done;
- **execution** — which files to change, what code to write, which commands to run.

In the observed sessions, users made about 70% of planning decisions while Claude made about 80% of execution decisions.

For Agent Relay, the important implication is:

> **Execution autonomy does not imply planning authority.**

An agent may be allowed to autonomously edit many files, run commands, or operate a deployment while remaining prohibited from changing the mission, architecture, acceptance criteria, or definition of done.

### Nine work modes

Anthropic classifies sessions into nine work modes:

- building;
- fixing;
- testing;
- orchestrating;
- operating software;
- understanding;
- planning;
- analyzing data;
- communicating / document work.

These should not become Agent Relay roles. They describe the **kind of work**, not the responsibility/authority model.

### Verified success

Anthropic distinguishes transcript-judged success from **verified success**. Their strict measure requires judged success plus at least one hard verifiable signal, such as matching Git activity, a passing test suite, or other strong evidence.

Agent Relay already says evidence beats assertions and has an evidence hierarchy. The opportunity is to make the **maturity of a specific relied-upon claim** explicit and portable across passes.

### Recovery from trouble

The report treats errors, failed tests, repeated attempts, and user pushback as failure/trouble signals. Sessions with greater task-specific expertise recover more often from trouble.

Agent Relay should not score or simulate human expertise. It can, however, encode the useful recovery behavior: repeated failed attempts or contradictory evidence should trigger a **protocol escalation**, not indefinite same-role retries.

### Task-specific expertise

Anthropic explicitly treats expertise as task-specific rather than occupational or general ability. Their classifier looks at framing precision, requested verification, and whether the user corrects the agent or vice versa.

Agent Relay should not adopt a `novice/intermediate/expert` user rating. The actionable substitute is to measure whether the **planning context required for safe autonomous execution is complete**.

## Design principle

**Separate responsibility, scrutiny, work type, decision authority, and evidence strength.**

The existing axes remain:

```text
Role
  = who is responsible for the pass

Reviewer lens
  = what a Reviewer scrutinizes
```

This RFC proposes additional orthogonal axes:

```text
Mission mode
  = what kind of work is being performed

Decision authority
  = which decisions this actor/pass may make

Evidence maturity
  = how strongly a relied-upon claim is established

Escalation state
  = whether continuing the same route is still justified
```

None of these should create a sixth role.

Add a protocol concept describing **which classes of decisions are delegated to which actor/role for the current mission**.

Example:

```text
Decision authority:
- Mission / desired outcome: User
- Architecture / acceptance criteria: User + Integrator
- Implementation mechanics: Builder
- Environment procedure: Executor
- Evidence interpretation: Verifier
- Readiness / reconciliation: Integrator
```

Issue #2819: [RFC]: Workload-Aware KV Cache Hints for Mooncake: `session_id` and `priority`

### Changes proposed

## Summary

This RFC proposes a first-stage workload-aware KV Cache interface for Mooncake.

The first stage only introduces two optional external hints:

- `session_id`
- `priority`

The goal is to let upper layers such as SGLang, vLLM, or llm-d pass lightweight workload information to Mooncake without changing the correctness semantics of existing `PUT` / `GET` operations.

If these hints are not provided, Mooncake behavior should remain unchanged.

## Motivation

Agentic and multi-turn workloads often reuse long prefixes across requests. However, the KV Cache objects generated by these workloads are not all equally valuable:

- KV objects belonging to the same session are often related in lifecycle and reuse pattern.
- Some requests are more latency-sensitive or more valuable to retain than others.
- Upper layers already have partial knowledge about session identity and request priority.

Mooncake currently provides object-level KV storage, lookup, transfer, replication, and eviction. To support workload-aware KV Cache management, Mooncake should be able to consume a small amount of external context while still keeping policy decisions inside Mooncake.

This RFC intentionally starts with the smallest useful surface: `session_id` and `priority`.

## Background

Recent SGLang main already exposes both signals:

- `session_id` is available as a top-level request field in SGLang's internal request path and OpenAI-compatible serving path.
- `priority` is available as an integer request field and is already used by SGLang scheduling / radix-cache logic.

SGLang also already has a Mooncake HiCache path that can pass `ReplicateConfig.group_ids`. Those `group_ids` currently represent page-level physical grouping, such as K/V objects, split-head shards, MLA objects, and sidecar objects derived from the same logical HiCache page.

This RFC does not propose replacing that existing `group_ids` behavior.

## Goals

1. Add optional `session_id` and `priority` hints to Mooncake object-level write paths.
2. Preserve existing behavior when the hints are absent.
3. Keep existing `group_ids` semantics unchanged.
4. Allow Mooncake to store session/priority metadata for KV objects.
5. Allow Mooncake to use priority as a coarse retention hint.
6. Provide a foundation for future session-level statistics, lifecycle handling, and eviction policy improvements.

## Non-Goals

This RFC does not propose:

- A new agent hint standard.
- Changes to OpenAI-compatible API standards.
- Changing `GET` semantics.
- Treating `session_id` as a cache key namespace.
- Treating `session_id` as hard pinning.
- Treating `priority` as a lease.
- Replacing existing `group_ids`.
- Adding placement hints such as `preferred_segment`.
- Adding replica hints such as `replica_num`.
- Adding explicit movement APIs such as prefetch/copy/move/demote.

Those can be discussed in later phases.

## Proposed API Semantics

### `session_id`

`session_id` is an optional string hint.

Semantics:

- It identifies the session or workload that caused the KV object to be written.
- It is metadata associated with the object.
- It should not be part of the object key by default.
- It should not prevent eviction by itself.
- It should not override `group_ids`.

Expected usage:

- Associate KV objects with sessions.
- Support session-level observability.
- Enable future session-level lifecycle operations, such as bulk release, demotion, or statistics.
- Help upper layers correlate Mooncake cache behavior with request/session routing.

Important distinction:

- `group_ids` groups related physical objects derived from the same logical page.
- `session_id` identifies the workload/session that produced or used the object.

These are orthogonal and should both be preserved.

### `priority`

`priority` is an optional integer hint.

Mooncake should treat it as a cache retention hint, not as a scheduler priority.

Recommended Mooncake-side semantics:

- Higher normalized priority means the object is more valuable to retain.
- Default priority should behave exactly like today's behavior.
- Priority should influence eviction only as a soft preference.
- Priority should not directly change lease duration.
- Priority should not imply hard pinning.

Because different upper layers may define request priority differently, the integration layer should normalize priority before passing it to Mooncake when needed.

For example, SGLang uses integer priority, but its scheduling direction may be configured. Therefore, Mooncake should not need to understand SGLang's scheduling flags. The SGLang-Mooncake adapter should map SGLang request priority into Mooncake's cache-retention priority.

## Proposed Data Model

The exact implementation should follow Mooncake's current coding style and binding constraints. Conceptually, the write configuration should support:

```cpp
struct ReplicateConfig {
  // Existing fields.
  // ...

  // Optional workload/session identity.
  // Empty string means unset.
  std::string session_id;

  // Optional cache-retention priority.
  // 0 means default/normal behavior.
  int32_t priority = 0;
};
```

If Mooncake already has a better internal optional-field convention, we should follow it.

For `batch_put`, the minimal first-stage behavior can treat `session_id` and `priority` as applying to all objects in the batch.

If a caller needs to write objects from multiple sessions or priority classes in the same batch, it can split the batch in the first stage. If this becomes a performance issue, we can add per-object vectors later, similar to the existing `group_ids` pattern:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> session_ids;
std::vector<int32_t> priorities;
```

This RFC does not require per-object vectors in the first implementation.

### When hints are absent

Behavior must be unchanged.

Existing clients, tests, and SGLang integrations should continue to work without modification.

Issue #214: Consolidate the storage layer of the three fixed schemas (rollout as reference) + support arbitrary user-defined schemas

## Summary

`lance-context-core` currently ships **three independently-written fixed-schema stores**:

| Store | File | Key column | Schema |
|---|---|---|---|
| `RolloutStore` | `crates/lance-context-core/src/rollout_store.rs` | `id` | `rollout_schema()` (36 cols) |
| `ContextStore` | `crates/lance-context-core/src/store.rs` | `id` | `schema_with_options()` (26 cols) |
| `DatagenStore` | `crates/lance-context-core/src/datagen_store.rs` | `event_id` | `datagen_log_schema()` (33 cols) |

They are structurally parallel but share almost no code. Over time they have **forked at the storage layer**, and their observable behavior now differs in ways that are bugs, not design choices.

This is a **parent ticket** covering two related goals:

1. **Consolidate the low-level storage layer** of the three stores onto one shared implementation, taking **`RolloutStore` as the reference/canonical behavior**.
2. **Support arbitrary user-defined schemas** on top of that shared layer, with a small set of enforced constraints (notably a required `id` field), while keeping `add` and `merge` semantics identical to the fixed-schema stores.

---

## Part 1 — Consolidate the storage layer (rollout store is the reference)

### Divergences we need to fix

**Write / `add` path**
- `RolloutStore` and `DatagenStore` keep a **resident `ShardWriter`** and do `put` → `force_seal_active` → `wait_for_flush_drain` on every add, so a generation is durable and cross-instance-visible when `add` returns.
- `ContextStore` opens and closes a **new writer per call** (`write_entries`), with **no seal and no drain**. Its writes are only visible after an internal Lance flush. It also has no fence-retry handling, because it never holds a writer.
- Result: `add` means three different things depending on which store you call.

**WAL -> base merge**
- `RolloutStore::merge_own_shard` is the correct implementation: close writer, scan generations, `WriteMode::Append`, `claim_epoch` + `commit_update` with a surgical generation drain, then remove the shard dir. Triggered by both a count threshold (`maybe_merge_own_shard`) and a time threshold (`cleanup_own_shard`).
- `DatagenStore::merge_own_shard` is a near line-for-line copy (plus a background cleanup task), and buffers every flushed generation fully in memory.
- **`ContextStore` never merges at all.** WAL generations accumulate forever and every read pays a full `LsmScanner` reconstruction over all shard manifests.

**Compaction**
- `RolloutStore`: synchronous, single-compactor, `defer_index_remap: true` to work around a Lance panic on the fieldless MemWAL index.

### Related Issues / PRs

#6821 covers latest-checkpoint selection in InMemorySaver. #8448 covers a Postgres pagination bug. Neither covers the SQLite delta-history parent walk.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
import asyncio

from langgraph.checkpoint.base import empty_checkpoint
from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite import SqliteSaver
from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite.aio import AsyncSqliteSaver


def checkpoint(checkpoint_id, values):
    value = empty_checkpoint()
    value["id"] = checkpoint_id
    value["channel_values"] = values
    return value


def run_sync():
    with SqliteSaver.from_conn_string(":memory:") as saver:
        config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "t", "checkpoint_ns": ""}}
        root = saver.put(config, checkpoint("z-older", {"ch": "seed"}), {}, {})
        saver.put_writes(root, [("ch", "write-root")], "task")
        child = saver.put(root, checkpoint("a-newer", {}), {}, {})
        print(saver.get_delta_channel_history(config=child, channels=["ch"]))


async def run_async():
    async with AsyncSqliteSaver.from_conn_string(":memory:") as saver:
        config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "t", "checkpoint_ns": ""}}
        root = await saver.aput(
            config, checkpoint("z-older", {"ch": "seed"}), {}, {}
        )
        await saver.aput_writes(root, [("ch", "write-root")], "task")
        child = await saver.aput(root, checkpoint("a-newer", {}), {}, {})
        print(await saver.aget_delta_channel_history(config=child, channels=["ch"]))


run_sync()
asyncio.run(run_async())
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell
No exception is raised. Both calls silently return:

{'ch': {'writes': []}}

The expected result is:

{'ch': {'writes': [('task', 'ch', 'write-root')], 'seed': 'seed'}}
```

### Description

Both SQLite saver overrides use `DELTA_STAGE1_SQL`, which filters with `checkpoint_id <= target_id` and orders by checkpoint ID. This assumes that every child checkpoint ID sorts after its parent.

The checkpoint contract identifies ancestry through `parent_checkpoint_id`; it does not require IDs to be lexicographically monotonic. In the reproduction, the child `a-newer` points directly to `z-older`, but the range predicate excludes the parent. The optimized SQLite implementation therefore loses the parent's seed and pending write. Calling the base saver implementation against the same rows returns the expected history.

I reproduced this with `langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite==3.1.1` and current `main` at `658541c4960f329864a2523fc7d52427e8190bed`.

A scoped fix would replace the ID-range scan with a recursive SQLite CTE that starts at the target and follows `parent_checkpoint_id` within the same thread and namespace. I can implement the fix and sync/async regression tests if maintainers agree. Could this issue be assigned to @lylelllll?

Issue #1020: Teams DynamoDB store: three update-expression rules to carry into the S04b state store

## Context

While reviewing the now-superseded [#987](https://github.com/layervai/qurl-integrations/pull/987) (Go Teams app), three defects turned up in its DynamoDB store. They are recorded here because they are **properties of the access pattern, not of Go** — the Teams OAuth-state store planned for S04b in [#1001](https://github.com/layervai/qurl-integrations/pull/1001) will use the same nested-map shape and can reproduce all three.

Each is rejected by real DynamoDB but accepted by a stub that only records the emitted expression string, which is why none surfaced in CI.

## The three defects

**1. Nested `SET` needs its parent map to already exist.**
`SET alias_bindings.#alias = :rid` fails with `ValidationException: The document path provided in the update expression is invalid for update` when `alias_bindings` is absent from the item. Nothing initialised it, so the *first* alias bind in any channel scope failed. DynamoDB does not auto-create intermediate maps.

**2. One update expression may not touch two overlapping document paths.**
The natural-looking fix for (1) — seeding and writing in one statement:

```
SET personal_conversation_refs = if_not_exists(personal_conversation_refs, :empty_map),
    personal_conversation_refs.#actor = :ref
```

is rejected with `ValidationException: Invalid UpdateExpression: Two document paths overlap with each other`. In #987 this shipped in `SavePersonalConversationRef`, where it failed on *every* call, not just the first.

The working pattern is two writes, which is what `apps/slack/internal/slackdata/aliases.go` already does (`ensureAliasBindingsMap`): seed the parent under `attribute_not_exists(parent)`, swallow the `ConditionalCheckFailedException` as success, then write the nested key. `slackdata` uses `if_not_exists` nowhere, deliberately.

**3. `ExpressionAttributeNames` must be nil, not empty.**
The AWS SDK guards on `!= nil`, not `len() > 0` (`dynamodb@v1.60.1/serializers.go:3843`), so a non-nil empty map is serialized as `"ExpressionAttributeNames": {}` and DynamoDB rejects it. In #987 this hit the common revoke path — a resource exposed to a scope with no alias bound to it built no placeholders but still passed `map[string]string{}`.

## Why CI did not catch any of them

The package's test double returned `&dynamodb.UpdateItemOutput{}, nil` unconditionally and never parsed `UpdateExpression` or evaluated `ConditionExpression`. A stub like that cannot fail on an expression the service would reject, and it also makes every conditional-write branch unreachable — `ErrAliasAlreadyBound`, `ErrAliasNotFound`, and the bind-conflict classification were all untestable.

## Suggested action for S04b

- Use the two-write seed-then-set pattern for any nested map attribute; do not reach for `if_not_exists` on a path you also write into.
- Leave `ExpressionAttributeNames` nil when empty.
- Make the store's test double *evaluate* expressions rather than record them, so these three rules are enforced at test time. A working reference implementation exists on the `feat/teams-bot` branch at commit `66d6edac` (`apps/teams/internal/teamsdata/ddbfake_test.go`) — an in-memory client that applies `SET`/`REMOVE`/`ADD`/`DELETE`, evaluates `attribute_exists`/`attribute_not_exists`/`contains`, and returns a real `ConditionalCheckFailedException`. All seven accompanying lifecycle tests fail against the pre-fix code.
- Alternatively, run the store tests against DynamoDB Local so the semantics come from the service itself.

Issue #209938: [Flang] Missing error for recursive invocation of NON_RECURSIVE procedures

## Summary

According to the Fortran 2023 standard, NON_RECURSIVE procedures are prohibited from invoking the procedures themselves. However, when such procedures are involved in defined assignment/operation, Flang seems to overlook this restriction.

### Reproducer

* test.f90


Issue #70: Propagate W3C trace context

> **As** an SRE debugging a request that crossed six services,
> **I want** Poseidon to continue the caller's trace instead of starting a new one,
> **so that** the trace is one connected tree rather than six disconnected roots.

## Context

Nothing propagates trace context today. `grep -rn "traceparent\|tracestate"` over the whole tree returns **no hits**.

`Tracing()` (`middleware/tracing.go:76`) calls `Tracer.StartSpan(ctx, name)` and never inspects the inbound field section, so every span it creates is a root span. Distributed tracing is therefore structurally impossible: each hop starts a new trace.

The vendor-neutral `Tracer`/`Span` interfaces are a good decision and should stay — the missing piece is the extract/inject step around them, which needs no new dependency (a `traceparent` value is a fixed-format 55-byte string).

Related gap: `StructuredAccessLog` (`middleware/slog.go`) emits no trace or span id, so logs cannot be correlated to traces either.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Parse `traceparent` and `tracestate` per W3C Trace Context, including the version/flag rules and the "malformed header is ignored, not fatal" rule.
- [ ] Expose the extracted span context on the request context, and pass it to `StartSpan` so adapters can make the span a child.
- [ ] Inject `traceparent` on outbound-facing surfaces where the server is the caller's peer.
- [ ] `StructuredAccessLog` emits `trace_id` and `span_id` when present.
- [ ] The sampling decision is honoured and exposed, so a downstream adapter does not re-decide it.
- [ ] Conformance tests named `TestConformance_W3CTraceContext_*` quoting the normative sentence, with rows added to `docs/RFC_COVERAGE.md`.
- [ ] Zero new dependencies.

## Proved by

`make conformance-gate` — the W3C Trace Context recommendation has normative MUST-level text, and the repo already has the machinery to assert against a spec (`docs/RFC_COVERAGE.md`, `TestConformance_*`).

Issue #134: Projects: Linear-style project entity grouping tasks with derived progress

## Background

With #130 (simplified task center), #131 (department assignment), #132 (sub-tasks), and #133 (task dependencies), OPC gains a solid task layer — but tasks still have no higher-level container. Users coming from tools like Linear expect a **Project**: a named initiative that groups related tasks, has its own status and timeline, and rolls up progress automatically.

This issue proposes a **Project** concept above the task layer, modeled on Linear's projects.

> Depends on #130; composes with #131 / #132 / #133. Not scheduled for immediate implementation — this is a design placeholder to be picked up later.

## Goal

Introduce `Project` as a first-class entity: a container that groups tasks toward a shared outcome, with its own metadata, lifecycle, and derived progress — without disturbing the single-assignee task model underneath.

## Requirements (draft — to be refined when scheduled)

- New `Project` entity: `{ id, name, description?, status, leadId?, targetDate?, createdAt, updatedAt, ... }`.
- Project status lifecycle (Linear-like): e.g. `backlog → planned → in_progress → completed | cancelled` (possibly `paused`).
- `Task` gains an optional `projectId`; a task belongs to at most one project. Existing tasks stay project-less (projects are opt-in).
- **Derived progress**: project detail shows task-count / completed-count (and per-status breakdown) computed from member tasks — never manually maintained.
- Project membership is organizational, not a new permission silo: visibility and management follow the task role model from #130 (project lead + task creators/assignees); decide whether a lightweight `project.lead` role can manage membership and status.
- Project detail view: task list grouped by status, progress rollup, lead, target date, and a project room (one conversation per project, reusing the room model) for discussion and event fan-out.
- Mobile: a Projects tab/section — list, detail (progress + tasks), create/edit project, add/remove tasks.

## Open questions

- Project lead: single accountable lead (Linear model) or shared ownership?
- Can a task move between projects, and is that recorded in task history?
- Do projects interact with #131 (assign a *project* — or its unassigned tasks — to a department pool)?
- Do projects interact with #133 (cross-project dependency chains — allowed or restricted)?
- Milestones (Linear-style project milestones) — include now or defer?
- Does project status auto-advance from task events (first task started → in_progress; all tasks completed → completed), or stay manual?
- Multi-tenancy boundary: are projects org-wide, or scoped to departments (which #130 deliberately decoupled from tasks)?

## Acceptance criteria (to be refined)

- Users can create a project, add/remove tasks, and see derived progress that updates automatically as tasks change status.
- A task without a project behaves exactly as before (#130 semantics untouched).
- Project lifecycle and membership management are covered by server e2e tests; mobile project screens covered by Maestro flows.

## Out of scope

- Cycles/roadmaps (Linear "Cycles"), sprints, velocity tracking.
- Custom workflows per project (status sets stay global).
- Resource allocation / workload planning.
- Cross-project rollups (initiatives/portfolio views).

Issue #3: Plan future matcher and flow support for retained semantic fact identities

## Summary

  The canonical semantic fact stream intentionally retains several identities that are not yet consumed by current
  matchers:

  - `Reference.value`
  - `MemberRead.value`
  - `PropertyWrite.source`
  - `Call.callee`
  - `Construction.callee`
  - `Construction.result`
  - `FunctionSummary.owner`

  These fields currently have narrowly scoped `#[allow(dead_code)]` directives. They are retained because computing
  them during the shared semantic pass preserves information needed for future matcher expansion without requiring
  another AST traversal or a parallel semantic model.

  This issue tracks the intended consumers for those fields and the conditions under which their allowances can be
  removed.

  ## Planned uses

  ### 1. Reference value identity

  Field: `Reference.value`

  Use the resolved `ValueId` to represent an identifier use as a connected semantic event.

  Potential capabilities:

  - Match a proven value when it is referenced or consumed.
  - Connect declarations and assignments to later uses.
  - Express generic value-use sinks that are not calls or property writes.
  - Distinguish same-name bindings across scopes and assignment versions.

  The matcher must never fall back to the raw identifier spelling in strict mode.

  The allowance can be removed when at least one production semantic projection reads `Reference.value`.

  ### 2. Member-read value identity

  Field: `MemberRead.value`

  Use the resolved member value to connect reads such as:

  ```js
  const handler = object.callback;
  consume(object.callback);
 ```

  Potential capabilities:

  - Treat a member read as a flow source or sink.
  - Follow a proven member value through aliases.
  - Connect property writes to later reads of the same receiver, property, and binding version.
  - Support lifecycle matching where reading a configured member is significant.

  Dynamic property names or invalidated receiver provenance must fail closed.

  The allowance can be removed when member-read flow consumes this identity.

  ### 3. Property-write source identity

  Field: `PropertyWrite.source`

  Use the RHS identity to model the value being stored:

```js
  container.handler = callback;
  options.transport = client;
```

  Potential capabilities:

  - Match a proven value flowing into a property.
  - Connect the stored value to a later read or call.
  - Support property-write sinks whose condition depends on RHS identity or provenance.
  - Extend current static-string property matching to connected values without weakening it.

  This must remain distinct from:

  - target: identity of the complete member expression;
  - receiver: identity of the object being mutated;
  - static_value: bounded static-string projection of the RHS.

  The allowance can be removed when the flow projector or a matcher index consumes source.

  ### 4. Call callee identity

  Field: `Call.callee`

  Use the callee identity for callable value flow:

```js
  const invoke = importedFunction;
  invoke(value);

  let callback = handler;
  callback();
```

  Potential capabilities:

  - Connect calls to callable aliases by identity.
  - Model higher-order functions where a callable is passed, returned, stored, and later invoked.
  - Match invocation of a proven value independently of its current spelling.
  - Improve interprocedural call edges where target_function alone is insufficient.

  Call.callee complements rather than replaces call provenance, rooted chains, or target_function.

  The allowance can be removed when call matching or summary construction consumes the callee identity.

  ### 5. Construction identities

  Fields:

  - `Construction.callee`
  - `Construction.result`

  Use callee to identify the constructor value and result to identify the newly allocated object:

```js
  const instance = new Constructor();
  instance.configure(value);
  consume(instance);
```

  Potential capabilities:

  - Treat construction as an object-flow source.
  - Follow the constructed result through aliases.
  - Apply configuration and lifecycle requirements to constructed objects.
  - Match constructors passed through aliases or higher-order transformations.
  - Connect a constructed instance to later member calls, property writes, and sinks.

  The result identity must remain allocation-specific and bounded. Separate construction sites must not share
  object state accidentally.

  Both allowances can be removed when construction-source flow consumes these fields.

  ### 6. Function ownership

  Field: `FunctionSummary.owner`

  Use the lexical owner relationship for closure-aware summary propagation:

```js
  function outer(value) {
      function inner() {
          consume(value);
      }

      return inner;
  }
```

  Potential capabilities:

  - Represent nested-function relationships without reconstructing scope ancestry.
  - Propagate proven captured-value effects into closure summaries.
  - Distinguish lexical capture from ordinary argument flow.
  - Invalidate summaries conservatively when capture, reassignment, or dynamic scope cannot be proven.
  - Support returned or passed closures while keeping same-name sibling functions isolated by FunctionId.

  Ownership alone is not proof of capture. Capture identities and assignment versions must still be established
  explicitly.

  The allowance can be removed when closure-aware summary construction consumes owner.

Issue #330: Re-entrant layout builds silently corrupt page structure since ACP2E-4040 (isolated reader context)

### Summary

Since 6194581 (ACP2E-4040, imported from upstream Magento 2.4.9), building the same shared layout twice within one request silently corrupts the generated structure: blocks scheduled into a container by an `<update>`-included handle lose their parent and disappear from the rendered page.

Before that change, `Magento\Framework\View\Layout::generateElements()` handed the shared `Reader\Context` to the generator pool, which consumed the `ScheduledStructure` in place — after a build it was empty, so a (rare but possible) second build re-interpreted into clean state. Since ACP2E-4040, generation runs on a clone (`createIsolatedReaderContext()`), so after a build the shared context retains all scheduled rows and materialized paths. A second `generateElements()` re-interprets the layout XML on top of that dirty state, and `Layout\ScheduledStructure\Helper::_overrideElementWorkaround()` treats the re-read declarations as overrides of the leftover rows — silently destroying the children scheduled under their paths.

### How a double build happens with core code only

1. A controller uses the common pattern `$resultPage->getConfig()->getTitle()->set(...)`. `Page\Config::getTitle()` triggers a full early layout build.
2. During that build, block generation lazily instantiates a class depending on the deprecated `Magento\Framework\App\ViewInterface` (e.g. `Magento\Customer\Helper\Session\CurrentCustomer`, injected by a block or view model). `App\View::__construct` eagerly runs `$pageFactory->create(true)`; the throwaway `Result\Page` constructs a `Page\Builder`, whose constructor unconditionally calls `$this->pageConfig->setBuilder($this)` on the **shared** `Page\Config` — replacing the already-built builder.
3. `Result\Page::render()` → `publicBuild()` → the swapped-in builder (`isBuilt = false`) re-runs `loadLayoutUpdates()` / `generateLayoutXml()` / `generateElements()` on the same shared layout instance.
4. The second pass corrupts the structure. Log fingerprint (developer mode):
   `Broken reference: the 'google_gtag_analytics' tries to reorder itself towards 'head.hyva-scripts', but their parents are different: 'head.additional' and '' respectively.`

The eager page creation in `App\View` and the builder swap in `Page\Builder::__construct` are long-standing quirks; they were harmless while a second build started from a consumed (empty) reader context. ACP2E-4040 made re-entrant builds destructive.

### Observed impact

On a Hyva storefront (Mage-OS 3): the `head.additional` children contributed by the theme's `default_hyva` handle (`head.js`, `head.hyva-scripts`, `speculationrules`) vanish from the page, breaking all `hyva.*` JavaScript on affected routes (e.g. third-party customer-account controllers that set the title early and then render blocks using `CurrentCustomer`). Any layout where a handle included via `<update handle="..."/>` schedules blocks into a re-declared container is susceptible.

### Suggested direction

Either make re-entrant builds safe again (reset the shared `Reader\Context`'s `ScheduledStructure` and the layout's `Data\Structure` when `generateElements()` runs on an already-built layout), or prevent the rogue rebuild at its sources: create `App\View`'s page lazily in `getPage()` instead of the constructor, and/or don't let `Page\Builder::__construct` replace an already-built builder on the shared `Page\Config`.

### Workaround

DI-detach `App\View`'s eager page from the shared `Page\Config` for injection points that are constructed mid-build: a virtual `Result\Page` with `isIsolated=true` plus a non-shared `Page\Config` (via a virtual `Template\Context`), wired into `App\View`'s `pageFactory` argument for e.g. `CurrentCustomer::$view`.

Identified on a client site with Mage-OS 3.4 + Hyva Theme + Amasty B2B suite, on an account-area controller.

Issue #561: fix(agent): pty:kill and spawn-replacement must use killProcessTree

> **Size:** S — Inconsistent process tree cleanup in PTY handlers
> **Parent / Sub-issues:** none

## User story
**As a** terminal user,
**I want** killing a terminal tab or replacing it to fully terminate all child processes (including CLIs spawned by Claude),
**so that** orphaned processes don't consume resources or interfere with subsequent operations.

---

## Context
The app manages PTY processes in `ptyProcesses` Map (electron/main.ts:111). When terminating a PTY:
- `teardownChildren()` (line 543–550) correctly uses `killProcessTree(p.pid, 'SIGKILL')` to terminate the shell and all descendants
- `pty:kill` handler (line 1599–1602) calls `IPty.kill()` directly — only signals the shell, leaving child CLIs orphaned
- `pty:spawn` replacement path (line 1519–1520) also calls `existing.kill()` instead of `killProcessTree()`

The asymmetry means a PTY killed via the UI handler leaks child processes, while the same PTY cleaned up on app exit reaps them correctly.

## Current scenario
1. User spawns a PTY and runs a long-lived CLI (e.g., `claude` agent) inside it
2. User clicks "Kill Terminal" → renderer calls `pty:kill` handler
3. Handler calls `ptyProcesses.get(id)?.kill()` (IPty.kill() only signals shell, pid ~N)
4. Shell process ~N exits; child CLI process ~N+X continues running
5. Process tree is orphaned

Same occurs when replacing a PTY (pty:spawn with same id): line 1520 `existing.kill()` before spawning replacement.

## Problem
1. `pty:kill` uses IPty.kill() instead of killProcessTree, orphaning descendants
2. `pty:spawn` replacement uses existing.kill() for the same reason
3. `teardownChildren` already has the correct pattern — inconsistency across handlers

## Consequences of the problem
- **Resource leak**: Agent CLIs and other child processes accumulate and persist after terminal close
- **Data corruption**: Orphaned agents may continue writing to vault files after user expects terminal to be dead
- **User confusion**: Terminal appears closed but backend work continues silently
- **Process accumulation**: Repeated kill+respawn cycles leak PID table slots

---

## Proposed solution
1. Replace `existing.kill()` at line 1520 with `killProcessTree(existing.pid, 'SIGTERM')`
2. Replace `ptyProcesses.get(id)?.kill()` at line 1600 with `killProcessTree(pid, 'SIGTERM')` (graceful) and verify exit before hard kill if needed
3. Verify both paths use the same termination strategy as teardownChildren (currently SIGKILL on full teardown; use SIGTERM for user-initiated kill, matching normal shell behavior)

Import killProcessTree if not already imported (it is, line 46).

## Expected result
- After kill signal reaches UI: shell and all descendants terminate within grace period
- Replacing a PTY fully reaps the previous tree before spawning new shell
- No orphaned processes leak from terminal operations
- Behavior matches teardownChildren's process tree handling

---

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] pty:kill terminates the full process tree (shell + descendant CLIs)
- [ ] Replacing a PTY with the same id kills the previous tree before spawning
- [ ] No orphaned agent CLI remains after killing a terminal from the UI (verified)
- [ ] Behavior matches teardownChildren's killProcessTree usage

## Out of scope
- Grace period tuning (use killProcessTree's existing default/strategy)
- Renderer-side kill confirmation UI changes

## References
- electron/main.ts:543–550 (teardownChildren — correct pattern)
- electron/main.ts:1519–1520 (pty:spawn replacement — wrong pattern)
- electron/main.ts:1599–1602 (pty:kill handler — wrong pattern)
- electron/proc-group.js (killProcessTree implementation)
- electron/main.ts:46 (killProcessTree already imported)

Issue #6997: [zephyr] Persist/cache a distributed dataset across jobs (avoid re-reading a large table every iteration in a driver loop)

## Summary

Zephyr has no way to **materialize a distributed dataset once and keep it resident** (in cluster memory, spilling to disk) so that multiple downstream jobs — especially the successive rounds of an iterative driver loop — can reuse it without re-reading or re-shuffling it each time. This is the single biggest gap for **iterative join / graph-traversal workloads**, and it's the classic reason plain MapReduce is poor at iterative algorithms (the founding motivation for Spark's in-memory persistence).

Requesting a `Dataset.persist()` / `.cache()` primitive analogous to Spark's `RDD.persist()` / `DataFrame.cache()`.

## Motivating workload

We're porting a graph resolver off a single ~2 TB-RAM box onto a cluster of many ~64 GB workers (Software Heritage → Nemotron enrichment). Its shape is representative of iterative joins generally:

- One large, **static** table `DIR_EDGE` (directory edges), on the order of hundreds of GB.
- A driver loop of **K dependent rounds**. Round `k` joins a small, **sparse frontier** (≈ one row per input row, collapsing toward ~1 candidate per row) against `DIR_EDGE` by key, producing the next round's frontier.
- The large table never changes across rounds; only the small frontier does.

## Current behavior / limitation

- The only join is `sorted_merge_join`, which requires both sides to already be `group_by`'d into identical co-partitioned, sorted shards (per its docstring: "same number of shards / corresponding shards contain the same key ranges / sorted by join key"). It is a streaming merge with **no persistence** of either side.
- There is **no `persist` / `cache`**: each round re-reads `DIR_EDGE` from storage (and, if joined via `group_by`, re-shuffles it). Cost is `K × read(DIR_EDGE)` even though the big side is immutable and each round's frontier only needs a handful of keys per shard.
- The best workaround today (pre-partition `DIR_EDGE` to disk with a shared partition function, re-open matching shards with `map_shard` each round) still re-reads the whole table from disk every round and leans on the OS page cache, which is unmanaged and evicted under memory pressure.

## Requested capability

`Dataset.persist(...)` / `.cache()` that:

- Materializes a dataset's shards once and **pins them in cluster memory** (implementation's choice — e.g. Ray object store / worker-resident), returning a handle reusable by later jobs **within the same driver process**.
- **Preserves partitioning and sort order**, so a persisted, hash-partitioned dataset can be re-joined (via `map_shard` / `sorted_merge_join`) across rounds **without another `group_by` shuffle**.
- **Spills to disk under memory pressure** rather than OOM-ing — important on many ~64 GB workers, where aggregate cluster RAM can hold the table even though a single worker cannot.
- Optionally exposes an **eviction / lifetime** API so the driver can release the dataset after the loop finishes.

## Benefit

- Converts `K × disk-read(DIR_EDGE)` into `1 × disk-read + K × in-memory-scan` — bounded by memory bandwidth, not storage bandwidth or repeated shuffle.
- Makes **iterative** Zephyr jobs (graph walks, connected components, iterative joins, multi-pass enrichment) practical without a single giant-RAM machine, which is the whole point of moving to the cluster.

## Non-goals / possible follow-ons

- **Indexed point lookups** on the cached side (so a sparse frontier probes only matching keys instead of scanning the whole cached table each round) would take this from `K × in-memory-scan` down to `K × O(frontier)`. That's a further optimization; **persist/cache is the prerequisite and the main blocker**, so it should land first. Happy to file the indexed-probe follow-up separately.
- Not asking for full Spark-style RDD lineage / automatic recompute-on-failure. Re-materializing a lost cache from source is acceptable initially.

## Spark analogues

- `RDD.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)`, `DataFrame.cache()` — the canonical fix for iterative algorithms (PageRank, connected components, iterative ML) that re-use a large static dataset across passes.

## Relation to existing work

- #4368 (Zephyr Improvements) — general gap brainstorm.
- #5992 (Zephyr Burndown epic).
- The Rust/polars pushdown direction — an Arrow-backed persisted dataset would compose cleanly with pushed-down operators.

## Alternatives considered (workarounds today)

- **Pre-partition `DIR_EDGE` to disk + `map_shard` re-open each round** — avoids re-shuffle but still re-reads from disk every round; relies on the OS page cache (unmanaged, not guaranteed across memory pressure).
- **External KV / sorted-SSTable service** for point lookups — works, but pushes state outside Zephyr and duplicates infrastructure.

Issue #2209: session_digest: model tasks_claimed as related entities, not a nested JSON array

## Problem

`session_digest.tasks_claimed` is a JSON array of objects, each carrying `claim`, `status_claimed`, `evidence_pointers`, `verification_state`, and `verification_note`. That array is doing the work of an entity plus a relationship, and it fails on four counts:

**1. Elements cannot be corrected independently.** `correct` replaces the entire field. Stage 3 of the session-task pipeline (`/verify-work`) exists specifically to upgrade individual claims from `verification_state: "intent"` to `confirmed`/`refuted`/`unverifiable`. With a nested array, upgrading one claim means rewriting all of them — a read-modify-write on a field another process may have changed in between. This is the same merge hazard the Ateles project instructions call out for plan `decisions`/`todos`, where rebuilding a field from a stale in-memory copy silently deletes other entries. A sweep of 154 digests averaging ~7 claims each means roughly 1,000 claims, every one of which currently requires a whole-field rewrite to verify.

**2. Elements cannot be queried.** "Every outstanding claim citing neotoma#2163" is a full scan plus JSON parse today. As entities with `REFERS_TO` edges it is a graph query — which is the point of storing this in a graph.

**3. The nesting invites a known silent failure.** A `tasks_claimed` written as a JSON-encoded *string* parses fine for a human reader but returns zero items to any consumer that iterates it. This has occurred at least once and hid an entire digest's contents. A relationship cannot fail this way. (Audited 50 digests from the 2026-08-24 sweep: zero occurrences, so this is a latent hazard rather than an active one.)

**4. It duplicates downstream state.** Stage 4 (`/reconcile-tasks`) creates real `task` entities from these claims. The same obligation then exists twice — once as an array element, once as an entity — with no link between them, so dedupe is by string matching rather than by identity.

## Proposal

Model each claim as its own entity (`session_claim`, or a `task` in a claimed state), linked `PART_OF` the digest, with `REFERS_TO` edges to the artifacts it cites. Then:

- `/verify-work` corrects one small entity per claim instead of rewriting a multi-element blob.
- `/reconcile-tasks` promotes or dedupes against entities that already exist rather than minting parallel ones.
- Evidence pointers that are real entity ids become real edges.

`commitments` and `artifacts` have the same shape of problem and should be considered in the same pass.

## General principle worth settling

The test for array-vs-relationship: does an element have an independent lifecycle — is it corrected, queried, or linked on its own? `topics` and `lineage_files` are inert values and are fine as arrays. `tasks_claimed`, `commitments`, and `artifacts` all fail that test. It would be worth stating this as guidance so new schemas do not repeat it.

## Migration note

There are ~220 existing `session_digest` entities carrying populated `tasks_claimed` arrays, and three skills (`/review-sessions`, `/verify-work`, `/reconcile-tasks`) that read or write the field. Any change needs a backfill path and coordinated skill updates; this is not a drop-in replacement.

## Provenance

Surfaced during a full session-task pipeline run on 2026-08-24/25 while preparing 154 forensic digests for `/verify-work`. The correction hazard in (1) was about to be hit at scale, which is what prompted filing. Neotoma entity: `ent_44aca410fc0b00ec354d0b2f`.

Issue #2238: Resolved Nostr event cards reload and change layout every time a chat opens

## Observed behavior

On GrapheneOS, opening a chat that contains a referenced Nostr-event preview first renders incomplete/loading content. When relay resolution finishes, the preview changes content and size and the conversation visibly jumps. Leaving and reopening the same chat repeats the loading-to-complete transition every time, even after that preview already resolved successfully.

## Source-confirmed mechanism

Reviewed at White Noise Android `231f5b6b1fee876d66b9b67ad8ac9211da0d2b28` and MDK `2d225ed1ecbbca339998638f659df5d609ae9935`.

1. Event cards are extracted from the typed Markdown tree and appended inside the message bubble ([extraction and call site](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/whitenoise-android/blob/231f5b6b1fee876d66b9b67ad8ac9211da0d2b28/app/src/main/java/dev/ipf/whitenoise/android/ui/conversation/messages/BubbleContentBlocks.kt#L488-L507), [card placement](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/whitenoise-android/blob/231f5b6b1fee876d66b9b67ad8ac9211da0d2b28/app/src/main/java/dev/ipf/whitenoise/android/ui/conversation/messages/BubbleContentBlocks.kt#L625-L642)). The outer timeline row key is stable, but its measured height changes when the nested card changes.
2. Each `ConversationScreen` constructs its own resolver and destroys it on navigation disposal ([resolver lifecycle](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/whitenoise-android/blob/231f5b6b1fee876d66b9b67ad8ac9211da0d2b28/app/src/main/java/dev/ipf/whitenoise/android/ui/conversation/ConversationScreen.kt#L1250-L1259)). The resolver's first state is always `Loading`, and its access-ordered map is cleared by `close()` ([memory-only state](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/whitenoise-android/blob/231f5b6b1fee876d66b9b67ad8ac9211da0d2b28/app/src/main/java/dev/ipf/whitenoise/android/ui/conversation/nostr/NostrEventCardResolver.kt#L76-L102), [teardown](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/whitenoise-android/blob/231f5b6b1fee876d66b9b67ad8ac9211da0d2b28/app/src/main/java/dev/ipf/whitenoise/android/ui/conversation/nostr/NostrEventCardResolver.kt#L252-L279)).
3. A relay result changes the card once from loading to verified event content, then may change it again after a separate kind-0 author lookup ([two-stage publish](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/whitenoise-android/blob/231f5b6b1fee876d66b9b67ad8ac9211da0d2b28/app/src/main/java/dev/ipf/whitenoise/android/ui/conversation/nostr/NostrEventCardResolver.kt#L134-L173)).
4. The loading branch is a short status/action row, while a loaded card adds a 32 dp author header plus optional title, three-line summary, and metadata; there is no shared reserved envelope ([loading branch](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/whitenoise-android/blob/231f5b6b1fee876d66b9b67ad8ac9211da0d2b28/app/src/main/java/dev/ipf/whitenoise/android/ui/conversation/nostr/NostrEventCards.kt#L174-L240), [loaded geometry](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/whitenoise-android/blob/231f5b6b1fee876d66b9b67ad8ac9211da0d2b28/app/src/main/java/dev/ipf/whitenoise/android/ui/conversation/nostr/NostrEventCards.kt#L245-L280)).

This is a remaining correctness/performance gap in [#1778](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/whitenoise-android/issues/1778) / [PR #2099](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/whitenoise-android/pull/2099), not a duplicate of that completed feature. It is the event-card analogue of the cached first-frame work in [#2103](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/whitenoise-android/issues/2103), but unlike timelines, event previews currently have no durable MDK projection to seed from.

## Required behavior

- After a preview has resolved successfully once, every later first committed frame for that message renders the complete last-known verified event card, including cached author metadata when previously available. Reopening the chat, recreating navigation/controller state, restarting the process, or reopening offline must not regress the card to a fetch-driven loading/incomplete state or change its outer geometry.
- Consume the typed account-scoped durable projection from https://github.com/marmot-protocol/mdk/issues/1547. Do not add an Android Room, DataStore, SharedPreferences, file, or second protocol cache. A cache hit may refresh in the background without replacing known-good content with `Loading`, a transient miss, an older addressable event, or incomplete author data.
- Before any event has ever resolved, render a deterministic bounded placeholder envelope without blocking the conversation. Its outer bounds must remain stable through `Loading` → `Loaded`, `NotFound`, `Invalid`, or `Failed`; state-specific content and retry actions may change inside that envelope.
- Preserve stable timeline/message/card keys and current scroll/unread anchors. Resolving a visible or off-screen card must not move another message, the viewport anchor, or the composer.

| `note` and `nevent` event IDs | Exact ID lookup; kind-aware card | FILED — reuse verified event + author projection on every later first frame |
| `naddr` addressable coordinate | Exact `(kind, author, d)` lookup; newest verified match | FILED — reuse last-known coordinate projection and refresh monotonically |
| Directly referenced text notes, replies, quote/repost events | Note for kind 1; otherwise bounded Generic card | FILED — same durable projection; do not recursively expand references inside fetched content |
| Article kind 30023 | Article card + in-app reader | FILED — cached title/summary/body/metadata must not rehydrate after first paint |
| Video kinds 21/22/34235/34236 | Video card + in-app player | FILED — cached media URL/type/dimensions/duration must not change bubble geometry after first paint |
| Release kind 30063 and file kind 1063 | Release/File cards | FILED — event-derived metadata participates in the same projection |
| Other valid event kinds | Generic card | FILED — same cache/layout contract |

Issue #3636: REN-2026-08-30-D23-06: no regression guard pins the resize ordering that keeps the presentation descriptor off a destroyed upscale view

- **Severity**: LOW
- **Dimension**: FSR/Presentation
- **Location**: `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/context/resize.rs:1005-1051` (`recreate_swapchain_core`), test module at `resize.rs:1394+`
- **Status**: NEW
- **Description**: `FrameUpscaler::recreate` is an unconditional `destroy` + `Self::new`
  (`frame_upscaler.rs:1005-1024`), so every resize and every preset switch replaces the
  output `VkImage`/`VkImageView` handles. `PresentationPipeline` writes those views into its
  descriptor sets exactly once, in `create`/`write_inputs`. The only thing preventing the
  presentation descriptor from naming a destroyed view is the source ordering in
  `recreate_swapchain_core`: `presentation.take()` → `destroy` → `upscaler.recreate()` →
  `PresentationPipeline::new(..., &upscaled_views, ...)`. That ordering is load-bearing, is
  the highest-value source-provable invariant in this dimension, and has no test.
  `resize.rs`'s test module already uses exactly this static-source-landmark technique for
  three sibling invariants (#654, #2141, #2142, #2156), so the mechanism is established.
- **Evidence**:
  - `resize.rs:1005-1012` — the comment states the invariant ("Presentation descriptors
    reference the upscaler's output views, so retire presentation before replacing those
    views") but nothing asserts it.
  - `frame_upscaler.rs:1013-1024` — `unsafe { self.destroy(device, allocator) }; *self = Self::new(...)?;`
    → new image/view handles on every call, including a same-output-extent preset switch
    (Quality→Performance changes only `render`, but the outputs are recreated anyway).
  - `presentation.rs::write_inputs` is called only from `create`; there is no
    `rebind_upscaled_views` equivalent to `composite.rs::rebind_hdr_views`.
  - The existing four static-order tests in `resize.rs`'s `mod tests` cover the swapchain
    view handoff, the SSAO failure rebind, the water set-2 rebind and the upscaler-switch
    rollback — but none cover this pair.
- **Impact**: A reordering (e.g. hoisting `upscaler.recreate` above the `presentation.take()`
  so the `allocator` borrow reads more naturally) would leave every presentation descriptor
  sampling a destroyed image view on the first post-resize frame. Invisible to `cargo test`,
  and on the default render path.
- **Needs RenderDoc**: no
- **Suggested Fix**: Add a static-source test to `resize.rs::mod tests` in the style of
  `ssao_recreate_failure_rebinds_binding_7_to_the_placeholder`: assert
  `find("unsafe { presentation.destroy(&self.device) }")` < `find("upscaler.recreate(")` <
  `find("PresentationPipeline::new(")` inside `production_src()`, with a message naming the
  descriptor-vs-view lifetime as the reason.

Issue #3663: PERF-D4-2026-08-30-01: the instance / previous-model / indirect dirty gates are defeated by the per-frame depth re-sort, so the documented steady-state saving only materialises with a parked camera

- **Severity**: MEDIUM
- **Dimension**: SSBO Sizing & Upload
- **Location**: `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/scene_buffer/upload.rs:557-566` (`upload_instances`
  gate), `:612-616` (`upload_previous_models`), `:730-736` (`upload_indirect_draws`);
  `byroredux/src/render/mod.rs:519-530` (the opaque `draw_sort_key` arm) and `:545-571`
  (`sort_draw_commands`); `byroredux/src/render/static_meshes.rs:409` (`sort_depth`
  computation); `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/context/draw.rs:2801-2806`, `:3056`, `:3311-3319`
  (instances built in sorted order, then uploaded)
- **Status**: NEW
- **Description**: The three sibling dirty gates skip the copy + flush when the current
  frame's slice hashes byte-identical to the last one written into this frame-in-flight slot.
  Their docstrings justify the win as *"static interiors produce byte-identical slices each
  frame"*. That premise does not hold whenever the camera moves. `gpu_instances` is built by
  walking `draw_commands` **after** `sort_draw_commands`, and the opaque sort key's
  penultimate component is `cmd.sort_depth` — a full-precision `f32`-to-sortable-`u32`
  reinterpretation of clip-space `w`, recomputed per draw per frame. Any camera translation or
  rotation that inverts the depth order of two draws sharing a `mesh_handle` permutes their
  `GpuInstance` entries. The bytes are the same multiset; the *slice* is not, so the hash
  differs and all three gates miss.

  Instanced batching guarantees the collision case is the common one: the whole point of
  grouping on `mesh_handle` is that real cells place the same mesh many times, and those are
  exactly the draws whose relative order `sort_depth` arbitrates. The per-instance payload is
  otherwise stable under camera motion — `GpuInstance.model` is render-origin-relative and the
  origin only re-snaps on a cell-grid crossing (`RENDER_ORIGIN_SNAP`), and
  `texture_index` / `material_id` / `flags` do not depend on the view.

  The codebase already documents the reordering, in the field that exists to work around it:
  `GpuInstance.surface_id` is *"Stable draw identity used by temporal direct-shadow reservoirs.
  Unlike the per-frame instance-buffer index, this follows the ECS entity when **depth sorting**
  or animated actors **reorder draw commands**"* (`gpu_types.rs:157-160`), pinned by
  `restir_history_uses_stable_surface_id_not_instance_order`. So one part of the renderer treats
  per-frame instance reordering as a given while another part's optimisation assumes it away.
- **Evidence**:
  ```rust
  // byroredux/src/render/mod.rs:519-530 — opaque arm of draw_sort_key
  (rt_only, 0u8, 0u8, cmd.render_layer as u32, cmd.two_sided as u32, 0, 0,
   pack_depth_state(cmd) as u32,
   cmd.mesh_handle, // group identical meshes
   cmd.sort_depth,  // front-to-back within group   <-- view-dependent, recomputed per frame
   cmd.entity_id)
  ```
  ```rust
  // byroredux/src/render/static_meshes.rs:409
  let sort_depth = f32_sortable_u32(clip.w);   // f32 bit pattern, no quantisation
  ```
  ```rust
  // crates/renderer/src/vulkan/scene_buffer/upload.rs:566
  let hash = hash_instance_slice(&instances[..count]);
  if self.last_uploaded_instance_hash[frame_index] == Some(hash) { return Ok(()); }
  ```
- **Impact**: In gameplay the gates are not merely ineffective, they are net negative: a miss
  pays the full `FxHasher` pass over the slice **and** the memcpy + flush it was meant to
  avoid. At the docstring's own MedTek reference workload (7 359 draws) the per-frame read
  overhead is `7359 × (160 + 64 + 20) B` ≈ 1.80 MB hashed, on top of the same 1.80 MB copied —
  ~108 MB/s each at 60 fps. The documented ~54 MB/s saving is realised only while the camera is
  completely still (menus, `--bench-hold`, a parked bench camera), which is also the only state
  the gates were ever observed in. Nothing renders incorrectly.
- **Related**: #1134 (`upload_instances` gate), #878 (`upload_materials` gate), #1809
  (`upload_indirect_draws` gate), #2036 (`upload_lights` gate), #2692 (the 112→128 B figure
  correction in the same docstring, now itself 160 B). Distinct from #3246 (animated material
  float bits in the *material* dedup key — a different gate and a different mechanism).
  `PERF-D2-2026-08-30-01/-02` (this session) cover the sort's *cost*, not its effect on the
  upload gates.
- **Suggested Fix**: Quantise the opaque tiebreaker — replace `cmd.sort_depth` at slot 9 with a
  coarse bucket (e.g. the top 8–10 bits of the sortable `u32`) so sub-bucket camera motion no
  longer permutes the slice while front-to-back early-Z ordering is preserved at the granularity
  that actually matters. Failing that, correct the three docstrings so the next reader does not
  budget for a saving that only exists at rest.

- **Severity**: MEDIUM
- **Dimension**: SSBO Sizing & Upload
- **Location**: `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/scene_buffer/upload.rs:771-863`
  (`upload_terrain_tiles`), `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/context/draw.rs:3361-3374` (the call,

  `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/context/init.rs:1471`
  (`terrain_tiles: vec![None; scene_buffer::MAX_TERRAIN_TILES]`),
  `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/texture.rs:826` (`wait_for_fences(&[fence], true, u64::MAX)`)
- **Status**: NEW (sibling of **CLOSED #2719**, the same defect class fixed for the UI overlay)
- **Description**: This is the one upload in the whole scene-buffer path whose byte count is
  `O(MAX_*)` rather than `O(live)`. `terrain_tiles` is a fixed 1024-entry `Vec<Option<_>>`;
  `fill_terrain_tiles` does `dest.extend(tiles.iter().map(|t| t.unwrap_or_default()))`, so the
  scratch is always exactly 1024 × 96 B = 98 304 B no matter how many slots are occupied. One
  tile is allocated per terrain quad (`byroredux/src/cell_loader/terrain.rs:639`), so a
  radius-3 exterior grid holds on the order of 49 live tiles — roughly 95 % of every upload is
  `GpuTerrainTile::default()` padding.

  The bigger cost is the delivery mechanism. Each dirty upload creates a fresh 98 KB staging
  buffer (`create_staging_buffer` → create + allocate + bind + map), memcpys into it, then calls
  `with_one_time_commands`, which submits to `graphics_queue` and does a blocking
  `vkWaitForFences(…, u64::MAX)` — draining everything previously submitted on that queue —
  before destroying the staging buffer and its fence. All of this runs on the render thread in
  the middle of `draw_frame`'s command recording. `terrain_tiles_dirty` is set by **every**
  `allocate_terrain_tile` and `free_terrain_tile` call (`resources.rs:65`, `:49`), so the upload
  fires on every frame in which any terrain slot was touched — i.e. a run of consecutive frames
  during exterior grid streaming and cell unload, not the "few times a minute" the function's own
  comment assumes.
- **Evidence**:
  ```rust
  // context/resources.rs:15-27 — always 1024 entries, live count irrelevant
  dest.clear();
  dest.extend(tiles.iter().map(|t| t.unwrap_or_default()));
  ```
  ```rust
  // upload.rs:805-847 — transient staging per upload, then a blocking submit
  let (staging_buffer, staging_alloc) =
      super::super::buffer::create_staging_buffer(device, allocator, byte_size, "terrain_tile_staging")?;
  …
  let result = super::super::texture::with_one_time_commands(device, queue, command_pool, |cmd| { … });
  ```
  ```rust
  // upload.rs:792-796 — the comment the frequency claim rests on
  // "Terrain tile uploads run at cell-transition frequency (a few times
  //  a minute at most), so skip the StagingPool reuse overhead"
  ```
- **Impact**: A full graphics-queue drain plus a buffer create/allocate/bind/map/destroy cycle,
  on the render thread, on each frame of an exterior cell crossing — precisely the frames whose
  frame time already spikes from streaming. This is the same failure mode as CLOSED #2719 ("UI
  overlay allocates a fresh VkImage and does a blocking one-time submit every frame"), which the
  project treated as worth fixing at a comparable payload size.
- **Related**: #2719 (closed, same class), #497 / #470 (the design this function implements),
  #2463 (the `GpuTerrainTile` 96 B pin), `PERF-D3-2026-08-30-03` (the 32 B doc row).
- **Suggested Fix**: Track a live high-water slot index and upload only `[0 ..= high_water]`;
  take the staging buffer from the existing `StagingPool` rather than creating one per call;
  and record the copy into the frame's own command buffer with a TRANSFER→SHADER_READ barrier
  (as `record_bone_world_copy` already does) instead of a synchronous one-time submit.
