  was closed with only the CPU-fill third fixed; the code comment says so and names no successor)
- **Description**: `bone_world` is a sparse array indexed by `slot_id × MAX_BONES_PER_MESH`
  (144), sized to `(max_used_slot + 1) × 144` matrices. `upload_bone_worlds` memcpys **the whole
  array** into the per-FIF staging buffer and `record_bone_world_copy` issues a single

  `skin_palette.comp` dispatch (`bone_input_upload_bytes`). The only gate is #1811's
  `clean_skin_frames` streak: it skips the trio entirely while **no** pose changed, and runs the
  full-width trio as soon as **any** pose changed. There is no per-slot granularity.

  `261 × 144 × 64 B` ≈ 2.4 MB of host memcpy **plus** 2.4 MB of device copy **plus** a
  proportionally-sized compute dispatch, every frame, to deliver 9 KB of changed data. The
  information needed to narrow it already exists and is already threaded to the renderer:
  `SkinSlotPool::pose_dirty()` is passed into `FrameInputs.pose_dirty` (`app_frame.rs:540`) and

  the bone-world copy is the one consumer that ignores it.

  ("the full `MAX_BONES_PER_MESH`-wide stride … most of which is padding tail beyond that
  entity's own bone count") and defers it as "the remaining two-thirds of the issue's
  three-fold cost". The *across-slot* multiplier — copying clean slots at all — is not named in
  that comment, in #1794's body, or anywhere else. `max_used_slot` is a high-water figure that
  `sweep` only compacts when the freed set includes the contiguous top of the range, so a single
  surviving high-numbered entity keeps the full span alive.
- **Evidence**:

  let required_slots = (pool.max_used_slot() as usize + 1) * MAX_BONES_PER_MESH;
  bone_world_out.resize(required_slots, IDENTITY_4X4);
  ```
  ```rust
  // upload.rs:238-259 — no dirty-slot narrowing; whole array, one range
  let count = bone_world.len().min(MAX_TOTAL_BONES);
  let byte_size = (std::mem::size_of::<[[f32; 4]; 4]>() * count) as vk::DeviceSize;
  std::ptr::copy_nonoverlapping(bone_world.as_ptr() as *const u8, world_mapped.as_mut_ptr(), byte_size as usize);
  world_buf.flush_range(device, 0, byte_size)?;
  self.bone_input_upload_bytes[frame_index] = byte_size;

  // crates/core/src/ecs/resources/skin_slot_pool.rs:355-357
  pub fn max_used_slot(&self) -> u32 { self.next_slot.saturating_sub(1) }

  Full-pool worst case (1365 slots) ≈ 12.6 MB/frame ≈ 755 MB/s."* Those figures still stand for
  the memcpy + copy halves; only the CPU identity-refill was removed (verified INTACT this
  session by sibling Dimension 1).
- **Impact**: The dominant per-frame host→device transfer in any scene with actors — larger
  than the instance SSBO — and it scales with skinned-entity *density and slot fragmentation*
  rather than with how much actually animated. It is also the sizing input for the

Issue #3667: PERF-D5-2026-08-30-02: `copy_depth_to_history` runs a full-render-resolution depth copy plus four layout barriers every frame for a feature most frames don't use, and no GPU timer covers it

- **Severity**: MEDIUM
- **Dimension**: GPU Pipeline
- **Location**: `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/context/post_passes.rs:54-145`
  (`copy_depth_to_history`); unconditional call site
  `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/context/draw.rs:3676`
- **Status**: NEW
- **Description**: Immediately after the main render pass, every frame, the engine
  transitions the depth image `DEPTH_STENCIL_READ_ONLY_OPTIMAL → TRANSFER_SRC`,
  the history image `SHADER_READ_ONLY → TRANSFER_DST`, issues a full-extent
  `vkCmdCopyImage` of the D32 depth buffer, then transitions both back. The sole
  consumer is the soft-particle depth fade in `crates/renderer/shaders/triangle.frag:970-983`,
  which is itself gated on `(mat.materialFlags & MAT_FLAG_EFFECT_SOFT) != 0u &&
  mat.softFalloffDepth > 0.0`. A scene with no soft-effect material pays the entire
  copy for a texture nothing samples.
- **Evidence**: `draw.rs:3676` calls it with no predicate of any kind:
  ```rust
  self.copy_depth_to_history(cmd);
  ```
  The shader-side gate is the *only* read of `depthHistoryTex`
  (`crates/renderer/shaders/include/bindings.glsl:333` declares it; `triangle.frag:973`
  is the single `texture(depthHistoryTex, …)` call site).
- **Impact**: Derived from the checked-in `D32_SFLOAT` depth format and
  `frame_extents.render`: 8.3 MB read + 8.3 MB write per frame at 1920×1080,
  33.2 MB each way at native 3840×2160 — plus two full `vkCmdPipelineBarrier`
  pairs that sit directly between the render pass and the whole post chain. This
  is also the **only per-frame GPU pass in the frame with no `gpu_timers`
  bracket**: it falls in the gap between `cmd_main_render_end` and
  `cmd_svgf_start`, so it is invisible to the console/bench per-pass summary and
  cannot be measured today without adding an instrument. That is the same
  measurement-gap shape as `PERF-2026-08-27b-02`.
- **Related**: `PERF-2026-08-27b-02` (a pass whose own doc defers tuning to a
  measurement no timer can produce). The `caustic_splat` pass next door already
  demonstrates the CPU-side skip pattern this wants.
- **Suggested Fix**: Two independent, cheap steps. (1) Add a
  `copy_depth_to_history` bracket to `GpuPerFrameTimers` (the query pool grows
  28→30, `active_bits` has spare bits) so the cost is measurable before anything
  is changed. (2) Gate the copy on a scene-level "any loaded material carries
  `MAT_FLAG_EFFECT_SOFT`" bit rather than a per-frame draw-list scan — a
  per-frame predicate would leave a newly-appearing FX sampling arbitrarily stale
  depth on its first frame, whereas a scene-level bit cannot. The skip is
  layout-neutral: the helper leaves the depth image in the same
  `DEPTH_STENCIL_READ_ONLY_OPTIMAL` it found it in, which is also the precondition
  `depth_capture_record_copy` documents on the very next line — so omitting the
  call cannot break the layout contract of anything downstream. Confidence on the
  layout-neutrality argument: high (in/out layouts are literally identical); on
  the magnitude: unmeasured, which is what step (1) is for.

Issue #3668: PERF-D5-2026-08-30-03: `memory-budget.md`'s G-buffer VRAM row understates the live attachment set by 4–10× and contradicts its own two columns

- **Severity**: MEDIUM
- **Dimension**: GPU Pipeline
- **Location**: `docs/engine/memory-budget.md:538`; ground truth
  `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/gbuffer.rs` (format constants + the seven
  `Attachment` fields) and `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/context/helpers.rs:190-223`
- **Status**: NEW
- **Description**: The row reads
  `| G-buffer (8 attachments × 2 FIF, incl. FSR reactive/transparency masks) | ~23 MB | ~47 MB (4K) |`.
  Every neighbouring row labels its columns 1080p / 4K. Computed from the shipped
  formats, the seven `GBuffer` attachments are 22 B/px → **91.2 MB** at 1080p ×2 FIF
  and **365.0 MB** at native 4K ×2 FIF. Read as the row's own "8 attachments"
  (i.e. including the `R16G16B16A16_SFLOAT` HDR colour) plus depth and
  depth_history, it is **141.0 MB** and **564.0 MB**. Either way the figures are
  4× to 10× low. The row is also self-inconsistent: a 4K "peak" only 2× the 1080p
  "typical" is impossible for a resolution-scaled allocation with 4× the pixels.
- **Evidence**: `git log -L538,538` shows the numbers were **incremented, never
  recomputed**, across the attachment-count churn: `78540d8e` seeded
  `7 attachments → ~35 MB / ~70 MB`; `ca874e41` (the `#1583`/`#1590` reservoir
  removal) wrote `6 attachments → ~22 MB / ~45 MB`; `2cb86be5` (the FSR mask
  addition) wrote `8 attachments → ~23 MB / ~47 MB` — i.e. two whole attachments,
  one of them 8 B/px, were added for +1 MB.
- **Impact**: `memory-budget.md` is named in `_audit-common.md` as an authoritative
  doc auditors are told to prefer over re-deriving, and this row feeds the
  `~1.74 GB` / `~3.4 GB at native 4K` totals two rows below. Understating one
  resolution-scaled subsystem by ~200 MB at 1080p and ~500 MB at 4K makes the
  "inside the < 4 GB target" conclusion unsound at native 4K — the same class of
  ledger error as `PERF-2026-08-27b-01` (vertex/index pool) and `#3447` (Instance
  SSBO), on a different row of the same table. `docs/engine/shader-pipeline.md`'s
  G-Buffer Layout table is, by contrast, correct and current.
- **Related**: `PERF-2026-08-27b-01`, open `#3447`. Both are the same defect class;
  neither covers this row.
- **Suggested Fix**: Replace the row with the computed figures and split HDR
  colour / depth / depth_history out explicitly, then re-total the table. Better:
  derive the number in code the way the volumetrics section already does
  (`FROXEL_BYTES_PER_SLOT` is read by a regression test *and* the boot log) — a
  *GBUFFER_BYTES_PER_PIXEL* constant next to the format constants, asserted by a
  test, would make this row impossible to drift again.

Issue #3669: PERF-D6-2026-08-30-01: `SKINNED_BLAS_REFIT_THRESHOLD` has no per-entity stagger, so a cell's NPC cohort drops and rebuilds its skinned BLASes in lockstep every 601 dirty frames

- **Severity**: MEDIUM
- **Dimension**: Skinning & BLAS
- **Location**: `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/context/skinned_blas_refit.rs:270-281`; `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/acceleration/constants.rs:68`; `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/acceleration/predicates.rs:107-109`; `crates/renderer/src/vulkan/acceleration/blas_skinned.rs:130-200,297-300,366`
- **Status**: NEW
- **Description**: `refit_count` starts at `0` for every skinned BLAS the moment its
  fresh BUILD registers (`blas_skinned.rs:366`) and is advanced by exactly one per
  *dirty* frame. `should_rebuild_skinned_blas_after` is a bare
  `refit_count >= SKINNED_BLAS_REFIT_THRESHOLD` with no per-entity offset, jitter, or
  per-frame rebuild budget. Every entity that first-sights in the same frame and then
  animates continuously therefore reaches 600 on the *same* frame, and
  `record_skinned_blas_refit` drops all of them and re-queues all of them into the
  same frame's `first_sight_builds` batch. An NPC playing any looping idle animation
  is pose-dirty every frame (the idle clip moves bones, so the FNV-1a pose hash
  changes), so "animating continuously" is the normal case for a populated interior,
  not a corner case.
- **Evidence**:
  ```rust
  // skinned_blas_refit.rs:270-281 — unconditional, per entity, per frame
  if accel.should_rebuild_skinned_blas(entity_id) { … accel.drop_skinned_blas(entity_id); }
  let needs_blas = accel.skinned_blas_entry(entity_id).is_none();   // now true → first_sight_builds
  ```
  ```rust
  // acceleration/predicates.rs:107-109 — no stagger term
  pub(super) fn should_rebuild_skinned_blas_after(refit_count: u32) -> bool {
      refit_count >= SKINNED_BLAS_REFIT_THRESHOLD          // = 600, constants.rs:68
  }
  ```
  The rebuild is *not* cheap per entity: `build_skinned_blas_batched_on_cmd` does a
  host `get_acceleration_structure_build_sizes` (`blas_skinned.rs:142`), a fresh
  `GpuBuffer::create_device_local_uninit` for the AS store (`:150`), and a
  `create_acceleration_structure` (`:170`) **per entity**, then records the builds
  with a full `record_scratch_serialize_barrier` between every pair
  (`:297-300`) — the same shared-scratch serialization #1797 documents for refits,
  but with BUILD-sized work instead of UPDATE-sized work.
- **Impact**: A periodic, self-synchronising frame spike roughly every 10 s of
  continuous NPC animation (600 dirty frames @ 60 FPS), scaling with the cohort size.
  Checked-in baselines put the resident skinned population at `skin_pool_live = 248`
  (`.claude/audit-baselines/runtime/fo4-InstituteBioScience.tsv`), `206`
  (`fnv-FreesideAtomicWrangler.tsv`) and `83`
  (`skyrim_se-WhiterunDragonsreach.tsv`). The cell loader's spawn budget
  (`byroredux/src/cell_loader/work_budget.rs`) spreads first-sight over the load
  window, so the cohort is several sub-groups rather than one — the burst is spread
  over a handful of frames, not concentrated in one — but it recurs on a fixed
  10 s period and nothing damps it. The spike is already observable without new
  instrumentation: `first_sight_attempted` / `first_sight_succeeded` and
  `cpu_skin_chain_ns` on `SkinCoverageFrame` (`skin.coverage` / `bench-stats
  --break-down skin`) jump together on the rebuild frame, and `gpu_skin_blas_refit_ms`
  covers the device side.
- **Related**: #679 / AS-8-9 (introduced the threshold), #1797 (the shared-scratch
  serialization ceiling this rides on — BUILDs share the same barrier chain as
  refits), #1196 (the refit gate that decides which entities advance `refit_count`),
  #1812 (`built_this_frame`, which correctly suppresses the *redundant refit* after a
  rebuild but does nothing about the rebuild clustering itself).
- **Suggested Fix**: Make the threshold per-entity rather than global — e.g. compare
  against `SKINNED_BLAS_REFIT_THRESHOLD + (entity_id % SKINNED_BLAS_REFIT_JITTER)`
  inside `should_rebuild_skinned_blas_after`, or cap the number of threshold-triggered
  rebuilds admitted per frame and let the rest slip to the next. Both are a change to
  one pure predicate plus a constant, and both are unit-testable exactly the way
  `should_rebuild_skinned_blas_after` already is.

Issue #3670: PERF-D7-2026-08-30-01: one dispatch batch parses the same NIF once per cell that references it, and the main thread then throws every duplicate away

- **Severity**: MEDIUM
- **Dimension**: Streaming & Cells
- **Location**: `byroredux/src/app_step.rs:178-182`, `byroredux/src/scene/world_setup.rs:833-836`, `byroredux/src/streaming.rs:877-908` (`queue_loads`), `byroredux/src/streaming.rs:1310-1322` (`pre_parse_cell`'s cache filter), `byroredux/src/cell_loader/partial.rs:44-50`
- **Status**: NEW (residual of #862, which is CLOSED and whose guard is intact — this is the gap the #862 design leaves open by construction, not a regression of it)
- **Description**: `cached_keys` is a **single snapshot of `NifImportRegistry`
  taken once, before the whole batch is queued**, and it is `Arc`-cloned into
  every `LoadCellRequest` (`streaming.rs:899`). The worker is one thread
  draining requests serially (`cell_pre_parse_worker`, `streaming.rs:1086`) and
  keeps **no memo of what it already parsed in this batch**: `pre_parse_cell`
  dedups `model_paths` within a cell (`HashSet`, `streaming.rs:1321`) and
  filters against the snapshot (`:1317`), but nothing filters against the
  cells earlier in the same batch. A model shared by K cells queued in one
  dispatch is therefore BSA-extracted, parsed and imported K times.

  The duplicate work is then **provably discarded**: `finish_partial_import`
  opens with #864's already-cached early-out (`partial.rs:44-50`), so every
  duplicate `PartialNifImport` the worker produced past the first is dropped
  unread. All that survives is the wall-clock and the peak RSS.
- **Evidence**: The bootstrap call site documents the worst case in its own
  comment (`world_setup.rs:830-832`): *"On initial-radius dispatch the cache is
  normally empty, so this typically returns an empty set and the worker parses
  everything"*. `stream_initial_radius` queues the whole initial radius in one
  `queue_loads` — 49 cells at `--radius 3`, 225 at the documented `--radius 7`
  ceiling — against that empty snapshot. Adjacent exterior tiles in a
  worldspace share the overwhelming majority of their statics (the #862 issue
  title itself measured ">95% cache hits on shared statics" on WastelandNV once
  the cache was warm), so K is the number of cells in the batch that reference
  a given rock/road/fence, not 1.

  The payload channel is `mpsc::channel()` — **unbounded**
  (`streaming.rs:772`) — and the main thread only blocks until the *centre*
  cell arrives (`bootstrap_waiting`, `world_setup.rs:843`). The remaining

  target_count]` (`morph_compute.rs:165`) — a permanently right-sized staging buffer.

  early-out at `morph_compute.rs:189` can never fire in steady state.

  ```rust
  // byroredux/src/render/skinned.rs:285-292 — per frame, per morph slot
  for (&entity, slot) in ctx.morph_slots.iter_mut() {
      let Some(weights) = weights_q.get(entity) else { continue; };
      let target_count = slot.target_count() as usize;
      let flat: Vec<f32> = (0..target_count).map(|i| weights.get(i)).collect();   // malloc
      slot.stage_weights(flat);                                                   // free of the old one
  }
  ```
  ```rust
  // crates/renderer/src/vulkan/morph_compute.rs:175-183
  pub fn stage_weights(&mut self, weights: Vec<f32>) {
      …
      self.pending_weights = weights;        // discards the pre-sized buffer
      self.pending_weights_dirty = true;     // unconditional → flush can never early-out
  }
  ```
- **Impact**: Bounded and small per entity, but it is squarely on the per-frame
  per-entity render path the #2923/#3061 hot-path rule exists to keep clean, and it is
  the last remaining allocator traffic on that path. Size is unmeasurable today
  because `SkinCoverageFrame` carries no morph counter — the number of live
  `MorphSlot`s is a strict subset of `skin_pool_live` (248 / 206 / 83 on the FO4 /
  FNV / Skyrim baselines) but is not itself recorded anywhere. This finding is
  deliberately LOW: it is allocator churn and a redundant small mapped write, not a
  per-frame leak.
- **Related**: `PERF-D6-2026-08-24-01` (origin), #3061 (CLOSED — covered only the
  hashing half), #3231 (landed the morph path), #3244 (the dual-fence rule

  wait, only make it conditional).
- **Suggested Fix**: Change `stage_weights` to take `&[f32]` (or a closure) and write

Issue #2032: Pre-push hook gate recomputes a stamp a direct run reports as fresh, then queues on the lock

### Goal

A push from a worktree whose gate stamp is already warm reuses that stamp instead
of paying a full gate run and then queuing on the machine-wide lock.

### Context and links

The pre-push hook's gate run does not reuse a stamp that a direct run reports as
fresh. Observed 2026-08-24 during #2030: four push attempts over ~50 minutes, one
of which expired at the gate's default 1800s lock wait behind another worktree's run.

Same session, same nominal base, seconds apart:

- `pnpm agent:quality-gate --run --skip-if-fresh --base origin/main` →
  `Previous successful agent quality gate run is still fresh; skipping mapped
  commands`, exits without touching the lock.
- The hook's own run → goes straight to waiting for the lock, i.e.
  `is_fresh_success_stamp` returned false for it.

This is the symptom #1899 fixed one cause of (the untracked-add `create mode`
line moving `validation_content_signature`).

**Ordering is not the problem**, re-verified on `main` at `18e6e13b`:
`is_fresh_success_stamp` is checked at `scripts/agent-quality-gate.sh:2283`,
before `acquire_gate_run_lock` at `:2298`, and again at `:2326` after the wait.
So the hook computes a different `stamp_line()` than the direct run.

`stamp_line()` (`:2203`) is seven fields, and `--parallel` is not one of them:

```
v2  base=<base_oid>  paths=<changed_paths_hash>  plan=<command_plan_hash>
    implementation=<implementation_hash>  content=<validated_content_hash>
    packageRisk=<package_script_risk_changed>  allowPackageScripts=<...>
```

The hook is defined at `.trunk/trunk.yaml:130-137`:

```
run: git fetch --quiet origin main && bash scripts/agent-quality-gate.sh --run --parallel 3 --skip-if-fresh --base origin/main
```

### Leading hypothesis, not yet confirmed

**`base_oid` moves because the hook fetches first.** The hook runs
`git fetch --quiet origin main` immediately before the gate. A stamp warmed by a
direct run resolves `origin/main` to whatever the worktree last fetched; the
hook then advances that ref and resolves `--base origin/main` to a newer OID via
`ref_oid` (`:1872`). Every field downstream of the base — `changed_paths_hash`,
`command_plan_hash`, `validated_content_hash` — moves with it, so the stamp
misses whenever `main` advanced between the warming run and the push. `main`
takes roughly 90 commits/week, so that window is open most of the time. This
also matches the observation that the hook's run was not merely slower but
computed a different stamp for what looked like the same base.

The hook's own advice text, `scripts/agent-quality-gate.sh:1649`, is what makes this
concrete:

```
Pushing? Warm the stamps with 'pnpm agent:quality-gate --run' first, then push:
--skip-if-fresh cache-hits and exits before this lock.
```

That command names neither a fetch nor `--base origin/main`, so following the
advice literally warms a stamp against a base the hook is about to move.

Confirm or refute it before designing a fix; do not assume it. A second
candidate, if the base OIDs turn out identical: the hook executes under trunk's
persistent daemon, which captures the environment of the shell that launched it,
so `allowPackageScripts` or a path-resolution input can differ from an
interactive run.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `stamp_line()`'s seven components are individually observable under an
      opt-in debug env var (e.g. `AGENT_QUALITY_GATE_DEBUG_STAMP=1`), printed to
      stderr, so a mismatch names the field that moved instead of failing an
      opaque equality. Off by default; no change to stamp content or format.
- [ ] The two stamps are captured back to back — the direct run and the hook's
      exact command line from `.trunk/trunk.yaml:137` — and diffed. The first
      differing field is recorded in this issue or the PR.
- [ ] The mover is fixed, or — if it is inherent, as the `base_oid` hypothesis
      would make it — the hook's advice text stops advertising stamp-warming as a
      reliable way to skip the lock wait, and says what actually warms a stamp the
      hook will reuse (for example, fetching before warming).
- [ ] A repeat of the scenario reuses the stamp: warm, then run the hook's
      command line, and the second run reports the stamp as fresh and exits
      before the lock.
- [ ] `bash scripts/agent-quality-gate.test.sh` passes.

### Expected files or package area

`scripts/agent-quality-gate.sh` (`stamp_line`, `is_fresh_success_stamp`, the
lock-wait advice text), `scripts/agent-quality-gate.test.sh`,
`docs/notes/agent-quality-gate-mechanics.md`, possibly `.trunk/trunk.yaml`.

### Verification commands

```
AGENT_QUALITY_GATE_DEBUG_STAMP=1 bash scripts/agent-quality-gate.sh --run --skip-if-fresh --base origin/main
AGENT_QUALITY_GATE_DEBUG_STAMP=1 bash -c 'git fetch --quiet origin main && bash scripts/agent-quality-gate.sh --run --parallel 3 --skip-if-fresh --base origin/main'
bash scripts/agent-quality-gate.test.sh
```

No push is required to reproduce: the hook's command can be run directly.

**Run the gate unsandboxed.** Under the agent sandbox, `stat` on `**/.env.*` and

bug and are not.

The gate holds a machine-wide lock at `~/.cache/agent-quality-gate/run.lock`;
other worktrees on the same machine hold it for 45 minutes at a time. Pass
`--lock-wait 3600` rather than concluding the lock is stuck.

the symptom disappear — a stamp that survives an input change is a gate that
skips checks it should run. Debug output must be opt-in and must never print to
stdout, which the gate's own output parsing reads.

Two user-visible consequences today:

1. **Every tile link's accessible name is polluted by the pin button's label.** The link name is computed from all descendants, so the links list / voice-control target for each tool reads like `Chess Pin Chess`, or `Files NEW Pin Files` for a tile with the NEW badge. 2. **Keyboard tab stops through the launcher double** — each tile now yields two stops (link, then pin), so traversing the grid takes ~48 stops instead of 24.

## Evidence
- ARIA snapshot of a grid tile (Chromium 1280×800, `/`):
  ```
  - link "Files NEW Pin Files":
    - /url: /tools/files/
    - text: Files NEW
    - button "Pin Files": ☆
  ```
- `document.querySelectorAll('.launcher__pages a.launch-tile .launch-pin')` → **25** focusable buttons inside anchors (24 tools + Files).
- Sequential-focus trace starting from the Chess tile: `launch-pin|Pin Chess → launch-tile|Quick Notes ☆ → launch-pin|Pin Quick Notes → launch-tile|Color Picker ☆ → …` (alternating link/button stops).

- Note: axe-core's `nested-interactive` rule does **not** flag button-in-link (its matcher only covers children-presentational widget roles), so automated scans pass — this won't be caught by CI or a Lighthouse run.

`e332283` ("launcher: pinned tools band and new-tool badges", 2026-07-04) has no body and no linked PR/issue discussing the nesting. The same commit carefully added `aria-pressed`, per-state `aria-label`s and Enter/Space handlers — accessibility was clearly intended, the nesting looks like an oversight. ## Suggested fix
Render the pin as a **sibling** of the anchor inside the (already `position:relative`) tile wrapper — the ☆ is absolutely positioned anyway, so the visual result is identical; or switch the tile to the overlay-link pattern used by feed cards. Either restores clean link names ("Chess") and one tab stop per tile plus one per pin outside the link.

severity:minor — the pins remain operable by mouse, keyboard and touch; the harm is screen-reader name pollution on all 24 tool links, doubled keyboard traversal of the launcher, and spec-invalid markup whose AT behavior is known to vary.

**Context**

A SCORM package is arbitrary third-party HTML and JavaScript, uploaded by a customer, often produced by a vendor neither of us has met. The standard's API discovery walks `window.parent` for `API` or `API_1484_11`, which is a same-origin operation — so the shortest path to a working player is to serve packages from the application origin. The AI Adapter track (#19092, #17097) is building "Natural Language to Infrastructure" — feeding the LLM Meshery **Models / schema definitions** so it can generate valid designs. - `topology.query` — query the cluster-safe topology graph (resources + relationships) for a given context/connection.

- "Which of my Services have no ready endpoints across all connected clusters?" answered by an agent over real topology.

- A safe first step for agentic / MCP integration that carries no mutation risk.

## Status

**In progress, 2026-08-27.** RFC-0137 was re-accepted and reached `3-integrated`
(metel-docs#43-#46); both blocking design gaps (Open Questions 5-6) were resolved
during that pass. This umbrella issue's scope below was then split into two scheduled
slices, each with its own issue and its own acceptance criteria (superseding the
Scope/Acceptance-criteria sections below, kept here for history):

- #857 (slice 1 -- representation + branded projection, RFC-0137 §1-4): **done**,
  merged in metel-core#861 + metel-docs#47.
- #858 (slice 2 -- move-triggered narrowing/widening, row-bounded `Drop` dispatch,
  RFC-0137 §2/5-6): open, not started. Depends on #857's representation
  (`Type::Residual`/`InferType::Residual`), which it must reuse as-is.

Split out of #827 once RFC-0137 reached `2-accepted` (2026-08-25); that issue tracked
getting the RFC reviewed and accepted, this one tracks building it.

## Scope

RFC-0137 (Nominal Types as Branded Rows, `2-accepted`): every `struct`, not only
RFC-0120's opt-in `record` kind, is represented for type-checking purposes as
`(brand, row)` — a fixed, compile-time-only identity tag minted at declaration, paired
with the set of fields currently present. Fixes the motivating bug found while fixing
#740/#774: `Self.{ fd }`/`Handle.{ fd }` currently accepts an unrelated anonymous record
exactly as readily as a value actually derived from the struct, since RFC-0116's shipped
projection carries no brand at all.

### 1. Representation and narrowing (RFC-0137 §1-2)

- Every `struct` declaration mints a brand at declaration time (a fourth surface use of
  the identity kind `brand-kind-unification.md` §8 already unifies allocator tags,
  lifetime anchors, and RFC-0076 brands under — not a new mechanism).
- Whole-value construction and use are unaffected: a freshly-constructed value's row is
  its full field set, and every program that never triggers narrowing typechecks exactly
  as before.
- A partial move (`move h.name`, under `--move-check`) and a struct's own field
  projection (`h.{ fd }`, RFC-0116 §4) both narrow the value's static type to
  `Brand.{ remaining-fields }` — the same brand, not a bare anonymous record. These two
  are one mechanism: projection is narrowing performed explicitly on a copy of the
  reference, rather than as a side effect of consuming the original.

### 2. Eligibility gate (RFC-0137 §3)

Separate "has a row" (universal, every struct) from "row is visible to structural
matching" (stays exactly as opt-in as RFC-0120's existing three-tier model):

- A single per-declaration flag records whether a struct's row is ever visible to
  `HasField`-style checks and row-conditional impl resolution. Narrowing or projecting —
  at any width, including full width — never touches that flag; it is fixed once at
  declaration, not reconsidered by row content.
- Regression case (RFC-0137 §3's worked example): a plain `struct Handle { fd, name }`
  projected to `h.{ fd, name }` must stay rejected against a bound requiring
  `record T: { fd, name, .. }`, even though its row is then identical in content to an
  actual `record NamedHandle { fd, name }`'s.

### 3. Passing a residual to a function (RFC-0137 §4)

- A parameter typed `SomeStruct.{ field }` (or `Self.{ field }` inside `extend`) is
  ordinary type-matching against a real, branded type — it must accept a value actually
  narrowed/projected from that struct and reject a same-shaped anonymous record literal
  or a same-shaped residual of a different brand. This is the direct fix for the
  #740/#774 motivating bug.
- No implicit truncation at the call boundary: passing a wider residual than the
  parameter's row must still be rejected, requiring the caller to narrow first. (A
  `.narrow()` convenience utility is explicitly out of scope — see below.)

### 4. `Drop` dispatch against a narrowed residual (RFC-0137 §5)

- For each `Drop` impl, compute once at compile time the union of fields the destructor
  body reads directly, plus — transitively, as a fixed point over the type's own method
  set — the required sets of every `self`-method it calls (mutual recursion among the
  type's own helpers handled via ordinary visited-set tracking). A call passing some
  other struct's value reasons against that struct's own, independently-computed set,
  not this one's.
- Relax `--move-check`'s current `MoveViolationKind::PartialMoveOfDropType` check (real,
  tested, and enforced today per RFC-0071 §7's unconditional ban) so that a partial move
  of a `Drop`-implementing struct is allowed exactly when the residual's row remains a
  superset of that impl's computed required set — rejected only when the destructor
  could observe a field that's actually gone.

### 5. Generic structs (RFC-0137 §7)

- A generic struct's brand is tied to its declaration, not to any one instantiation
  (`Pair<i64>` and `Pair<String>` share one brand). Narrowing a generic struct's value
  needs nothing beyond what generic field access already provides — a field's symbolic
  type pre-monomorphization composes the same way it already does for ordinary field
  access.
- §4's Drop-dispatch required-set computation must not depend on any generic parameter
  `T` — the same fixed set applies across every instantiation of a generic `Drop` impl.

Issue #900: RFC-0150: Nested Row Narrowing -- review, accept, and implement

## Purpose

Review, accept, and implement **RFC-0150 — Nested Row Narrowing**.

Split from RFC-0117 (Row Narrowing) on 2026-08-29. RFC-0117's pre-acceptance
review established that narrowing a field *of* a record-typed field **in place**
(`o.inner.a`, leaving `o : Outer.{ inner: Inner.{ b }, tag }`) needs a recursive
residual type system RFC-0117 deliberately avoids. RFC-0117 ships flat for
v0.13.0; this is the recursive follow-up.

## Design surface (from RFC-0117's review)

1. **Residual type grammar** for a branded row whose field type differs from the
   declaration — `Outer.{ inner: Inner.{ b }, tag }` is new syntax, or needs an
   internal desugaring.
2. **Recursive type identity** — `(brand, recursively-canonical field map)`;
   history-independent; anonymous records never acquire a brand.
3. **Tuple-field residuals** — RFC-0071 §9a tracks tuple elements like struct
   fields, so `o.t.0` partially moves `o.t`; either define tuple residuals or
   reject nested narrowing through a tuple-typed field.
4. **Recursive `Drop` receiver shapes** — RFC-0137 §5's flat required-field set
   must become a receiver shape/tree; dispatch checks nested field types
   recursively. Depends on RFC-0147/0148's narrowed-`drop`-receiver syntax.
5. **Control-flow joins** for path-dependent nested residuals — lift the move
   checker's existing join/fixpoint behavior into the spec for the nested case.
6. **RFC-0119 round-tripping** — `to_record` must carry nested residual field
   types through; `from_record` to the full type stays widening / Construct.
7. **Termination domain** — `R(T)` over finite product type trees only;
   references, enums, arrays, functions, unconstrained generics are atomic.

## Dependencies

- **RFC-0117** (flat narrowing) — the base this extends.
- **RFC-0137** (`3-integrated`) — `(brand, row)` representation, §5 `Drop` dispatch.
- **RFC-0147 / RFC-0148** (`1-under-review`) — narrowed `drop` receiver forms;
  §4's recursive shape is declared in their syntax, so RFC-0150 is scheduled
  after them.
- RFC-0116 (grammar addition), RFC-0071 §9a (tuples), RFC-0119, RFC-0114.

## Not urgent

RFC-0117 is complete and acceptable without this — nested narrowing is an
additive capability, not a gap in the flat rule. Milestone is provisional
(v0.14.1, with RFC-0147/0148) and likely to move as those dependencies settle.

Issue #302: Enumerate a website authoritatively from sitemap indexes

## Objective

Implement a complete, bounded sitemap inventory that can drive crawler discovery and deletion reconciliation without fetching HTML to learn page membership.

This is **P1**. Sitemap inventory is the first network release because it fits the existing discover-then-fetch connector contract; arbitrary link traversal does not.

## Dependencies

- #300 URL scope and SSRF-safe HTTP policy
- #301 robots and bounded transport behavior

## Required behavior

- Support XML sitemaps and sitemap indexes.
- Follow nested sitemap indexes through the shared URL/HTTP policy.
- Normalize and scope every `loc` before it enters membership.
- Bound compressed bytes, expanded bytes, XML depth, sitemap nesting, sitemap count, URL count and total run bytes.
- Detect cycles and duplicate sitemap/page URLs.
- Stream XML rather than materializing an unbounded document.
- Preserve deterministic source-native batches for durable journal admission.
- Record `lastmod` as metadata only; it is not a trustworthy sole version token.
- Yield one stable, duplicate-free, authoritative page inventory in deterministic order.
- Distinguish a genuinely empty complete sitemap from a failed, bounded, cancelled, cyclic or partially read inventory.
- Only true exhaustion of the complete sitemap graph can authorize deletion reconciliation or a candidate watermark.

## Acceptance criteria

1. Plain and indexed sitemaps enumerate exact normalized membership.
2. Duplicate page entries collapse without losing diagnostics; conflicting metadata follows one documented rule.
3. Nested indexes reach the real end and preserve bounded page admission.
4. Cycles, malformed XML, cross-origin entries, media-type mismatch and decompression expansion fail closed.
5. Reaching any configured limit produces an incomplete inventory and no deletion proof.
6. An explicitly empty valid sitemap is complete and may reconcile an empty site subject to the normal deletion ceiling.
7. `lastmod` cannot cause an unchanged skip by itself.
8. Cancellation/interruption advances no watermark.
9. Memory remains bounded independently of sitemap URL count.

## Required tests

Generate synthetic streaming sitemap trees. Cover plain/index forms, exact boundary counts, deep nesting, duplicates, cycles, cross-origin URLs, malformed XML, compressed input, expansion bombs, empty complete inventory, later-page failure, cancellation and deterministic batching.

Issue #220: infra(security): shrink workflow-token blast radius — dedicated bot account (public_repo+project classic PAT), token expiry policy

## Motivation

The #208/#209 automation (`mutants-report.yml`, `board-triage.yml`) authenticates with two classic PATs stored as repo secrets (`KWIKI_MUTANTS_REPORT_TOKEN`, `KWIKI_BOARD_TRIAGE_TOKEN`), both `repo` + `project` scopes — forced by a real API gap: fine-grained tokens and `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot write **user-owned** Projects. Classic PATs are account-scoped credentials, not project-scoped: a leaked token with `repo` grants read/write to **every repository the account can access** (personal + every org membership, incl. client orgs without SAML enforcement), and `project` grants control of **all** user projects. The workflow engineering is already sound (secrets only in Actions, schedule/workflow_run triggers only, no fork-PR path, explicit `permissions:` blocks, fail-loud on missing secrets); the residual risk is purely the credential blast radius.

**Priority: low** (single-maintainer repo, no exposure path today), but it hardens before collaborators ever join.

## Scope

### 1. Immediate (minutes, no code)

- [ ] Set **90-day expirations** on both classic PATs; calendar reminder to rotate. Rotation drill: revoke → re-create → update the two repo secrets → next scheduled run self-heals.
- [ ] Add **branch protection on `main` requiring review for `.github/workflows/**`** changes (blocks the echo-the-secret exfiltration path for any future collaborator).

### 2. Structural — dedicated bot account (identity isolation; org migration ruled out)

Research verdict (2026-08-30): GitHub Apps **cannot** access user-owned Projects v2 (not supported as project collaborators; the App "Projects" permissions cover only org/classic projects), and fine-grained PATs remain unreliable for user-project GraphQL (community evidence conflicts; `actions/add-to-project` maintainers state fine-grained doesn't work there). The only reliable credential for a user-owned board is a classic PAT with `project` scope — so isolate the **identity** instead of the scope: the classic PAT lives on a dedicated bot account whose entire existence is the two objects the automation needs.

Setup:

- [ ] Create the bot account (e.g. `mguinada-kwiki-bot`): unique email (dedicated mailbox or plus-address), **2FA enabled**, nothing else — no org memberships, no other repos, no other projects.
- [ ] Grant exactly two things:
      | Target | Role | Covers |
      |---|---|---|
      | K-Wiki Kanban (project) | **Write** collaborator | Lane/field writes only — no project settings, no admin |
      | mguinada/k-wiki (public repo) | **Triage** collaborator | Create/update the rolling survivor issue |
- [ ] Bot's classic PAT scopes: **`public_repo` + `project` only**. The repo is PUBLIC (verified), so `public_repo` suffices for issue writes — the token **cannot touch any private repo or any org content at all**, even orgs without SAML enforcement. No `repo`, no `read:org`, no `workflow`.
- [ ] Set an expiration on the bot PAT anyway (90 days; the rotation drill below applies).
- [ ] Replace both repo secrets' values with the bot PAT (`KWIKI_MUTANTS_REPORT_TOKEN`, `KWIKI_BOARD_TRIAGE_TOKEN` — or collapse to one secret; the workflows are unchanged either way).
- [ ] Update the workflow comments/post-merge notes that document the classic-PAT requirement — the rationale text changes from "fine-grained gap" to "bot-isolated classic PAT".
- [ ] Kill-switch drill (documented in the issue): revoke PAT → remove both collaborator grants → board and issue writes stop; re-grant + new secret to restore. Two clicks, no account-wide exposure either way.

Blast radius after: a leaked bot PAT grants *write to one public repo's issues + one project*. Not the owner's account, not client orgs, not private repos, not other user projects. Attribution bonus: board moves and issue updates show as the bot — a clean audit trail separating automation from human actions.

**Rejected alternatives (recorded for posterity):**
- Org project migration — ruled out by the operator (not convenient); would have enabled fine-grained tokens.
- GitHub App — cannot access user-owned Projects v2 (research-confirmed).
- Local launchd board-sync with keyring auth (zero CI credentials) — genuinely more secure by construction, but moves board freshness onto the local Mac and discards the CI automation #209 built; kept in reserve if the bot account is ever deemed too much.

### 3. Policy

- [ ] Note the token policy in the repo docs (AGENTS.md or `.github/`): workflow tokens are fine-grained, single-repo, expiring; classic PATs only where an API gap forces them, always with expiry, one per purpose.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Both owner-account classic PATs are revoked; the workflows run green on the bot PAT (manual `workflow_dispatch` of both)
- [ ] Bot blast radius proven small: with the bot PAT authenticated, `gh api` against a second repo the owner can access and against a second user project both fail closed (403/404)
- [ ] Board moves and rolling-issue updates land attributed to the bot account
- [ ] Branch protection verified: a workflow-file change without review is rejected

- **Blocks: nothing.**
- **Blocked by: nothing** (merging #212/#214 first avoids churn on the same workflow files' comments — soft ordering, not a formal edge).

Issue #648: wxc-host-prep can recursively rewrite descendant ACLs on data-drive roots

### Relevant area(s)
Windows (AppContainer + DACL host preparation)

### Brief description
`wxc-host-prep prepare-system-drive --target <data-drive-root>` can recursively rewrite security descriptors throughout the target volume even though the two ACEs it adds are non-inheriting. On a large data volume the command therefore appears to hang and touches thousands of descendants.

I intend to submit a focused fix after filing this issue, as required by CONTRIBUTING.md.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Use a Windows data volume whose directory tree contains legacy or inheritance-inconsistent ACLs.
2. Run elevated: `wxc-host-prep.exe prepare-system-drive --target E:\`
3. Observe filesystem security activity below the root with Process Monitor.

On the affected 2 TB volume, a 15-second capture showed 10,684 `SetSecurityFile` operations below `E:\`, including package-cache and recycle-bin descendants, while host prep had only printed the first root ACE.

### Expected behavior
Only the DACL on the requested drive root changes. Descendant files and directories remain byte-for-byte unchanged, matching the documentation's “non-inheriting” contract.

### Actual behavior
The implementation writes the new root DACL with `SetNamedSecurityInfoW`. Windows documents that this API automatically propagates inheritable ACEs and applies the current inheritance model to existing children. This can normalize a large pre-existing hierarchy even when the newly added ACE itself is non-inheriting, making preparation extremely slow and unexpectedly mutating descendant ACLs.

The same risk exists in `unprepare-system-drive`, whose precise-revoke helper also ends by calling `SetNamedSecurityInfoW`.

### Proposed direction
Keep the existing read/merge/rebuild logic, but use a non-propagating security-descriptor write for the persistent system-drive prepare/unprepare path (for example `SetFileSecurityW`). Leave the runtime DACL manager's intentional propagation behavior unchanged. Add a Windows regression test proving a child DACL is unchanged.

## Summary

I would like to propose a new capability for OpenMausBot tentatively called **Teach Me**.

The goal is to allow a user to demonstrate a repetitive task once, have OpenMausBot capture the structured interaction and context, and compile that demonstration into a reusable, parameterized Skill.

The resulting Skill could then be executed manually or invoked by existing Routines and Webhooks.

The proposal is **not** to introduce another browser automation engine, another computer-use system, or another scheduler.

Instead, Teach Me should build on OpenMausBot's existing browser/computer-use infrastructure and add the missing layer that transforms a human demonstration into a reusable Skill.

## Motivation

Many repetitive tasks can be demonstrated more easily than they can be described.

For example, a user may be able to demonstrate:

1. Open an application.
2. Navigate to a process.
3. Enter a process number.
4. Search for the process.
5. Generate a document.
6. Verify that the document was generated.

Today, turning this into a reliable reusable automation requires the user to describe the workflow to the agent or construct automation logic manually.

Teach Me would allow the user to simply perform the task once.

OpenMausBot would then produce something conceptually equivalent to:

```text
generate_document(process_number)
```

The Skill could subsequently be invoked manually, by a Routine, or through a Webhook.

This would make repetitive workflows teachable by demonstration rather than requiring users to program them.

## Existing OpenMausBot capabilities

OpenMausBot already provides important building blocks for this proposal.

The existing browser architecture uses Electron's embedded Chromium and CDP, including accessibility-tree information and screenshots.

The existing computer-use architecture also favors accessibility-based targeting over pixel coordinates.

Therefore, Teach Me should **reuse these capabilities instead of introducing a separate browser recorder or browser automation engine**.

The existing structured browser representation is particularly valuable because actions can be associated with the interface state that existed when the user performed them.

For example, a demonstration could conceptually capture:

```text

  @e1 = input "Process Number"
  @e2 = button "Search"
  @e3 = button "Generate"

action:
  fill @e1 "12345"

snapshot:
  @e1 = input "Process Number"
  @e2 = button "Search"
  @e3 = button "Generate"

action:
  click @e2
```

The transient element reference is useful as grounding evidence for the demonstration.

The compiler should retain semantic and structural information sufficient to resolve the corresponding element again during future executions.

### 1. Demonstration Trace

A structured, provider-independent representation of a teaching session.

The trace should preserve, where available:

- browser/computer actions;
- transient element references;
- accessibility information;
- DOM/context information;
- URL and navigation state;
- screenshots when useful;
- values entered by the user;
- observed outputs;
- ordering of actions;

The Demonstration Trace is an intermediate artifact.

Issue #248: Proposal: `koza layer` — orchestration verb for extending an existing merged graph with new sources

## Motivation

Downstream KGs that build **on top of** a released upstream KG are becoming a real pattern — e.g. `monarch-bdc-kg` layers BDC-specific sources (SemMedDB procedure edges, SNOMED has-focus edges) onto a released `monarch-kg.duckdb`. The released duckdb is already a koza graph database, so the base layer is a file copy and `append` does the heavy lifting (~1s for 70k edges onto a 6.7GB / 15.8M-edge base).

But making the result *correct* currently requires a hand-rolled conform step around `append`. The relationship we want:

> `merge` : `join` :: `layer` : `append`

`merge` orchestrates join → normalize → prune for building a graph from per-source files. `layer` would orchestrate the same lifecycle for extending an existing graph database:

```
koza layer bdc-kg.duckdb --base monarch-kg.duckdb --input-dir overlays/ [--mappings ...]
```

internally: copy base → append overlays → normalize (new edges only) → prune → refresh derived tables.

## What layer needs beyond today's append

Each of these was hit in practice on the first real layered build:

1. **Type conformance to the target schema** — append currently stringifies jsonl arrays into scalar columns (#247). A layer verb must coerce to the base graph's conventions (e.g. monarch's `force_single_valued` `category`/`in_taxon`/`type`).

2. **Node collision policy** — overlay files carry endpoint stubs (MONDO/HP nodes referenced by their edges) that already exist in the base with richer records. Blind append produced 4,784 duplicate node ids, which fan out the `denormalized_edges` view join (70k appended edges → 122k view rows). Default should be **base wins** (drop overlay node rows whose id exists), with property-merge as a possible later option. Collisions *between* overlays need the same treatment (first wins / declared order).

3. **Provenance stamping** — `join` has `generate_provided_by`; `append` has nothing. Overlay files need `provided_by` stamped from the file stem so per-source QC and coverage attribution work. (Per-file control rather than one global flag would also benefit `merge`.)

4. **Scoped normalize** — the base graph's edges are already normalized; re-running SSSOM normalization over 15.8M edges to cover 70k new ones is wasted work. Normalize should be scopeable to edges whose `provided_by` was just appended. Monarch's closure filter is three string literals in an awk line —
`monarch-ingest/scripts/after_download.sh:32`:

```sh

```

Phenio's relation graph emits **79.3M rows** over hundreds of predicates
(`phenio/src/ontology/phenio.Makefile:309-321`, no predicate restriction); **21.3M survive** (27%).

`BFO:0000051` — the predicate `config/mappings-to-upheno-oba.rules` generates for every
`UPHENO:phenotypeToTrait` mapping — is **dropped**. The rows exist upstream
(`HP:0003074 BFO:0000051 OBA:VT0000188`, and 10 more OBA targets) and never reach the closure file.
In the shipped DB, `HP:0003074`'s closure has 126 members and **zero** OBA terms.

## 2. Closure is not a path, and existentials do not invert

`koza/src/koza/graph_operations/_closurize_engine.py:242-246` groups by `subject_id`:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE closure_id AS
SELECT subject_id AS id, ARRAY_AGG(object_id) AS closure FROM closure GROUP BY subject_id
```

So `LOINC`'s closure would gain `OBA:xxx`, and `HP`'s closure would gain `OBA:xxx`. **Neither contains
the other.** For the Solr filter query
(`monarch-app/backend/src/monarch_py/implementations/solr/solr_query_utils.py:118-127`) to fire, the
`MONDO → HP` association's `object_closure` would have to literally contain `LOINC:2345-7`. OWL does
not entail that: `A ⊑ ∃p.B` does not give `B ⊑ ∃p⁻.A`, and no property chain connects them.
`RO:0009006` as proposed points the wrong way.

## The mechanism does work when the direction is right

`UPHENO:0000001` survives the filter and points HP → CHEBI. Consequence, measured on the shipped DB:
a CHEBI glucose page's **All** tab already aggregates **9,310** phenotype associations. Same shape we
want — but with the non-phenotype node on the **object** side of the closure row.

## What would work: an inverse plus a property chain

- assert `OBA:xxx SubClassOf: measured_by some LOINC:2345-7`
- add `SubObjectPropertyOf: BFO:0000051 o measured_by → measured_by`
- add `measured_by` to the awk clause

relation-graph then materializes `HP:0003074 measured_by LOINC:2345-7` directly, with no need to

- `moon check --target all` and `moon bundle --target all` materialize several backends.
- Every plan rewrites the same file, so only the last backend remains visible to IDE and documentation tooling.

```text

  index.json
  js/
    packages.json
  native/
    packages.json
```

Issue #1827: [Topological graph theory] Extend combinatorial embeddings to orientable surfaces and exact genus

## Summary

The continued conjecture, benchmark, and operation-catalog audit found a structural gap immediately above #1728's planar-embedding boundary:

```text
connected finite graph + cyclic rotation at every vertex
    -> exact orientable cellular embedding
    -> complete face walks and Euler characteristic
    -> exact embedding genus
    -> dual combinatorial map / multigraph

bounded graph
    -> embedding of genus <= g
    -> exact minimum orientable genus only after lower-genus exhaustion
```

#1728 already owns the foundational `CombinatorialEmbedding`, dart, face-walk, and planar/Kuratowski semantics. This issue must **reuse and generalize that same rotation-system value** rather than create a second graph-embedding representation.

The missing operation is not a graph-drawing service or a general surface-topology framework. It is the exact finite combinatorics of rotation systems on orientable surfaces and the bounded optimization problem they induce.

This issue must not become a map-enumeration platform, Heawood/Ringel–Youngs theorem wrapper, arbitrary topology DSL, persistent embedding session, or conjecture solver.

Audit baseline: current `main` on 2026-08-17.

## Research and library evidence

Rotation systems encode orientable cellular graph embeddings combinatorially. Their dart permutations determine face boundary walks, and for a connected cellular embedding the genus follows exactly from:

```text
chi = |V| - |E| + |F|
chi = 2 - 2g.
```

This finite boundary recurs in:

- graph genus and minimum-genus problems;
- dual maps and embedded graph invariants;
- topological graph theory and excluded-surface arguments;
- map coloring and face-width questions;
- polyhedral maps and cellular decompositions; and
- benchmark certificates that need more than planar/nonplanar status.

Reference ecosystems:

- Sage graph theory documentation: https://doc.sagemath.org/html/en/reference/graphs/
- NetworkX planar/combinatorial embedding documentation: https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/reference/algorithms/planarity.html

Maintained implementations may be private producers or conformance oracles. Public authority remains the exact rotation system, dart permutations, and replayed Euler relation.

## Scope discipline

### Initial public scope

Version 1 should support **connected finite loopless graphs embedded cellularly in closed orientable surfaces**.

The initial graph carrier may be:

- the existing `SimpleUndirectedGraph`; and
- later #1680's edge-ID multigraph value, which is necessary for fully general embedded duals and maps with parallel edges.

Connectedness is not cosmetic. For disconnected graphs, a rotation system alone can describe componentwise surfaces or embeddings whose faces have several boundary components, and the naive connected Euler formula becomes ambiguous. Start with connected graphs and add a separately specified disconnected convention only when its surface-component semantics are explicit.

### Explicit non-goals for version 1

Do not silently include:

- nonorientable surfaces, which require signed rotation systems or equivalent additional data;
- graph drawings or coordinates;
- embeddings with boundary/punctures;
- arbitrary CW complexes;
- map isomorphism/canonical enumeration at large scale; or
- minimum-genus claims from a heuristic embedding alone.

## Reused and extended values

### 1. `CombinatorialEmbedding`

Reuse #1728's graph-bound value:

```text
for every vertex v:
  one cyclic order of exactly the incident darts/edges
```

For simple graphs a dart may be represented by an oriented endpoint pair. For multigraphs it must include stable edge ID.

Required invariants:

- every incidence appears exactly once in the local rotation;
- every graph edge contributes exactly two opposite darts;
- no undeclared incidence appears;
- local list rotation is presentation-equivalent;
- reversing every local rotation gives the orientation-reversed embedding on the same orientable surface;
- graph identity remains bound; and
- no NetworkX/Sage embedding object crosses the public boundary.

### 2. `OrientableCellularEmbedding`

Extend the checked rotation system with derived exact permutations:

```text
alpha: dart -> opposite dart
sigma: dart -> next dart around its tail vertex
phi: dart -> next dart on a face boundary
```

Fix one public convention, for example:

```text
phi = sigma^{-1} o alpha
```

or its equivalent orientation choice. The choice must be used consistently in every face/dual operation.

The value includes:

```text
complete dart domain
complete vertex cycles of sigma
complete edge transpositions of alpha
complete face cycles of phi
V,E,F
Euler characteristic
genus
```

The face cycles are the mathematical boundary walks. A bridge or repeated vertex may occur multiple times in one face walk; do not require faces to be simple cycles.

### 3. `EmbeddedDualMap`

The dual of a cellular embedding has:

```text
one dual vertex per face
one dual edge per primal edge
incidence determined by the two dart sides of that edge
one induced cyclic rotation at each dual vertex
```

The dual may have loops and parallel edges even when the primal graph is simple. Therefore the public dual result should consume/return #1680's edge-ID multigraph value once available, not force the result into `SimpleUndirectedGraph` or silently merge edges.

```text

  complete face-walk family

  Euler characteristic chi
  exact genus g
  orientation-reversal relation

INVALID_EMBEDDING:
  first concrete incidence/permutation/face obstruction
```

Issue #99: Add an attachment-prune subcommand for orphaned attachments

markfluence never deletes, so an attachment it uploaded stays on the page after the page stops referencing it. There is no way to clean those up except by hand in the Confluence UI. Add `attachment-prune PAGE` to remove them.

## What makes an attachment prunable

Two conditions, both required:

- **Unreferenced.** The page body does not name it. `cmd/export/export.go` already computes this as `referencedNames(storage)`, matching `ri:filename` anywhere in the raw storage rather than only inside `ac:image` — an attachment link target or a reference inside a passthrough macro counts as referenced.
- **Managed by markfluence.** `client.AttachmentMeta.Managed` is true only for attachments carrying the `markfluence: ` comment prefix. This half is not optional: an attachment someone added in the Confluence UI is unreferenced by definition if it is not embedded, so pruning on "unreferenced" alone would delete a PDF a human attached for reference. That is a [S5](https://github.com/mozilla/markfluence/blob/main/docs/guarantees.md) violation.

## Report the checksum, do not branch on it

Every managed attachment records a SHA-256 in its comment, which makes it possible to say whether deleting an orphan loses content: if its checksum matches an attachment the page still references, the bytes survive under another name. If it matches nothing, this is the only copy on the page.

That distinction should be **reported, not encoded as different behaviour**. Branching on it guesses; showing it lets the operator decide.

```
$ markfluence attachment-prune docs/guides/index.md --dry-run
  orphan  assets%2Fbrand.png     content also attached as ..%2Fassets%2Fbrand.png
  orphan  old-diagram.png        only copy on this page
  keep    handbook.pdf           not managed by markfluence
```

Worth noting that the second case is usually still safe: a managed attachment came from a local file, so republishing reproduces it. The exception is when that file has since been deleted from the repo — which is exactly when the checksum will not match anything.

## Guarantees

This command exists in the shape it does because of [docs/guarantees.md](https://github.com/mozilla/markfluence/blob/main/docs/guarantees.md):

- **S4** — removal is a command's stated purpose or it does not happen. This is why pruning must not be a step inside `update`. Publishing that quietly deleted things would be removal as a side effect.
- **S5** — markfluence removes only what markfluence created. The `Managed` gate.
- **S6** — a command that removes says what it will remove first and honours `--dry-run`.

S4-S6 are currently **Vacuous**: nothing in markfluence removes anything. This would be the first command to exercise them, so their status changes when it lands.

## Shape

`attachment-prune PAGE`, matching its three siblings — singular noun, noun-first, so `attachment-<TAB>` still completes as a group. PAGE goes through `internal/pageref` like the others, so it accepts a page id, a Confluence URL, **or a `.md` file with a `page_id`** — pointing at the markdown file whose images just changed is the obvious way to invoke this.

Single page to start, like `attachment-list`. Batch pruning across a space has a much larger blast radius and can follow if it is wanted.

## Prerequisites

- **A delete method in the client.** There is none: `http.MethodDelete` appears only in `send`'s idempotent-methods list.
- **`referencedNames` has to move somewhere shared.** It is local to `cmd/export` today, and export and prune must not each have their own scanner — same rule as the traversal clamp in `internal/attachfile`.
- **A schema entry**: the `command` enum plus an `if/then` branch constraining `results.items` and `summary`, or `internal/schematest` fails.

## Relationship to the file-organization work

The root-relative naming model in `_plans/025_file-organization.md` removes the most common source of orphans: today, moving a markdown file renames every attachment it references, because the name encodes the path relative to the referencing file. Under that model moving a *page* changes nothing, so nothing is stranded.

This command handles what is left over: moving or renaming an **asset** (whose identity does follow its location, by design), removing an image from a page, and orphans that already exist from before the model lands. It is a cleanup tool for the residual rather than a fix for the naming problem.

Issue #604: nowcast: resolve second-pass dependencies per generation instead of capturing Arcs at construction

## Problem

`NowcastEngine` captures its second-pass dependencies as `Arc`s at construction time — `source` (`Arc<dyn MapEngine>`), `lightning_source` (`Arc<dyn EventSource>`), and now `impact_source` (`Arc<dyn FeatureEngine>`, #603).

Because those `Arc`s are captured rather than looked up, a rebuilt dependency can never propagate into a live wrapper. `reusable_collections` (`crates/server/src/admin.rs:989`) correctly compensates by refusing to reuse a nowcast unless **every** dependency was also reused:

```rust
if base.contains(&nc.source)
    && nc.lightning_source.as_deref().is_none_or(|ls| base.contains(ls))
    && nc.impact_source.as_deref().is_none_or(|is| base.contains(is))
```

That is the right call — the alternative is silent staleness — but it composes badly with another correct rule. `csv`/`geojson` engines are excluded from the reuse pool unconditionally (`admin.rs:997`), because they read their data file once at construction and a reload is the only mechanism by which they can re-read it.

Net effect: **a nowcast with a `geojson` impact source rebuilds on every reload**, even when nothing about the nowcast, its raster source, or its own config changed. The natural impact source is a municipality/region polygon file, so this is the common configuration rather than an exotic one.

## Cost of an avoidable rebuild

A fresh `NowcastEngine` starts empty (`generations: BTreeMap::new()`, `cell_history: Vec::new()`) and nothing warms it at build time — the first generation runs on the poll loop's immediate first tick. So each reload costs:

- **A serving gap.** WMS/Maps/Tiles for the collection return nothing until the first generation completes; health reports `degraded` / "waiting for first nowcast generation". Measured ~37 s for a cold FMI S3 generation.
- **Loss of the retained cell-snapshot history** (`CELL_HISTORY_SNAPSHOTS = 48`, ~4 h). `?datetime=` into the past returns 0 features and refills only over the following hours.
- **Track identity discontinuity.** `next_track_id` resets to 1, so a client following a cell across a reload is silently looking at a different storm.

This matters most where reloads are frequent — with `watch_collections_dir = true` a palette edit under `colormaps_dir` triggers a full reload, blanking an unrelated nowcast collection.

## Proposal

Give the wrapper an indirection so a rebuilt dependency is picked up without rebuilding the wrapper: resolve dependencies at use time from a registry snapshot rather than holding a captured `Arc`.

Sketch: the server owns an `ArcSwap` registry of live engines by collection id; the nowcast holds a handle to that registry plus the configured ids, and resolves per generation (which is already the only place these are read — the impact join, the lightning fetch, and the source frame fetch all happen inside `generate()` / `poll_loop`, never per request).

With that in place, `reusable_collections` can drop the dependency conjunction entirely: a nowcast becomes reusable whenever its own config is unchanged, and a rebuilt geojson source is observed on the next generation.

## Design constraints

- Resolution must stay O(1) and lock-free at use time (`ArcSwap` read), consistent with Critical Rule 10.
- A dependency that disappears between reloads must degrade the way a source error already does — no impact/flash context for that generation, never a failed generation — rather than panicking or failing the collection.
- The load-time validation must not weaken: a `impact_source`/`lightning_source` naming a non-existent or wrong-shaped collection must still fail the collection at load, which means config validation and runtime resolution become two separate concerns rather than one lookup.
- Must not reintroduce the declaration-order hazard fixed in #603 (`base_feature_engines` snapshot): registry resolution has to be order-independent by construction.
- `nowcast`-as-a-dependency stays rejected (chaining is unsupported for `source`; cells are points, not areas, for `impact_source`).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A nowcast with a `geojson` impact source is reused across a reload when its own config is unchanged: no serving gap, cell history retained, track ids continuous.
- [ ] Editing the impact source's GeoJSON file and reloading changes the impact context served by the nowcast without rebuilding it.
- [ ] Removing a dependency collection from config degrades that join gracefully; the nowcast keeps serving frames.
- [ ] `reusable_collections` no longer needs the dependency conjunction, and its tests are updated to assert reuse where they currently assert rebuild.
- [ ] Load-time validation of dependency ids and shapes is unchanged (existing failure tests still pass).
- [ ] Resolution is declaration-order independent (the #603 regression test still passes).

## Non-goals

- Changing how `csv`/`geojson` themselves reload — always rebuilding those is correct.
- Hot-swapping a nowcast's own tuning (`horizon`, `max_pixels`, weights) without a rebuild; a config change to the nowcast itself should still rebuild it.
- Generalizing this to every engine that wraps another; do it for `nowcast` first and see whether a second consumer appears.

## Anchors

- `crates/server/src/admin.rs:989` — `reusable_collections` and the dependency conjunction
- `crates/server/src/admin.rs:997` — the `csv`/`geojson` exclusion
- `crates/server/src/admin.rs:2700` — `base_raster_engines` / `base_feature_engines` pre-pass snapshots (#603)
- `crates/engine-nowcast/src/engine.rs` — `ImpactCfg`, `lightning`, `source` fields and the `with_*_source` setters
- `crates/engine-nowcast/CLAUDE.md` — the documented consequence this issue removes
- `crates/server/CLAUDE.md` — incremental reload rules (#574)

Found while wiring #603; documented there rather than fixed, since the workaround (serve the polygons from a `postgis` collection, which reuses normally) is a config change rather than code.

Issue #113: Design durable child-step resume for composite external effects

## Summary

A single Mycelium ledger entry represents one effect transition: one effect identity, one side-effect boundary, one external-operation reference, and one terminal outcome.

When a ledgered function performs multiple independently observable external effects, those distinct outcomes are compressed into one transition. After a crash, Mycelium can safely fail closed, but it cannot represent which internal effects completed or automatically resume at the first incomplete effect.

## Illustrative example only

The following generic sequence illustrates the failure shape; it is **not** the domain or intended scope of this issue:

```python
def composite_operation():
    external_effect_a()
    external_effect_b()
    external_effect_c()
```

If execution crashes after `external_effect_b()`, the outer ledger knows that `composite_operation()` did not complete. It does not have independent durable state for effects A, B, and C.

## Current guarantee

Mycelium does the safe thing: an ambiguous retry of the composite function can hard-block instead of blindly replaying every internal effect.

What it cannot currently provide is automatic partial-progress recovery. Doing that requires each independently observable effect to have its own durable identity, outcome, provider reference, and reconciliation decision.

This is a recoverability and modeling gap—not a claim that Mycelium currently duplicates effects under ambiguity.

## Why this matters

- Hidden multi-effect functions are common integration boundaries.
- A single `external_operation_ref` cannot describe multiple provider outcomes.
- Safe hard-blocking preserves correctness but can unnecessarily stop progress.
- The runtime and documentation need an explicit, honest definition of effect granularity.
- Any first-class composition feature affects identity, persistence, fencing, reconciliation, replay, migrations, and public API design.

## Current safe pattern

Each independently observable effect should be a separately ledgered operation with a stable identity:

```text
Ledger effect A -> record outcome
                -> Ledger effect B -> record outcome
                -> Ledger effect C -> record outcome
```

On deterministic replay, completed child effects should return their stored results, while execution proceeds from the first unresolved child effect. Each child independently owns its provider reference, reconciliation strategy, terminal state, and retry policy.

## Design decision needed

Decide whether Mycelium should:

1. Treat this strictly as an effect-boundary/documentation concern;
2. Formally support composition through existing nested ledgered operations; or
3. Add a small first-class parent/child operation primitive.

The decision must answer:

- How are stable parent and child identities derived and versioned?
- Are children ordinary linked `LedgerEntry` records or a new persisted shape?
- What are the exact semantics when orchestration code or step order changes?
- How are concurrent resumes fenced?
- How are child outcomes aggregated without erasing ambiguity or overstating parent completion?
- How does reconciliation operate independently per child effect?
- Where is the boundary that keeps Mycelium from becoming a general workflow engine?
- What compatibility and migration behavior is required for existing ledgers?

## Candidate minimal capability—not a decided design

- Durable parent operation identity and definition version.
- Stable child effect identities.
- One normal ledger entry and external-operation reference per child effect.
- Explicit dependency or ordering metadata.
- Deterministic replay that reuses completed child results.
- Resume from the first unresolved child effect.
- Per-child reconciliation and retry decisions.
- An aggregate parent view derived from, but never replacing, child evidence.

Mycelium must not imply that arbitrary function bodies are transactional or that it can infer hidden effect boundaries.

## Good-first-issue scope

The first contribution is a design/RFC plus an executable spike, not a production protocol rewrite:

- [ ] Document current nested-ledger identity and context behavior.
- [ ] Add a provider-neutral three-effect crash example.
- [ ] Demonstrate whether deterministic replay safely skips completed, separately ledgered child effects.
- [ ] Compare documentation-only, nested-ledger, and first-class parent/child approaches.
- [ ] Propose the smallest persisted metadata and API surface needed.
- [ ] Record non-goals and rejected alternatives.
- [ ] Split any chosen implementation into independently reviewable follow-up issues.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A reviewed design explicitly chooses one of the three approaches above.
- [ ] The design defines identity, version changes, ordering, fencing, concurrency, reconciliation, and aggregate outcomes.
- [ ] Failure semantics are specified before, during, and after each child effect.
- [ ] Required deterministic, process-kill, redispatch, and durable-backend tests are enumerated.
- [ ] Documentation states that one ledgered transition should represent one independently reconcilable external effect until stronger composition semantics ship.

## Relevant implementation areas

- `sdk/mycelium/action_ledger.py`: `LedgerEntry`, `ActionLedger`, ledger decorators, and active-transition context
- `sdk/mycelium/transition.py`: effect identity, effect boundary, outcomes, capabilities, and causation metadata
- `sdk/mycelium/reconcile.py`: reconciliation of one ledger entry
- `sdk/mycelium/verify/proof/crash_sweep.py`: crash-point proof machinery
- `sdk/tests/test_handoff_identity.py`: existing parent/child causation foundations
- `sdk/tests/test_effect_protocol_proof.py`: effect-protocol invariants

## Non-goals

- Inferring effect boundaries inside arbitrary user code.
- Providing atomic transactions across unrelated external systems.
- Building a scheduler, queue, or general-purpose workflow product.
- Weakening fail-closed

Issue #26: [Bug] Iterate element-set keys when resolving integral attachment dependencies

## Summary

`SWEP:GetDependentIntegralSlots` attempts to remove elements that are still supplied by another attachment slot, but it iterates the values of the element set instead of its keys. Because `SWEP:GetElements()` returns `{ [elementName] = true }`, the current loop repeatedly removes `eles[true]` and leaves every real element name unchanged.

This can make valid attachment changes appear to enable/disable integral slots even when another installed attachment continues to provide the same element.

**Suggested severity: Medium attachment-system correctness.**

## Evidence

Reviewed at `main` commit `0f51e3236948c5f00fcd15f4dcd27e3efb1b69d7`.

- `lua/weapons/arc9_base/sh_elements.lua` — `SWEP:GetElements`
- `lua/weapons/arc9_base/sh_attach.lua` — `SWEP:GetDependentIntegralSlots`, `SWEP:GetSlotMissingDependents`, `SWEP:CanAttach`

`GetElements` converts its list into a set:

```lua
local eles2 = {}
for _, ele in pairs(eles) do
    eles2[ele] = true
end
return eles2
```

The dependency code then does:

```lua
local othereles = self:GetElements({[addr] = true})
for _, e in pairs(othereles) do
    eles[e] = nil
end
```

Here `e` is the value `true`, not the element-name key.

## Impact

With two or more slots providing the same element, ARC9 can incorrectly:

- consider an integral slot newly enabled when it was already enabled;
- consider an integral slot affected by a detach even though another provider remains;
- require the player to own an unnecessary dependent attachment;
- reject `CanAttach` through `GetSlotMissingDependents`;
- produce inconsistent behavior depending on attachment order and duplicate element providers.

## Suggested change

Iterate set keys:

```lua
for e in pairs(othereles) do
    eles[e] = nil
end
```

Add a regression test or test fixture covering duplicate providers for both `ActivateElements` and slot `InstalledElements` / `UnInstalledElements`.

## Acceptance criteria

- Elements supplied by any non-excluded slot are removed from the set of elements affected by the proposed change.
- Attaching/detaching one of two equivalent providers does not report dependent integral slots as newly enabled/disabled.
- `GetSlotMissingDependents` blocks only when the proposed change truly creates an unfillable integral slot.
- Single-provider behavior remains unchanged.
- Cache invalidation still refreshes dependency decisions after attachment changes.

## Validation notes

Create a test weapon with two independent slots that provide the same element and an integral slot gated by that element. Test attaching and detaching each provider in both orders, with and without a compatible integral attachment in inventory. Static GLua review only; live customization validation is required.

Issue #36: Table / BufferPtr use-after-free across compile and perform_ksmps


`Table` and `BufferPtr` are views into engine memory, not copies. Csound frees and reallocates that memory during ordinary operation. Both paths below are confirmed `heap-use-after-free` under AddressSanitizer, reachable from **safe code** (no `unsafe` in the caller).

Came up while working on #35. `reset()` taking `&mut self` closes one related case; these two remain because `compile_orc` and `perform_ksmps` still take `&self`.

## 1. Recompiling resizes a function table while a `Table` handle is alive

```rust
let cs = Csound::new().unwrap();
cs.set_option("-n").unwrap();
cs.set_option("-d").unwrap();
cs.compile_orc("sr=44100\nksmps=32\nnchnls=1\n0dbfs=1\n\
                gi1 ftgen 1, 0, 16, 2, 1\ninstr 1\nendin\n", 0).unwrap();
cs.start().unwrap();

let table = cs.get_table(1).unwrap();
cs.compile_orc("gi2 ftgen 1, 0, 1024, 2, 2\n", 0).unwrap(); // reallocates table 1
let _sum: f64 = table.as_slice().iter().sum();               // UAF
```

## 2. An `f` statement in the score reallocates one during `perform_ksmps`

```csound
<CsScore>
f 1 0.05 1024 2 2
i 1 0 0.5
e
</CsScore>
```

```rust
let table = cs.get_table(1).unwrap();
while !cs.perform_ksmps() {}        // score replaces table 1 partway through
let _sum: f64 = table.as_slice().iter().sum(); // UAF
```

Both report:

```
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free
```


## Proposed fix

Take `&mut self` on `perform_ksmps` and the compile family. That is the same rule as `reset(&mut self)` in #35: if a call can free or reallocate the memory a handle points into, it must conflict with the handle's borrow.

`while !cs.perform_ksmps()` still works; callers just need `let mut cs`. The breaking part is anyone who hoists a `Table` or `BufferPtr` out of the performance loop — which is the unsound pattern, so rejecting it at compile time is the point.

A generation counter on each deref would catch this at runtime without a signature change, but it adds a branch on the audio path (`BufferPtr`). Leaving it documented keeps the UAF in safe code. Neither matches what `reset` already does.

If this is the direction, it is worth doing before more handle types land, since it would touch the same call sites.
