# Bug: async-delegation wakeup turns persist without `_source` and render as raw user bubbles

## Summary

When a background `delegate_task` fan-out completes and its `[ASYNC DELEGATION COMPLETE — …]` / `[ASYNC DELEGATION BATCH COMPLETE — …]` summary is delivered to an idle WebUI session, the delivery is persisted as a plain user-role message **without** the `_source: "process_wakeup"` stamp. The frontend gates the collapsed background-wakeup card on that stamp, so the transcript renders the full multi-kilobyte raw envelope as a normal user bubble instead of the intended collapsed wakeup card.

Two independent faults contribute:

1. **Server — the wakeup turn loses its provenance during turn settlement.** When the session runs in the default deferred save mode, no eager checkpoint row exists when the agent turn settles, so `_settle_current_turn_boundary` takes the adoption branch in `api/streaming.py` that marks the agent-returned user row with `_mark_active_turn_checkpoint`. That helper historically wrote only `_active_turn_token` and never routed through `stamp_message_source`, so `_source` (and the `_wakeup_meta` display metadata that rides along) is silently dropped before the row is promoted into the display transcript. The materialize branch of the same settlement does stamp, so only the adoption path is affected — which is exactly the path the default save mode takes.
2. **Client — no display grammar for the async-delegation envelope.** Even a correctly stamped async-delegation delivery gets no collapsed card, because `_parseProcessWakeupBody` in `static/ui.js` only recognizes the two `[IMPORTANT: Background process …]` grammars, and the server's `wakeup_display_meta` deliberately returns `None` for the async-delegation shape. The delivery then falls through to the raw process-wakeup notice dump.

## Environment

- WebUI: `exp-v0.52.263` (Experimental) — observed on a live deployment
- Fault verified unchanged through current `master` (`exp-v0.52.264`): `git log exp-v0.52.263..exp-v0.52.264 -- api/streaming.py static/ui.js` is empty and the faulty helper is byte-identical across both tags
- The faulty adoption helper dates to the turn-ownership settlement change first released in `exp-v0.52.155`

Issue #84: Recompute per-checkpoint LM loss on a fixed Pile slice, then test λ_ca-vs-loss collapse

Prerequisite for the collapse test, and it is **not a download — it is a computation**.

## Pythia per-checkpoint loss is not obtainable

The eval JSONs at `github.com/EleutherAI/pythia/tree/main/evals/pythia-v1` (831 files, 21
variants × {zero-shot, five-shot} × 27 steps) carry only `acc`, `acc_norm`,
`likelihood_difference` and `lambada_openai.ppl` — **no loss** — and contain **no 14m or 31m
directories at all**.

Loss exists only in the maintainers' self-described *"(messy!)"* W&B project
`wandb.ai/eleutherai/pythia`, with no CSV or JSON export path.

## Recompute it instead

LM loss on a **fixed held-out Pile slice**, same slice for every model and every checkpoint.
Cheap at these sizes, covers 14M and 31M which the published evals do not, and — the actual
reason to prefer it — it evaluates on **exactly the token distribution driving the λ_ca
lattice**, rather than on downstream task accuracy.

> Note: `experiments/loss_baseline.py` already does this shape of computation against a fixed
> **WikiText-103** slice (`results/loss_baseline.json`). That was deliberately scoped as a
> shape-only comparison because WikiText is not the training distribution. This issue is the
> Pile version — same machinery, correct corpus — and should extend that script rather than
> start over.

## The test

Does λ_ca **collapse** when plotted against loss rather than against step? If it does, the
transition is a property of *how good the model is*, not of *how long it trained*, and the LR
confound in C20 dissolves as a side effect.

## Hold it to the right standard

arXiv:2507.02119 (Qiu et al., "supercollapse") sets the bar: **the collapse residual is measured
against a per-model seed noise floor, not eyeballed.** Anything less will read as curve-fitting.

Getting that noise floor needs multiple seeds per configuration — **scope that cost into the
issue rather than discovering it mid-run**. PolyPythias (arXiv:2503.09543) provides 9 seeds ×
14M–410M and may supply the floor without new training; check whether its checkpoint spacing is
compatible.

## Frame it as an extension, not an invention

arXiv:2403.15796 (Du et al.) already owns loss-reparameterisation collapse for *task metrics*.
Our contribution would be extending it to a **dynamical** observable — a quantity measured from
the model's own generation dynamics rather than from its outputs on a benchmark. State it that
way or a reviewer will state it for us, less charitably.

Issue #7250: Dependency-tree walk enqueues every child twice and propagates parents before their children

**Version:** `dev-2026-08:a7c8a4b94`, x86-64 Linux

## Summary

`check_update_dependency_tree_for_procedures` (`src/checker.cpp`, the live `#else` branch):

1. every child is enqueued twice, so task count grows as `2^depth` in procedure-literal nesting;
2. a parent propagates its dependencies upward without waiting for its children, so dependency sets come out nondeterministic and short.


## Origin

Both lines arrived together in 629777b98 ("Multithread `check_update_dependency_tree_for_procedures`", 2025-09-10); the region has not been touched since. That commit redefined `check_walk_all_dependencies` to be nothing but `thread_pool_add_task(...)`, and kept the sequential version's loop body verbatim:

```cpp
for (DeclInfo *child = decl->next_child; child != nullptr; child = child->next_sibling) {
	thread_pool_add_task(check_walk_all_dependencies_worker_proc, child);
	check_walk_all_dependencies(child);   // <- now the same enqueue, not a recursion
}
add_deps_from_child_to_parent(decl);      // <- no longer runs after the children
```

One line broke two things. In the sequential form, `check_walk_all_dependencies(child)` *returning*
meant the subtree was complete, which is what made the following `add_deps_from_child_to_parent`
correctly ordered. As a non-blocking enqueue it guarantees nothing, and that merge is only correct
bottom-up. The `#if 0` block directly above still shows the intended shape.


Note: Local attempts to eliminate the redundant work and make it deterministic had sufficient perf regressions that I'm just filing an issue instead.

every stated requirement — recursive CTEs for the (small, bounded) encounter-local graph,
JSON1/JSONB attributes, append-only + content hashes + FKs + ACID, immutable

multi-host/concurrent shared writers, high write concurrency, or HA-replication/PITR
compliance requirements.

SQLite for the current deployment shape, or is there a durability/concurrency requirement
that mandates PostgreSQL?

`_gate_documentation_minimum` currently passes when a clinical action (description) is

actor structure). Claude deliberately did NOT strengthen it: tightening beyond "action

interact with the fail-closed boundary to block real claims.

event is eligible for retrieval? (e.g., service requires action + target/site when the

over-broad (it widens the duplicate-merge candidate scope). The F5 dedup is now pair-aware

unsafe. Finer per-session grouping would need session/operative timestamps that the
current extraction does not capture.

Decision needed: is per-DOS episode grouping acceptable, or should extraction capture
session/operative-time signals to support finer episodes? (Extraction-schema change +
grouping refinement if the latter.)

Issue #5084: Proposal: a governed context-layer example (Genie/Unity Catalog semantics + Lakebase GraphRAG)

Floating this as an issue rather than a PR to check whether maintainers want it before I write it — I have two example PRs open already (#3170, #2725) and would rather not add a third unreviewed one if the answer is no.

## The gap

Searching the repo, there is no ontology or knowledge-graph concept anywhere: no hits for `ontology`, `pgvector`, or `knowledge graph`. What *is* already here is most of the substrate for one:

- `deploy/databricks/` already depends on **Lakebase Postgres as the state store**, so pgvector + recursive-CTE graph traversal need no new infrastructure.
- Unity Catalog functions are already wired as agent tools (`docs/databricks.md`).
- Genie over managed MCP is what my open #3170 adds.

So the missing piece is the layer above: giving an agent a *governed semantic model* to ground answers in, rather than letting it guess which table is authoritative.

## What the example would show

A two-layer context model, which is the pattern I keep hitting in customer architectures:

1. **Certified core** — the head of the business modelled explicitly in Unity Catalog (metric views, glossary terms, domains, certified tables). Curated, authoritative, small.
2. **Inferred long tail** — relationships derived from tables, queries and docs, served from Lakebase: pgvector for the semantic seed, recursive CTEs for traversal.

Everything authority-ranked, so certified definitions win over inferred ones and an answer can cite which source it came from. The agent asks the context layer "what is authoritative for revenue?" before it asks the warehouse for numbers.

Issue #106: Installed system service loses a boot race against Docker Desktop and stays failed

## Summary

On a Linux host whose Docker is provided by Docker Desktop (WSL 2 integration),
a system-scope install generates a systemd unit with **no ordering dependency on
Docker at all**. The unit starts right after `basic.target`, fails because Docker
is not yet available, and exhausts its entire restart budget in about one second
— roughly 20 seconds before Docker Desktop finishes wiring up the WSL
integration.

The service then stays `failed` until someone starts it by hand. It has never
once survived a boot on this host.

## Environment

```text
reploy   0.7.0.dev1 [08d1ee835c, built 2026-08-15 22:36:02 PST]
OS       Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (WSL 2), kernel 6.6.114.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2
systemd  255 (255.4-1ubuntu8.17)
docker   Docker Desktop 4.87.0 (236836), server 29.7.2
install  --scope system --to /opt/arbiter --service arbiter
```

There is no `docker.service` on this host — Docker Desktop provides the CLI and
socket through bind mounts instead:

```console
$ systemctl show docker.service -p LoadState
LoadState=not-found

$ ls -l /usr/bin/docker
/usr/bin/docker -> /mnt/wsl/docker-desktop/cli-tools/usr/bin/docker
```

## Observed

The generated `/etc/systemd/system/arbiter.service` has an empty `[Unit]`
ordering section:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Reploy Docker service (arbiter)
# Managed-By: reploy
# Reploy-Service: arbiter
# Reploy-Target: /opt/arbiter
# Reploy-Compose-Project: arbiter-03ee1bb5

[Service]
Type=notify
...
Restart=on-failure
```

Boot timeline (`journalctl -b`, boot `b1eb3e86`):

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 22:50:11.875 | `arbiter.service` starts (immediately after `basic.target`) |
| 22:50:11.940 | fail — `exec: "docker": executable file not found in $PATH` |
| 22:50:12.786 | **5 restarts exhausted** → `Start request repeated too quickly` (0.91s total) |
| 22:50:33 | Docker Desktop mounts `cli-tools` — **21.2s too late** |
| 22:50:34.167 | retry (10s start-limit window elapsed) |
| 22:50:35.270 | fail — `dial unix /var/run/docker.sock: connect: no such file or directory` |
| 22:50:36.229 | **exhausted again** (2.06s total) |
| 22:50:38 | `docker.sock` bind-mount activates — **1.8s too late** |
| +5h48m | recovered only by a manual `sudo systemctl start arbiter.service` |

The same failure occurred on the three most recent boots (Aug 19, Aug 21,
Aug 23). Two distinct error signatures appear depending on how far Docker
Desktop got:

1. `reploy service-container error: ... inspect Docker endpoint: exec: "docker": executable file not found in $PATH`
   — `/usr/bin/docker` is a dangling symlink; the `cli-tools` mount does not exist yet.
2. `reploy service-container error: ... failed to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock; check if the path is correct and if the daemon is running: dial unix /var/run/docker.sock: connect: no such file or directory`
   — CLI tools mounted, socket bind-mount not yet.

## Expected

An installed service survives a host reboot without manual intervention when
Docker becomes available a normal amount of time into boot.

## Cause

Two independent contributing defects.

**1. Backend selection ignores the Docker runtime.**
`hostPlatform.installBackend` (`internal/dockerdeploy/platform.go`) dispatches on
`GOOS` alone:

```go
case "linux":
    return installBackendLinuxSystemd
```

So WSL + Docker Desktop gets the systemd backend, which assumes a
`docker.service` exists, rather than the Docker Desktop backend whose
reboot-resistance story is Docker's own restart policy (as recorded in
`docs/archive/WINDOWS_PORT.md` and `docs/archive/MACOS_PORT.md`). The codebase
already detects Docker Desktop — `dockerRuntimeDockerDesktop` in the same file —
but that detection never reaches backend selection.

**2. Absence of `docker.service` is treated as "no gating needed".**
`inspectProviderInstallHostToolsWithV1`
(`internal/dockerdeploy/provider_install_host_tools.go`) decides whether to emit
an ordering dependency by shelling out:

```go
result.IncludeDockerUnit = tools.run(
    CommandSpec{Name: systemctlPath, Args: []string{"cat", "docker.service"}},
    RunOptions{Context: ctx},
) == nil
```

That command exits 1 here, so `providerInstallSystemdFileV1`
(`internal/dockerdeploy/provider_install_systemd.go`) emits an empty ordering
block:

```go
dockerUnit := ""
if includeDockerUnit {
    dockerUnit = "Requires=docker.service\nAfter=docker.service\n"
}
```

The detection is technically correct — there genuinely is no `docker.service` to
depend on — but the fallback should be "Docker readiness must be established
some other way", not "no gating needed".

**Amplifier: the restart policy is off by an order of magnitude.**
`Restart=on-failure` with systemd defaults gives `RestartSec=100ms`,
`StartLimitBurst=5`, `StartLimitIntervalSec=10s` — a ~1 second total retry budget
against a ~22 second wait. That converts a transient unavailability into a
permanent failure.

There is also no readiness wait in the service path. `--docker-timeout` (default
5s) is a daemon *responsiveness* timeout, it is not passed in the generated
`ExecStart`, and it would not help signature 1 regardless — that fails at
`exec.LookPath` before any daemon contact.

## Note for whoever picks this up

The obvious narrow fix — `After=` on the Docker Desktop WSL mount units — does
**not** work. Those units are synthesized from `/proc/self/mountinfo` and have no
unit file:

```console
$ systemctl show 'mnt-wsl-docker\x2ddesktop-cli\x2dtools.mount' -p FragmentPath -p SourcePath
FragmentPath=
SourcePath=/proc/self/mountinfo
```

systemd does not know about them at dependency-resolution time, so the ordering
constraint is silently a no-op and the unit proceeds anyway.

## Suggested fix

Either or both:

- Add a bounded Docker readiness wait in `_service-container` before the first
  Docker call, covering both the missing-executable and missing-socket cases.
- Scale the restart policy to real Docker Desktop startup time (e.g. a longer
  `RestartSec` with a `StartLimitIntervalSec`/

Issue #3717: Enhancement: make the edge probe's shape cues language-aware in the engine (deterministic — not the #652 LLM classifier)

## Pre-submission checklist

- [x] Improves existing behavior — does not add a new command, workflow, or concept.
- [x] Searched existing issues — not already proposed.
- [x] Read CONTRIBUTING.md; will wait for `approved-enhancement` before any code.
- [x] Can describe a concrete benefit, not just "nicer."

## What existing feature or behavior does this improve?

`SHAPE_CUES` / `classifyShape` in `src/edge-probe.cts` — the deterministic prose→shape classifier the spec-phase Step 5.5 edge-completeness probe uses to decide which of the closed 8-category edge taxonomy applies to each requirement.

## Current behavior

`SHAPE_CUES` is five English word-boundary regexes. A project running with `response_language` set writes its SPEC requirements in that language, so every requirement matches no cue, classifies to zero shapes, and surfaces as the `unclassified` sentinel (#1110). The taxonomy contributes nothing and `--auto` resolves nothing.

**#2773 shipped the stopgap the triage approved** (PR #3713, merged): spec-phase Step 5.5 now feeds the probe a faithful **English translation** of each requirement's `text` while the SPEC keeps its original language. That works — measured against the compiled engine:

| Requirement text handed to the probe | `classifyShape` | categories raised |
|---|---|---|
| `O sistema mescla intervalos sobrepostos em uma lista ordenada` | `[]` | none |
| `The system merges overlapping intervals in a sorted list` | `["collection"]` | `adjacency`, `empty`, `ordering` |

But it is a **documented instruction, not an enforced contract**. The engine still cannot read anything but English, so the correctness of every non-English spec's edge coverage rests on the model following a prose instruction, with no machine check that it did. The triage on #2773 said so explicitly:

> Option 1 is a two-line markdown change and removes the silent no-op today; **option 2 is the durable fix.**

and closed with:

> **The durable engine fix is a separate follow-up, not blocked by this** … worth a follow-up enhancement issue once the doc stopgap lands.

This issue is that follow-up.

## Proposed behavior

Make the engine itself language-aware, **staying fully deterministic**. Three candidate forms, in rough order of cost:

1. **Scan an English `text_en` field when present.** `Requirement` becomes `{ id, text, shapes?, text_en? }`; `classifyShape` reads `text_en ?? text`. Smallest change; makes the current translation step an explicit, validatable field instead of an invisible convention, and lets a contract test assert that a `response_language` project actually populated it.
2. **A `lang` hint + per-language cue sets.** `SHAPE_CUES` becomes `Record<lang, Record<Shape, RegExp>>` with `en` as the default. Genuinely reads the author's own prose — no translation step at all — at the cost of maintaining a cue table per supported language.
3. **Both** — `lang` where a cue set exists, `text_en` as the universal fallback.

Whichever form is chosen, the acceptance bar should include a **parity assertion** that the shape vocabulary stays single-sourced across the cue table and `VALID_SHAPES` (the `DEFECT.GENERATIVE-FIX` class), and a fixture pair proving a non-English requirement classifies identically to its English equivalent.

## Reason and benefit

The probe exists to catch domain-boundary edges the author never wrote down — the failure mode it targets is precisely a *silent* one. Leaving the language handling as prose reproduces that shape one level up: if the instruction is not followed, coverage silently degrades to `unclassified` and nothing fails.

The concrete gap the stopgap cannot close is the **partly-classified** case. Step 5.5's `$APPLICABLE = 0` warning fires only when *every* requirement is unclassified, so a spec where a few requirements happen to carry English loanwords (`API`, `upload`) classifies partially and raises **no signal at all**. An engine that knows the input language can fail closed there; a prose instruction cannot.

## Scope of changes

- `src/edge-probe.cts` — `SHAPE_CUES`, `classifyShape`, and (for forms 1/3) `Requirement` + `validateRequirement`.
- `CONTEXT.md` — the `EdgeCompletenessProbeModule` glossary entry records the export surface as locked, so a new field or a re-shaped `SHAPE_CUES` is a glossary update and likely an **ADR-550 amendment** rather than a silent change.
- `gsd-core/workflows/spec-phase.md` + `gsd-core/references/edge-probe.md` — the #2773 translation instruction becomes redundant or changes shape.
- `docs/FEATURES.md` §144, `docs/how-to/probe-edges-in-a-non-english-project.md` — both currently describe the translation workaround.
- Fixtures under `gsd-core/references/edge-probe-fixtures/` and `tests/edge-probe*.test.cjs`.

None intended if `en` stays the default and `text` keeps its current meaning — both proposed forms are additive. Nothing here seeks to re-open that.

Another topic related to the discussion in #10255

### Relationship to #10255 & #10265
This proposal complements the learner progression and curriculum structure discussed in #10255 (`Courses: course-pipeline overhaul`) and #10265 (`Courses: centralized myProgress learner dashboard overhaul`).

### Current Problem
- **Unrestricted, Out-of-Order Course Enrollment**: In Planet Learning, all courses in the catalog can be joined independently with no sequential requirements or curriculum tracks.
- **Missing Curriculum Dependencies**: Educators creating progressive multi-part subject tracks (e.g., *Introductory Algebra* → *Calculus*, or *Foundational Literacy* → *Advanced Reading*) have no mechanism to require that foundational coursework be completed before learners attempt advanced material.
- **Fragile Link Integrity on Renames**: Relying on course titles or textual descriptions breaks whenever a prerequisite course is renamed, updated, or translated into another language.
- **Orphaned Dependency Traps on Deletion**: If a prerequisite course is deleted or archived, learners could become permanently blocked from taking advanced courses if the system lacks graceful dependency resolution.

### Proposed Solution: Optional Course Prerequisites & Progression Tracks
We want to introduce configurable course prerequisites with referential ID tracking, circular dependency safeguards, and intuitive learner-facing unlock states:

1. **Course Authoring & Prerequisite Configuration (`CoursesAddComponent`)**:
   - **Multi-Select Prerequisites (`prerequisiteCourseIds: string[]`)**: Add an optional multi-select chip/autocomplete control in `src/app/courses/add-courses/courses-add.component.html` allowing educators to select one or multiple prerequisite courses.
   - **Circular Dependency Guardrails**: Prevent a course from selecting itself as a prerequisite or forming circular dependency loops (e.g., Course A → Course B → Course A).
   - **Immutable ID Referencing**: Store immutable CouchDB `_id` values on the course document so that **renaming a course title** never breaks existing prerequisite links (titles and metadata are resolved dynamically).

2. **Resilient Deletion & Sync Handling**:
   - When evaluating course prerequisites, if a referenced prerequisite `_id` is missing from the database (due to course deletion or selective offline sync), the system gracefully skips the missing ID and treats the requirement as satisfied/waived, preventing learners from being permanently locked out by orphaned IDs.

3. **Learner-Facing Prerequisites Overview & Lock States (`CoursesViewComponent`)**:
   - **Prerequisites Status Card**: On the course overview page (`courses-view.component.html`), display a dedicated **"Prerequisites"** card listing all required courses:
     - ✅ **Completed** (green badge / checkmark)
     - 🔒 **Required** (clickable course link directing the learner to enroll and take the prerequisite)
   - **Smart Enrollment & Navigation Protection**:
     - If prerequisites are incomplete, the primary **Join** button is disabled with an explanatory tooltip (e.g., *"Complete [Course Name] to unlock this course"*).
     - Direct URL navigation to step views or exams (`/courses/step/:courseId/:stepIndex`) evaluates prerequisites and gracefully redirects back to the course overview with an informative notification if prerequisites are incomplete.

### Justification & Practical Impact
- **Structured Pedagogical Pathways**: Enables educators and community managers to build structured learning tracks, multi-grade curricula, and certificate sequences.
- **Referential Integrity**: ID-based tracking guarantees that course renames, multi-lingual translations, and deletions never corrupt student learning paths.
- **Self-Directed Learner Guidance**: Gives students clear, visual visibility into what foundational knowledge they need before tackling advanced subject matter.

## Summary

Create an Open Suite administration and access-management portal at `admin.<domain>` (the demo would be `admin.demo.opensuite.online`) where an authorized administrator can manage a person once and control that person's access to every installed Open Suite application.

This is a **proposal and research issue only**. No implementation should begin until the decisions at the end of this issue are made.

The portal should centralize:

- user lifecycle (joiner, mover, leaver, rehire);
- coarse application entitlement (may this person enter app X?);
- supported app roles and scopes (what may this person do in app X?);
- provisioning/deprovisioning and drift reconciliation;
- approvals, audit, connector health, and manual exceptions.

It must **not** claim to centralize permissions that an application cannot expose or enforce. Authentication, lifecycle/provisioning, app entitlement, and domain authorization are different layers and must stay explicit.

A search of all current `open-suite/open-suite` issues, plus targeted searches for `admin`, `access`, `provisioning`, `permissions`, `users`, `SCIM`, and `IAM`, found no overlapping issue as of 2026-08-02.

## Executive recommendation

Build a small, permissively licensed **Open Suite desired-state control plane over upstream Keycloak**, not a new IdP and not a universal authorization engine.

- Use **Keycloak client roles** for app entitlement and stable app-local capabilities; use only a few realm roles for truly suite-wide administration.
- Add an Open Suite portal/API and asynchronous reconciliation controller. It discovers installed apps from declarative capability manifests and applies desired access through SCIM or app-native APIs.
- Enforce coarse app entitlement at the edge **and** in the app/token boundary. An OIDC login alone is not an entitlement check.
- Preserve each app's real semantics in the UI and connector. Normalize presentation and orchestration, not authorization meaning.
- Use events to reduce latency, but use a durable work table and periodic full reconciliation to recover from missed events and repair drift.
- Do **not** add OpenFGA, SpiceDB, Casbin, or OPA in the MVP. Add one only when cooperating applications have a real policy enforcement point and a demonstrated shared authorization model.

The Codex App needs a recoverable or degraded-running task state. Confidence: `Confirmed`

The task-status UX lacks an aggregate recoverability state that incorporates active descendant execution when the parent response is suppressed or marked as a system error.

## Expected behavior
When a parent task cannot display content but one or more descendants remain active, the App should show a non-terminal degraded/recovering state, identify that background work is continuing, and reserve terminal blocked/error presentation for cases where no execution path can progress.

## Likely solution direction
Confidence: `Likely`

Add a derived degraded-running or recovering state based on descendant activity and durable task state. Preserve the safety-hidden content boundary, but expose safe operational facts: whether work continues, whether user action is needed, the last safe checkpoint, and whether resume would duplicate an active execution path.

## Likely affected surface
| Surface | Confidence | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codex App task-status aggregation and sidebar/detail status presentation | Likely | The mismatch is visible between parent status presentation and descendant execution state. |
| Task resume affordance | Possible | A resume action should warn or remain unavailable while a descendant is actively continuing the same workflow. |

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A parent with a hidden or errored response and at least one active descendant is not presented as terminally blocked.
- [ ] The App visibly distinguishes degraded-but-running, paused/checkpointed, needs-user-action, and system-blocked states.
- [ ] The degraded state exposes only safe operational metadata and does not reveal content that the safeguard withheld.
- [ ] The operator can see whether background work is continuing and whether manual resume risks duplicate execution.
- [ ] When all descendants stop, the displayed state deterministically transitions to completed, recoverable, needs-user-action, or system-blocked.

## Unknowns and non-goals
**Unknowns**
- Whether the parent systemError originates in the safety-response layer, task aggregation, or a separate transport error.
- Whether descendant activity is already available to every App status-rendering surface.

**Non-goals**
- Weakening, bypassing, or exposing content hidden by safety safeguards.
- Changing cybersecurity policy or Trusted Access eligibility.
- Automatically retrying arbitrary failed prompts without durable-state reconciliation.

Issue #40605: Codex Desktop write thread cannot reliably retrieve exact output from a read-only planning thread, breaking autonomous planner→implementer loops

### What version of the Codex App are you using?

Codex Desktop `26.819.11345`.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS.

### What issue are you seeing?

A production-style multi-thread orchestration flow cannot reliably continue autonomously from a read-only Planner thread into a workspace-write implementation thread because the write-side thread cannot retrieve the exact final output of the read-only Planner thread through the supported cross-thread/thread-reader path.

In the reproduced workflow:

1. A dedicated read-only planning thread produced the final implementation plan.
2. A separate workspace-write implementation/orchestrator thread was required to retrieve that exact Planner result unchanged, validate it, persist it, and continue implementation.
3. The write-side thread could not retrieve the exact final Planner result through the supported thread reader.
4. The workflow stopped with an explicit blocker equivalent to:

```text
INSTRUCTION400_EXACT_NONCANONICAL_PLAN_NOT_RETRIEVABLE
```

5. No product work could continue until the user manually copied the complete Planner output from the read-only thread into the write thread.

This is not a simple UX inconvenience. It breaks unattended / continuous engineering workflows that intentionally separate roles and permissions:

```text
read-only Planner
      ↓ exact result handoff
workspace-write Orchestrator / Implementer
      ↓
implementation → tests → review → next loop
```

If the downstream write-capable thread cannot programmatically read the exact upstream read-only result, the loop requires manual copy/paste at every permission boundary. That prevents reliable 24/7 autonomous engineering even when both threads belong to the same Codex project and the user has already authorized the workflow.

### Why exact retrieval matters

For governed multi-agent workflows, a summary is not sufficient. The downstream thread may need to prove that it consumed the exact upstream result unchanged.

Examples:

- validate a Planner result against a schema;
- compute and compare SHA-256;
- persist the exact plan bytes;
- preserve provenance and auditability;
- avoid reconstructing native/subagent output from prose;
- prevent the implementer from silently rewriting the Planner result before acceptance.

In this reproduction, the write-side thread correctly refused to substitute a summary or reconstruct the missing output. Manual user transfer was the only path forward.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open Codex Desktop on macOS.
2. Create two tasks/threads in the same project:
   - Thread A: Read only.
   - Thread B: Workspace write.
3. In Thread A, generate a substantial final planning result that Thread B must consume exactly.
4. In Thread B, use the supported cross-thread/thread-reading mechanism to retrieve Thread A's exact final result.
5. Require exact content rather than a summary, because the next step computes a hash or validates a structured contract.
6. Observe that Thread B may be unable to retrieve the exact result even though the user can open Thread A manually and see it.
7. The orchestration blocks until the user manually copy/pastes Thread A's result into Thread B.

### Expected behavior

Codex should provide a first-class, permission-safe handoff/read mechanism for exact cross-thread result retrieval within an authorized project/workflow.

At minimum, a downstream authorized thread should be able to retrieve:

```text
source_thread_id
source_turn_id
final_result_bytes_or_exact_text
content_sha256
source_permission_profile
result_status
```

with clear provenance and no normalization.

A workspace-write consumer does not need write access to the read-only source thread; it only needs read access to the source result.

The mechanism should preserve exact bytes/text so a downstream validator can verify integrity without requiring user copy/paste.

### Actual behavior

The result is visible to the user in the read-only source thread, but the downstream workspace-write thread cannot reliably retrieve that exact result through the supported reader/handoff path.

The workflow therefore requires a human to manually bridge the threads.

### Impact

This blocks or degrades:

- Planner → Implementer loops;
- Reviewer/Tester → Fixer loops;
- read-only audit → write-side remediation loops;
- role-separated security workflows;
- long-running unattended Codex orchestration;
- 24/7 autonomous engineering loops;
- exact provenance / hash-based governance;
- restart-safe continuation across permission-separated threads.

The problem becomes more severe when permission separation is deliberate. A safe architecture often wants Planner/Reviewer/Tester threads to remain read-only while a separate implementation thread owns writes. Without a reliable exact-result bridge, least-privilege multi-agent design and autonomous continuation conflict with each other.

A first-class handoff/receipt API would solve this better than exposing whole thread internals.

For example, when a role finishes, Codex could persist a terminal receipt containing:

```text
producer_thread_id
producer_turn_id
producer_role
producer_permission_profile
result_kind
exact_result
result_sha256
completed_at
```

The authorized downstream thread could then consume that immutable receipt by ID.

Important properties:

- read-only source threads remain read-only;
- downstream threads get result read access, not source-thread mutation access;
- exact content is preserved byte-for-byte;
- provenance is machine-verifiable;
- restart/resume does not lose the handoff;
- no manual copy/paste is required;
- summaries remain optional convenience, not the only transport.

Issue #41009: Codex Desktop leaves high-CPU grep and Python child processes after an interrupted task on macOS

## Summary

A Codex Desktop task that performed broad local CSV searches was interrupted, but its shell child processes were not cleaned up. Four `grep` processes and one Python process remained running after the task was interrupted, each consuming approximately one CPU core.

## Environment

- macOS on Apple Silicon
- Codex Desktop
- Large local CSV archive

## Related Codex task

- Task: **Assess zinc coulombic register**
- Task reference: `01a040b8-9e96-7dc3-9882-b51155163f99`
- Task state: interrupted

## What happened

The task launched several long-running searches and a Python CSV-analysis script. After the Codex task was interrupted, the descendant processes continued running in the background.

Observed remaining workload:

- Four recursive `grep` searches across large CSV and project directories
- One Python process loading and profiling a large collection of CSV files
- Each active process used approximately 80–95% CPU
- The processes continued for several minutes until manually terminated

## Expected behavior

When a Codex task is interrupted, completed, cancelled, or its parent process exits, all shell descendants started for that task should be terminated as a process group after a short graceful shutdown period.

## Actual behavior

The owning Codex task ended, but its descendant `grep` and Python processes remained active and continued their scans.

## Impact

- High sustained CPU use
- Fan activity and reduced system responsiveness
- Orphaned work can accumulate across interrupted tasks
- The user must inspect Activity Monitor and manually terminate the processes

## Suggested fix

Launch each shell command in a tracked process group or job. On task completion, cancellation, interruption, crash, or app shutdown:

1. Send graceful termination to the complete child process group.
2. Wait briefly for cleanup.
3. Force-terminate any remaining descendants.
4. Surface a visible warning if cleanup fails.

## Related reports

This appears related to existing reports of Codex child-process cleanup failures and high-CPU orphaned processes, especially #37770 and #21994.

With `sandbox.mode: "all"` and `sandbox.scope: "agent"`, concurrent sandboxed runs (especially many isolated cron `agentTurn`s at the same minute) intermittently omit eligible workspace skills from `<available_skills>` because a shared materialized skills directory is wiped/rebuilt while other runs rescan it for prompt construction.

5. For each run, inspect the compiled system prompt / trajectory `context.compiled` and extract `<available_skills>` names.
6. Compare catalogs across concurrent runs and against `openclaw skills check --agent <id>`.

### Expected behavior

Every concurrent sandboxed run for the same agent should see a stable, complete set of eligible skills in `<available_skills>` (or a documented truncation with a clear note). Concurrent runs must not observe a partially synced skills directory.

Observed on `2026.7.1-2` (`0790d9f`) at `2026-08-12T07:00:05Z`: three concurrent `agent:main` cron runs saw **11 / 21 / 25** skills respectively. - skills block ≈ 8.5k chars

2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f); race still present on current `main` as of e3488e1d73 (2026-08-12)

Linux x64

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

  await prepareSyncedSkillsDirectory(targetSkillsDir); // deletes every entry under target

Run B: acquires lock, wipes shared skills dir, starts copying
Run A: builds <available_skills> by scanning that dir → partial/nested subset

As a course author using the Manage & Apply Competencies authoring flow, I want to fetch the current `CompetencyCriteriaGroup` tree (root, course-level, and leaf groups) and the `CompetencyCriterion` leaves under it for a competency I'm managing, so that the authoring UI can render what's actually already associated — existing groups, existing criteria, which subsections are already tagged — from persisted backend state, rather than tracking or guessing at that state client-side, and so that my next write action (add or remove an association) acts against ground truth instead of a stale local copy.

## Description

This ticket adds a single GET endpoint returning every non-archived `CompetencyCriteriaGroup` and `CompetencyCriterion` for one competency, as two flat lists. It is the read-side counterpart to the write-side family already drafted: \#665 (create a criterion), \#674 (remove a criterion), and \#675 (remove a group subtree).

**Current state**

No endpoint exists today to retrieve `CompetencyCriteriaGroup` or `CompetencyCriterion` rows. \#674 and \#675 were both written assuming this endpoint filters archived rows out by default (their own lookups deliberately do not, "unlike the future read/list path"), so that expectation is a settled input to this ticket, not an open question.

**Requested change**

`GET /cbe/rest_api/v1/competencies/<int:competency_tag_id>/criteria-groups/` returns, for a given competency: every `CompetencyCriteriaGroup` in that competency's tree with `archived=False` (root, every course-level group, every leaf, across every course at once — no `course_id` or date-window scoping parameter), and every `CompetencyCriterion` with `archived=False` under those groups. The response is two flat arrays, `groups` and `criteria`, each row carrying its own `parent_id`/`competency_criteria_group_id` for client-side reconstruction, matching this repo's existing tree-shaped GET precedent (`TaxonomyTagsView`) rather than introducing a nested/recursive serializer this codebase has never used. A competency with no criteria structure yet returns 200 with two empty arrays, not a 404\. Windowing by course-run dates and pagination for competencies with many associations are explicitly deferred to \#682, not built here — see Explicitly out of scope.

**Explicitly out of scope**

- Any write behavior (create, update, archive, delete) — covered by \#665, \#674, \#675.  
- Windowing by course-run date and pagination for large result sets — \#682's scope. This ticket returns the whole non-archived tree unconditionally, correct for now per ADR 0002's own note that `course_id is null` branches are expected to stay small.  
- Any convenience signal indicating whether a row can be safely removed without a warning (e.g. a `deletable` field). Not built here: Studio currently has no way to know this without attempting the delete and observing whether it archives instead. Revisit if a future ADR settles on a concrete mechanism for this.  
- An explicit audit endpoint or parameter for retrieving archived rows. Default-exclude is the behavior for MVP; no consumer has asked for archived visibility.  
- Learner progress/mastery status (`StudentCompetency*Status` tables) — this endpoint returns authoring structure only, not evaluation results.  
- Any UI.

Issue #108: Sub-zones give coverage, identifiers give lineage — aggregation needs a third relation: unique ownership. Proposal for an "owned sub-zone" term and an optional Zone Query capability

OGC API — DGGS Part 1 (21-038r1) builds its hierarchy machinery on the
**sub-zone** relation (term 4.11): a zone at greater refinement level
*at least partially contained* in the parent zone — a **coverage**
relation, currently being sharpened to interior-intersection in #106.
Coverage is the right relation for its jobs: zone listing under
`parent-zone`, hierarchical paging with `zone-level`, and the
deterministic sub-zone ordering that the data encodings serialise
against at a `zone-depth`.

But for every non-congruent DGGH (every hexagonal or pentagonal system;
congruent quadtrees are the special case where all the distinctions
below vanish), coverage is one of **three** distinct hierarchy readings,
and the other two are load-bearing for common workflows:

1. **Coverage (the Standard's sub-zone, 4.11)** — every zone at relative
   depth d whose interior intersects the parent's. Right for retrieval
   and exploration. Not a partition: a zone straddling a boundary is a
   sub-zone of **two or more** parents, so counts are not Nᵈ and
   aggregating over `parent-zone` listings double-counts the straddlers.

2. **Lineage (identifier truncation)** — what native DGGRS libraries
   actually compute (e.g. H3 `cellToParent`). **Transitive** by
   construction (`parent∘parent = grandparent`), cheap — but iterated
   lineage *decoheres*: deep descendants drift outside the ancestor's
   region by a system-specific, measurable amount. The Standard already
   documents this symptom in its own words — Note 2 to 4.11: "In some
   DGGHs, the children of the children of a parent zone (relative depth
   of 2) are not all sub-zones of that parent zone."

3. **Ownership (unique geometric assignment)** — each zone at relative
   depth d belongs to **exactly one** ancestor (under a documented
   ownership convention for the straddlers). This is the relation
   aggregation, roll-up statistics and multi-resolution joins need:
   counts are exactly Nᵈ, descendant sets partition the domain, nothing
   is double-counted. Its price: it is **non-transitive** —
   `owner(z, K)` need not equal `owner(owner(z, M), K)` — which is
   precisely why it cannot be recovered by composing one-level steps
   and must be defined (and served) at its target depth.

These cannot be collapsed into one relation: for non-congruent zones, no
unique-parent assignment makes iterated parenthood agree with
containment at all depths. The Standard currently names only reading
(1); readings (2) and (3) are left to implementations, which silently
differ.

## Reproducible example (H3, 5 lines)

Lineage vs geometry, using only a native library:

```python
import h3
leaf = '87390d509ffffff'                                # res 7
idx  = h3.cell_to_parent(leaf, 5)                       # lineage ancestor
geo  = h3.latlng_to_cell(*h3.cell_to_latlng(leaf), 5)   # zone containing its centre
print(idx, geo, idx == geo)
# 85390d53fffffff 85390d57fffffff False
```

Different res-5 cells; neither is wrong — they answer different
questions. A client mixing native-library lineage with API sub-zone
queries is silently mixing relations (1) and (2).

## Measured magnitude

Enumerating one anchor zone's lineage-descendants three levels finer and
classifying each by overlap with the anchor region (anchor at 40°N 3°W;
counts are anchor-dependent, the qualitative behaviour is not;
reproduction script:
<https://github.com/MrBenGriffin/hex9/blob/main/docs/dggs/dggs_nesting.py>):

| System | descendants | entirely outside the ancestor |
|---|---|---|
| S2 (congruent quadtree) | 64 | 0 — all three relations coincide |
| H3 (aperture 7) | 343 | 12 (3.5%) |
| A5 (aperture 4, pentagonal) | 64 | 22 (34%) |
| Hex9, lineage relation | 729 | 108 (14.8% — exactly 1/6 of the area, structurally) |
| Hex9, ownership relation | 729 | 0 (27 rim zones straddle by construction) |

The last two rows are the same grid under two relations — the divergence
is a property of the *relation*, not the grid. Ownership is exactly
computable when the system documents the exact substructure its
refinement recurses on (its **carrier** — for Hex9 a rep-9 half-hexagon;
for S2 the cell quadtree itself; H3 has no finite polygonal carrier, but
an ownership rule is still exactly computable in lattice arithmetic).

## Proposal

1. **Add a term: owned sub-zone** (alongside 4.11's sub-zone): a
   sub-zone at relative depth d assigned to exactly one super-zone under
   the DGGRS's documented ownership convention. Every zone at depth d is
   the owned sub-zone of exactly one level-K zone; owned sub-zone sets
   partition the globe; their counts are exactly the DGGRS's aperture to
   the power d. (The existing deterministic sub-zone ordering gives the
   owned subset a well-defined induced order, so data encodings carry
   over unchanged.)

2. **An optional Zone Query capability** exposing it — e.g. an
   `owned-only` (boolean) refinement of the existing `parent-zone` +
   `zone-level` query, returning only zones the parent owns. No new
   endpoints and no new depth machinery: `zone-level` already provides
   exactly-at-depth semantics. Aggregation clients then have a
   partition; exploration clients keep coverage.

3. **DGGRS metadata SHOULD declare the properties** of the hierarchy
   relations it exposes: transitivity (lineage: yes; ownership: no),
   count regularity (exactly Nᵈ?), containment or bounded excursion,
   and partition. These four are not simultaneously satisfiable on
   non-congruent zones — which is exactly why they should be declared
   rather than assumed. Congruent systems satisfy all four under every
   reading at no cost.

4. **Relate the readings in prose.** A short informative subsection (or
   an extension of 4.11's notes) naming the three relations and their
   intended uses would prevent the silent-mixing failure mode. Note 2
   already contains the seed of this; #106 sharpens reading (1); this
   proposal completes the taxonomy with reading (3).

Issue #302: Factory lines — plugin-style program bundles (epic)

## Goal

Turn the factory-line pattern we already ran (HAR 1.0.0, epic #225) into a **product primitive**: a repeatable, gated, multi-station program any repo can **install** — without baking in how *this* repo happened to execute *that* migration, and **without putting the program on the default verify pipeline**.

**Out of the 1.0.0 release.** This is `post-1.0.0`. 1.0 ships the primitives; factory lines compose them.

## Closed architecture (2026-08-29)

A factory line is a **plugin-style bundle** with the same authoring and distribution path as [os-factory/har-plugin](https://github.com/os-factory/har-plugin), and the **opposite apply rule**.

| | Verification plugin | Line bundle |
|---|---|---|
| Template | `os-factory/har-plugin` | `os-factory/har-line` (#322) |
| Author locally | `har plugin create <id>` | `har line create <id>` |
| Install | `har env add-plugin <spec>` | `har line add <spec>` |
| Resolve | path → git → bundled → npm | **same resolver** (`plugin-resolve.ts`) |
| Writes | Stage scripts, optional CI, package merge | Program (`line.json`: stations, skills, MCP hints, gate) + optional extra stages |
| `stages.json` | Register **and** append `verificationStages` | May **register** stages; **must not** append `verificationStages` |
| Default verify | Gets those stages — that is the point | **Unchanged** list and duration |
| Agents run it | `har env verify` / `har_run_stage` | `/factory-line` → `har line gate` / `run-stage` |
| Ledger | `.har/plugins.json` | `.har/lines.json` (sibling file, not a fourth marketplace) |

`har env add-plugin` on a line bundle must **refuse** (pointer to `har line add`). `har line add` on a verification plugin must refuse. Kind confusion is how a Docker occupancy lab or `fixture-e2e` ends up on every `verify --full`.

This closes the old “line vs plugin vs composition” debate in #302: **same pipes, different apply.** It is not a new marketplace UI. It is not `add-plugin` with empty `verificationStages` (today that field is required and always patched — `patchStageRegistry` in `src/harness/plugins.ts`).

Two existing skills already describe themselves as a "Factory line for…":

- `new-plugin` — research the docs, build the template, register it everywhere, validate on a real repository, open a PR

That's two unrelated jobs converging on the same shape. A **harness** is already a manufacturing word (a jig that holds a unit in a known state so you can measure it). The product name's etymology extends; it isn't a borrowed analogy.

| Holds | Breaks |
|---|---|

Issue #813: Derive NIP-68 image format from exact bytes for every composition source

Parent: #216
Blocked by #750, #811, and #857
Blocks: #746 and #862

## Consequence

Every current or proposed NIP-68 construction path can publish a MIME label that was not derived from the bytes:

- direct upload supplies a caller `Content-Type` and receives a descriptor `type`;
- BUD-05 transformed output receives a descriptor `type`;
- `nmp-asset::VerifiedAsset` may prove only exact-byte identity;
- `nmp-nip68::PictureImage` currently copies a MIME claim from `BlobDescriptor`, `VerifiedUpload`, or the in-progress neutral asset into `imeta m`.

Hash/size proof does not prove media family. Request/response string agreement does not prove media family. Treating direct and transformed sources differently would duplicate the same policy and let one path remain weaker.

## Owning boundary

`nmp-nip68` owns the closed image vocabulary it publishes. Therefore it owns one private, bounded byte-to-format classifier used by **all** NIP-68 picture composition, regardless of whether the bytes came from direct Blossom upload, BUD-05 transformed retrieval, another storage backend, or an in-memory app asset.

`nmp-asset` remains protocol-neutral exact bytes + digest only. Blossom owns descriptor and transport claims. `nmp-media` may orchestrate stages but does not classify formats. Native SDKs do not sniff media.

## Exact proof claim

The classifier proves bounded structural container-family conformance sufficient to derive exactly one governed NIP-68 MIME:

- `image/apng`
- `image/avif`
- `image/gif`
- `image/jpeg`
- `image/png`
- `image/webp`

It does not prove pixel validity, successful rendering, safety, authenticity, semantic content, or full codec decode.

The input is the exact immutable bytes held by `VerifiedAsset`. The result is consumed privately to mint the existing `PictureImage`; do not add a public `VerifiedMedia`, `DetectedMime`, transformed-only witness, classifier service, registry, or runtime callback.

Descriptor MIME, request `Content-Type`, URL extension, HTTP headers, platform frameworks, and caller strings are claims only. They never select the result. After byte derivation, any present descriptor/request claim may be compared byte-for-byte for consistency; disagreement is a typed refusal, never authority. The emitted NIP-68 `m` is always the byte-derived closed value.

## Parser contract

- Apply one explicit byte cap before parsing. Runtime is linear in that bounded input; all length/offset arithmetic is checked; extra memory is bounded independently of blob length.
- Do not decompress pixels or codec payloads.
- Dispatch through pairwise-disjoint container families and then validate that family. Do not use first-match magic-byte guessing.
- PNG/APNG: validate signature, required chunk ordering, checked lengths/CRCs, `IDAT`, exact `IEND`, and an APNG state machine that cannot silently downgrade malformed animation to PNG.
- JPEG: validate SOI, checked marker/segment framing, supported SOF, SOS/entropy framing, and exact EOI.
- GIF: validate 87a/89a framing, table/block/sub-block bounds, at least one image descriptor, and exact trailer.
- WebP: validate RIFF size/padding, `WEBP`, one coherent VP8/VP8L/VP8X family, required animation relationships, and no trailing bytes.
- AVIF: validate complete ISOBMFF box coverage, `avif` image brand (not `avis` sequence mislabeled as image), coherent primary image item/extents/config/property relationships, and bounded no-copy traversal.
- Truncated, malformed, unsupported, over-limit, overflow, concatenated-container, and resource-exhausting inputs have reachable closed refusals. Do not add an `Ambiguous` variant unless an actual byte corpus proves it reachable.
- Third-party parser strings never cross Rust or FFI.

## Exact source census/target

At audited `origin/master` `c51fc80a8b5a2a54fcedf7881ca4eef139a1b512`:

- `crates/nmp-nip68/src/image.rs::PictureImage::from_descriptor` and `from_verified_upload` mint `m` from descriptor text.
- `crates/nmp-media/src/upload.rs::UploadedAsset::{picture_image,into_picture_image}` bypass any byte classifier.
- `crates/nmp-media/src/prepare.rs::PreparedUpload` has the direct bytes but loses them at the upload boundary.
- #750 deliberately stops at transformed hash/size verification.

Required target:

- one private classifier and one closed refusal taxonomy in `nmp-nip68`;
- one `PictureImage` construction boundary that requires `&VerifiedAsset` exact bytes and derives `m`;

Issue #108: Unscoped candidate sets are O(house) on the wire: 1.8 MB / 912 ms measured, and the compaction lever we reverted

## The measurement

A candidate set puts every candidate on the wire, so an unscoped set is linear in house size. On a
real instance (1069 entities), `pkl-demo` — which says `q.from(dump.all).where(state == on)` —
evaluates to:

| | |
|---|---|
| total wire JSON | **1.8 MB** (57% of it candidate sets) |
| per candidate | **982 B** — 2× the 459 B the design estimated |
| eval time | **912 ms**, against 209 ms for the same dashboard's set-free siblings |

The old `LayoutNode.Dynamic` expressed the same query in ~1 KB, O(1) in house size. That is a real
regression for **unscoped** sets, and it is the trade the redesign made knowingly (build-time entity
identity in exchange for shipping the candidate list). Scoped sets — a room's lights — are cheap and
strictly better. Nothing here argues for undoing the redesign; the question is what to do about the
unbounded case.

`dashboard.json` never reaches the browser, so this costs **eval time, server memory and editor
latency**, not client bytes. 900 ms per save is felt in the edit loop.

## Where the bytes actually go

Measured over the 1069-member set:

| | per member | share |
|---|---|---|
| `onclick` slot | 333 B | **42%** |
| `value` slot | 138 B | 18% |
| `label` slot | 104 B | 13% |
| guard (`when`) | 63 B | 8% |
| node scaffolding | 58 B | 7% |
| `entity_id` | 36 B | 5% |
| everything else | ~54 B | 7% |

And the decisive fact for any dedup scheme:

```
distinct clause nodes: 1069 of 1069
distinct slot objects:    7 of 3255
```

Every node differs (each carries its own `entity_id` and baked `label`), so node-level dedup gains
nothing. But the **slot objects are almost entirely identical** — `onclick` and `value` are the same
JSONata for every member, because they resolve `$entity_id` at runtime rather than naming it.

## Four independent levers

### 1. Fold `toggleTap` — #106, already tracked

`onclick` is 42% of the bytes: one large `$lookup($domain)` JSONata repeated 1069 times. #106 turns
it into a per-entity literal (`sse/action/light/toggle/light.taklys`, ~70 B). **The single biggest
win, and it is already scoped work.** Note the interaction with lever 3: folding makes the string
small but per-member (not dedupable), where interning makes it shared but large. Either helps;
they do not compound as much as their individual numbers suggest.

### 2. Scope the set (authoring guidance)

`q.from(dump.all)` is the expensive pattern, and `pkl-demo` demonstrates it. Most real dashboards
want a room or a floor. Cheapest fix, but it does not make the general case safe — it just avoids
it.

### 3. The compaction mechanism we designed, built, and reverted

This existed. `docs/plan-dynamics-one-entity-lifecycle.md`, "Rejected: the compressed format", has
the full account. Summary, because it is the obvious lever and its rejection should not be
re-litigated from scratch:

**The shape** — shared `shapes` and `conditions` tables, members as thin rows of indices plus their
varying literals (`vars`) and nested sets (`fills`), with `holes` marking where a shape's children
vary.

**Measured then**, on N synthetic post-fold lights:

| candidates | compressed | expanded | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 2.1 KB | 4.4 KB | 2.1× |
| 50 | 9.2 KB | 22.3 KB | 2.4× |
| 200 | 36.1 KB | 89.4 KB | 2.5× |
| 1000 | 180.7 KB | 448.0 KB | 2.5× |

Per-candidate cost is flat either way (185 B compressed, 459 B expanded), so both grow linearly and
the ratio settles at ~2.5×. No exponential term.

**Why it was reverted:** the 2.5× cost four concepts (`shapes`, `conditions`, `holes`/`fills`,
`vars`) and two classes of bug, both found in the spike and both *structurally impossible* in the
expanded form — a clause carrying another clause's literals, and two cards with different cells
silently sharing a shape. It also needed a rule for whether a literal is shared or per-member, which
then had to be made count-independent to stop identical authoring emitting two different structures.
Judged a bad trade **for a server-side artifact**.

**What the new evidence changes.** The plan set an explicit revisit condition:

> Revisit only if memory or Pkl eval time on a large real dashboard actually bites.

It bites — 1.8 MB and 912 ms. And the 7-distinct-slots-of-3255 figure suggests compaction would beat
its own 2.5× benchmark here, because that benchmark was measured on synthetic lights with fewer
slots than a real `entityCard`. A slot-level table alone (not the full shapes/holes/fills machinery)
might get most of it for one concept instead of four.

**If this is revived, the two reverted bug classes come back**, and the spike scenarios that guard
them (S18–S22: a member whose clauses point at different shapes carries each shape's own literals,
and the fallback never renders with blanks; C11–C13: two sets over the same entity keep independent
members) were deliberately not ported to `query.test.pkl` *because the expanded format makes them
unrepresentable*. They would have to be ported first.

### 4. Backend interning at load

The plan's own "cheaper first move": intern identical terms when the dashboard is loaded, recovering
the sharing without putting any of it on the wire. Given 7 distinct slot objects out of 3255, this
would collapse **memory** dramatically. It does **not** help eval time or JSON size — the bytes are
still generated and parsed. Worth knowing which problem is actually being solved before picking.

## Guard against silent regression

None of this was caught by CI: no test pins wire size, so the 1.8 MB arrived and passed. Whatever is
done above, something should fail when a dashboard's evaluated wire crosses a threshold — or at
minimum when a set's candidate count does. A `Dashboard.validate` warning above N candidates is the
cheap version and would have surfaced this at authoring time.

- SDK availability, versions, install commands and compatibility facts come from the generated SDK catalog/release artifacts.

## Scope

1. Establish the version-controlled documentation source structure and ownership rules.
2. Build system routes/navigation for `/docs` and all descendants outside the editorial page resolver/publication system.
3. Generate the API Reference from the released OpenAPI contract, including security schemes, request/response models and canonical error envelopes.
4. Generate SDK overview/language pages from the released SDK catalog.
5. Author canonical guides for:
   - Developer Account creation/sign-in;
   - Project creation;
   - Subscription selection;
   - development client and first request;
   - confidential server clients;
   - public/distributed clients, enrollment and DPoP;
   - token lifetime, refresh/cache and resilience;
   - credential rotation/revocation and secure storage;
   - canonical `MC-*` error handling and support correlation with `errorId`;
   - SDK version/API compatibility and upgrade behavior.
6. Generate language-specific quickstarts from tested snippets tied to the exact published SDK version.
7. Integrate system docs into Portal navigation/search/sitemap as appropriate without exposing them as CMS-editable pages.
8. Define redirect/version/deprecation behavior for renamed or removed documentation paths.

- Reusable conceptual prose has one canonical Markdown/MDX source.
- Code samples must be compile/test fixtures or generated from such fixtures where practical.

Issue #70747: executor: collect producer-side evidence for precise statement RU accounting

## Enhancement

Statement RU accounting can now traverse the whole physical-plan forest (Main, deduplicated CTE definitions, and scalar-subquery trees), but its calibration remains `Incomplete`. The current value is deliberately neither an exact value nor a mathematical upper/lower bound because several formula inputs have already lost execution-lifecycle or response-level information by the time the statement-RU consumer runs.

This issue tracks the producer-side evidence needed to tighten that contract without inferring execution from missing rows or multiplying shared CTE work by consumer count.

### Missing evidence

1. **Physical scan bytes per response/request.**
   - Cloud TiKV can provide total key size for scan and point-get responses.
   - TiDB should consume that response-level total directly (including close-time unconsumed responses) and aggregate it under the request root.
   - Until then, estimating bytes from merged `ScanDetail` ratios can bias either upward or downward when requests have different key-size distributions.

2. **Formula-ready Sort/TopN work per executor lifecycle.**
   - Repeated CTE rounds and correlated Apply executions merge row counts by plan ID.
   - `sum(n_i * log(n_i))` cannot be reconstructed from `sum(n_i) * log(sum(n_i))`; the latter overestimates repeated work.
   - Sort/TopN producers should publish a bounded sufficient statistic plus begun/completed/incomplete coverage, rather than an unbounded vector of row counts.

3. **Direct recursive-CTE and Apply execution-opportunity state.**
   - Preserve three distinct states: intentionally skipped, executed with zero rows, and required evidence missing.
   - CTE evidence should be keyed by `IDForStorage` and classify seed/recursive phase attempts, legal skip reasons, and completed rounds.
   - Apply evidence should classify outer rows, filters, cache hits, logical inner invocations, and physical inner executions/cancellation.

### Ownership and lifetime

The direct executors should publish display-neutral, value-only snapshots into the statement-owned runtime evidence collector before live CTE/Apply objects are closed. Synchronization stays private to the provider/container; copied snapshots contain only scalar values and enums. Plan ID remains an execution-evidence lookup key, not an occurrence identity.

The statement-RU consumer should continue to:

- count each CTE producer once through the `IDForStorage`-deduplicated definition forest;
- keep skipped, executed-zero, and missing evidence distinct;
- fail closed on invalid or structurally inconsistent evidence;
- avoid treating positive aggregate rows or EOF as proof that every physical opportunity was attempted.

### Acceptance criteria

- Response-level scan/point-get total key size is consumed without reconstructing it from merged ratios.
- Repeated Sort/TopN work uses producer-accumulated per-lifecycle sufficient statistics.
- Recursive CTE and serial/parallel Apply expose complete opportunity/disposition snapshots.

A maintainer on the project piskuliche/RBFENetworkMap (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #43: --design-total-ns can allocate 0.0 ns to a selected edge

`--design-total-ns` divides a simulation budget across the selected edges by predicted
information gain. The aggregate is right -- the per-edge `simulation_ns` values sum to
exactly the budget -- but there is no lower floor, and on a real series it reaches zero.

Planning the 16-ligand Tyk2 set with

```
--scorer variance --planner optimal --design a_optimal --n-edges 44 --design-total-ns 400
```

gives 44 edges summing to 400.0 ns, λ windows 12-24, median 7.85 ns, max 36.02 -- and **two
edges at exactly 0.0 ns**: `ejm31~ejm42` and `ejm31~ejm46`. The next smallest is 5.16 ns, so
this is not a rounding tail; it is a cliff.

Zero is self-contradictory rather than merely small. Both edges are *selected*: they are in
`edges.dat`, they have `atommap_*.runconfig` files, and those runconfigs instruct a run of no
length. Whoever executes the network either runs nothing and has a hole in the graph, or
notices and picks a number by hand, which is the allocation the flag was supposed to make.

Before #42 this was one edge at 0.0139 ns, which read as a floor problem. Now that the
candidate pool is complete it is two edges at flat zero, which reads as a modelling problem:
the design says these edges carry no information given the rest, and the allocator faithfully
gives them nothing.

Three plausible resolutions, and I do not think it is obvious which is right:

1. **Drop them.** If the design gives an edge zero weight, it does not belong in the network;
   emit 42 edges and say two were dropped as uninformative.
2. **Floor them.** Clamp to some minimum runnable length and renormalise. Keeps the topology
   the planner chose, at the cost of spending budget the design says is wasted.
3. **Refuse.** Treat a zero allocation as a contradiction between `--n-edges` and
   `--design-total-ns` and make the user resolve it.

Whichever it is, silently writing a runconfig for a zero-length simulation is the one option
that should be off the table.

Note the upstream method (NetBFE, Li et al., *JCTC* 2022, 18(2) 650-663,
doi:10.1021/acs.jctc.1c00703) is *iterative* -- it re-optimises allocation each round from
measured variances -- so a near-zero allocation there is a signal the next round reconsiders.
This package implements the static first pass, where there is no next round.

Issue #4056: perf: pin Python deps and install offline (postinst pip resolution costs ~20s per job and corrupts the shipped site-packages)

## Context

Measured on `ci / build / merge-python-site-packages`, job-level instrumentation step (`plengauer/opentelemetry-github@571cbe85`, v5.60.0), runner image `ubuntu-24.04` / `20260810.271.1`.

The whole step takes **~33.2 s**. `postinst configure` (backgrounded via `run` from the fast-deb path) runs from ≈`12:05:40.06` to `12:06:01.94` = **~21.9 s**, and 19.4 s of that is exposed as naked latency in the `::group::Waiting for background init jobs` block. It is by far the biggest single cost in the step.

## Problem

`meta/debian/postinst` runs `pip3 install -r requirements.txt` against a live index for both the `/opt/opentelemetry_shell/venv` chunk and the per-version `agent.instrumentation.python` chunk. Because the requirements files pin only some packages, the prebuilt artifacts (`python_site_packages.tar.xz`, `/root/.cache/pip` from the dependencies cache) **never fully satisfy them**, so every job pays a full PyPI resolution plus real downloads.

Evidence from a single run's log:

- `idna>=3.15` floats: chunk (b) reports `Requirement already satisfied: idna<4,>=2.5 ... (3.18)` while chunk (c) does `Downloading idna-3.19-py3-none-any.whl.metadata` — two different versions of the same dep in the same run.
- Freshly downloaded (not cached) every run: `charset_normalizer-3.5.1` (248 kB), `grpcio-1.83.0` (**7.0 MB**), `protobuf-7.35.1` (327 kB), `wrapt-2.3.0` (172 kB).
- The result is a tree pip itself declares broken:
  ```
  ERROR: pip's dependency resolver does not currently take into account all the packages that are installed. ...
  opentelemetry-instrumentation-asyncclick 0.65b0 requires wrapt~=1.0, but you have wrapt 2.3.0 which is incompatible.
  ```
  i.e. install time mutates `python_site_packages.tar.xz` — the artifact this very job builds — into an inconsistent state.
- `type uv` fails on GitHub-hosted runners, so the `uv pip install --offline` fast path in postinst is dead code and we always take the slow `python3 -m venv` + `pip3` branch. `/root/.cache/uv` in the dependencies cache key on `main` is therefore dead weight.

## Proposal (output-equivalent)

1. Generate a **fully pinned lock file** (e.g. `pip freeze` of the tree that the build job actually produces, or `pip-compile`) and commit it alongside the current requirements. Once nothing floats, the shipped artifacts satisfy the requirements exactly and pip has no work to do.
2. Install with `--no-deps --no-index --find-links=<wheelhouse shipped in the deb>`, falling back to the network only on failure — the same offline-then-online shape the existing `uv` branch already has.
3. Better still: **ship a prebuilt `/opt/opentelemetry_shell/venv` in the deb** (the install path is fixed, so `python3 -m venv --copies` output is relocatable enough) and reduce postinst to a sanity check.
4. Either install `uv` as part of the flow or drop the `uv` branch and `/root/.cache/uv` from the cache paths, so the code reflects what actually executes.

Side effect: this also fixes the `wrapt` incompatibility above, which is a correctness bug independent of performance.

**Expected saving: ~22 s → 2–4 s on the critical path.**

## Caveat

The exact split of the 21.9 s between venv creation, pip resolution, download, and xz extraction is **not** measurable from the log, because `run` pipes output through `perl -0777 -pe ''`, which slurps the whole stream and flushes at exit — every postinst line carries the same `12:06:01.9xx` timestamp. See the companion issue on instrumenting the `run` wrapper.

Issue #1917: SDK drift: Python's errors.py exposes hosted error classes via a module-level __getattr__ lazy re-export; TypeScript's errors.ts explicitly refuses to re-export them at all

## Drift
Python's `errors.py` submodule implements a module-level `__getattr__` that lazily re-exports the hosted error classes (`HostedTradingError`, `InsufficientEscrowBalance`, `OrderSizeTooSmall`, `InvalidApiKey`, `OutcomeNotFound`, `CatalogUnavailable`, `BuiltOrderExpired`, `InvalidSignature`, `NoLiquidity`, `MissingWalletAddress`) from the private `_hosted_errors` module. This means `from pmxt.errors import HostedTradingError` (and `pmxt.errors.HostedTradingError`) work in Python even though these classes are not defined in `errors.py` itself.

TypeScript's `errors.ts` has no equivalent mechanism and explicitly documents that it never will: a comment states hosted errors are intentionally NOT re-exported from `errors.ts` because doing so creates a circular dependency that crashes tsx/CJS module loaders, even though `tsc`/`ts-jest` tolerate it. So `import { HostedTradingError } from "./errors"` (or the compiled equivalent) does not work in TypeScript — only `index.ts` (package root) or `./hosted-errors` directly expose it.

This is distinct from #1329 (which is about `pmxt/__init__.py` package-root exports vs `index.ts`): this finding is about the `errors`/`errors.ts` *submodules themselves* diverging in whether they expose hosted error classes as attributes, independent of what the package root does.

## TypeScript SDK
`sdks/typescript/pmxt/errors.ts:172-175`
```typescript
// Hosted error classes live in ./hosted-errors. Re-exported from index.ts
// at the package root, NOT here — re-exporting from errors.ts creates a
// circular dependency (hosted-errors imports PmxtError from errors.ts)
// that crashes tsx/CJS module loaders even though tsc and ts-jest tolerate it.
```
No hosted error class is accessible via the `errors.ts` submodule under any import path — only via `index.ts` or `./hosted-errors` directly.

## Python SDK
`sdks/python/pmxt/errors.py:177-197`
```python
_HOSTED_ERROR_EXPORTS = frozenset(
    {
        "HostedTradingError",
        "InsufficientEscrowBalance",
        "OrderSizeTooSmall",
        "InvalidApiKey",
        "OutcomeNotFound",
        "CatalogUnavailable",
        "BuiltOrderExpired",
        "InvalidSignature",
        "NoLiquidity",
        "MissingWalletAddress",
    }
)


def __getattr__(name: str) -> Any:
    """Lazily re-export hosted errors without creating an import cycle."""
    if name in _HOSTED_ERROR_EXPORTS:
        from . import _hosted_errors
        return getattr(_hosted_errors, name)
```
`from pmxt.errors import HostedTradingError` and `pmxt.errors.HostedTradingError` both succeed in Python, sourcing the class from the private `_hosted_errors` module transparently.

## Expected
The two "errors" submodules should present the same import surface. Either TypeScript's `errors.ts` should gain an equivalent lazy/dynamic re-export mechanism for hosted error classes (mirroring Python's `__getattr__` shim, without reintroducing the documented circular-dependency crash — e.g. via a lazy getter or a separate non-circular indirection), or Python's `errors.py` should drop its `__getattr__` shim and rely solely on the package-root `__init__.py` for hosted-error discoverability, matching TypeScript's approach.

## Impact
Python users can reach hosted error classes through two submodule import paths (`pmxt.errors.X` and, once #1329 is fixed, `pmxt.X`) with an undocumented `frozenset` allowlist that must be kept manually in sync with `_hosted_errors.py`'s actual class list — a new class added there silently becomes unreachable via `pmxt.errors` until someone remembers to add it to `_HOSTED_ERROR_EXPORTS`. TypeScript users have no submodule import path at all for hosted errors (`./errors` never exposes them), only the package root. Code or documentation written assuming `pmxt.errors`/`./errors` are equivalent, mirrored submodules across languages will behave inconsistently.

Issue #13434: perf(pacquet): avoid nested tarball extraction parallelism without regressions

## Problem

On a cold frozen install of the pinned Next.js workspace from https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13305, the TypeScript CLI completed in 11.30s while the Rust CLI completed in 13.84s on the same machine and dependency graph.

Investigation indicates that many tarballs are downloaded concurrently while each tarball with at least 32 files also uses inner parallel extraction. This nested parallelism increases scheduling and filesystem contention. As an experiment, effectively disabling per-tarball parallel extraction improved Rust fetch performance, but applying that globally could regress workloads with one or a few very large tarballs.

The concurrent integrity/extraction benchmark added by https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/pull/13433 provides a deterministic regression workload for the many-tarball case.

## Proposed investigation

Test an adaptive, globally bounded extraction strategy rather than simply increasing or removing `PARALLEL_EXTRACT_THRESHOLD`:

- preserve inner parallel extraction when only a few large tarballs are active;
- prefer sequential extraction within each tarball when many tarballs are already in flight;
- prevent outer package concurrency from multiplying unboundedly with per-tarball file concurrency.

Before choosing an implementation, parameterize the integrity benchmark across:

- 1, 8, 32, 128, and 256 concurrent tarballs;
- 8, 32, 64, 256, and 2,048 files per tarball;
- small and large files;
- compressible and incompressible content.

## End-to-end validation

Validate baseline Rust against candidate Rust on:

1. The pinned Next.js cold frozen-install reproduction.
2. All 48 installation scenarios from https://github.com/vltpkg/benchmarks/pull/132:
   - fixtures: Next.js, Astro, Svelte, Vue, Large, and Babylon.js;
   - states: clean, cache, cache plus lockfile, cache plus `node_modules`, cache plus lockfile plus `node_modules`, lockfile, lockfile plus `node_modules`, and `node_modules`.
3. The vlt `build`, `build-cache`, and `run` scenarios as correctness checks.
4. Single-large-tarball microbenchmarks that exercise the workload most likely to benefit from inner parallel extraction.

Run at least five measured iterations after warmup. Repeat apparent regressions with baseline/candidate order reversed so machine drift is not mistaken for an implementation effect.

## Acceptance criteria

- The Next.js cold frozen install improves by at least 10%.
- The concurrent-tarball microbenchmark improves materially.
- No repeatable vlt installation scenario regresses by more than 3%.
- Single-large-tarball scenarios do not regress by more than 3%.
- Aggregate vlt performance does not regress.
- Package counts, exit codes, lockfiles, and installed dependency graphs remain equivalent.

The optimization should not be merged if it only exchanges the Next.js regression for a regression in low-concurrency or large-tarball workloads.
