Issue #59: [P1] Add dependency-aware skill/provider lockfiles and capability manifests

## Problem

#30 protects direct provider installation/configuration with source, version,
binary identity and hashes.

That is necessary but not sufficient once skills/providers have their own
dependencies.

A top-level skill can invoke:

- another skill;
- a package-manager dependency;
- a local executable;
- a remote service;
- an MCP server;
- a credentialed API.

Auditing only the top-level artifact hides transitive capability and
supply-chain changes.

## Evidence

"Skills Are Not Islands" analyzes more than 1.43 million skills and reports
mixed skill/package/service dependency graphs where inspecting only a top-level
skill misses security-relevant signals. It recommends typed dependency
manifests and lockfile-like records:

https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01136

"Skills That Don't Exist" finds systemic hallucinated skill recommendations
across 15,000 prompts:

https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12340

Recent malicious-skill evaluation:

https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05223

Supply-chain poisoning evaluation:

https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03081

## Goal

Extend #30 from direct binary provenance into dependency- and
capability-aware locking.

## Proposed artifacts

    skills.lock
    providers.lock

Each entry records where applicable:

- canonical ID/name;
- exact source;
- publisher/owner;
- exact version or immutable revision;
- content/binary digest;
- direct dependencies;
- resolved transitive dependencies;
- external services;
- requested filesystem capabilities;
- requested network capabilities;
- requested credentials;
- install/approval provenance.

## Capability manifest

Example:

    skill: deploy-service
    version: 1.4.2
    capabilities:
      filesystem:
        read: ["deploy/**"]
      network:
        - "api.example.invalid"
      credentials:
        - "deployment-token"
      process:
        - "kubectl"

A version update that adds a new credential or network capability is a
security-relevant diff even when the package name is unchanged.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Skill/provider identity can be pinned to immutable provenance.
- [ ] Lockfile records direct dependencies.
- [ ] Supported ecosystems record resolvable transitive dependencies.
- [ ] External service dependencies are representable.
- [ ] Requested capabilities are part of the locked review surface.
- [ ] Protected execution detects binary/content/dependency drift.
- [ ] Capability expansion requires a new approval.
- [ ] Model-generated nonexistent names are never silently resolved by
      installing similarly named registry artifacts.
- [ ] `agentos doctor` can report missing, drifted, or unexpectedly expanded
      dependencies.
- [ ] Lockfiles are deterministic for a fixed dependency graph.

## Tests

- top-level skill unchanged, transitive package changes;
- dependency introduces new service;
- skill version requests a new credential;
- binary swapped at same path;
- hallucinated nonexistent skill;
- removed dependency;
- deterministic regeneration.

## Dependencies

- Extends #30.
- Uses #7 approval receipts.
- Protected behavior uses #11.
- Capability declarations should share the sandbox-capability schema.

## Non-goals

- Reimplementing npm/pip/etc. lockfile resolution.
- Automatically trusting a dependency because its package manager considers it
  valid.

Issue #482: RFC: review_tiers seam key — declare blast-radius paths so required review depth is schema, not per-PR judgment

Status: RFC — a design question, not a settled direction. Filed to capture the gap and force reconciliation with adjacent in-flight work (#438, #400, #392) before any seam surface is added.

## Gap

Review depth is currently tiered by prose judgment, not by declared risk. The Adversarial Review Gate (`workflows/pr-processing.md`) is required for "high-risk, concurrent-batch, or RC PRs" — but *high-risk* is decided per-PR by the coordinating agent or operator. A consumer repo has no way to declare "changes under these paths always get the full gauntlet." That determination lives inside a load-bearing merge gate as unstructured judgment, which is the pattern the Process Gap Disposition rule exists to push toward `schema`.

External framing: Addy Osmani, [Agentic Code Review](https://addyosmani.com/blog/agentic-code-review/) — route review layers by cost of failure ("tier by risk, not author"): a config tweak gets lint + a glance; a payments/auth/migration path gets types, tests, heterogeneous reviewers, domain owner, security pass. The pack has the gates; it lacks the routing declaration.

## Proposal (for discussion)

A `review_tiers` key at the repo seam (`.agents/agent-workflow.yml`): path patterns and/or change classes mapped to required review depth — e.g. which of {adversarial review, security pass, human review, N configured reviewers} are mandatory before the Review Completion Gate can close. The gates consume the declaration; absence of a declaration preserves today's judgment-based behavior, so adoption is opt-in per consumer repo and fully portable.

## Open design questions this RFC must settle

1. **Relationship to #438** (policy-aware merge assurance / `diff_identity`): is tiered review depth a facet of that policy model, or a separate intake-side contract? If #438's design subsumes it, close this in favor of #438.
2. **Relationship to #400/#392**: risk-based model routing and task-scoped review packets both classify work by risk — one classification vocabulary should serve all three, not three parallel ones.
3. **Classification basis**: path globs are cheap but coarse (a one-line comment fix in a payments file is not a payments change); change classes are truthful but need derivation. Probably globs first, class overrides later.
4. **Whether to build at all**: there is **no motivating miss** — no observed case of a high-blast-radius path receiving a shallow review. Under the disposition rule that is a legitimate reason to park. The counter-weight is that this gap's failure mode is silent (a shallow review that ships is only discovered by incident), so waiting for the miss means paying for it.

## Disposition

- Mechanism target: `schema` (seam key + validation in `agent-workflow-seam-doctor`), contingent on RFC acceptance.
- Motivating miss: none observed — filed preventively from external review; question 4 above is the honest treatment of that.
- Replay evidence: if accepted, a fixture consumer repo (`test/fixtures/consumer-repo/`) declaring a tier and a replay showing the gate refuses to close without the mandated reviews.
- Non-goal: no new review mechanisms — only routing of the existing gates; no default tiers imposed on consumer repos.

## Severity
[P1]

`4055e225e81a2cbe1afc5f864b4aaba4d8b3fc15`

Track active calls/generations per slot and make unregister wait for quiescence, with defined self-unregister behavior.

## Severity

Foundations and asset/data pipeline

## Evidence

PR #356 closes the POSIX half of #338. Its Windows half is explicitly not implemented, and the PR body says so and asks for a linked follow-up before #338 is closed. This is that issue, filed so the residual scope lives on the tracker rather than only in a PR body (`CLAUDE.md`, working conventions: "Residual scope from a partial fix gets its own linked issue").

- `core/src/durable_replace.cpp:57-64` — `production_open_parent_directory` returns `kDirectoryDurabilityUnavailable` unconditionally under `_WIN32`; no directory is opened and nothing is synced.
- `core/src/durable_replace.cpp:69-77` — `production_sync_directory` returns `false` under `_WIN32`; unreachable today because the open short-circuits first.
- `core/src/durable_replace.cpp:180-182` — that sentinel maps to `ReplaceOutcome::ReplacedDurabilityUnavailable`, which `core/src/atomic_file.cpp:113-126` maps to `commit() == true` with **no log at all** (only `ReplacedNotDurable` logs).
- `core/src/durable_replace.h:29-36` names the intended remedy — `MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH` / `ReplaceFile` — and records that it is not implemented.

Windows is the canonical build/test platform in `CLAUDE.md`'s Build/test section and the first editor target in the product vision, so the platform the durability work has not yet reached is the primary one.

## Failure scenario

Identical to #338's, on Windows: a scene, prefab, save, editor setting, input map, or cooked output is written; `commit()` reports success; power is lost; on recovery the destination holds the pre-save file, or nothing where the entry was newly created. Nothing in the log indicates the save was never made durable, because the `ReplacedDurabilityUnavailable` branch is deliberately silent.

The silence is defensible as a design choice — logging an error on every save on a whole platform would be noise — but it means the gap is invisible in the field, which is a reason to close it rather than to leave it reported-by-omission.

## Closure requirements

- Implement the Windows durable-replacement primitive behind the existing `ReplaceOps` seam so the protocol, not the call sites, gains the platform behaviour: `MoveFileEx(..., MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING | MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH)` or `ReplaceFile` with its write-through semantics, and decide explicitly whether a successful write-through rename reports `Durable` (it should, if the API's contract is met) or keeps a distinct outcome.
- Regression, red on base: the injected-ops test in `tests/unit/durable_replace_test.cpp` already covers every branch platform-independently; add the Windows production-ops case and a case asserting that `ReplacedDurabilityUnavailable` is no longer reachable on `_WIN32`. `check_production_path`'s current durability assertion (`log.errors == 0`) is vacuous on Windows for exactly this reason — see the PR #356 review — so it must be tightened in the same change, otherwise the new behaviour is untested there.
- Verification must run on a real Windows lane (the canonical clang-cl one, plus the MSVC compatibility lane), not be inferred from a POSIX run.
- Boundaries: destination absent vs. present, destination open by another handle (Windows rename semantics differ from POSIX here — worth an explicit test), a path on a network or removable volume where write-through may be refused, and repeated commits to the same destination.
- #338 stays open until this closes, per its own scope table.

## Origin

PR #356 review; deferred row of that PR's scope/closure table. Residual scope of #338.

Issue #18: Cycle errors render as inspect noise instead of the actual cycle

## Summary

Cycle detection is a headline feature (convention rule 3), but when it fires, the user sees inspect noise instead of the cycle:

```
$ rwm check
Convention violations found:
  - Dependency cycle: ["topological sort failed: [\"alpha\", \"beta\"]"]
```

```
  - Dependency cycle: alpha → beta → alpha
```

## Where

Three layers each mangle it a little:

- `DependencyGraph#topological_order` ([`lib/rwm/dependency_graph.rb:80`](https://github.com/sidbhatt11/ruby-workspace-manager/blob/33834f9/lib/rwm/dependency_graph.rb#L80)) wraps TSort's message string as `CycleError, [[e.message]]` — the "cycle" is a one-element array containing prose.

Don't parse TSort's exception message — extract real cycles: `each_strongly_connected_component` yields components; any component with size > 1 (or a self-edge) is a cycle whose members are package names. Both `check!` output and the raw `CycleError` message then agree. `execution_levels`' "possible cycle" branch should reuse the same extraction.

## Tests

- Two-package cycle → `Dependency cycle: alpha → beta → alpha`, exit 1.
- Three-package cycle renders the full loop.
- Multiple independent cycles each listed.

Issue #5035: Define atomicity and rollback semantics for OCI artifact publication

<!-- Issue title: Define atomicity and rollback semantics for OCI artifact publication -->

**Description**

<!--Tell us about the bug. What went wrong? How can we reproduce it? What should the correct behavior be?
-->

Cosign publishes OCI artifacts through several registry operations. A config and all referenced layer blobs must exist before an artifact manifest is accepted, so the OCI Distribution API provides no transaction spanning the complete publication.

The writers do not currently share an explicit partial-failure contract. In particular, the local-layout referrer path in `WriteSignedImageIndexImages` uploads the config and attempts the manifest before uploading its bundle layers. A conforming registry rejects that manifest because referenced blobs are missing; AWS ECR reports `BLOB_UPLOAD_UNKNOWN` in #5030. The layer loop is therefore never reached, while image, index, signature, or attestation objects written earlier by the same call may already be committed. Manifest-last writers such as `WriteReferrer` avoid that ordering failure, but a config, layer, cancellation, authentication, transport, artifact-manifest, or discovery-index failure can still leave partial state.

The affected publication protocols have different commit points and must not be treated as one blanket transaction:

| Path | Published state | Transaction concern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WriteReferrer`, `WriteSignaturesExperimentalOCI`, `WriteAttestationNewBundleFormat`, `WriteAttestationsReferrer` | Blobs, digest-addressed artifact manifest, optional referrers-tag fallback manifest | The artifact may exist even if fallback discovery fails; fallback read-modify-write can lose concurrent updates. |
| `WriteSignedImageIndexImages` / `cosign load` | Image/index, legacy signature and attestation tags, then local-layout referrers | Earlier objects may be committed before a later referrer fails; its current referrer ordering is invalid. |
| `WriteSignatures`, `WriteAttestations` | GGCR-managed blobs and mutable `.sig` / `.att` tag manifests | Retry or concurrent tag replacement is not automatically idempotent. |
| Attach SBOM, upload WASM, recursive image/index writes | GGCR-managed blob and one or more manifest writes | Ordering and retry units are owned by GGCR; multi-object callers may still partially commit. |

The exact CLI callers and GGCR-owned behavior should be mapped before selecting code changes; the immediate ordering correction belongs to the known local-layout path, while this issue defines the cross-writer contract.

Generic client-side rollback is unsafe:

- Blob deletion is optional, policy-dependent, and may be unavailable to the publishing identity.
- Blobs are content-addressed and may already exist or be shared by other manifests.
- A client cannot generally prove that it created a blob exclusively during the failed attempt.
- Deleting a shared blob can corrupt an unrelated artifact; failed deletion still cannot restore atomicity.
- An invocation-owned monolithic or chunked upload session is distinct from a completed shared blob and may have a capability-scoped cancellation operation.

The desired baseline is therefore manifest-last publication with idempotent retry, preserved failure causes, and no implicit delete rollback. Before changing the public behavior, maintainers should agree on the following contract:

1. What are the commit points and retry unit for each publication path?
2. Should publication errors identify the failed phase and successfully processed descriptors, without exposing credentials or registry responses containing secrets?
3. Is cleanup ever allowed without an explicit registry capability and proof that the invocation created exclusive content?
4. How should cancellation, authentication, transport, and manifest-conflict errors remain distinguishable?
5. When an artifact manifest succeeds but its fallback discovery-index update fails, is the result partial success, and how should retry discover and repair it?
6. Must fallback indexes use conditional requests or conflict retry to prevent concurrent lost updates?
7. Should the client cancel only an exact upload-session UUID it owns, when the registry supports that operation?
8. Which writers require code changes versus documentation-only treatment?

Proposed design:

- Perform all locally available structural and publication-option validation before the first mutation; network authentication remains subject to expiry and TOCTOU failure.
- Upload every required blob before publishing the manifest.
- Model phases as blobs, artifact manifest, and any optional fallback discovery-index read/conditional update.
- Stop on the first failure within a publication unit; report which earlier commit points succeeded.
- Return the original cause with publication-phase context.
- Treat content-addressed blob and digest-addressed artifact operations as reusable on retry; do not extend that claim to mutable tags, fallback indexes, or multi-object workflows without conflict-safe proofs.
- Never delete a completed blob or artifact manifest merely because a later discovery update failed.
- Decide separately whether to cancel an exact invocation-owned upload session; do not infer permission to delete completed content.
- Leave completed unreferenced blobs subject to registry retention and garbage-collection policy, which may retain them indefinitely; expose enough phase/descriptor information for operators to diagnose storage accumulation without leaking credentials.
- Do not promise atomicity across repositories or nonstandard registry APIs.

Required failure-injection coverage:

- Each config, layer, and manifest step fails independently.
- Existing and newly uploaded blob digests.
- Shared digests and registries where deletion is unsupported or forbidden.
- Exact upload-session cancellation supported, unsupported, forbidden, and interrupted.
- Retry after every partial-failure point, with idempotence asserted only per proven operation.

Issue #1777: FA-10-002: smc watch can miss declared dependency manifest changes outside the imported module graph

Umbrella: #1617
Module: **10 — `smc-cli`**
Audit HEAD: `4ac4d1a169902777e760e23eaee92aa233edc04d`
Severity: **P1**
Classification: **FAIL-OPEN · FALSE-READY · IDENTITY/TRUST-GAP · QUALIFICATION-GAP**

## Trigger

Run `smc watch` on a project whose package graph contains a declared dependency relationship that is not represented by the source import graph currently traversed by `module_graph_fingerprint`.

Then change a dependency's own governing manifest while leaving:

- the watched entry/source graph unchanged; and
- the entry package's own governing manifest unchanged.

Representative residual case from the historical repair log:

```text
root package manifest unchanged
→ dependency A manifest changes (identity / declared sub-dependency / pin)
→ no imported source edge makes that manifest part of the current module_graph_fingerprint signal
→ fp remains unchanged
→ smc watch does not enter its rebuild/reset branch
→ declared dependency graph cache is not reset/revalidated
→ watch keeps the prior admission result
```

## Claim / confidence source

`cmd_watch` resets the package-admission caches only inside:

```text
if last_fp != Some(fp) {
    reset_pinned_dependency_fingerprint_cache();
    reset_declared_dependency_graph_cache();
    ...
}
```

The accompanying comment says `module_graph_fingerprint` folds each module's governing manifest content into the fingerprint so relevant manifest changes reach this branch.

The SSF repair log DL-023 in #1598, however, explicitly documents a deliberately accepted residual gap: the fingerprint does not cover every manifest transitively reachable through the declared dependency graph, and a dependency's own manifest can change without changing `fp` until another event causes a rebuild.

## Actual guarantee

`incremental.rs::collect_module_graph` follows source `Import` edges and folds the nearest manifest for modules that are actually visited. It does not independently walk the entire declared dependency graph merely to construct the cheap watch fingerprint.

Therefore the watch-change signal and the admission validity surface are not identical.

## Gap

`smc watch` uses a narrower fingerprint as the sole trigger for invalidating broader package-admission state.

A package can therefore move from admitted to invalid on the declared-dependency axis while the watch loop sees an unchanged fingerprint and performs no re-admission.

This is the Phase-A pattern:

```text
trust/provenance input changes
→ change signal misses it
→ stale admission evidence retained
→ successful continuation
```

The gap is especially important because the code comment presents the conditional reset as sufficient, while the historical rationale itself records the known exception.

## Historical context

#1598 DL-022/DL-023 repaired an earlier `smc watch` invalidation/performance problem by making the cheap fingerprint sensitive to each visited module's governing manifest and moving resets back under the fingerprint-change branch.

DL-023 explicitly left the transitive declared-manifest case unresolved as an accepted residual gap. Phase A records that known residual as a current readiness finding rather than reopening the historical repair in-place.

- `crates/smc-cli/src/app.rs::cmd_watch`
- `crates/smc-cli/src/incremental.rs::module_graph_fingerprint`
- `crates/smc-cli/src/incremental.rs::collect_module_graph`
- `crates/smc-cli/src/package_manifest.rs`
  - declared-graph validation cache/reset
- #1598 — DL-022 and DL-023, including the explicit residual-gap note

## Repair note

**Phase B only.** Make the watch invalidation signal cover every trust/provenance input whose change can invalidate package admission, or decouple package-admission revalidation from the narrower source-module fingerprint. Preserve a cheap idle poll, but do not use a signal known to be narrower than the state it authorizes as the sole freshness gate.

Issue #1: OpenLineage support: emit data lineage for Bento pipelines

## Use case

Bento sits in the middle of data platforms (Kafka to S3, CDC to warehouse, S3 to Elasticsearch) but is invisible to lineage tooling. A platform that runs Spark, Flink and Airflow can already draw a dataset graph across all three, because each has an OpenLineage integration. Every Bento pipeline in that platform shows up as a gap in the graph: datasets go in one side and come out the other with no recorded edge between them.

[OpenLineage](https://openlineage.io) is the open standard those tools emit. Adding support would let a Bento pipeline appear as a job with input and output datasets in Marquez, DataHub, OpenMetadata, Dataplex, or any other OpenLineage consumer, and let impact analysis traverse *through* Bento rather than stopping at it.

This issue proposes a shape and asks for a direction decision before any code is written. Nothing is implemented.

## The `tracer:` slot cannot host this

The obvious first idea is a `tracer: openlineage` plugin sitting alongside `jaeger` and `open_telemetry_collector`, with a `SpanProcessor` folding spans into OpenLineage `RunEvent`s. That does not work, for three reasons:

1. **The constructor sees only its own config.** `OtelTracerProviderConstructor` is `func(conf *ParsedConfig) (trace.TracerProvider, error)` (`public/service/plugins.go:175`). No `*Resources`, no manager.
2. **Tracers are built before the pipeline exists.** `public/service/stream_builder.go:993` passes `TracersInit` a `tmpMgr` constructed from an empty `manager.NewResourceConfig()`. The comment above it calls this "a very lazy way of instantiating a manager". A tracer therefore never sees what the input or output is. Metrics exporters have the same limitation, from the same `tmpMgr`.
3. **Spans carry no dataset identity.** Span names are `"input_" + typeStr` and `"output_" + typeStr` (`internal/component/input/async_reader.go:205`, `internal/component/output/async_writer.go`). The span stream says `input_kafka` and `output_aws_s3` — the component type, never the topic, bucket or table.

Point 3 is the decisive one. Dataset names are the entire content of a lineage event, and they are not in the spans.

There is also a model mismatch. OpenLineage is run-oriented (`START` → `RUNNING`* → `COMPLETE`/`FAIL`/`ABORT`) over a dataset *graph*; OpenTelemetry is a per-request span *tree*. OpenLineage [describes the difference](https://openlineage.io/blog/openlineage-takes-inspiration-from-opentelemetry/) as graph-vs-tree and dataset-level-vs-row-level. A Bento stream is one long-running OpenLineage run, not one per message.

## What Bento already has

- **A stream-level lifecycle hook.** `public/service/stream.go:126-137` calls `Shutdown(ctx)` on the tracer provider at stream stop, if it implements it. That is a usable `COMPLETE`/`FAIL` emission point.
- **Dataset identity in message metadata.** `kafka_topic` (`internal/impl/kafka/input_kafka_franz.go:494`), `s3_bucket` and `s3_key` (`internal/impl/aws/input_s3.go:734-735`), and equivalents across the impl tree.
- **Dataset identity in the static config**, which `stream_builder.go` already sanitises and scrubs of secrets for the root HTTP endpoint.
- **A CLI home** for a design-time command, next to `lint`, `list` and `create` in `internal/cli/`.
- **The optional-interface idiom**, used throughout: `internal/component/processor/interface.go:59`, `public/service/metrics.go:212`, `public/service/stream.go:131`, `internal/manager/type.go:931`.

## Prior art

Nothing exists in Benthos or Redpanda Connect. Three patterns exist elsewhere:

**Plan introspection — Flink and Spark, both official OpenLineage integrations.** Flink registers `OpenLineageFlinkJobListener` on the `StreamExecutionEnvironment` through Flink's own `JobListener`. On submission it pulls `Transformations` out of the `ExecutionEnvironment` and keeps only Sources and Sinks, since those are where Flink touches external systems, then watches checkpoints as the liveness signal for a long-running job. They instrument the *plan*, not the traces, which is the same conclusion the blockers above force here.

**Pass-through lifecycle hook — Kafka Connect.** No official integration exists. Factor House maintains an [`OpenLineageLifecycleSmt`](https://docs.factorhouse.io/playground/data-lineage-labs/kafka-connect-lineage): a Single Message Transform that modifies no records and exists purely as a lifecycle hook. `RUNNING` on the first record, `COMPLETE` from `close()`, `FAIL` on unhandled exception. It does not parse the connector config. Users hand-declare `connector.class`, `topics`, `dataset.namespace`, `dataset.names`, and the SMT applies role logic, so topics are outputs for a source connector and inputs for a sink. It requires `tasks.max: "1"`, because parallel instances would each emit their own run events.

**Connector-native emission — Debezium**, [native since 3.2](https://debezium.io/blog/2025/06/13/openlineage-integration/), enabled with `openlineage.integration.enabled`. It derives input datasets from its own connector configuration: each monitored table becomes an input dataset. Config introspection performed by the component that owns the config, rather than by a central engine.

## Proposed shape

**Datasets come from the components, not from a central registry.** The Debezium model applied to Bento: an optional interface that inputs and outputs may implement, type-asserted at stream start.

```go
// Implemented by inputs and outputs that can name the datasets they touch.
type LineageDataset struct{ Namespace, Name string }
type LineageAware interface{ LineageDatasets() []LineageDataset }
```

The alternative, one central resolver per component type, means a hand-written resolver for every connector, maintained forever across Bento's very large impl surface. It will rot. Components that do not implement the interface fall back to datasets declared in config, the Kafka Connect approach.

Issue #2: `canonicalManifestForSigning` depends on key insertion order — sibling service already solves this with `sortDeep`

**Labels:** bug

---

`src/snapshot.ts:41-43`:

```ts
export function canonicalManifestForSigning(manifest: IndexManifest): string {
  return JSON.stringify({ ...manifest, sig: "" });
}
```

`JSON.stringify` emits keys in insertion order, so the signed byte string depends
on the order in which the object was constructed — not on its content. Today that
works, because exactly one object literal builds the manifest (`:76-87`) and the
spread preserves its order.

It breaks for any reader that reconstructs the object before verifying, which is
easy to do without realising it's forbidden:

- round-tripping through IndexedDB / structured clone, or any cache layer that
  rebuilds objects (canopy persists query data via `idb-keyval`)
- re-serializing after adding or stripping a field
- verifying in another language — Python `dict` ordering, Go `map` ordering, and
  most JSON libraries make byte-identical reproduction awkward or impossible
- any future producer change that reorders the literal, which would silently
  invalidate every signature for readers that hardcoded the old order

The failure is a *valid* signature that fails verification, which is the worst
shape for this bug: it looks like an attack, and it appears only for some readers
on some platforms.

### Fix

`freedom-adblock-service` already does this correctly for the same signing scheme
— recursive key sorting before serialization (`src/manifest.ts:78-83`):

```ts
/** Recursively sort object keys so serialization is deterministic. */
function sortDeep(value: unknown): unknown { … }
```

Adopting the same helper here makes the two sibling services consistent and makes
the canonical form reproducible from content alone. The spec
(`docs/index-protocol.md:49-51`) should state the canonicalization explicitly
rather than implying it via a `JSON.stringify` snippet — ideally naming sorted
keys (or [RFC 8785 JCS](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785)) so
implementers in other languages have something to target.

### Migration

Changing the canonical form invalidates signatures across the change. Since no
reader verifies today (canopy doesn't), the window to fix this at zero cost is
now — once a reader ships verification, this needs a schema bump and a
dual-accept period.

### Aside

This is the one place where [recordstore](https://github.com/petfold/recordstore)'s
core property is directly relevant, language differences aside: it makes
encodings deterministic so that equal content produces an equal root reference
regardless of the history that built it. Same principle, applied to signature
inputs — content-determined bytes, not construction-determined bytes.

Issue #19513: ACL parent cycle causes infinite recursion in BasicLookupStrategy.convert()

`AclImpl.setParent()` only rejects direct self-parenting (`newParent.equals(this)`); it does not detect indirect cycles (A → B → A, or longer chains). Once such a cycle is persisted via `JdbcMutableAclService.updateAcl()`, every subsequent lookup of any ACL in the cycle recurses forever.

**Where:**
- `AclImpl.setParent(Acl)` (`acl/src/main/java/org/springframework/security/acls/domain/AclImpl.java`) only guards `newParent.equals(this)` — no ancestor walk.
- `JdbcMutableAclService.updateObjectIdentity(MutableAcl)` (`acl/src/main/java/org/springframework/security/acls/jdbc/JdbcMutableAclService.java`) writes `parentId` with no cycle check.
- `BasicLookupStrategy.convert(...)` (`acl/src/main/java/org/springframework/security/acls/jdbc/BasicLookupStrategy.java`, ~lines 386-431) recurses on `StubAclParent` ids with no visited-set, so a stored cycle causes unconditional infinite recursion / `StackOverflowError` on every future read. `JdbcMutableAclService.clearCacheIncludingChildren(...)` has the same unguarded recursive shape.

**Repro sketch:**
1. User owns (or has `CHANGE_GENERAL` on) two ACL-protected objects A and B.
2. `aclA.setParent(aclB); aclService.updateAcl(aclA);`
3. `aclB.setParent(aclA); aclService.updateAcl(aclB);`
4. Any subsequent `aclService.readAclById(...)` for A or B recurses forever.

**Suggested fix shape:**
- In `AclImpl.setParent(Acl)`, walk `newParent`'s ancestor chain via `getParentAcl()` and reject (`IllegalArgumentException`, same unchecked pattern as the existing self-parent `Assert.isTrue`) if `this` is reachable.
- In `JdbcMutableAclService.updateObjectIdentity(MutableAcl)`, walk the proposed parent's stored ancestry before writing `parentId` and reject on a match, for the case where the in-memory check is bypassed (e.g. a custom `MutableAcl` implementation, or direct DB manipulation).
- Add a visited-`Set` guard in `BasicLookupStrategy.convert(...)` and `clearCacheIncludingChildren(...)` so that already-corrupt data (e.g. from before this fix, or written through a path that skips the new checks) fails fast with a clear exception instead of a `StackOverflowError`.

This should be additive/non-breaking: a stored parent cycle is already guaranteed to crash every future read of the affected ACLs, so no working application depends on being able to create one. Rejecting the write earlier, with a clear exception, doesn't remove any capability that currently functions.

Platform Improvement

P1

Publishing content updates through the CMS may not immediately reflect on production because of CDN caching.

Manual cache purging introduces:

- inconsistent user experiences

- Maintain high CDN cache hit ratio.

- URL-level purge
- Cache Tag purge (where applicable)
- Asset invalidation
- Automatic cache warming for high-traffic pages

The solution should support:

- Single page updates
- Scheduled publishing
- Bulk publishing
- Rollbacks

---

- Cache Tags
- Webhook-based publishing
- Retry mechanism
- Failure monitoring
- Purge audit logs

Avoid:

- Purging entire CDN
- Manual intervention

- Publishing remains asynchronous.

- Frontend Platform

- Race conditions during large-scale deployments.

- Regional cache preloading.
- Predictive cache optimisation.

Issue #125: Next breaking release: thread Result through IERS-table-dependent frame transforms

## Background

The IERS precession-nutation tables (tab5.2a/b/d.txt) are the one data dependency that panics instead of returning an error when unavailable: `frametransform::ierstable::table()` has an infallible `-> &'static IERSTable` signature and panics on load failure (src/frametransform/ierstable.rs). Every other data-dependent subsystem (EOP, space weather, JPL ephemerides) surfaces the same condition as `Err`/`None`.

The panic fires on the first full-accuracy frame transform (`qcirs2gcrs` → `qitrf2gcrf` / `qgcrf2itrf` / `rotation(ITRF, GCRF, t)` / state transforms) on a machine with no data directory and no network (or a build without the `download` feature).

This was deliberately left out of the panic-hardening pass (#124) because fixing it properly is a breaking cascade. Mitigations already in place: the table parser is panic-free, and `init_from_bytes` / `init_from_path` let applications preload the tables at startup and handle the `Result` there.

## Planned fix (for the next breaking release)

Thread `Result` through the IERS-table-dependent transform chain so a missing/corrupt table surfaces as an error, consistent with the rest of the crate:

- `ierstable::table()` → fallible accessor
- `qcirs2gcrs` / `qcirs2gcrs_dxdy` → `Result<Quaternion>`
- `qitrf2gcrf`, `qgcrf2itrf`, `rotation()`, and the state-transform functions that sit on top
- Python bindings: map to a clean exception
- Decide what the propagator force model does (it has no error channel): likely validate/preload the tables up front in `propagate()` so the force closure can keep an infallible path

Explicitly rejected alternative: silently degrading to `qgcrf2itrf_approx` — degraded accuracy without an error is worse than a loud failure.

## References

- Panic audit + hardening PR: #124
- Deliberate-panic comment: src/frametransform/ierstable.rs (`table()`)

# ClientSurge OS — Cross-Phase Product Contracts

## Purpose
Create the authoritative product contracts inherited by Phase B Business Intelligence and Phase C Customer Operations. These rules prevent inconsistent semantics across Morning Brief, Business Health, Opportunity Center, Revenue Intelligence, Website Intelligence, AI Workforce, Client Timeline, Communication Center, and Customer Success.

## Worker ownership
- Worker #1 / Codex: implements approved contracts and validates behavior.
- Worker #2 / Chief Product Architect: owns these contracts and final product interpretation.
- Worker #3 / UX Director: reviews rendered clarity, accessibility, consistency, and friction.

## 1. Universal data-truth contract
Every displayed metric, score, trend, event, recommendation, or outcome must support:
- source identifier and human-readable source name
- verification class
- observed/processed timestamp
- displayed freshness state
- confidence where inference is involved
- unit and period
- account, client, tenant, and permission scope
- partial-coverage disclosure
- estimated versus verified label
- user-facing explanation

### Verification classes
- `verified`: directly supported by an authoritative connected source
- `derived`: deterministic calculation from verified inputs
- `estimated`: model or heuristic estimate with assumptions disclosed
- `reported`: manually supplied or third-party reported, not independently verified
- `unknown`: insufficient evidence

Never silently promote estimated, reported, or unknown information to verified.

### Freshness states
- `live`: actively updating or near-real-time within the source contract
- `current`: within the expected freshness window
- `stale`: outside the expected freshness window but still viewable
- `delayed`: source confirms processing delay
- `unavailable`: source cannot currently be reached or queried
- `not_connected`: required integration is absent
- `permission_restricted`: user lacks access
- `unknown`: freshness cannot be determined

Every module must define its own expected freshness window by source. Do not use one arbitrary global duration.

- initial loading
- refreshing
- current data
- partial data
- empty but valid
- stale data
- delayed source
- unavailable source
- not connected
- permission restricted
- error with recovery
- unknown

Use the following meanings consistently:
- `healthy`: operating within the documented contract
- `degraded`: operating but with reduced performance or incomplete capability
- `attention_needed`: human review is recommended but operation may continue
- `action_required`: a specific intervention is required
- `blocked`: progress cannot continue because a dependency is unmet
- `offline`: a previously active capability is not operating
- `not_configured`: capability has never been completed or enabled
- `paused`: intentionally stopped by an authorized actor
- `unknown`: status cannot be verified
- `unavailable`: status cannot currently be retrieved

Rules:
- Unknown is never healthy.
- Not configured is not the same as offline.
- Paused is not an error.
- Degraded requires a documented reason.
- Action required must include a resolution path where one exists.
- Color may reinforce status but must never carry meaning alone.

A health score or label may ship only when all of the following exist:
- eligible contributors
- weighting or aggregation rules
- minimum evidence threshold
- unknown-data treatment
- stale-data treatment
- confidence calculation
- contributor explanation
- anti-gaming rules
- score history policy
- recalculation trigger
- user-facing explanation
- test fixtures for edge cases

A module may use qualitative status without a numeric score when a defensible score contract does not exist.

Implement the **User Management, Role Management, and Access Control (ACL)** foundation for the Warehouse Koperasi application based strictly on the existing `PRD.md`.

Before writing or modifying any code, read and understand the entire relevant section of the PRD. Treat the application as a **multi-tenant SaaS system** at all times. Do not design authentication, users, roles, permissions, or database relationships as if this were a single-company application.

### 1. SaaS and Tenant Model

The fundamental tenant in this application is a **Company**.

Every operational user must belong to a company/tenant, except for platform-level accounts explicitly defined by the PRD.

Tenant isolation is mandatory. A user belonging to Company A must never be able to access, enumerate, modify, assign permissions to, or otherwise interact with Company B's users or resources unless the PRD explicitly defines a platform-level privilege allowing it.

Design the implementation from the beginning so future warehouse, inventory, purchasing, cooperative, reporting, and other business models can be scoped securely by company.

Do not rely only on frontend/UI restrictions for tenant isolation. Enforcement must exist at the backend/application authorization layer.

* Kepala Gudang
* Staff Admin
* Purchasing
* Koperasi users

The registration must atomically create:

* the new Company/tenant;

Issue #2784: feat(logging): carry an operation cause through the call graph

[mode: plan]
[model: opus]
[effort: high]

## Summary

Give the system a way to say why a piece of work is happening, by carrying a cause through the
call graph to the places that do the work.

## Problem / Motivation

Log entries record effects with no attributable cause, because the code itself does not carry
one. This cannot be fixed by editing log statements. The provider client logs what it has, and
what it has is a URL. It cannot say which rule triggered it, because nothing told it. The cause
was discarded several layers up.

Every enrichment the rest of this epic asks for depends on this. So it is a plumbing change
first, and richer logs are a consequence of it rather than the work itself.

Verified at HEAD: no cause or trigger value is carried anywhere. The provider package does
already use the context-value idiom for other deep parameters, so this follows an established
pattern rather than introducing one.

## Proposed Solution

Carry the cause on the request context and read it at the points that already log.

Adding a parameter to every signature between the cause and the work is the alternative and is
worse here: provider calls are made from rule fixers, from request handlers and from the
orchestrator, and the adapters have independent request paths with no shared base. The context
already flows unmodified from every caller down to the work, and the codebase already uses it
for exactly this kind of deep parameter.

The cause should identify the class and the specific instance, for example a rule and which
rule, a scan, a scheduled task, or a user action.

Set it at the call sites that know why: the rule fixer, the bulk rule executor, the scanner, and
the request handlers that trigger a refresh or a provider fetch.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A cause can be attached to a context and read back, and reading an absent cause returns an
      empty value rather than panicking.
- [ ] The accessor lives beside the other deep-parameter context keys in the provider package and
      follows their shape.
- [ ] The cause is set at every call site that knows one: rule fixing, bulk rule execution,
      scanning, and the user-initiated request handlers.
- [ ] The cause is read once at the shared provider fetch point rather than in each adapter, and
      appears on the log lines that point already emits.
- [ ] Provider calls made with no cause set log an explicit unattributed marker, not a blank
      attribute that reads as if attribution succeeded.
- [ ] Tests assert the cause survives the full path from a rule fix to a provider fetch, by
      wiring the real path and reading the emitted attribute, not by asserting the setter and
      getter in isolation.
- [ ] A test proves the cause does not leak between concurrent operations.
- [ ] No public signature changes, and no new log lines are introduced by this issue.

## Additional Context

This is the foundation. B, C and D all depend on it and should not start before it lands, per
the repository's decompose-before-building rule.

Related: #2476, where one rule fired a provider query per artist and none of the 870 resulting
outbound requests could be attributed to the action that caused them.

Issue #192: Resolve external JSON Schema refs through XMD filesystem and fetch capabilities

## Motivation

The initial `<Parse>/<SafeParse>` contract accepts self-contained JSON Schema
draft-07 values and resolves only fragment references within the supplied
schema. Larger schema systems should later be able to compose definitions from
files and network resources without bypassing XMD runtime capabilities.

## Intended behavior

- Resolve relative external `$ref` values against contextual `Env.cwd`.
- Read referenced files through XMD's built-in filesystem capability rather
  than direct host filesystem calls.
- Resolve HTTP and HTTPS `$ref` values through XMD's built-in fetch capability
  rather than `globalThis.fetch`.
- Preserve URI fragments when selecting definitions from a referenced
  document.
- Resolve each canonical reference once per parse operation.
- Detect reference cycles and report a bounded reference chain.
- Apply the same resolution behavior to `<Parse>` and `<SafeParse>`.
- Compile the complete schema graph before expanding the content being parsed.

## Runtime constraints

- Filesystem and network access must remain subject to the active permission and
  sandbox policy.
- Fetches must use the runtime fetch API so tests can stub them and durable
  execution can journal and replay them.
- Resolution errors must identify the referring schema, unresolved reference,
  and underlying filesystem or fetch failure.
- A referenced document must itself be valid JSON and a valid draft-07 schema.
- No model or repair behavior participates in reference resolution.

## Testing

- Markdown tests use `<TempDir>` and `<File>` for relative schema references.
- Runtime tests stub the built-in fetch capability for successful HTTP(S)
  references, non-success responses, malformed JSON, and transport failures.
- Tests cover nested references, fragments, duplicate references, cycles,
  permission denial, deterministic caching, and replay without live I/O.
- No test depends on the public network.

## Documentation

- Document file and HTTP(S) reference resolution, base URI rules, capability
  requirements, caching scope, and failure diagnostics.
- Add a website example for file composition and a separately stubbed network
  example.

## Not included

- Additional JSON Schema drafts.
- Non-JSON schema formats.
- Model-assisted schema repair.

Issue #146: [BUG] tarfilter lacks POSIX classes and locale-aware GNU regex escapes

## Parent boundary

Follow-up to #36 and regex-dialect issue #108. Related zero-length reference hang: #144.

## Current retained behavior

The retained tarfilter transform candidate compiles patterns with Python `re` over Python strings.

Consequences:

- POSIX bracket classes such as `[[:digit:]]` and `[[:alpha:]]` are not implemented; Python treats them as a nested-set form, warns, and does not match the intended class.
- GNU word delimiters `\<` and `\>` do not carry GNU semantics in Python and silently miss intended matches.
- Python `\w`, `\W`, and `\b` use Python Unicode/ASCII rules rather than GNU regex behavior under the selected process locale.

## Confirmed GNU tar 1.35 matrix

### POSIX bracket classes

Under `LC_ALL=C`:

```text
a1b + s/[[:digit:]]/D/       -> aDb
a1b + s/[[:alpha:]]/L/g      -> L1L
a1b + s/[[:alnum:]]/Q/g      -> QQQ
```

Under `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `[[:alpha:]]` also matches `é`:

```text
é1_ + s/[[:alpha:]]/A/g      -> A1_
```

Python `re` does not implement those POSIX classes.

### GNU word escapes

Under both tested locales:

```text
foo-bar + s/\<foo\>/X/       -> X-bar
foo-bar + s/\bfoo\b/X/       -> X-bar
abc     + s/\w/W/g           -> WWW
```

Python does not implement GNU `\<`/`\>` word delimiters as such.

### Locale and byte/code-point divergence

For filename `é1_` under `LC_ALL=C`:

```text
GNU tar s/\w/W/g   -> éWW
GNU tar s/\W/X/g   -> XX1_
```

GNU's C-locale regex sees the two UTF-8 bytes of `é` as two non-word units. Python Unicode regex sees `é` as one word character:

```text
Python Unicode \w  -> WWW
Python Unicode \W  -> é1_
```

Python `re.ASCII` still operates on one Unicode code point:

```text
Python ASCII \w    -> éXX
Python ASCII \W    -> X1_
```

Neither Python mode reproduces GNU tar's C-locale bytewise `\W` result.

Under `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, GNU tar and Python Unicode agree on the explored `\w`/`\W` classification for `é1_`, while POSIX bracket syntax remains unsupported by Python.

## Required local correction

- make the transform regex locale/encoding contract explicit;
- implement or reject named POSIX bracket classes before Python compilation;
- implement GNU `\<` and `\>` semantics;
- define `\w`, `\W`, `\b`, and `\B` behavior for C and UTF-8 locales;
- decide whether C-locale parity requires a byte-oriented matching path and reversible filename encoding;
- preserve archive member and link-target strings without lossy decode/encode cycles;
- compare C and C.UTF-8 behavior directly with GNU tar;
- add ordinary ASCII controls plus multibyte member and link-target cases;
- treat zero-length global boundary expressions with a timeout because GNU tar 1.35 can hang (#144);
- reject unsupported collating elements/equivalence classes deterministically until implemented;
- retain a durable investigation, raw matrix, reusable note, cleanup receipt, and exact-head review.

## Boundary

This issue owns POSIX class syntax, GNU word escapes, and locale/encoding parity. Basic-versus-extended operator spelling remains #108. Expression lists remain #117. Replacement case conversion remains #125. Reference hangs remain #144.

The imported source remains unchanged; retain local evidence and a candidate patch only. No upstream contact is authorized.

Issue #5: P2 — Policy packs and historical simulation

roadmap-slug: p2-policy-packs-simulation

## Phase / priority
P2 — Differentiate and expand / High

## Problem
Teams cannot safely predict how a policy change will alter investigations, approvals, or reactions before activation. Direct activation makes governance changes hard to review and risky to reverse.

## Target users / jobs to be done
Security owners, platform leads, and workflow owners need to test, compare, approve, distribute, and roll back policies with evidence.

## Product outcome
Every policy activation has an explainable impact preview. Reusable policy packs are immutable, attributable, versioned, signed where shared, and tenant-scoped.

## In scope
- Draft, published, active, retired, and superseded policy-pack states.
- Historical dry-run simulation and current-versus-candidate outcome comparison.
- Explanations for matched rules, changed decisions, and unmatched inputs.
- Signed, versioned import/export with provenance for shared published packs.
- Authorized human activation, rollback, and immutable audit history.

## Out of scope
- Executing reactions during simulation.
- Autonomous policy generation or activation.
- Cross-tenant history access or permission inheritance from imported packs.

## Functional and operational requirements
1. Users can select a candidate, workspace, historical range, and event/action classes.
2. Simulation returns allow, deny, approval-required, invalid, and unmatched outcomes without changing production state.
3. Comparison identifies every changed outcome, affected resource/action scope, matched rule, and reason.
4. Aggregate results drill into authorized, redacted examples and declare retention gaps or unsupported historical data.
5. Shared published packs require verifiable provenance and signatures; incompatible or tampered packs are rejected.
6. Activation requires an authorized human to approve the exact immutable version after reviewing the diff.
7. Rollback creates a new audited activation; history is never rewritten.
8. Every later decision records the exact policy version used.

## User journeys and administrative experience
Simulation is visibly marked as non-executing. Progress, cancellation, partial-data warnings, zero-match results, and failures are explicit. Activation presents material behavior and scope changes before confirmation. Operators can find the current version, prior versions, approvals, and rollback history from one timeline.

## Acceptance criteria
- Given historical inputs, when simulation runs, then no reaction, approval, incident, entitlement, or external-system state is mutated.
- Given current and candidate policies, every changed decision shows old/new outcome, matched rule, affected scope, and reason.
- Given a shared published pack, import fails if signature, provenance, compatibility, or tenant authorization fails.
- Given an approved activation, all subsequent decisions reference the immutable activated version.
- Given rollback, prior behavior is restored through a new auditable activation record.
- Cross-tenant simulation access is denied and tested.

## Failure/abuse/revocation/concurrency/degraded-mode scenarios
Retention-deleted evidence, schema drift, cancelled jobs, partial evaluation, zero matches, invalid rules, expired signatures, and unavailable historical payloads must produce explicit non-success states and cannot be mistaken for a clean result.

## Security, privacy, and compliance
Preserve tenant isolation, least privilege, evidence redaction, audit retention, provenance, and payload-access auditing. Imported content cannot grant permissions. Shared published packs require signatures; private drafts remain tenant-contained.

## Dependencies and relationships
Depends on mature policy schema, durable evidence/audit, hosted auth, and tenant repositories. Enables `p3-graduated-autonomy`; informs `p2-private-edge-deployment` and `p3-enterprise-governance`.

## Success and guardrail metrics
Simulation completion rate, candidate-to-activation rate, median review time, post-activation rollback rate, and policy-caused incident rate.

## Rollout and release gates
Internal fixtures, no-write verification, cross-tenant tests, explanation usability review, signed-pack tamper tests, and rollback drill must pass before limited beta. General availability requires audited activation history and no critical authorization findings.

## Do / don't
Do default users toward simulation before activation and surface uncertainty. Do require human activation of shared packs. Don't describe simulation as proof of future safety, execute reactions, or allow packs to expand importer authority.

## Fixed product decisions and launch defaults
- Simulation is always non-executing and cannot create approvals, incidents, usage, or reactions.
- Shared published packs require verifiable provenance and signatures; private drafts remain tenant-contained.
- Activation and rollback always require an authorized human acting on an exact immutable version.
- Retention gaps, unsupported history, and partial results block any claim of complete coverage and must be reviewed explicitly.
- Automatic policy generation, activation, permission inheritance, and cross-tenant simulation are deferred.

## Definition of done
All requirements and acceptance criteria pass; user and administrator documentation describes lifecycle and limitations; security/product review approves the signed-pack and activation model; telemetry for listed success metrics is available; rollback and tenant-isolation release gates are evidenced.

Issue #113: Add reachability analysis for Go findings

Deputy reports every advisory that matches a dependency's version range, with no signal about whether the vulnerable code is actually reachable from the scanned code. For Go specifically that is now a conspicuous gap:

- The Go toolchain ships symbol-level reachability for free, and it emits machine-readable output including a VEX form.
- The Go vulnerability database publishes per-symbol data (`ecosystem_specific.imports[].symbols`) under an open license, so the data is consumable directly.
- Two other open-source scanners began consuming that symbol data this year, so the capability is moving from differentiator to expectation for Go.

Deputy is a Go tool that scans Go projects, which makes this the most natural place to start.

The measured benefit is meaningful but should not be oversold: an independent study using conservative call-graph analysis removed about 62% of alerts across a multi-language corpus and about 74% on its Go subset. Vendor claims in the 90s are self-reported without published methodology and should not be used as a target.

## Proposal

Consume the symbol-level data rather than reimplementing analysis. Two levels, useful separately:

1. **Symbol presence**: when an advisory names vulnerable symbols and the scanned binary or module does not reference them, mark the finding as such. This needs no call graph.
2. **Call-graph reachability** for source scans, delegating to the existing toolchain analysis rather than writing one.

Important: treat the result as a **confidence and prioritization signal, not a filter**. The underlying analysis documents its own false negatives (invisible to reflection, unsound under `unsafe`, conservative on interface and function-pointer calls), and binary mode silently degrades to module-level matching when symbols cannot be extracted. Deputy should record which mode ran and whether symbol extraction succeeded, and never present "not reachable" as proof of safety.

This also connects to the VEX work: an unreachability determination is exactly the evidence that would justify one specific VEX justification, and it is the only one of them that can be substantiated automatically.

## Scope note

Other ecosystems publish similar data in incompatible shapes (one other ecosystem's advisories carry affected function lists), and there is an open upstream proposal to standardize a symbols field. Worth watching, but Go alone is the valuable first step.

Issue #22: Define the life–computing overlap doctrine and flow constraints

## Relation to #21

Issue #21 defines composite fields, recognition, commitment, and sovereign adoption receipts.

This companion issue captures the broader design doctrine that emerged immediately afterward: TranchNode should not merely imitate biology or decorate software with organic metaphors. It should locate the **proportional overlap** between the life field and the computing field, then give the emergent third field explicit structure.

## Core statement

> Bring the life field into proportional overlap with the computing field, and structure the new field that emerges.

This is not:

- biology as a literal software specification;
- software architecture justified by metaphor alone;
- importing every biological mechanism into code;
- claiming that all growth follows phi or any one geometric law.

It is:

- identifying structural invariants that appear meaningfully in both domains;
- preserving each domain's irreducible differences;
- using the overlap to derive new computational primitives;
- rejecting mappings that distort either side;
- treating the emergent overlap as its own field with its own laws.

## Candidate overlapping invariants

From the life field:

- lineage;
- differentiation;
- recognition;
- local autonomy;
- circulation and return;
- growth without ancestor erasure;
- regeneration;
- stewardship;
- inherited constraint;
- coexisting variation.

From the computing field:

- canonical identity;
- addressability;
- append-only history;
- deterministic replay;
- explicit type and capability boundaries;
- cryptographic integrity;
- executable validation;
- queryable projections;
- machine-verifiable receipts.

The emergent field should not be reducible to either list. Its primitives must be justified by the overlap itself.

## Flow must be first-class

The architecture must not model only static objects and edges.

A field participates in flow by being:

- received;
- recognized;
- composed;
- projected;
- proposed for adoption;
- adopted or refused;
- made available for later recognition.

```text
field
  -> recognition
  -> composite
  -> proposal
  -> adoption/refusal receipt
  -> derived lineage/view
  -> future field participation
```

The exact loop is not necessarily closed or periodic, but return paths must be representable. Recognition and adoption can influence later descendants without rewriting ancestors.

## Proportional overlap

A mapping is valid only when it preserves the important proportions and authorities of both source fields.

Examples:

- `lineage` may map well to immutable ancestry plus inherited receipts;
- `recognition` may map well to attributed composite fields;
- `growth` may map well to append-only differentiation;
- `metabolism` probably does not map directly unless a concrete computational invariant is identified;
- `phi` may serve as a visual or generative heuristic, but must not be smuggled in as a biological law.

A proposed life-to-computing mapping should therefore declare:

```yaml
mapping:
  life_pattern: recognition
  computing_pattern: attributed composite artifact
  preserved:
    - source integrity
    - recognizer attribution
    - non-destructive growth
  distorted_or_unmapped:
    - embodied perception
    - metabolic cost
  status: proposed
```

## Required constraints

1. No biological analogy becomes normative without an explicit computational invariant.
2. No computing convenience may erase witness, lineage, or local authority merely because a graph can be flattened.
3. The overlap must preserve differences as well as correspondences.
4. Flow events must be representable independently from static field structure.
5. Return paths must not imply retroactive mutation.
6. Emergent primitives require characterization examples from both life-like and computing contexts.
7. Geometry and visual language may guide discovery but must remain distinguishable from executable law.
8. The architecture must state where a mapping is lossless, lossy, or unavailable.
9. A useful overlap can remain partial; completeness is not required.
10. The third field must be allowed to develop concepts not present verbatim in either source domain.

Create a short doctrine/ADR plus one executable or fixture-backed characterization table containing at least five mappings:

| Life-field pattern | Computing-field analogue | Preserved | Lost or unavailable | Resulting TranchNode primitive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| lineage | immutable ancestry | provenance and descent | embodiment | lineage refs |
| recognition | composite reference graph | attributed noticing | lived perception | recognition field |
| differentiation | append-only descendant | history and variation | biological development | derived field |
| adoption | authorized inherited receipt | local sovereignty | organism-level assimilation | adoption receipt |
| circulation/return | replayable flow with return path | recurrence without rewrite | continuous physiology | flow receipt / return edge |

The slice should identify at least one rejected analogy to prove that the doctrine is discriminating rather than decorative.

The originating visual intuition is a triadic/toroidal set of fields, with new fields spiraling outward in proportional steps. Each step behaves like another landing in a spiral staircase: prior fields remain intact while new recognition fields emerge and participate in later flow.

This geometry is currently a conceptual and diagrammatic aid, not a frozen data structure.

We know individual phases are byte-exact on small inputs, but the **envelope of Nim language features that compile-and-run on the SVM is unmeasured**. Stand up a conformance suite: a gated fixture set exercising the language surface — generics, exceptions (`raise`/`try`/`except`), closures, methods (dynamic dispatch), `seq`/`string`/`Table`, floats, iterators, `case`/variant objects, `ref` types + ARC destructors — each compiled through the full pipeline (native oracle where a `svm-leng` translate-and-run is possible) and asserted to match.

## Why

"Full Nim breadth" (the #954 goal) is only meaningful if measured. A tracked suite turns "does X work?" into a green/red matrix, and each red files a specific `svm-leng`/runtime ticket — the "add a grammar arm, not rearchitect" ethos (NIM.md §3a). It also guards against regressions as breadth grows.

## Relationship to #760

#760 is the `svm-leng` **totality** long-pole (every Leng construct real Nim emits translates or fails closed). This suite is the **driver + oracle** that surfaces #760's remaining arms from the *language* side (rather than from translating nimony's own source), and measures end-to-end *run* correctness, not just translation.

## Acceptance

A committed, toolchain-gated conformance suite with a feature→status matrix; each unsupported feature has a filed sub-issue; the suite gates against regressions. Initial pass documents which features run today vs. fail-closed.

NIM.md §3a (W1 totality) · #760 (svm-leng totality) · `svm-leng/tests/nim_e2e.rs` (the existing e2e harness to extend).

Issue #2720: [Bug] PipelinePlanning misses transitive buffer dependencies through scalar bindings, producing invalid stage assignments

## Summary

`PipelinePlanning` produces an invalid stage assignment when a `T.copy` in a `T.Pipelined` loop indexes its source through a scalar `Bind` whose value is loaded from a shared buffer written earlier in the same loop body. The scalar-producer propagation pulls the `Bind` statement into the producer stage (stage 0), but the buffer store that the `Bind` reads from stays in the compute stage — so a stage-0 statement ends up depending on a stage-1 statement. The invalid schedule is not caught by `PipelinePlanning` itself; it is caught later by `InjectSoftwarePipeline`'s dependency validation, which fails with an `InternalError`:

```
Check failed: src_info.stage <= dst_info.stage (1 vs. 0)
```

The minimized dependency chain is:

```
copy
  ← scalar offset binding      (offset = index_shared[0])
  ← shared-buffer load         (reads index_shared)
  ← shared-buffer producer     (index_shared[0] = k * 32)
```

This was found while working on the fix for #2527 (PR #2681), but it is an independent, pre-existing bug in the generic software-pipeline planning path — see the section below.

## Reproduction

The kernel is the existing `producer_bind_kernel` from `testing/python/language/test_tilelang_language_let.py`. On targets where the copy is TMA-eligible (Hopper) the loop is lowered through the TMA path and the failing generic pipeline path is not exercised, so the simplest reproduction that avoids TMA entirely is to lower for a non-TMA target such as `sm_80`:

```python

from tilelang import language as T

@T.prim_func
def producer_bind_kernel(A: T.Tensor((64,), T.float16), B: T.Tensor((64,), T.float16)):
    with T.Kernel(1, threads=256):
        index_shared = T.alloc_shared((1,), T.int32)
        A_shared = T.alloc_shared((32,), T.float16)
        for k in T.Pipelined(2, num_stages=2):
            index_shared[0] = k * 32
            offset = index_shared[0]
            T.copy(A[offset], A_shared)
            for i in T.Parallel(32):
                B[k * 32 + i] = A_shared[i]

tilelang.engine.lower(producer_bind_kernel, target={"kind": "cuda", "arch": "sm_80"})
```

This crashes with the `InternalError` below. The pipeline-planning code involved (`src/transform/pipeline_planning.cc`, `src/transform/inject_pipeline.cc`) is identical between current `main` (verified at `3b37333c`) and the PR #2681 branch; only the TMA-eligibility change in `src/cuda/op/copy_analysis.cc` differs, and it does not affect the `sm_80` reproduction.

Any other way of making this copy take the generic pipeline path triggers the same error on Hopper, e.g. an eligibility check that rejects dynamic offsets that cannot be proven 16-byte aligned (an intermediate version of the #2527 fix did exactly that, which is how this surfaced via `test_producer_bind_kernel`).

Note: when re-running experiments, use a fresh `TILELANG_CACHE_DIR` (or a new process) — the kernel cache can otherwise mask lowering changes.

`PipelinePlanning` emits (statement order: store, bind, copy, consumer loop):

```

software_pipeline_order = [2, 0, 1, 3]
```

i.e. the invalid assignment

```
stage 1: index_shared[0] = k * 32     (write index_shared[0])
stage 0: offset = index_shared[0]     (read index_shared[0] into offset)
stage 0: T.copy(A[offset], A_shared)  (use offset in copy)
stage 1: consumer loop
```

```

    index_shared = T.Buffer((1,), "int32", scope="shared.dyn")
    T.reads(index_shared[0])
    T.writes()
    offset: T.int32 = index_shared[0] in stage 0 cannot depends on statement with T.sblock("", no_realize=True):
    T.reads()
    index_shared = T.Buffer((1,), "int32", scope="shared.dyn")

    k = T.int32()

If no legal stage assignment can be constructed for a statement chain, planning should fall back gracefully (e.g. keep the whole chain in the same stage, or decline to pipeline the offending statements) instead of emitting a schedule that a downstream pass rejects with an internal dependency error.

Issue #17: Deep call-path queries (e.g. "trace HTTP insert → nativelog write") return no result — sparse C++ call graph + agent doesn't use path_between

## Symptom

Asking the chat agent a call-path question like **"Trace the call path from HTTP insert to nativelog write"** (one of the empty-state suggested questions) returns *"I could not find a documented call-path…"* even though the endpoint entities exist. The agent runs ~9 `search_entities` keyword calls and gives up.

## Root cause (two compounding factors)

**1. The agent treats it as keyword search, not graph traversal.**
The trace shows 9 `search_entities` calls and **zero `path_between` / `neighbors`**. "Trace the call path from A to B" is inherently a `path_between(A, B)` question — find the two endpoint nodes, walk the `calls` edges. The agent never attempts a traversal, so it never reconstructs a path.

**2. Even with the right tool, the path isn't in the graph.**
Measured on `proton-enterprise@v3.3.1`:
- Call graph is **sparse**: only ~38% of function/method nodes (22,715 / 60,467) have *any* outgoing `calls` edge.
- `InterpreterInsertQuery` (the INSERT entry point) has **0 outgoing `calls` edges** — a leaf in the extracted graph, so nothing to trace from it.
- proton is ingested **code-only (AST)**. C++ AST call extraction misses virtual dispatch, templates, and callbacks — exactly how ClickHouse/proton dispatches *between* layers via abstract interfaces (`IStorage`/`IInterpreter`, `indirect_call` is only 851 edges vs 46k direct `calls`).
- The real path (HTTP handler → parser → interpreter → storage → WAL/nativelog) is many layers deep, beyond `path_between`'s `MAX_PATH_DEPTH = 6` cap (`src/tpk/tools.py:52`).

The individual entities *are* findable (`InterpreterInsertQuery`, `NativeLog` ×92, `HTTPHandler` ×22) — browsable in Explorer — but the end-to-end chain connecting them can't be reconstructed from the current data.

## Options

**A. Small — nudge the agent to use `path_between`/`neighbors` for trace questions.**
Improve the agent system prompt / tool descriptions so "trace"/"call path"/"how does X reach Y"/"what calls X" questions drive `neighbors` (single-hop: what calls X / what X calls) and `path_between` (endpoint-to-endpoint). Makes single/few-hop call questions work reliably. Does **not** fix deep cross-layer traces — the agent can't invent edges that aren't extracted. Low effort, real value for the common "what calls X?" case.

**B. Large — richer call-graph extraction.**
Either a semantic (LLM) extraction pass on proton (currently code-only), or a proper C++ call-graph analyzer (e.g. clang-based) that resolves virtual dispatch/templates. This is the real fix for deep-path questions, but a substantial effort. Possibly also raise/parameterize `MAX_PATH_DEPTH` for deep codebases.

## Suggested near-term action

Do **A** (small agent-prompt improvement) and set expectations in the UI: consider replacing the "Trace the call path from HTTP insert to nativelog write" suggested question with one the current graph can answer well (e.g. "What calls `CheckpointCoordinator::trigger`?"), keeping deep-trace as a target for **B**.

## Context

Found while debugging chat answers. Related fixes already merged this cycle: stale bare-name node keys re-ingested; repo-filter now accepts bare name or `name@ref` (#14). This issue is specifically about call-path reconstruction depth/coverage and agent tool selection, which those did not address.

A maintainer on the project tomerwave/godlint (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #57: architecture/no-cycle needs module resolution, and that is a new subsystem

Last rule in Phase 4, deliberately deferred to its own pull request.

## Why it is different in kind

Every rule shipped so far **resolves nothing** — it reads what the source spells, and the roadmap states that boundary repeatedly. A cycle cannot be found that way. To know that `src/a.ts` importing `"./b"` is an edge to `src/b.ts`, something has to map a module spelling to a file.

That makes it the first rule to need module resolution, which is a new subsystem rather than another rule.

## Agreed approach: convention-based resolution per language

Chosen over the two alternatives (relative-only, or repository-declared roots).

- **JavaScript / TypeScript** — `./x` and `../x` probe `x.ts`, `x.tsx`, `x.js`, `x.jsx`, `x.mjs`, `x.cjs`, then `x/index.*`. Bare specifiers are dependencies, not repository edges, and are skipped. `tsconfig` path aliases are explicitly out of scope for a first version.
- **Python** — `a.b` probes `a/b.py`, `a/b/__init__.py`; a relative `from .b import` resolves against the importing file's package.
- **Rust** — `crate::a::b` probes `src/a/b.rs` and `src/a/b/mod.rs`. `self::`/`super::` resolve against the importing module.

An import that resolves to no file in the scan is not an edge. That is the honest failure mode, and it must be observable rather than silent — a resolution that quietly finds nothing would make the rule report no cycles and look like it passed.

## What the rule then does

Build a directed graph over resolved edges, find strongly connected components, and report **the complete edge chain** for each cycle, not just a pair. The finding needs a range, so it should be reported at the import that closes the cycle.

## Where it interacts with what exists

- `ImportFact` already carries the module spelling and the importing file, which is everything resolution needs as input.
- Issue #45's kernel (`report`) takes an iterator of `(source, range, violation)`, so a graph-shaped rule fits the existing driver without a sixth copy of the severity gate.
- This is the first rule whose evaluation is not per-file, so it will need the whole fact set at once — `evaluate` already receives `&[SourceFacts]`, so no signature change.

## Sequencing

Resolution should land as its own reviewed change with its own tests, before the rule that consumes it. A resolver that is wrong is worse than no cycle rule, because it fails quietly.

Issue #1573: Honor reclaim-guard expiry when admitting references

## Problem

A reclaim guard carries a lease.
[`ReclaimGuard::is_expired_at`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-ha/src/reclamation.rs#L7-L16)
defines it, and
[`compare_and_arm_reclaim_guards`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-storage/src/meta/reclaim_guard.rs#L13-L51)
honors it: a lapsed row is available and a new collector may take it. The reference-admission check disagrees.
[`commit_driver_txn_at_with_commit`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-storage/src/meta/index.rs#L344-L354)
rejects the commit whenever a row is present, reading no clock at all, so an expired guard blocks a write exactly like a
live one.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[purge_orphaned_blobs arms 300s guard] --> B[blobs.delete]
    B --> C[disarm guard]
    B --> D[process dies or delete errors]
    D --> E[guard lapses, row remains]
    E --> F[commit_driver_txn_at_with_commit ignores expiry]
    F --> G[MetaError::BlobReclaiming forever]
    class A,E accent
    class F good
    class B,C,D,G warn
    classDef accent fill:#dbe6f5,stroke:#4a6f9f,color:#16304d
    classDef good fill:#d8ebe1,stroke:#3f8467,color:#14402f
    classDef warn fill:#f6e2d0,stroke:#b06f36,color:#5a3212
```

[`purge_orphaned_blobs`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-ha-distributed/src/reclaim_guard.rs#L36-L86)
arms a 300-second guard over each orphan candidate, deletes its bytes, then disarms. Kill the purge in that loop, or let
one `blobs.blocking().delete` return an error, and the guard survives with a timestamp that soon lies in the past.
Nothing clears it:
[`release_absent_expired_guards`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-ha-distributed/src/reclaim_guard.rs#L88-L110)
disarms an expired guard only when `blobs.head` reports the bytes gone, so a failed delete keeps its guard forever, and
a successful delete keeps its guard as soon as a client re-uploads the bytes. No test pins expired-guard admission:
`crates/peryx-storage/tests/unit/tests/meta/reclaim_guard_tests.rs` covers only a live guard.

## Example

A confirmed purge arms the guard over `sha256:9f1c…`, then the node is killed mid-loop. Five minutes later the lease has
lapsed, but a client re-pushing that exact layer gets `MetaError::BlobReclaiming` and is told to "publish the reference
again once its deletion finishes" while no deletion is in flight. The digest stays unpublishable until an operator runs
another confirmed purge that reaches both the delete and the disarm.

## Required change

- Give the admission check the transaction's clock and treat a guard as blocking only while
  `!ReclaimGuard::is_expired_at(now)`, matching the arming side.
- Remove the lapsed row in the same write transaction that admits past it, so an abandoned guard cannot outlive its
  lease.
- Extend `release_absent_expired_guards` to clear an expired guard whose blob is still present; an expired guard proves
  the arming purge no longer holds it.
- Distinguish a collector guard from a claim-backed one before expiry may clear it, so the rule cannot release a live
  distributed delete claim.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A driver commit that references a digest whose guard has a past `expires_at_unix` succeeds instead of returning
      `MetaError::BlobReclaiming`.
- [ ] The same commit against a guard with a future expiry is still rejected.
