Issue #19: Spec (2/2): Fortran HLI MVA integration (consumes the Rust engine)

**Spec / PRD — part 2 of 2** · the **Fortran HLI multi-version-agnostic (MVA) integration**, consuming the Rust same-major projection engine specified in [#18](https://github.com/yohannmarguier/IMAS-Fortran/issues/18).

This specification is the implementation hand-off for the Fortran-owned decisions from map [#1](https://github.com/yohannmarguier/IMAS-Fortran/issues/1): the MVA definition and static-typing boundary (#2), fixed schema-blind Core boundary (#3), parity target (#4), hybrid architecture (#5), multi-version build/code generation (#6), runtime discovery and diagnostics (#7), facade/backward compatibility (#8), Fortran side of same-major projection (#9), explicit cross-major seam (#10), backend/serialization treatment (#11), conformance strategy (#12), and the per-open MDSplus/UDA evidence (#14). It also owns build/FFI obligations created by the Rust decisions (#15–#16).

> **Normative split.** Everything users, generated Fortran, CMake, packaging, and IMAS-Core-facing wrappers touch is specified here. XML comparison, projection-map construction, cached per-node verdicts, and engine-level loss facts are specified in #18 and consumed only through its C ABI.

## Problem Statement

IMAS-Fortran currently generates one set of statically typed IDS derived types and I/O routines from one `IDSDef.xml`. One build is tied to one DD version and installed as a versioned library. A user who needs another DD version switches builds, and one program cannot naturally use two generated DD layouts at once.

IMAS-Python can build dynamic trees from runtime XML. Fortran cannot copy that mechanism: `%` component selection and derived-type layout are compile-time facts, and Fortran has no reflection or `__getattr__`. Typed access to a DD version that was not compiled is therefore impossible.

At the same time, IMAS-Core cannot solve the mismatch. Its C ABI is a schema-blind path/datatype/buffer data plane. It carries no DD identity or schema handle, performs no DD path projection, and does not discover DD artifacts. The stored DD version is ordinary IDS data, not Core metadata.

The required design must therefore make one installed IMAS-Fortran handle multiple DD versions while preserving the existing typed API, module names, linker expectations, validation behaviour for the default version, and same-version fast path.

## Solution

Deliver **data-level MVA (R2)** in one installed binary:

- compile a finite **curated set** of typed **working versions** into one library;
- expose every curated version under stable tagged module names;
- expose the build's default version again under all existing untagged module names through zero-wrapper re-export facade modules;
- select a typed working version by the Fortran type/module used by the program, not by a runtime version argument;
- discover additional DD XML artifacts lazily at runtime;
- on a same-major stored/working mismatch, keep the normal generated walk and project its context/timebase paths inline through #18 before calling Core;
- on an exact match, do not call the Rust engine;
- report skipped/dropped data non-fatally and structurally;
- provide a separate explicit typed→typed `ids_convert` seam for cross-major conversion, with the semantic rules corpus absent and disabled;
- keep backend conversion logic centralized, with only a thin schema-preparation hook for schema-bound backends; and
- prove the behaviour at the public Fortran API, backed by pinpoint C-ABI tests in #18.

A newly published non-curated same-major version becomes readable/writable when its XML is discoverable, without rebuilding the installed binary. Making it a new typed working version, or supporting a new semantic conversion corpus, remains a release event.

## User Stories

### Existing-user compatibility

1. As an existing user, I want every current `use ids_schemas`, `use ids_routines`, `use ids_types`, and `use ids_utilities` statement to compile unchanged, so that upgrading requires no source migration.
2. As an existing user, I want every current per-IDS module name to remain available under its untagged spelling, so that direct module imports do not break.
3. As an existing user, I want existing derived-type, component, procedure, and generic names to remain unchanged, so that declarations and calls retain their meaning.
4. As an existing user, I want existing `ids_get`, `ids_put`, `ids_get_slice`, `ids_put_slice`, `ids_validate`, `ids_copy_struct`, `ids_deallocate_struct`, and `ids_delete` calls to remain source-compatible, so that the MVA release is additive.
5. As an existing user, I want the facade to add no wrapper procedure or runtime dispatch layer, so that ordinary calls resolve directly to the tagged implementation.
6. As an existing user, I want exact-version I/O to avoid the Rust engine completely, so that the common case keeps the direct path.
7. As an existing user, I want hand-written special validation to continue for the default working version, so that current validation coverage is preserved.
8. As a downstream build, I want the default-version library name and unversioned link alias to remain available, so that existing link discovery continues to work.
9. As an existing installation consumer, I want the default `IDSDef.xml` to remain at the legacy installation location, so that existing tools and UDA fallback assumptions remain valid.

### Curated typed working versions

10. As a tool author, I want two or more curated working versions compiled into one library, so that several typed layouts can coexist in one executable.
11. As a tool author, I want each version's generated modules to have stable release-tagged names, so that an explicit import never changes meaning when the default moves.
12. As a tool author, I want the type inside each version module to keep its ordinary unversioned name, so that the common single-version coding style stays clean.
13. As a tool author, I want to resolve type-name clashes with normal Fortran `use ... => ...`

> - **Category:** `对话 / Agent 交互 · Agent chat / interaction`
> - **Agent framework:** `ZCode Agent（自研）`

**Environment:** Windows 11 x64 · ZCode desktop 3.7.7 · engine `zcode.cjs` 0.16.3 (build 81fa9054) · GLM Coding Plan channel.

## 使用场景 · Use case

Subagents today are strictly leaves: only the main conversation can dispatch subagents — a subagent cannot spawn further subagents, so a delegated task can never delegate.

This blocks three real workflow shapes:

1. **Orchestrator-as-subagent.** Move an entire pipeline (plan → implement → review) into one coordinator subagent that owns and sequences specialist children, keeping the main conversation clean. Today the coordinator must be the main conversation itself — every intermediate result lands in the context the user actually reads, which is exactly the problem subagents exist to solve.
2. **Fan-out inside a delegated task.** A reviewer subagent that spawns one fresh verifier per finding: each verification runs in a clean context and none of that noise reaches the main thread.
3. **Specialist lookup agents owned by worker subagents.** For example a planning or implementation subagent that dispatches read-only code-graph verification subagents (the scout/verify/auditor tiers of codebase-memory-mcp).

Current workaround: flatten the pipeline into the main conversation (context bloat), or split it across manually created sessions (loses programmatic handoff).

## 建议方案 · Proposal

Make the dispatch tool grantable per subagent definition, with guards:

1. **Per-definition grant** — allow the Agent (dispatch) tool in a subagent's `tools` list; omitting it keeps today's leaf behavior. At the depth limit, the tool is simply withheld from the child.
2. **Bounded, configurable depth** — conservative default (e.g. one nested layer below a top-level subagent), raised via a setting or env var.
3. **Runaway caps** — max subagents per session and max concurrent subagents.
4. **Inheritance & safety** — children inherit the parent's permission mode and tool allowlists; interactive approval stays at the main-conversation boundary (a nested agent must not be able to prompt the user).
5. **Observability** — lineage on child sessions (ancestry marker in the session id, `parent_agent_id` in payloads/spans) and a tree view in the subagent panel.

## 预期价值 · Value

Context management is the core value of subagents — as the Claude Code lead put it when shipping nesting there, "agents kicking off agents as a way to better manage context." Nesting pushes noisy intermediate work further from the conversation the user cares about: a deep run costs the main thread one summary regardless of how many children ran. It also composes with what ZCode already has or has requested — per-subagent model selection (#177, shipped) and cost-tiered executors (#299) become strictly more useful when a coordinator subagent can own them instead of the main conversation.

## Parity

- **Claude Code** — nested subagents shipped in v2.1.172 (initially 5 levels); depth later made configurable (`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH`, current default 3 layers), with per-session (200) and concurrency (20) caps; the subagent panel renders the tree. Their defaults moved around (nesting off in 2.1.217–218, re-raised in 2.1.219), which suggests conservative default + knob is the workable middle ground. Docs: code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents, "Let subagents spawn their own subagents".
- **OpenAI Codex** — supports nested agents with a user-configurable `max_depth` (default 1).

It is not advertised as the browser entry anywhere in mermaid's README.

The practical difference: `mermaid.core.mjs` keeps `from "dompurify"` as an external import, so a bundler resolves it from `node_modules`. `mermaid.esm.min.mjs` has **zero** external dompurify imports — the library is compiled in, currently at version 3.4.0.

Consequence: the `overrides` block in `nicegui/elements/mermaid/package.json` never reaches the shipped bundle.

```
overrides: { "lodash-es": "^4.18.0", "dompurify": "^3.4.0", "uuid": "^14.0.0" }
```

The `dompurify` override resolves `node_modules/dompurify` to 3.4.12, while `nicegui/elements/mermaid/dist/` still contains DOMPurify 3.4.0. Running `npm update dompurify && npm run build` produces a **byte-identical** `dist/` — the override is inert. This is not specific to dompurify: every transitive dependency of mermaid is frozen inside that artifact, invisible to Dependabot and unpatchable by us.

It also makes our alert bookkeeping misleading. Dependabot alert 344 (dompurify in `nicegui/elements/mermaid/package-lock.json`) was closed by the lockfile bump in `bd746a15` without any change to what users receive.

### Suggested change

Import `mermaid` instead of the pre-bundled artifact and let rollup bundle the dependency tree from `node_modules`, so `overrides` and lockfile updates actually reach `dist/`.

**This is not a one-liner.** A trial build fails: mermaid's core pulls in CommonJS dependencies (`dayjs`, `cytoscape-fcose`) while `nicegui/elements/mermaid/rollup.config.mjs` has no `@rollup/plugin-commonjs` — unlike the json_editor element's config, which does. There are also circular `d3-selection` imports and `this`-rewrite warnings to work through. Bundle size and chunk layout will change, so expect a large diff that needs checking across diagram types rather than just a green test run.

### Why this is not urgent

The DOMPurify version we currently ship is old enough to be covered by several published advisories, but none of them appear to fire under mermaid's usage:

- The advisory behind alert 344 (GHSA-c2j3-45gr-mqc4) requires a registered `afterSanitizeElements` hook. mermaid registers only `beforeSanitizeAttributes` and `afterSanitizeAttributes`.
- Most of the remaining ones are `IN_PLACE`-mode specific, and mermaid sanitizes into a string.

An application passing its own `dompurifyConfig` through `ui.mermaid(config=...)` could widen that, but nothing in the default path does. So this is technical debt with a security flavour rather than a live vulnerability — worth fixing when the element is touched anyway, not worth rushing.

## Summary

  --max-instability-delta=0.05 \
  --max-distance-delta=0.05 \

- Table of packages with metric deltas
- Clear indication of which packages regressed and by how much
- JSON output with `regression` section for programmatic consumption

- [ ] Configurable delta thresholds for instability, distance, cohesion

- [ ] Clear CI output showing regression details
- [ ] JSON output includes `regression` section conforming to `metrics.ModuleGraph` schema
- [ ] Non-zero exit code on regression beyond tolerance
- [ ] Integrated into CI workflow

- **Depends on**: #2 — `vibe-check analyze` command
- **Related**: #3 (divisor-entropy agent)

## Executive verdict

This repo has a strong conceptual core: the default Claude session is explicitly framed as the orchestrator/front door, role agents have clear boundaries, and the hook/test layer meaningfully backs important policy with executable checks. The highest-leverage fragility is that several load-bearing orchestration capabilities are still represented as prose conventions or assumed external provisioning rather than verified, durable system state: if a required plugin/skill is absent, if a lane is interrupted, or if the PM/developer boundary is crossed, the user's intended “delegate real work and recover cleanly” workflow can degrade without an obvious failing test.

Highest-leverage change: add a real doctor/fixture layer for agent capabilities and orchestration state. The installer/tests should prove that every frontmatter skill and plugin-backed review agent is available, and the orchestrator playbook should have a durable lane/track representation that survives resume/recovery instead of relying only on transient TodoWrite + teammate mailboxes.

## Strengths worth preserving

- Clear one-orchestrator model: `core.md:5-12` makes thinking/verification/communication the lead session's job and delegates execution.
- Role boundaries are easy to inspect: `README.md:11-18` and each `agents/*.md` file state tools and responsibilities directly.
- Mechanical guardrails exist where prose would be too weak: `README.md:76-90`, `hooks/guard-git.sh:35-66`, `hooks/guard-config.sh:32-45`, and `hooks/guard-linear.sh:21-29` back publishing/config/board boundaries with hooks.
- The regression suite is broad and portable for the hooks it currently covers; `tests/run.sh:37-143` covers publishing/config/Linear gates and `tests/run.sh:145-321` covers process ownership/reaping.
- The install model is portable and mostly idempotent: `install.sh:19-22` handles symlink invocation safely, `install.sh:107-190` rewrites toolkit-managed settings entries, and `tests/run.sh:323-414` checks several installer edge cases.
